ARTHUR .WILLIAM BROUILLET
Grand Master 1945-1946

The 80th Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California was forceful
and energetic Arthur William Brouillet, who first opened his eyes at St.
Anne, Illinois, on January 21, 1884. He was born of French-Canadian
parents.
Arthur received his elementary and hi~h school education at Chicago.
In 1908 he moved to California where he continued his studies at the University of California. Graduating from the Hastings College of Law in
1911, he commenced the practice of law which he has since pursued with
marked success.
While attending college Arthur enlarged his income and also expanded
his experience by literally starting his career at the foot of the ladderas a shoe clerk. Perhaps it was at t'his point also that Arthur r eceived the
initial training which was to result in a speaker of unsual grace and natural
eloquence. Thereby, at any rate, he early in life became affiliated with the
labor moven'.ent (A. F. of L.) of the city and state. Entering actively into
~be leadership of the cause of labor, he became president of his Union and
in 1915 served as legislative agent for the San Francisco Labor Council at
the session· of the California Legislature. Later, in 1917, he· was president
of the Council.
During 1916-1917 Arthur c01;nmenced his long and distinguished career
of public service by enforcing narcotic laws as prosecuting attorney for the
State Board of Pharmacy. Presently, he is Deputy Inheritance Tax Attorney
of California, Northern District.
He has given freely of his exceptional talents to the good and welfare
of his chosen profession of legal science. Arthur was one of the outstanding leaders in the organization, prior to 1927, of the present statutory
State Bar. In ~935-1937 he was president of the Bar Association of San
Francisco. Later, in 1937-1940, he was California Commissioner on Uniform State Laws.
A lover of his adopted city of San ·Francisco, Arthur has also contributed generously to the civic betterment of the community. In 1930 he
served as an elected member and as secretary of the Board of Freeholders
which drafted the present charter of San Francisco. He is now vice-president of the Civic League of Improvement Clubs of San Francisco.

at Atherton.

A CONTINUAL - INCARNATION
Belief in God is fundamental in Masonry. This is revealed and attested
by the various titles used in Masonic ritual in addressing the Deity. Recall
some of them : "Our Heavenly Father ... Almighty and Eternal God ...
Creator of the Universe . .. Great Architect of the Universe ... 'Supreme
Ruler of the Universe .. . Supreme Grand Master."
Every candidate seeking knowledge of the rites and mysteries of Free
Masonry must affirm his belief in the Supreme Being. This is as it should
be. But the purposes of Masonry relative to the Great Architect of the
Universe, the Supreme Grand Master are not attained simply by the candidate's intellectual assent to the Creator's existence. That end is achieved
only when God becomes incarnate in a Mason's life, when the man expresses the Godlike.
·
St. John, the mystic writer of the New Testament, phrased his thought
concerning this with respect to Jesus in simple understandable language:
"The Word became flesh and dwelt among us." The perfectly clear meaning of this is that God became incarnate in him, and God lived in him down
here in this workaday world.
But the incarnation of God in human life was not something which took
place once and for all. God's most effective way of making himself known
to men has been through incarnation, not only in Jesus, but continually
in others,
The hand of God writing the pages of history always has written in the
flesh of man. The story of the creation could not have been told without
Adam and Eve. God could not have set forth the Ten Commandments
without a Moses. He could not have pictured the life of spiritual adventure without an Abraham. The record of the marvelous achievements of
those Old Testament prophets never could have stirred human hearts and
changed men's lives without an Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos and others.
The fact is this was the very principle the Master himself followed. He
wrote no letters; dictated no formulae, composed no creeds, published no
books. He lived his message in the presence of his disciples and left it
written upon their hearts. He intended them so to live that ~11 who knew
them would know God. In so doing he was foilowing a universal ·law of
life. That which gives significance to any movement is the Word made
flesh, an incarnation.
The history of our nation is a chronicle of the doings of those in whom
the Word was incarnated: Columbus Benjamin Franklin, Washiitgton,
Lincoln, Wilson. Liberty is one of t!A precious words of our language,
but standing alone the word may mean little or nothing. But when liberty
becomes incarnate in a Patrick Henry and his whole being is so on fire
with the meaning of the word that he i& able to set others aflame, liberty
becomes a reality in the life of a people. Freedom is another great word
in our language. This word, so far as Black people were concerned, w·a s
coined selfishly in the minds of the founders of the Republic. But seventy
years later it was incarnated in its true, full meaning in the person of
Abraham Lincoln. He issued the Emancipation Proclamation and shackles
fell from the limbs of four million slaves in our country.
We have heard a great deal in recent years about the Constitution.
To listen to some persons, one might conclude there is something 'Sacrosanct about the very word. I yield precedence to no one in my admiration
and reverence for this immortal document. I agree fully with the judgment of one in a position to know whereof he spoke when he said, "The

Constitution of the United States is the greatest document ever penned by
man for the government of a free people." At the same time, the Constitu' tion may ..be pf no more value than the paper on which it is written. This
is true, if it is only words on paper. But when the Constitution becomes
focarnate in the lives' of the citizens of this Republic, it takes on significance, character and greatness.
The same rule holds in other realms. For e:itample, the majority of us
enjoy beautiful music. What is music? Turning to the dictionary, this is
what I found: "Music is the science and art of rhythmic combination of
tones, embracing harmony and melody." Because this definition is in
Webster, we take for granted it is correct. But music is something more
than rhythm, harmony and melody. Instrumental music is the word made
flesh in a Heifitz, Kreisler, Menuhin, Rubenstein, Toscanini. Vocal music
that entrances and enthralls people is the word made flesh in a Jenny Lind,
Melba,
Caruso,
.
. Marian Anderson, Lily Pons, Paul Robeson.
Some of us on occasion like the drama. What is the drama? Webster
states:· "The drama is a composition acted on the stage, a play, hence any
series of dramatic events." Doubtless Webster correctly defines the drama.
But if that is all the drama is, it leaves me cold. The drama to me is the
word incarnate in a Booth, Barrett, Bernhardt, Katherine Cornell, Helen
Hayes.
.
Even more than music and the drama I am fascinated by real oratory.
I would rather listen to a brilliant orator than a gifted singer or great
actor. Again I turned to Webster. He states that an orator is one who
delivers an oration. Possibly so. In my time I have heard a good many
orators. Some of them were exactly what Webster said they were. . . .
"Orators delivering orations." As I think of some of them I am reminded
·of the answer the school boy gave to his teacher in reply to the question,
"What. is.. elocution?" He said, "Elocution is what they put people to
death with in some countries." Figuratively speaking that is not so far
wrong as a description of some so-called oratory. But real oratory is
Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg, bearing in his great soul the sorrows of
a race, the cestiny of a nation. Oratory is Booker T. Washington, pleading the cause of his people, with h~ heart on fire, his tongue aflame.
Oratory is Henry Ward Beecher in. his pulpit, to him a throne, proclaiming the infinite goodness of God, the word incatnate.
What is patriotism? Webster states, "Love of country, devotion to the
welfare of one's country, the passion to serve one's country." Technically
that may correctly define patriotism. But that alone is not enough for me.
Patriotism is the word made flesh in a Nathan Hale, that fine young man
of Revolutionary times, trapped, knowing the end was near, but without
bravado or flinching, saying, "I regret I have but one life to give for my
country." Patriotism is the spirit of our country incarnate in the lives of
couotless young men of our Republic, who in recent years on field of battle,
in the air, one the sea and in the sea revealed to all the world that Americanism is. Part of an inscription on a tombstone in a soldiers' cemetery in
Virginia reads, "Who they were no man knows, what they were all men
know." Because of what they were, there radiates and will continue to
radiate an influence that is a benediction.
The same principle holds in education. It is this which gives validity to
the statement of Garfield, "The best university is Mark Hopkins on one end
of a log and the student on the other end." In other words, education to be
valid and worthful mu.st be incarnate in personality. This is what Emerson

had in mind when he said, "What you are speaks so loud, I cannot hear
what you say."
What is Christianity? Webster states a Christian is one who believes in
Christ, one born in a Ch.ristian country or o·f Christian parents . . . a
decent, civilized, respectable or presentable person . . . a human being as
distinguished ·from one of the lower animals. Here again we assume that
Webster is correct. But in the main such conceptions are infinitely removed' from the Christ, the perfect revelation of God. It is a strange quirk·
of human nature which_ causes so many persons to think of the Godlike in
terms of some theological, denominational or other superficial label. I recall a statement made by Dr. Roy Smith, formerly pastor of the First
Methodist Church of Los An·geles. He said that he had graduated from
college and the seminary and was well into his first pastorate, when one
day he got the shock of his life. He discovered that God was not a Methodist. It is · rather an amazing thing how many people there are who think
God belongs to their particular church. Some go even to greater extremes,
and think of God as belonging only to their political party. They cannot
conceive of God being anything other than a Democrat, or a Republican,
. depending upon which party they happen to belong.
One of the tragedies in connection with Christianity through the centuries has been that something other than q1ri!>tlikeness, Godliness has
been the norm by which a person's Christianity was judged. To know and
appreciate fully a Christian, one must see the word "incarnate." So to me
a Christian is my father, my mother, or· any one of many persons I have
known and now know.
What is Masonry? Webster states: "The craft, the institutions or
mystery of Free Masons." Technically, Webster correctly defines Masonry.
There are other definitions, many and varied, that are given from time to
time. They all are more or less descriptive. At best they are quite inadequate as full and complete expositions of Masonry. There is no qu~s­
tion as to the height of the ideals, the loftiness of the principles, the quality
of the spirit of Free Masonry. But even these in the abstract are not
enough. Only as they become incarnate in the lives of the members of the
fraternity do they reveal the true character of the craft. In other words,
Masonry to have reality and power must be incarnate. So to me, Masonry
is William B. Ogden, Roy W. Bryan, John T. Bond, Lawrence Kelley,
Arthur Brouillet. John R. Moore, Earl Warren, and a host of others that
cannot" be numb~red who incarnate the ideals, the principles, the spirit of
Masonry. It is the word incarnate which gives dignity, character and
worth, not only to Masonry, but to personality in any sphere. Y~s, even
more than that, without such incarnation, God Himself cannot do His work
in the world.
As Antor:io Stradivarius said, "God could not make Stradivarius violins
without Antonio." He couldn't. God could not be a blessing to the
neglected Lc.brador folk without a Wilfred Grenfell. He could not ministei;
to the backward Black people of Africa without an Albert Schweitzer. He
could not have a Salvation ArplY without a General Booth. Even God Himself cannot have a worthy Masonic Order without worthy Masons.
Many persons wonde.r what is wrong with our world today. We ha~e
not far to seek to discover some of tie factors that enter the ~nswer to .this
question. For one thing we have been placing greater. emphasis upo~ things
than persons. A while ago Bernard Shaw made this· rather caustic co.mment about the people of our time. He said, "'I:his is the first generation
with a perfect system of communication, but with nothing to say." What

There is still another element in the answer to the question concerning
the cause of the trouble in our world. Glenn Frank in his "Thunder and
Dawn" hurls into the midst of our conferences for social reform this arresting phrase: "You cannot build a great civilization around sleazy individuals." If ever there was a generation that produced illustrations of this
truth, ours is that generation. Think of attempting to build a great civilization around such sleazy individuals as Hitler, Mussolini, Tojo or any of
that ilk.
Hitler's type of order in Europe that he said would last a thousand years
came to an inglorious end in a few brief years, with the maker of that order
going out of life in 'cowardly fashion by his own hand. The spectacle of
the end of the braggart Mussolini, posing for years as a modern Caesar,
was revolting in the extreme, but it strikingly illustrates the truth, that
while the mills of the gods may grind slowly, the miUs of the gods grind.
Tojo thought to make Japan great by assuming the role of assassin on a
colossal scale. His attempted suicide and the plight of his country are mute
witnesses of the end of an attempt to block the purposes of the eternal.

The Decla,~ation of Independence on parchment did not procure

REPORT · OF GRAND TREASURER
In the various ways that come to us as Masons we are to make God a
reality in our lives and the life of our world. This Masons have attempted
to do and have done from time immemorial. They have gleaned truth from
every quarter of the globe. They .have drawn teachings from many different
races and peoples. They have gained inspiration from all the great philosophies and religions.
In the sphere "of religion first place is given to that of the Holy Book
which, as we know, is always open when a Masonic Lodge is in session.
This is the great light in Masonry, the great law of the brotherhood. Thus
from the universal has come the fundamentals, and by the attrition of time
and the experience of uncounted men has come the unity we know as
Masonry. If it be said that Masonry has to do with the intangibles, the
contention is granted. At the same time attention is called to the fact that
all the great, most vital, and important things of life have to do with the
intangibles-love, friendship, patriotism, and religion. But the value of
Masonry as with these other intangibles is revealed only when personified.
We need to remember that Masonry is not' and never can be a finished
product. From its very character it requires a continual incarnation. As
Master Masons in the present, by incarnating its ideals, principles, and
spirit, we may forward Masonry to a fuller fruition.
·
J

Who than Masons are better fitted to usher in a finer human order, the
Golden Age of humanity? These words of Markham might well have been
written with Masons in mind, so prophetic are they:
·
"We men of earth have here the stuff
Of paradise we have enough;
We need no other stones to build
The stairs into the unfulfilledN o other ivory for the doorsN o other marble for the floorsN o other cedar for the beam
Artd dome of man's immortal dream.
Here on 'the paths of every day,
Here on the common human way
Is all the busy gods would take
To build a heaven, to mold and make
New Edens. Ours the task sublime
To build eternity in time."

course of the market was created by the Federal Reserve Board's report indicating potential inflationary possibilities because of progressive eligibility for
purchases of long-term secu.rities by commercial banks. In one report it was
suggested that certain procedures be adopted to curtail holdings and eligibility.
Recotnmc:ndations were made by investment houses to gradually replace some
. maturities with longer maturities, which also had an effect on the market. New
York banks iucreased interest rates to dealers on loans secured by governments
and also increa~ed call money and c0mmercial paper rates. Whatever the cause,
the market was unsteady, and al.so governments being at a premium, it was
deemed inadvisable to take a possible loss when there might be opportunity to
more certainly determine the course of the market. There was also the possibility of another Government issue which would be purchasable at par near the
end of the year or early in the coming year. Under th~ circumstances, to assure
a minimum loss and putting Grand Lodge in a short term position so that when
the market should steady and it became advisable, governments might be selected
which would yield a higher rate-to that end U. S. U Treasury Certificates
of Indebtedness, December l, 1946 maturity, to yield .81 approximately, were

REPORT OF GRAND SECRET ARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

I have the honor to present to you herewith my Fifth Annual Report
as your Grand Secretary.
This is the first full year of peace during which I have conducted the
Office of Grand Secretary, and whatever hopes I may have had that the
'return to peace would restore the office to normalcy have been smashed.
The volume of work has not only kept up but has actually increased, and
the problems of materials and labor have been as acute as during the war.
One of the bright spots in the situation Is the efficiency and zeal of the
Lodge Secretaries. It is not too much to say that both have been at the
highest peak during the past year of any time since my association with
the office.
War Program
Although the "shooting war" is over the activity aasociated with war
is by no means at an end. In my last report I 1tated that we had received
requests for Courtesy Degrees from other Grand Jurisdictions totaling 8,290
Degrees and that we had ourselves requested 2,603 Degrees. As of September 30th this year the former figure had grown to 10,054 and the
latter 3,323, indicating that this program is by no means at an end.
We continue to receive requests for contacts from other Grand Jurisdictions with their members in California hospitals, and with the assistance of the War Activities Committee every request is compiled with.
Since the war has not been officially declared at an end and men are
still being inducted into the service, we continue to register our service
men and to issue certificates to them. The last certificate issued was number 12,383.
Philippine Islands
The story of our wartime service to the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands and its members needs no repetition here. This phase of our war
program has been concluded as reported last October. I am glad to say
that we are still able to serve that Grand Lodge in numerous ways.
One such instance is in the service which we were able to perform for
Past Grand Master Harry E. Stafford and for Brother
,
reference to both of which may be found in the Report of the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes.
Dispensation Surrendered
Just as the dislocations of war enlarge·d the population of Chungking,
China, so the dislocations of war decreased its population. Like all others,

their former homes as rapidly as possible with the result that there was

General Offices of Grand Lodge
Visitations
The circumstances relative to Grand Lodge Officers during the year,
which is well-known to all, has made it necessary for all of us to undertake
more visitations than would have ordinarily been the case. It has been
my pleasun: to visit many Lodges during the year as well as to attend
the institution of all of the new Lodges with the exception of Oildale
Lodge U, :p.
- The conference of Grand Secretaries in Washington was resumed in
February, and I attended that meeting as well as the meeting of the George
Washington National Masonic Memorial Association of which I have the
honor to be a: Director.
An unusual and unexpected opportunity to visit Mexico on a purely
personal basis presented itself early in the year and in company with my
wife and daughter I visited that country in April. That time was selected
to make possible attendance at the Annual Communication of the York
Grand Lodge of Mexico. This was a most pleasant experience and made
the more so by the thoughtfulness of the Brethren of that city.
I cannot begin to name all who were so gracious to us, but I must
mention Most Worshipful Archie Seabrook, Grand Master, Fred Berger,
Grand Secretary, Past Grand Masters Marcus A. Loevy and Sydney Ulfelder, and Grand Treasurer and Past Master George Friedman and his
son, George, Past Master of Anahuac Lodge Number 3.
The opportunity thus had to see Masonry in Mexico at first hand was
invaluable, and although it made something of a "bus man's holiday" of a
personal vacation, it was very much worthwhile.
At the request of the Grand Master I represented this Grand Jurisdiction at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Washington
held at · Spokane. The genuine hospitality of Most Worshipful Grand
Mast'er Lee, Deputy Grand Master Gus Schultz and Grand Secretary John
Priessner made the occasion a most pleasant one as well as very profitable
from the knowledge gained of that Grand Jurisdiction.
At the close of that Communication, I flew from Spokane to Victoria,
B. C., where I attended the 75th Anniversary of that Grand Lodge.
Unfinished Business
.The following _items of unfinishedt business are brought forward from
the last communication:
1. The recommendation of Grand Master Morrison, relative to changes
in the form of application for d~grees. (See page 191, 1944 Proceedings.)

At the last Communication of Grand Lodge, $10,000 was appropriated
for the modernization of the Grand Lodge offices. A thorough and detailed study has been made and general plans approved, but the actual
work could not be undertaken because of problems of material, labor and
the governmental restrictions placed on such work.
The Grand Secretary recommends that a sufficient appropriation be
made to carry the work through during the present year if conditions
warrant.
Office Equipment
At the last Communication $3,000.00 was appropriated to replace wornout and out-moded equipment. It has been possible to purchase a portion
of the required equipment, $1,844.82 having been spent plus $369.48 for
the Grand Master's office. If we complete the modernization of the
Grand Lodge offices, additional new equipment will undoubtedly be required and it is recommended that an appropriation be made for this
purpose.
Employee Retirement
Miss Marian Van Buskirk has once more expressed her desire to retire
from the employ of Grand Lodge after approximately 30 years of service.
Twenty-five of these years were spent in association with John Whicher
during his tenure as Grand Secretary, and I am very certain that everyone in Grand Lodge knows that if John were here today he would have
difficulty in finding words to express his deep appreciation for the splen•
did service which has been performed by "Miss Van/' At the end of but
5 years as Grand Secretary, I find myself confronted with the same difficulty, and I can only say that I appreciate the work which she has done
and trust t~at Grand Lodge will find ways of expressing its appreciation.
Membership
In _p resenting the membership figures for the year I have supplied
figures commencing with the year 1941 for t.he purpose of showing what
the trend has been throughout the war period.
We continue to show a gain 'in the number of degrees conferred al~
though 'there is a smaller net gain in total membership in compariso~
with 1945. Our membership of 161,752 is the largest in our history.
Evidence that_: ~>Ur Lodges have been · extremely busy may be had
from the fact that. they have conferred 41,401 degrees on their own candidates in additfon 'to the courtesy degrees previously reported.

The Grand Master informed Grand Lodge that the gavel used
by him during the opening ceremonies was a gift to him from
the Pearl Harbor. Square Club during his visit to the . Hawaiian
Islands. He further stated that it was made of wood taken from
the battleship Missouri at a point on the ship approximately
where the Japanese delegates signed the surrender documents.

RESOLUTIONS
The following resolutions were read by the Grand Secretary,
the Grand Master referring each to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes :

31

Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:

Brethren:
I respectfully submit the following resolution for your consideration:
Be it resolved, That the brethren of this Grand Lodge who have served
ten consecutive years as Inspector, shall at the meeting of Grand Lodge
nearest to the conclusion of ten consecutive years of service, be formally
presented by Grand Lodge with a suitable and appropriate testimonial document, in appreciation of the services they have rendered.
Be H further resolved, That said document, if possible, be signed by the
Grand Master and all the Past Grand Masters under whom said Inspector
had served.
Be it further resolved, That, following the first ten consecutive years
tenure of office, a similar document be presented at the end of each fiveyear period thereafter.
Respectfully submitted,
. Ei;>GAR T.· HAM,
Past Master, San Bernardino Lodge N6. 348.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Resolved, That Section 70 of the Ordinances of the Grand Lodge of
California be amended to include the Committee on Lodge Financing.
HERBERT C. GOLDMAN,
Past Master, Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674.

October 8, 1946.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Jurisdiction of California:
Whereas, There is at present a growing resentment against the method
used in presenting the names of brethren, for election for Grand Lodge
offices, in particular the office of Junior Grand Warden;
And whereas, Something should be done to correct the cause for this
growing resentment;
Therefore be it resolved, That legislation is necessary to provide a
recognized committee representing this Grand Lodge, from each section of
this Grand Jurisdiction, whose duty it shall ·be to consider the qualification:;;
of all brethren suggested for an elective office in this Grand Lodge, and
after careful consideration, make necessary recommendations to this Grand
Lodge, before each annual election of Grand Lodge officers;
Be it further resolved, That this resolution be referred to the proper
committee or committees, with instruction to report back to this 1946 session, for final action by Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
CHAS. L. W. VocKE,
Past Master and Secretary of Valley Forge Lodge No. 587.
Whereas, Religion and. an unfaltering faith in the existence of a Supreme
Being, have always been the under-girding strength upon which the superstructure of Masonry is erected, and
Whereas, The Hc;>ly Bible has, from tim~ immenwrial, been revered by
Masons as the great light of Masonry, and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Whereas, The placing of the ballot box on the Bible during balloting
has caused open criticism of the custom on the part of many of the members of the Masonic fraternity;
Now therefore be it resolved, By Abell fodge No. 146, F. & A. M.,
that said custom is inconsistent with the principles and teachings of
Masonry in that it detracts from the supreme position in Masonry in which
the Holy Bible should be held, and
Be is further resolved, That a copy of this resolution be forwarded to
the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California, for presentation to the Grand Lodge at its next
regular communication in order that the necessary action be taken to
instruct, or order, or permit, subordinate Lodges to place the ballot box
during balloting in a position on the altar beside the Holy Bible and not
resting upon it.

Whereas, Upon investigation it has been found that the brethren· are
under the impression that they are seeking relief when they use the services of the E_mployment Bureau due to the use of the name East. Bay
Masonic Board of Relief and Employment, and
Whereas, Such a~ impression has caused a reluctance on the part of
some members to avail themselves of the Board's service, causing much
embarrassment to ;others of the fraternity, and
Whereas. Such an implication and embarrassment is not the intent of
the fraternity, and
••
Whereas, The services of the above mentioned Board is a Masonic
service open to all members of the Craft; therefore be it
Resolved, That this matter be brought to the attention of the Grand
Master in order that he may refer it to the proper committee for suitable
action at the next communication to be held during October, 1946, so that
the name of the organization can be changed to eliminate the word "Relief"
or any reference thereto in the new name.
Note: Resolutions identical with or similar to the above were adopted
and certified by the following Lodges:

in its stated meeting. for the month of February and that this is the original

ABELL LonGE No. 146.

At a meeting of Past Masters of Burbank Lodge No. 406, F. & A. M.,
held in Burbank, California, August 29, 1946, the following resolution was
read and unanimously adopted:
Whereas, During the last several years large numbers of new members
have been adde4 to our Craft; and
Whereas, Many of our members have been so busily engaged in the
work of war and the subsequent reconversion to peace time activities; and
Whereas, Scientific discoveries and swiftly moving events of a social,
economic, and religious nature of worldwide importance are a matter of
almost daily occurrence; and
Whereas, The continual growth, maintenance and prosperity of Freemasonry within the United States and as a worldwide institution is dependent on an active, vigorous, and well informed membership, therefore
be it
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California appoint a committee to study and determine sUltable
means whereby our membership may be kept informed of such events and
their relationship, and implication to Freemasonry.

Whereas. The building of a new order, and the preserva:tion of world

Proposed Amendment to Section 208 of the Constitution of Grand Lodge
of California, F. & A. M.
PROPOSAL No. 1
To add a further paragraph to Section 208 of the Constitution of the
Grand Lodge of the State of California, as adopted October 12, 1939, as
follows:
Where the applicant for the degrees of Masonry has a maim or defect
in his body which does not render him incapable of learning the art, and
he is physically able to conform substantially to what the several degrees
respectively required of him, though he employ the use of an artificial
member, such applicant may be deemed qualified; provided, however, that
nothing herein contained shall be regarded as authorizing the acceptance
of applicatiods for the degrees without artificial members.
Respectfully submitted,
DUDLEY H. NEBEKER,
Past Master, Yerba Buena Lodge No. 403.
Proposed Amendment to Section 208 of the Con1titution of Grand Lodge
of California, F. & A. M.
PROPOSAL No. 2
To add a further paragraph to Section 208 of the Constitution of the
Grand Lodge of the State of California, as adopted October 12, 1939, as
follows:
In determining the physical sufficiency of the qualifications of a candidate to receive the degrees of Masonry, the same shall be left to the sound
discretion of the Lodge. However, where a candidate is unable to literally
comply with the physical requirements, the Master shall state the nature
of and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before ballot is taken.

pass upon the physical fitness of an applicant, and thereupon where said
Masonic Inspector passes upon the physical sufficiency of the applicant's
gualifications, the same shall be binding upon said Master. In the event

Dear Brother Lloyd:
Again I am bringing up this subject. As I have written before I still
think California ought to have a time .limit on the candidate getting his
d~grees. Now more than ever we should have some way of cleaning up
· our tbooks in due course of time.
My suggestion is this: After a candidate has been elected he should have
twelve months to complete his degrees, unless it is the fault of the Lodge
in not getting to him 011 account of too much work, and then the Lodge
would be requested to ask Grand Lodge for an extension and give the
reason. If at the end of twelve months the candidate has not been raised
he shall be reimbursed with the amount due him for the degree or degrees
not received. The refund to be on a percentage basis as different Lodges
charge different amounts for the degrees. I suggest 70 per cent for the
First degree, 20 per cent for the Second degree, and 10 per cent for the
Third degree. After the refund has been made the candidate would have
to reapply and be reinvestigated and balloted on if he cared to finish his
degrees.
I just make this suggestion to you and if you think it merits attention
you carry on.
Yours fraternatly,
FRANK C. SHAW, P.M., Secretory,
Modesto Lodge No. 675.

AFTERNOON SESSION
Monday, October 14, 1946
Grand Lodge was called on at 1 :30 o'clock, the Deputy Grand
Master presiding.

Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller reported for the Jurisprudence Committee, all members concurring, as follows:
To thi! Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has given consideration to the present
and future status of .the Grand Master, and reports as follows:
That on the 24th day of October, 1945, only twelve days after he had
been installed as Grand Master, our beloved brother, Lawrence C. Kelly,
was taken by death, and under our law the then Deputy Grand Master
assumed the title of Grand Master, and succeeded to and was charged with
all the powers and duties of the office.
Since his succession to the office, the Grand Master has, at great personal sacrifice, fully and ably performed the duties Qf his high office, and
has earned <i.nd commands the respect and esteem of all with whom he has
come in cqntact.
Notwithstanding the fact that he has for practically the entire year
performed all of the duties required of him, under the provisions of Section
15 of our Constitution, he will not at the end of his term become a Past
Grand Master, as h~ was not elected and installed Grand Master.
Your committee feels that under these circumstances, to deprive the
. Grand .Master of the privi-leges accorded to a Past Grand Master would
be .an injustice 't o him and a reflection upon this Grand Lodge. We have
therefore prepared an amendment to Section 15 of the Constitution to
remedy this condition.
While giving consideration to the present situation, and to clarify the
law applicable to the powers and duties of a Deputy Grand Master as set
forth in Section 39 of the Ordinances, we deem it proper to submit to
Grand Lodge an amendment of that section, and therefore submit amended
Section 15 of the Constitution ·and amended Section 39 of the Ordinances·
of Grand Lodge, and recommend their adoption.
Respectfully submitted,
DANA R. WELLER,
GEORGE L. JONES,

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Brethren:

Where there is no vision, the people perish:
-Proverbs (Chap. 29-18).
When, at the last Annual Communication, I was elected Deputy Grand
Master of this Grand Lodge, little did I dream that within two weeks the
cold blast of death would remove from our midst our beloved Most
Worshipful Lawrence Carlyle Kelley. Such, however, is fate. He was
not spared us to round out his great Masonic career. During the entire
preceding year he had chosen with care those who were to serve under
and with him, had meticulously laid out an itinerary as to his official
visitations, mapped a course as to certain of our activities and I ani sure
would have appeared here today with various' recommendations and an
amazing report as to the accomplishments of our fraternity during "his
year."
It was my sad duty to convene a special communication of Grand
Lodge of Los Angeles on October 27, 1945 to conduct his funeral and
perform the last sad rites for our brother. P<!rticipating as Grand Lodge
officers were the following:

The report of the Committee on Necrology, will, I am sure, paint
more vividly his Masonic career and pay a more fitting tribute to his
memory than lies within my humble powers.
The proi;pect of taking over the guidance of Grand Lodge under such
tragic circumstances, on such short notice, and without any opportunity to
survey the work which lay before me was a challenge. I determined to
accept it and do my duty as Grand Master with such courage and wisdom
as was vouchsafed me by Divine Providence. I am sure that like all
humans I have made mistakes but they have been of the mind and not of
the heart. In everything which I have done in this exalted position, which
I reached by your suffrage only as Deputy Grand Master, my guiding
principle has been "What does Masonic Law and Custom" dictate? "How
does the solut.i on of a question affect the fair name of Masonry?" "Is not
the welfare and happiness of this fraternity greater than that of any individual or group of individuals within it."
The unconditional surrender of Japan, approximately three months
after Germany and three · months prior to our last Annual Communication,
led to a very natural desire on the part of the men of our armed forces to
be returned to this country and discharged from the various services as
soon as possible. This movement of armed personnel in conjunction with
lack of accommodations in hotels, inability to secure advance reservations
for ·travel by air, rail or steamer during the first months of my term rendered it well nigh impossible to make all the visitations which my predecessors had made prior to 1941. Much as I would have enjoyed visiting
all districts and more individual Lodges it seemed more Masonic for me
to refrain from traveling while our boys were coming home to their loved
ones. They deserved, and still do, every consideration which we can give
them. They cleaned up a nasty job in short order, under awful conditions.
They drank milk but thirsted for the blood of dictators. They maintained
the highest ideals and matche.d the patriotism of the founding Fathers
of their Republic. They put to shame the gray-beards of a few years ago
who thought they were irresponsible, and headed for hell and damnation
b~cause they ran around in a cut-down flivver or flirted with girls at the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

39

"Coke" corner. In short they acquitted themselves with a glory. such as
have few generations and we owe them our undying gratitude··.for a job
well, and may we hope, permanently done.
' ·
We are fortunate in that we have a substantial fund which I trust will
be made available to er.e ct within the walls of this Temple and in Los Angeles a fitting memorial to those of our fraternity who made the Supreme
Sacrifice in World Wars One and Two, and it is a memorial which will be
living and pulsating with daily life:
I have reference to the establishment of a Masonic Library to Masonic
Veterans of the World Wars.
General Remarks
At this po_int in my message I think it is appropriate that I should report to you that in numbers, in material wealth, and in an expanding membership, we are in a very fortunate condition. Also the high standards
for admission have been upheld. All of the Committees of Grand Lodge
have worked diligently and very effectively throughout the year, as their
various reports will indicate.
The ritudistic work under the able leadership of our V. W. Grand
Lecturer, his assistants, the Inspectors, Officers and Coaches of our constituent Lodges has reached a degree of such perfection that we are often
referred to as one of the outstanding jurisdictions in ritualistic · perfection.
Division of Inspectoral Districts
As the result of a survey and report, which I requested in the matter, it
was ascertained that Division A, containing eighteen Inspectoral districts,
was too large and unwieldly for one Assistant Grand Lecturer to properly
instruct and after consultation with the V. W. Grand Lecturer and M. W.
Gilbert C. DeForest, Past Grand Master, certain districts were excluded
from the former Division A and others excluded from Division B in order
to make an additional Division, over which district I placed W. Charles A.
Schwartz. I take this opportunity of expressing to M. W. Gilbert C. DeForest, and the other brethren who assisted in making this change possible;
my sincere thanks. I trust my action will receive the approval of Grand
Lodge.
I, therefore, recommend that in the future there be at least five Assistant Grand Lecturers, one of whom. shall preside over each of the
various Inspectoral Districts, as now, or may subsequently, be determined
by Grand Lodge, and that the new district be designated as the North
Central District or other suitable designation.
This seems a proper place to mention a newspaper clipping which
W. Brother Herbert R. Hargrave . r.ecently f~rwarded to me from the
front page of one of the leading dailies in Fresno, which carried a story
concerning a Negro who died as the result of a broken neck suffered during initiatory work in one of their Masonic Lodges.
While I am satisfied that nothing of this kind could happen itf any of
our constituent Lodges, it does at least pose a question as to whether or
not we should be protected ·by a l>lai:lket coverage against accidents to
candidates, members or visitors while in or about our Lodge rooms or
rooms adjacent thereto.

George Wa.s hington Masonic National Memorial Association
The first extendep trip which I made this year in my official capacity
was to the Grand Master( Conference, February 20-21st and the meeting
?f the G;orge •.Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, held
m Washmgton, D. C. February 22d. It was a distinct thrill to sit in the
same room with the Grand Masters of forty-eight other jurisdictions and
listen to the well-prepared papers on various subjects of Masonic interest.
One of them dealt with "Masonic Postwar Assistance to Veterans,"
others were "How can Masonry Avoid Repeating the Mistakes made
Following World War I," "Postwar Developments in Masonic Educational
Programs," "Will Additional Social Security Legislation Eliminate or
Minimize the Need' for Masonic Homes and if so What Other Charitable
Projects Should the Fraternity Sponsor" and "Clandestine Masonry Today-Is It a Menace, and If So, What Should Be Done About It."
As the Representative from this Jurisdiction I was honored by being
called upon to prepare and read a paper entitled "Extending Our Masonic
Cabletow to Mas&hs in War Devastated Countries," particularly our
brethren in the Philippines. It was a short recapitulation of what California Masonry did for our boys in the armed forces and in helping to
evacuate prisoners of war and other displaced persons who passed through
our ports. I think that without any impropriety I can modestly say it was
well received.
1:his· annual Con~erence should and does afford an opportunity for the
full mter-chang~ of ideas among· the various jurisdictions, but as it is apparently becommg an appendage to the George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association, I fear its usefulness may be lessened.
Why do I make this statement? My answer is, that when the usual Committee was appointed to select the time and place for the next annual
meeting of said Association and' M. W. Chas. S. Johnson, Grand Master
of Kentucky, a member thereof, filed a minority report recommending
that Cleveland, Chicago, or some mid-Western city be selected as the
place for the next annual meeting, he was unable · to even obtain a second
for the motion until I came to his rescue. See page· 168 of Conference
Report. The majority report, of course, was in favor of Washington, D. C.
This brought the minority report before the Conference for action prior
to. th~ vote of the majority report, and the entire argument against the
mmonty report was based upon the fact that the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial Association for a great many years now had
be.en meeting in W~shi~gton, D. C. annually on Washington's Birthday,
for the purpose of v1ewmg the Temple, accepting subscr.i ptions and secur-

41

ing some promises for the future and that it woul~ be impracticabl~ to
have the Grand Masters' Conference at any city distant from Washmgton, D. C.
This, my Brethren, indicates ho'w a movement which started subordinate
to a main movement sometimes overwhelms the greater move~~nt an~
the latter be·c omes a mere appendage. It is almost a case of the tail
wagging the dog." I am sure that if George Washington were alive he
would not want pressing proble,ms affecting our fraternity to be subordinated to discussions concernfog a monument to his memory.
There were several Grand Masters from the middle West ancl Pacific
Coast States that joined in the debate and pointed out the large expense
and time consumed by those of us in the West to always attend the meetings in , Washington, b~t this, however, was all to no avail.
On' the morning of Washington's Birthday the Grand Masters and
their 'wives were transported by.:bus to Alexandria, Vir~nia, for the p~r­
pose of taking part in the ceremonies at the George Washmgton Memorial.
As many of my predecessors have indicated, it stands on a beautiful
eminence which in Colonial Days was known as Shooter's Hill, and Commands a' view not only of the surrounding country but of · the beautiful
Potomac riYer and our own majestic Capitol in the distance. Personally,
I ;y.'.~1,1i'd not go into ecstasies, which some have, concer~ing the b~auty
of the building. To me it resembles too much a terraced old-fashioned
wedding cake. The Hall of Columns is indeed beautiful but lacks warmth.
After we were assembled in the Auditorium President Arn called the
meeting to order ~nd after the Invocati.o n of ~.he. Divine Ble~sing upon
the Convention and its deliberations, and the smgmg of America, a_n address of wekome by the Chairman, reports, .appointments of Comm1.ttees,
etc., the various Grand Masters announced the contributio~s of their respective jurisdictions.
Had I known that I was expected to appear on the platform with a
special check as our contribution from this Grand Lodge,. ~ would not
have attended the meeting. Personally, Brethren, I felt hum1hated and almost like the dull pupil who was in a corner of the school-room with a
dunce cap. After a long list of contributions had been announced I heard
one of the brethren near by, but who was obviously not aware of the
fact that I was near at hand, ask " Where is California's contribution?"
At our last Annual Communication the subjec't of what we were to do
towards the completion of the George Wa'shington Memorial. was again
before Grand Lodge. The special committee which had previously been
appointed by M. W. Claude H. Morrison made a rep?rt and recommendation, which will be found at page 144, 1944 Proceedmgs.
As I intend to make a definite recommendation before closirig this
report it seems to me that it would not be amiss for me to recapitulate
briefly the history of this movement in our Grand Lodge.
·
In 1908 our own M . W . Oscar Lawler, Past Grand Master, while on a
visit to Washington, urged the construction of a proper bui!ding within
which should . be placed the priceless relics of George Washmgton, th~R
owned by Alexandria Washington Lodge No. 22, A. F. & A. M. of Virginia. (Grand Master's Address-1927 Proceedings, page 387.) The original cost of the Memorial was suggested at $100,000.00.
The idea grew so that in· 1910 a Memorial to "George Washington,
A Man and Mason" was agreed upon and a definite decision to build such
a structure was made in 1911. By the time of the organization of the

Association jn 1922 it was proposed to erect a Memorial at a cost of
$500,000.00 and to provide an Endowment Fund of $200,000.00. Later in
that year plans were adopted providing for an estimated cost of the
Memorial of $2,100,000.00. To date the Memorial has cost $4,500,000.00
and the end is not yet.

and recommended that action be taken by this Grand Lodge so that we
may do our share in bringing an early completion of this structure.
The Ftnance Committee report of that year, written by Past Grand
Master Crites, provides for a per capita levy of twenty cents for four ·
years and again advised that whatever plan for financing that should be
adopted should fall equally upon an members of the Craft.
In 1928 Past Grand Master Fischer recommended the continuance of
the per capita levy and that the same continue as provided for in the previous year.
In 1929 Grand Master Hutaff recommended "the continuance of the
plan under which we are making annual payments on our quota."
In i931 Grand Master Ross recommended that "Grand Lodge take
proper action to continue our contribution to meet with the terms of the
so-called New York Plan." He also stated that when he presented the
check representing our fourth payment pledged by this Grand Lodg~, he
hoped that we would be able to have the fifth payment made during this
year, so that the amount might be used before May of 1932. Accordingly
as we had on hand $25,000.00 that by our previous custom would have
been held over to present at the next meeting of the Association, he caused
a check for that amount to be sent on the 13th of August as a part of our
1931 payment. He further stated that "the balance is available to be paid
at this time, which when paid will complete the payment of our original
quota, the amount heretofore pledged by this Grand Lodge."
In the same year M. W. George L. Jones, Past Grand Master, presented a resolution to Grand Lodge "that a per capita tax of ten cents be,
and the same is hereby levied upon the membership of this Grand Jurisdiction ·as a contribution to the George Washington National Memorial
Associati<;m, the same to be payable with other Grand Lodge dues."
It was referred to the Finance Committee, who presented the following resolution, which was adopted: "Resolved, that the sum of ten cents
be added to the tax levy, payable with the annual returns August 1, 1932,
upon the paying members of the jurisdiction."
There was no mention of the project in 1932 or 1933.
In 1934 Grand Master Gist, in his Annual Message, commented on the
Memorial but made no recommendation.
In ·1935 Grand Master Whiting called attention to the unfinished state
of the Temple and that although approximately four million dollars had
been expended thereon to that time, it seemed that the project would require about five hundred thousand more. He recommended that we should
make further contributions, as others are doing, when our financial condition would permit.
This language, in conjunction with the r~ference to the so-called New
York plan by Grand Master Ross, had the moral effect of raising our
contemplated contributions to the fund.
In 1941 Grand Master Wilson made no specific recommendation but
commented as follows: "This Grand Jurisdiction ought not to allow a
relatively few thousand dollars to forever keep it out of the honored list
of those Grand Jurisdictions which have had a full participation in the
completion of the project."
In 1942 Grand Master Smith commented on the Memorial but made n0
recommendation.
In 1943 Grand Master Wood made no comment on the Memorial.

In the 1935 report the President of the Association reported that the
architect estimated it would cost $493,000.00 to complete the structure.
In our Proceedings of 1912, at page 214, appears the resolution intro~uced by the late M. W. William P. Filmer, wherein after calling attention to the fact that there were thirty-five Grand Lodges in the United
States then in this movement and that it should be "A Memorial Hall to
Washington, the Mason" in which the Grand Jurisdictions might place
memorials to their distinguished Masons, he recommended an appropriation of $200.00 from the funds of Grand Lodge for membership in said
Association, which recommendation was concurred in and adopted by
unanimous vote.
Grand Masters Filmer in 1913, Burnett in 1916, and Hervey in 1918,
made favorable comment in their Annual Messages and suggested that
California participate.

The second contribution by this Grand Lodge was in 1922 and amounted
to $5,000.00 The entire sum of which was to be available not later than
November 1, 1923.
The cornerstone of the Memorial was laid on October 1, 1923.
In his Annual Message in 1924, Grand Master Crites called attention
to the fact that it was planned to have the Memorial financed by all the
Masons in the United States by each Jurisdiction raising its quota by
$1.00 per member. Our total contribution up to that time was $5,200.00.
The Grand Master also gave as his opinion "That California should lay
out a plan so that our full share of the undertaking will be paid within a
reasonable time." At that time our membership was about 107,000. Grand
Master Crites further stated that he was of the opinion that whatever
plan be adopted that it should bear equally upon all of our members.
. Pursuant to such recomm~ndations the Finance Committee recommended
an appropriation of $5,000.00 and that no further appropriation should be
made thereafter for the above purpose by this Grand Lodge.
In 1925 Grand Master Reese made no reference to the Memorial, nor
did the Financ,e Committee.
In 1926 Grand Master Boynton recommended reconsideration of the
position taken by Grand Lodge and expressed the opinion of two previous
Grand Masters that California should contribute to ' this movement, and
that whatever contribution that we made should bear equally upon all
members of the fraternity. Grand Master Boynton had stated "that ultimately our contribution will amount to at least $1.00 per member."
The Finance Committee, of which Past Grand Master Crites was a
member recommended that an appropriation be made from Grand Lodge
funds as the same became available above other requirements and recommended an appropriation for that year in the sum of $5,000.00.
• ,Jn 1927 Grand Master Jones in his Annual Message, which will be
found in the 1927 Proceedings, page 387, again reviewed the action taken
in this matter and among other things said, "the present plans call for an
expenditure of four million dollars for the entire cost of.. the Temple, while
a sum of one million dollars should be raised as an Endow,ment Fund,"

Boards of Relief and Employment Offices
During the past year I have visited all of the Boards of Relief and
Employment offices, with one exception, .and was rather critical abo11t
their appearance. In most instances the offices, insofar as furniture and
equipment was concerned, were not in accon;lance with my conception of
what this fraternity stands for.
Most of the quarters were rather cramped, the furniture was old, needed
cleaning or repairing and the general appearance was not in accordance
with modern standards.
As I have often said, the appearance of some of the offices might leave
one with the feeling that the fraternity needed assistance rather than the
one who was seeking it. As Grand Lodge funds are used toward the
support of these offices I felt that it was a matter which vitally concerned the Craft as a whole.
In view of the fact that members of our fraternity frequently patronize
private employment agencies I was curious to know the reason therefor,

47

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

One of our Secretaries explained it on the theory that they were probably
under the impression that they could secure better positions through
private employment agencies. I endeavored to fathom the reason behind
this theory and reluctantly came to the conclusion that as private employment agencies have a more prosperous appearance than our own the
reason was probably psychological.
I am very happy to report that the Board of Control has cooperated
with me to the fullest extent possible and local Boards of Relief have
been jarred into a sense of responsibility for the improvement of the
appearance of their offices and the necessity of employing file clerks,
stenographers or other assistants. Considerable painting and cleaning of
these office5 has been authorized or completed. As a· sample I suggest
you visit the offices in this very Temple.
. One further point, and that is the lack of 'adequate card index records
of applic~tions, positions filled, reasons for termination of employment and
other data. In one of the offices I visited there was no card index whatsoever and in another large office none worthy of mention. As a matter
of fact, in the latter office, I strongly suspect that accurate records are
not available because they would not justify the lurid claims made as to
the number of positions filled.
Furthermore Boards of . Relief should see to it that those who have
office hours from ten to twelve o'clock and two to four o'clock should at
least be available during those hours of the day.
A more cordial greeting would not be amiss in some of these offices.
On one occasion I visited one of these offices and asked for the Manager of
the Employment office. The lady in charge replied "out to lunch." I then
inquired for the Secretary of the Board of Relief and received the
identical answer, "out to lunch." As the lady in question knew who I
was, I am wondering what sort of reception an ordinary brother would
receive at her hands or how cordial the req:ption of a widow of a deceased brother would be. These are some of the things which should be
corrected without delay or much effort.
Several Secretaries of our Boards of Relief have called my attention
to the fact that the brethren are sometimes loathe to apply for assistance,
or even cash checks issued by the boards because of what they considered the objectionable word "relief."
·
We are all awa.re of the fact that the tendency in r ecent years has
been to eliminate as far as possible such words as "alms house," "poor
house," "county farm," and "relief." Social workers are unanimous in
their opinion that self respect should be maintained and the dignity of the
individual respected. I therefore trust that Grand Lodge will a,dopt remedial legislation to eliminate such words as "relief" and adopt some such
phrase as "Masonic Service and Employment Bureau." We would then
have a state-wide name, easily found in indexes or directories, and could
refer to various branches as, "San Francisco," "Oakland," " San Diego,"
"Los Ang eles," etc.

Courtesy Degrees
As the r eport of our V. W. Grand Secretary will indicate, we have
conferred approximately three degrees for every deg ree requested of
other Grand ] urisdictions during the war period. I admit that I have
probably been more liberal than some of my predecessors in consenting
to the conferring of Courtesy Degrees by our constituent Lodges for
other Grand ] urisdictions.
My reasons for this attitude, very briefly, were beca~se I think of
this fraternity as one great family, especially insofar as the Grand Lodges
of the United States and Canada are concerned. Due to the marriage
of young men and young women of our Armed Forces, which resulted
in new homes and family ties in this State, I have not adhered strictly
to our previous rule agairn~t conferring First Degrees as a courtesy to other
Grand ] urisdictions unless a candidate was in the Armed Forces.
As there are thousands of our former soldiers taking advantage of
the G. I. Bill of Rights at the Schools, colleges and universities of our
State, and have in numerous instances been induced to become citizens

Open Air Degrees
During my term of office several Lodges made application for Dispensations to permit them to meet on the highest hills, or in the lowest
vales near their community, usually in conjunction with some other Lodge,
at a moonlight ceremonial, or initiation . Under present tens e conditions
I refused all of these applications. My reasons briefly, were because of
the , apparent resurgence of the Ku Klux Klan movement, which according to newspaper accounts usually conducts its initiatory services among
its hooded members by candle light and under a fiery cross. It would
be so easy for the profane to confuse a perfectly _proper outdoor meeting
of a Masonic Lodge with the activities of an organization, whose principles are so un-Masonic that I refused to permit these meetings. I am
happy to report that in every instance where I called the attention of the
applying Lodge to the reason for my refusal, it invariably acquiesced.
Future Enlargement of Grand Lodge Offices
During the past year the offices of Grand Lodge have been· considerably improved and modernized, insofar as furniture, lighting equipment
and other essential services •are concerned. The Grand Master's office;
also, I think has been improved in .appearance. I certainly trust that as
many of the brethren as can possibly view the offices will take advantage
of the opportunity, to the end that they may determine for themselves as
to the wisdo'11 of the expenditures which have been made in that regard.
With our expanding membership and enormous future growth of this
State, it is inconceivable that we shall not, in the near future require all
of ·the space on the fourth floor of our TemP,le. As soon as construction
of office building is resumed so as to house our present Board of Relief
and Employment Office, it should be asked to move to a more central
location; to better serve the public, and at the same time make that additional space available for Grand Lodge offices.
Realizing the need for adqitional space, I feel certain that the Grand
Encampment of the Knights Templar would be willing to make their
space available also. As this Grand Lodge owns fifty-one per cent of
the stock in the Masonic Temple Association it has a right to use its
own property to its best advantage, and this without injuring any of the
other activities.

Retirement Plan for Grand Lodge Employees
This prompts me to call the attention of Grand Lodge to t!:te fact that
we have no provision for the retirement of employees, such as is provided for those in Federal, State or Municipal service and as is largely
found in . all up-to-date modern corporations.
The number of employees directly employed by Grand Lodge would
hardly justify the establishment of a retirement system qut I do believe
that with the number of employees at our Masonic Homes, which it is
true are under the jurisdiction of the Bo:trd of Trustees thereof. arid the
number of employees in Boards of Relief and Employment offices, the
latter of whom are sustained not entirely from funds from Grand Lodge
and which are sustained by contributions from the Lodges comprising
the same, prompts me to recommend that the incoming Grand Master should be
authorized to appoint some well qualified member, or committee, of our
Fraternity to make an actuarial investigation and report to the next annual
communication of Grand Lodge as to the feasibility of establishing such
a system for the benefit of the employees hereinabove referred to.
At first blush there may be those who believe that it is impracticable
to provide a system of retirement for employees of our Boards of Relief
for instance but my answer to that is that it should not be any more
difficult tha~ to provide a blanket bond for the Secretaries of our various
Lodges in conjunction with the employees of Grand Lodge.
In any broad aspect it seems to me that we should provide retirement
on the contributing basis by the employees and subject to retirement at
not less than twenty years' service and compulsory upon obtaining the
age of 64 years. Experience has indicated that the age at which our Army
and Navy retires those in the service, namely, at 64 years, is a pretty safe
yard-_:;tick to go by. It is true that age in men is relative. It is not
necessarily a matter of birthdays. Soine men are mentally old at fifty;
some men, like Benjamin Franklin and Oliver Wendell Holmes, and in
our present day; Jan Smuts, are mentally alert and nimble-minded at
eighty. .They, unfor~unately, are in the minority.

Visitation to Hawaiian Islands
On July 5th .we set sail for the official visit of a Grand Master to
the constituent Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands for the first time in five
years, with the Masonic emblem flying from the masthead of the "S. S.
Matsonia."
Upon arrival in Honolulu, with our emblem again at the masthead,
we were met by Worshipful Brothers Harold N. Mosher, Alexander
Douglas Potts, Cletus Chaussee, Paul Charles Peters, Frank Ahrendt,
Harry Colvin and William Beers, who escorted us to our hotel and thereafter commenced a round of visitations to the various Lodges, brethren
and prominent members of the Fraternity, for the ensuing sixteen days.
I visited the Islands of Kauai, Maui and Hawaii and met members of
various Masonic Clubs, or groups, on the different islands. I was honored
by being asked to address the Bar Association of the City of Honolulu
through the courtesy of Worshipful Brother Tavares, Attorney General
of the Islands.
Although not a member of the International Rotary I was asked
during the following week to address the members of the Rotary Club
on the Island of Maui.
Time and space do not permit of the description which I should like
to give the brethren of these beautiful Islands and the genuine hospitality
of their people.
Prior t9 my intended trip I had endeavored to make it quite plain to
Brothers M'osher and Potts that realizing their war-time difficulties I did
not wish to enhance their problems unless they felt that my visit would
result in some distinctive advantage to the Fraternity.
They assured me that the brethren in the Islands were most anxious
to have a visitation from the Grand Master that they might be given
somewhat of an opportunity to forget the trials and tribulations of war.
Those of us who merely went through the discomforts and inconvenience
of rationing or partial blackouts cannot appreciate what it meant to the
civilian population to live under curfew regulations and military discipline
for about four years on the doorstep of a conflict then raging in the
Pacific. War had been brought to these Islands too suddenly and with
consequences too terrible for the . lesson to have been forgotten. Be it
said to the undying glory of all our brethren in these Islands they carried
on with the noblest traditions of our fraternity, worked long hours, kept
their Lodges open, disbursed charity and extended the hand of fellowship
to the sojourning brethren of the Armed Forces under these trying. circumstances.
Their enthusiasm for our Grand 'Lodge is shown in many ways but
by none more visibly than by the generous contributions annually made
by their members to our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.

I a~ prone to admit that I have a very v:arm spot in m?' heart for
the Masons in the Hawaiian Islands. The exotic beauty of their trees and
flowers has been described by more capable authors on innumerable occasions and I feel that if I were to dwell upon the coloring of the waters,
the height of the mountains, the · verdure· of the hillsides, the beauty. of
their falls· and the vastness of the volcano, I would be suspected of bemg
disloyal to my beloved California.
There is a strong sentiment favoring Statehood for this Territory in the
not too far distant future but there is also a sentiment opposed to the idea
of Statehood. One who has read anything about the Islands can readily
understand the reasons actuating those who oppose Statehood, but personally I believe it is inevitable. From a selfish standpoint I should hate
to see this happen because our Lodges would inevitably form a Grand
Lodge of their own and thereby sever another tie by which. this Paradise of the Pacific has for so many years been he'd to the mamland.
One· of the most pleasing things about the Islands in general is the
manner in which the various races, nationalities and religions have made
a working thing of our democracy. It is an example worthy of all imitation.
In one individual there are sometimes as many as six or eight racial and
religious strains. But, as Professor Andrew W. Lind, Ph. D., Professor
of Sociology, University of Hawaii, in his introduction to "Hawaii~n
Types" recently said: "The one unifying racial strain in most of the hybrid
types is Polynesian. But in any event there is the unifying influence of
Island life which, on the evidence of th.e photographs themselves, seems
to be producing a growing congruity in appearance between peoples of
different racial extractions. It is as though the racial and ancestral masks
were becoming slowly transparent and a new character, thoroughly
Hawaiian and American in spirit, were forcing itself through to dominant
expression."
There is evidence that a clandestine Lodge of Masonry is operating
in the Islands and drawing into its fold numerous candidates of Polynesian; Chinese, Japa~ese and mixed extractions. Some of our seriousminded brethren on the Islands are of the opinion that it will not be long
before applications will be made for a Dispensation to charter a so-called
International Lodge. It will undoubtedly be the subject of much controversy. Grand Lodge may have to consider this question sooner than we
think. In its solution, if it is shown that the applicants are good men and
true, I hope that we may be as tolerant as the people in the Islands are
toward each other. If, on the other hand, the application should originate
from those who have selfish or mercenary motives, we should not hesitate
to deny the application.
Due to the dislocation of the communities and restri~tions during the
war years it was inevitable that our ritualistic work, as between the Lodges
on the four separate Islands comprising two lnspectoral districts, one of
which had been without an Inspector for more than a year, should develop
imperfections. For that reason I authorized V. W . Chester H. Warlow,
Grand Lecturer, to proceed to the I slands for the purpose of holding
schools of instruction and he departed, hence on the day that I returned
to San Francisco.
On the night before our departure we were tendered one of those neverto-be-forgotten. Hawaiian luaus.

stitution and Ordinances has previously been before Grand Lodge, I am
of the opinion that the subject will press upon us more than ever and we
should again give consideration to a possible relaxation of the strict rules

Sections of our Edicts and Resolutions hereinabove quoted, there are those

It would seem to me that if the action taken in the several instances

It is true that under · the Old York Constitution in 926 "a candidate
must be without blemish, and have the full and proper use of his limbs;
for maimed man can do the Craft no good," but this was at a time when we
were operative Masons. It seems to me that as we no longer work in
operative Masonry but speculative only, this custom has become obsolete.
Even the law of the land, which is supposed to be so conservative and
precedent-bound, recognizes the principle of law that where the reason for
a rule has ceased, the rule itself should cease. An examination of pages
414-417 of our 1944 Proceedings will show that this is a subject of prolific
discussion. Personally I b~iieve that we might we)! reconsider our former
stand on this subject and adopt _a resolution in conformity with that
adopted by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana in 1944 in the following form,
to wit:
"WHEREAS, It seems wise to. reconsider our traditional attitude on
the doctrine of physical perfection; therefore, be it
"RESOLVED, That physical qualifications for the Degrees in the
jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge be and the same are hereby defined as to
require o.nly that the candidate be able in a reasonable manner by the' use
of natural or artificial members to' give all the signs, grips, and steps; be
of sound mind; and self-supporting so as not to become a financial burden
, on the fraternity; be it further
"RESOLVED, That all edicts and general regulations in conflict herewith are hereby repealed; be it further
,
"R~SOL VED, That the constituent Lodges shall have the responsibility of determining that applicants meet these physical qualifications;
be it further
"RESOLVED, That we reaffirm our declaration that the inward and
not the outward qualifications are what we as Masons regard as of permanent importance."
To the end that this subject may again be brought before Grand Lodge,
I recommend adoption of the Louisiana resolution or similar resolution.

In.January I held a meeting with the Trustees of the Clubhouse, Univers~ty of California, Los Angeles, to determine upon the future policy of
continuance or abandonment of said clubhouse. A portion of the Board
was in favor of abandoning the project, selling the property and distributing the proceeds to the original donors. Another group was in favor
of giving the clubhouse a further trial and the third group was resolved to
make a success of the project. After visiting the clubhouse at Westwood
with its proximity to the campus and the fine character of the buildin~
and grounds, I concluded that so far as lay within my power I would do
anything necessary to resume activities as soon as the clubhouse was
available for use by the students. During the war the clubhouse had been
taken over by the Army as a mess hall for personnel attending special
classes at the University. At the close of the war the American Red Cross
rented the premises on a month to month basis. After the termination of
this tenancy the property was put in order and I am very happy to report
they officially reopened on September 24th and I was invited to be present
at an official reception on September 26th, which I was unable to attend
becau'se of a previous engagement.
·
On January 12th the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley held a dinnerdance and reception in my honor and I am most happy to report that I
was very favorably impressed with the appearance and fine manners of
the young men and women who patronized the Clubhouse on that occasion
and I have been assured that it was typical of the character of the young
people for whom we are rendering this truly worthwhile Masonic service.
Personally I cannot commend too strongly the continuance of both of
these activities. There are those I fear who look at activities of this kind
too much from the standpoint of "What does the fraternity gain in membership or direct prestige ?" Whereas I look at it from the standpoint of
being the rr..eans to provide a place of study and recreation for those of
Masonic affiliation. Some important discovery in science or contribution
made for the benefit and welfare of humanity by one of our guests would
far out-weigh the small annual per capita contribution which they cost
us. Although primarily social, their continuance gives visible proof to the
world that we are disciples of the arts and sciences.
Physical Qualifications
On numerous occasions Masters of constituent Lodges have endeavored
to shirk the responsibility cast upon them by our Constitution in determining the physical qualifications of applicants by asking me questions,
the answer to which is readily at hand. See Edicts and Resolutions
Sections 878a-885.
'
One of these cases, however, particularly impressed me. The candidate
who sought admission had suffered the loss of a foot · a short distance
above the ankle, . which had been replaced by an artificial foot enabling
him to walk, dance, and carry on his usual occupations without any
noticable effect. He is .happily married, has two children, owns his own
home and is in a good position. Jrle, of course, cannot understand why he
cannot be accepted. Much to my surprise I found that this artificial limb
was held in place not by metal braces or brackets, but by means of plastic
substances. Although this does not eradicate one of the objections to the
removabi!ity of an artificial limb, it does overcome another objection which
is sometimes raised in the very first degree.

Accord•ng to latest available information all of these Lodges are doing
very fine work.
For more than ten years, the brethren in Yosemite Valley had been
endeavoring to obtain a Dispensation to form a Lodge. Due to opposition
they were unsuccessful until I looked into the matter very carefully and
concluded that not only would it be a great convenience to those in the
valley who were members of the Fraternity to have a Lodge in their
midst, but it would provide a haven for innumerable sojourning brethren
from all parts of the world while vacationing in one of God's beauty spots.
The membership of Indian Wells Valley Lodge is at present composed
primarily of personnel of the United States Navy Experimental Rocket and
Torpedo Base out on the desert. I made a preliminary trip to lnyokern
with M. W. Arthur S. Crites and satisfied myself as to the enthusiasm of

as samples I note the following:
(a) I was asked to rule on whether or not a Lodge could receive a petition,

of thin~ing, comply with the provisions of Section 208 of our Constitution and
Ordinances, which undoubtedly must have reference to a candidate being capable

(g) Russian River Lodge No. 181 inquired as to whether it would be permissible for said Lodge to rent a building on its lot "for the use of a stationery

(k) On<! of the most difficult decisions which I was called upon to make
involves one who refused to serve in the Armed Forces during the late war,
on the ground that he was a "conscientious objector.'' Although the record is
long, the various actions of the Lodge and the correspondence are interesting,
and the principle involved merits serious consideration. To recapitulate the
facts, they are as follows :
On September 22, 1944, Truth Lodge No. 628 addressed a letter to M. W.
Claude H. Morrison, Grand Master, the pertinent portion of which follows:
"Most Worshipful :
"At the Stated Meeting held on September ·18th, at ·Truth Lodge No.

Nineteen voted for and two against:

'"RESOLVEP, that Truth Lodge No. 628, F. & A. M ., Los
Angeles, California, request the Grand Master to declare the office
of Master of Truth Lodge No. 628, to be vacant, and to petition
the Grand Master for a Dispensation to hold an election for Master
for the balance of this year.'"

Thereafter, and on October 3, 1944, M. W. Oaude H. Morrison, replied to

"If I accede to the request, it may have very serious consequences
and create a precedent which might be far reaching. Therefore, I am

Following up his letter of October 3, 1944, M. W: Claude H. Morrison wrote

It is necessary to bear in mind that the resolution of the Lodge, under date

First: "To declare the office of Master of Truth Lodge No. 628 to be

Second: "To grant a dispensation to hold an election for Master for
