The regularity of the meeting of Truth Lodge, just referred to, has itself
been questioned on the ground that the meeting was opened in the Third Degree
by the Secretary of the Lodge with the Master and both Wardens absent. The
Secretary then called from labor to refreshment, whereupon the Senior
Warden arrived and proceeded with the business of the Lodge.
Rather than seize upon this technicality to overrule the resolution of November 6, 1944, I have chosen to meet the issue presented on its merits.
The ruling of M. W. Claude H. Morrison in refusing to declare the office of
Master vacant and refusing to grant a Dispensation to hold an election for
Master was discussed, whereupon the Inspector of the District was quoted. as
having assisted in the formulation of the resolution last hereinabove referred
to. It will be noted that the effect of the resolution would be to do virtually by
indirection, that which was directly refused by the Grand Master.

It is only fair to state at this point, however, that the action of the Lodge
was undoubtedly warped by the heat of warfare.
" It should ~e note~ that the .r~solution stated that George X. Hickerson, Jr.,
has placed himself m the position where he could not serve as Master to the
end of his term" and "has not served the Lodge as Master since July I 1944
owing to his removal from the Jurisdiction."
'
'
The prim~ry question to be decided, however, is whether or not a Lodge can,
by a resolution at a Stated Meeting, declare the office of its Master vacant.
The question as to whether the Master has placed himself in a position where he
could. not serve to the end of his term by asserting his constitutional rfght to
refuse to bear arms in time of war, and whether his removal from the Juris~iction by military authorities disqualifies him from office, although collateral
issues, are ones upon which the Lodge predicated its action. This is borne out
by a letter to our V. W. Grand Secretary, by the Secretary of the above Lodge,
under date of February 7, 1945, wherein he states that after "The Government
Selective Service had taken him (George X. Hickerson, Jr.) under its protective wing," he had designated the Senior and Junior Wardens to assume his
official duties for the balance of the year, and further intimated in said letter
that the Lodge questioned Brother Hickerson's good faith in "his assumption
of the 'conscientious objector' role hardly seems exactly genuine and leaves
much to be desired."
The above substantially states the condition of the record at the time M. W .
Gilbert C. DeForest assumed office as Grand Master in October, 1944. Not
being a lawyer, he sought advice from members of the• legal frater.nity in our
Grand Lodge. As is not unusual, the lawyers disagreed.
' In due course, Brother George X. Hickerson, Sr., Past Master of the same
Lodge, who in the language of the Secretary of said Lodge, had ."been fighting
a one man war on behalf of his son," appealed to Grand Lodge for the customary Past Master's Certificate on behalf of his son, and tendered the .necessary fee in payment thereof. This, therefore, squarely presents the issue as to
whether or not, under the stated circumstances the Lodge had the right to deny
Brother George X. Hickerson, Jr., a Past Master's Certificate.
I am of the opinio~ that it has not, and I recommend that the Past Master's
Certificate be issued to George X. Hickerson, Jr., as Past Master of Truth
Lodge No. 628, for the following reasons:
Section 274 of our Constitution and Ordinances, being Article 2 of Part
3, declares as follows:
"Charges may be preferred against the Master of the Lodge for abuse
of his powers, violation of the Constitution or Regulations, or un-Masonic conduct of any kind, by any five Master Masons in good standing;
which charges shall be in writing, over their signatures, and shall be
presented to the Grand Lodge, if in session, or to the Grand Master
during vacation."

where he could not serve as Master to the end of 1944" because he asserted his
constitutional right by claiming to be a "conscientious objector." We may
individually, and as Masons, disagree with one who claims to be a "conscientious
objector". in time of war, but we have no right to deny him that privilege, if
made in good faith.
The Selective Service Act of 1940 recognized this right in our citizens, and
it behooves us not to s"et ourselves above the law of the land. It should be
borne in mind that during the most terrible days of fire, raids and bombing of
England, they so upheld the constitutional rights of their citizens who claimed
to be "conscientious objectors," and said claims were respected. If the action
of Truth Lodge is sustained, it would appear to me that we are trenching very
closely upon religious freedom.
The file in this case contains a copy of a resolution which was adopted by
the Commission on World Peace of the State of California-Arizona Conference
Committee in the Methodist Church in Los Angeles on April 5, 1945, which, by
resolution, denounced a bill then pending in the California Senate, which would
deny a conscientious objector the right to hold public office or employment after
the war. The resolution stated:
"l. The freedom of individual conscience is a fundamental principle
of American Democracy and a part of the freedom of worship guaranteed by the Bill of Rights.
"2, Civilian public service and non-combatant military service has
been· duiy provided by law through the Selective Service Act of 1940 as
alternatives to bearing arms. Therefore, those individuals who, because
of religious convictions, apply for such service have the full backing of
the law of the land.
"3. Such g·roups as the Quakers, Brethren, and Mennonites who have
historically opposed participation in war have nevertheless made great
contributions to American life and character. To debar such earnest and
sincere people from public life would be to impoverish our State."

58

If, as is implied in the correspondence which I have quoted, Brother Hickerson, Jr., claimed to be a 'conscientious objector" through cowardice or lack of
patriotism in bearing arms for his country, it would have been a very' simple
matter to prefer charges against him along those lines, and if proven, ask that
he be removed from office, whereupon the record would have been reviewed by
our Grievance Committee as to the sufficiency of the charges. I have no doubt
that if a charge of that kind had been proven it would have been construed to
be such un-Masonic conduct as to warrant reprimand, suspension, or expulsion.
This orderly procedure was not pursued, and in order to circumvent the
plain mandate of our law, the Lodge sought by artifice, to declare the office of
Master vacant, on the ground that he had "placed. himself in the position

The record in this case contains aspersions against the Brother in question,
which are evidently not borne out by his subsequent actions. After having been
sent into the Forestry Service during the first part of his enlistment, he was
thereafter sent to the United States Hospital at Livermore, as a medical aide.
A call was issued to take care of tuberculosis patients in one of the wards for
which service he volunteered, and for which he received $10.00 a month. I am
reliably informed that he was kept in the United States Army in the above kind
of service until July of this year.
It is well for us to remember that the President of the United States, on
October 11, 1945, conferred the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest
national award of heroism, upon Corporal Desmond T. Doss, who also was a
conscientious objector. The newspaper articles at the time said:
"As a medical corpsman, Doss saved scores of lives amid heavy fighting during which he was wounded badly. The twenty-six-year-old conscientious objector, when notified that he had been awarded his Nation's
highest honor, said:
"'My country's award of the Congressional Medal of Honor
to me, a conscientious objector, is probably as good proof as any
of the real freedom in America. I do not think they would do a
thing like that in any other country in the world.' "
The truth of the matter is that this Brother was denied a Past Master's
Certificate because he was a conscientio~s objector and let us not be naive
about it.

Another illuminating· instance of how far our country has gone in upholding the rights of conscientious objectors is in the decision of the United States
Supreme Court, last April, in holding that an alien may be granted American
citizenship, even though he refuses to bear arms in the Nation's defense because he was a conscientious objector. The conscientious objector was one
James Louis Girouard, a Canadian, who applied for American citizenship, but
declined to accept that section of the Naturalization Act which makes willingness to bear arms a requirement for admission to citiZenship. Girouard is a
member of the Seventh Day Adventist Church. .
Are we, as ~fasons, to flaunt the law of the land and deny a Brother his
constitutional privilege of claiming exemption on the ground of being a "conscientious objector" and by overruling a mandate of the Grand Master deprive
this Brother' to the right of a Past Master's Certificate? I think not.
While it may be true that he placed himself in a position wh~re he could
not serve as Master to the end of his term, I do not believe that any of the
previous Edicts or Resolutions o.f Grand Lodge justify the statement that
Brother Hickerson had removed himself from the Jurisdiction. The facts are
exactly the opposite. According to all information in the file, he has never
been out of the State of California. There was therefore no vacancy in that
office, as defined by Section 35 of our Constitution.
For the foregoing reasons I recommend that a Past Master's Certificate be
issued to George X. Hickerson, Jr., as a Past Master of Truth Lodge No. 628.
(I) Brother Cyril W. McClean, Secretary of Sequoia Lodge No. 349,
addressed a letter to me shortly after I assumed office, which was as follows :
"Having in mind Section 152 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge, as
amended in 1944, and Section 2261 of the Civil Code of California, as
amended in 1943, may we kindly have your ruling as to whether or not
there has been removed thereby the former limitations on the type of

including, but not by way of limitation, corporate obligations of every
kind, and stocks, preferred or cornmon,· which men of prudence, discretioi1 and intelligence acquire for their own account."

At about the same time, Brother McClean addressed a letter to the Grand
Treasurer on the same subject, but I am not entirely sure the question was
answered as clearly as it might have been by me, for the following reasons :
Realizing the danger of permitting Lodges to invest ' in common stocks, I
referred to Section 721 of our Edicts and Resolutions, indicating that it was the
clear policy of Grand Lodge tliat endowment funds should be invested only in
federal, state, county, or municipal bonds legal for savings banks.
I am convinced, however, that there is a very definite uncertainty in the
minds of various Lodge officers and trustees of Lodges by the retention of the
words "or trustees" in the first subdivision of our Section 152, as amended by
Grand Lodge in 1944, and as is indicated by the question propounded herein.
It seems to me that our present Section 152 of the Constitution leaves the
door wide open for the investment of Lodge funds in common stocks or equities,
because Section 2261 of the Civil Code of California, as amended in 1943,
states:
''.* * * * a trustee shall exercise the judgment and care, under the
circumstances then prevailing, which men of prudence, discretion, and
intelligence exercise in the management of their own affairs, not in regard to speculation, but in regard to the permanent disposition of their
funds, considering the probable income, as well as the probable safety
of their capital. Within the limitations of the foregoing standard, and
subject to any express provisions or limitations contained in any particular
trust instrument, a trustee is authorized to acquire evfry kind of property, real, personal, or mixed, and every kind of investment, specifically

61

Due to the uncertainty which exists, I am satisfied that numerous of our
constituent Lodges have already purchased common stocks or equities, and I
am quite certain that it is not the policy of Grand Lodge to permit Lodge
funds, and much less life membership funds, to be invested in securities of that
kind. I therefore recommend that the words "or trustees" in the first subdivision of Section 152 of our Constitution relative to the investment of Lodge
funds, be stricken out.
Recommended Changes in the Constitution and Edicts
Due to the fact that the five day week has come to be an accepted part of
our business life, and the increased inability to employ help for Saturday morning work, I recommend that Section 44 of paragraph 9th of our Constitution
be amended by eliminating the word "six" therein, and substitute in lieu thereof
"eight," and that the word "Saturdays" be inserted immediately preceding the
word "Sundays," so that when amended the paragraph will read as follows:
"To keep his office with all the books, papers and archives of the
.
Grand Lodge in a fireproof building in the City of San Francisco, and
to have the same open at least eight hours each day, except Saturdays,
Sundays and legal holidays for the transaction of Masonic business."
I recommend that in the event Grand Lodge should adopt my suggestion for
the establishment of a Masonic Library as a memorial to the Veterans of
World Wars I and II, that the 14th paragraph of Section 44 eliminate the
words:. "act as grand librarian" so that the sentences shall read:
"To take charge of the library of the Grand Lodge under such regulations as it may prescribe."
This recommendation is made in view of the fact that if a library is e~tab­
lished, such as I have in mind, a trained librarian should be placed in charge
thereof, and he, of course, would be under the direction of the Grand Secretary.
I recommend that Section 70 of our Constitution and Ordinances, relating
to Standing Committees, be amended by adding immediately following word
"Member" at the end of the first sentence thereof, the following: "Provided,
however, that no member shall be appointed on more than one committee."
So that, when amended, the first sentence will read as follows :
"The following Standing Committees shall be appointed by the Grand
Master at each Annual Communication just before the dose, viz.: On
Jurisprudence, on Policy and General Purposes, to consist of nine members each ; on Finances, on Grievances, on Credentials, on Pay of Members, on Charters, on By-Laws, on Accounts, on Returns, on Correspondence, on Library, on Grand Lodge Week Activities, on Clandestine
Masonry, to consist of seven members each ; and on Necrology, to consist of five members; provided, however, that no member shall be appointed on more than one committee."
This amendment is offered for the purpose of spreading the honors in Grand
,Lodge, and attracting younger men to serve us. A great American statesman
made a speech some years ago, the theme of which was : "Pass Prosperity
Around"; I think we can modernize the slogan by: "Let's Pass the Honors
Around."
This amendment is furthermore offered in view of the fact that the laudable
purposes sought to be obtained by providing for the appointment of "at least
one Master and one Warden on each of said committees" has not accomplished

Brotherhood Week
On July 5, 1946, under the seal of Paul Revere Lodge No. 462, a communication was addressed to me, in my capacity as Grand Master, calling my
attention to the fact that on that date a resolution had been adopted by the
Lodge reiterating our belief in the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of
Man, and the necessity of striving to bring about a Brotherhood of Nations
and eliminating bigotries and prejudices, etc., and wound up with an appeal to
all Blue Lodges in California:
"To petition the Grand Lodge of the State of California to endorse
the coming observance of Brotherhood Week as a fitting time to empha- ·
size the teachings of our Craft, and . call upon all Lodges within the
Jurisdiction to join in that observance to the end that human brotherhood
will be strengthened, and that the gospel of Freemasons as it pertains to
brotherhood will become the creed of all men throughout this land."
, It will be noted that the resolution in question was adopted on the same
day upon which I set sail for the Hawaiian Islands. I mention this, not beeause
I think the Lodge sought to take any unfair advantage of my absence, but in
explanation of the fact that by the time I returned from the Hawaiian Islands
the resolution had been sent to all or at least a great many of the constituent
Lodges throughout the State, and the harm, if any, had already been done.
Numerous brethren throughout the State wrote to me concerning said resolution and considered it a violation of Section 128 of our Constitution. If the
adoption by Grand Lodge of the resolution in question were deemed to be legislation then the action of Paul Revere Lodge was wrong.
As Grand Master, I have no objection to the wording of the resolution, but
I seriously doubt its wisdom. A communication of that kind going to Masons is
almost equivalent to asking them if they believe in the Ten Commandments or
the Golden Rule.
Furthermore, a resolution of that kind might lead to serious controversy in
Lodges, not from the laudable purposes which it seeks to accomplish, but from
an inquiry into the motives of its sponsors, or those who a,re seeking its adoption.
I make no recommendatio.n insofar as the resolution is concerned, but do
believe that although not specifically prohibited by our Constitution, it might be
well for Lodges, before adopting such resolutions, to make inquiry of the Grand
Master as to whether or not there is any possibility of its adoption causing
friction within the Lodges themselves.
It has further been suggested by our Right Worshipful Senior Grand
Warden that to endeavor to teach the gospel of Freemasons to all men throughout the land might do violence to the 23rd landmark.

Order of De Molay
On several occasions during the past year, I have been the guest of
honor at installations of officers and the conferring of Degrees by members of the Order of De Molay. On all such occasions I have been impressed with the fine appearance, manly qualities and ritualistic perfection

Candidates for Public Office
Complaint was made to me by several brethren in Southern California
against a candidate for Congress who, in the political literature which he
was sending out, gave the name and number of the constituent Lodge
of which he was a member. It should be noted, however, that the candidate gave the names of several other fraternal organizations of which he
was a member, as well as his church affiliations, and he did not use any
Masonic sign or emblem in connection with the advertisement. Under
the circumstances of this case, I am of the opinion that it did not violate
the Resolution adopted by this Grand Lodge in 1920, and numbered 750 of
Edicts and Resolutions.

Conclusion
Throughout my term and wherever possible, ,I have stressed racial
and religious tolerance.
To the "Four Freedoms" guaranteed under the Atlantic Charter I
believe we should add Freedom from abuse on account. of one's politlcal
party affiliations, and Freedom from abuse because of one's belief in labor
organizations.
I am persuaded to offer the first suggestion for I have noted that
most of our official family seems to be composed of the adherents of a
political party which is not in accord with the ideas of the present
dominant political party throughout the Nation. I happen. to belong to
the first of said parties, myself, but I have jealously guarded the rights
of others to disagree with my ideas of party loyalty. Some of our brethren too frequently forget that from the very foundation of our Republic
great men of those days disagreed as to the propriety of adopting the
present Constitution of the United States'. From the very incipiency of
our political history we have made gre.at strides under a two party system.
It has provtn not only beneficial, but salutary in the extreme, and well
may we rue the day if ever one political party becomes all powerful.
Have we already forgotten the one party man in Nazi Germany? Or
Fascist Italy? Does the present example of lack of cooperation with the
Western Powers on behalf of one of our recent allies indicate that the one
party system results in greater or less democracy in that country? I regret
to say that I have heard brethren in meetings adjacent to our Lodge room
speak in the most blasphemous manner concerning a late President of
the United States with whose policies they disagreed. Surely this is not
what is taught us in our Lodge rooms or ritual.
On the second proposition which I have suggested-verbal abuse of
some of our members because of their belief in or adherence to labor
organizations-may I be permitted to observe that most of our members,
so far .as I have noted, work for their living, and under present economic
conditions and trends of development, it will become increasingly necessary for them to belong to or join labor organizations.
No one can deny that for sometime past we have had a surfeit of
strikes, and the public in general is thoroughly disgusted with the interference toward a recovery leading to peacetime activities. There is evidence that those who have been responsible for this work stoppage are
beginning to realize the road to peace, prosperity, and plenty is not
through strife, but through labor and production of g oods and commodities which the people are cravin,g for.
Much as we deci:y this present interference with peacetime recovery,
w e should never forget that Freemasonry and the growth of labor ot-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE QF CALIFORNIA

ganizatio.ns from the inception of the Guilds is co-eval and the present
day ·abuse and jurisdictional disputes among labor unions is probably no
more annoying or intolerable than were the practices of the early day
Guilds. Society overcame those obstacles and I am certain will find means
of overcoming these present day obstacles.
In our work we have stressed the religious, philosophical and esoteric
to such an extent that we are sometimes apt to overlook our humble
origin. Let us not be like the ungrateful son who denies his father's humble birth-right, but rather let us be proud of our achievement for humanity during the years that we have functioned. Let us look forward to
a brighter day and with hope that the Golden Age is in the future, and
"As we sow, so shall we reap."
Great complaint is made against agitators. Were not Christ, Huss,
Washington, Bolivar, Garibaldi, Rosseau, and Voltaire agitators?· Were
it not for the fact ' that men like Galileo, Burbank, Pasteur, Einstein, and
other great scientists did not accept as facts things which they found
about them and proceeded to hunt greater truths, this age might well
be in the days of -Moses. All of the progress in the world has been due
to men and women who were not satisfied with the established order
of things. If we had no labor problem, we would have had no industrial
output which enabled us, in the shortest possible time and with thoroughness that overwhelmed and stunned our enemies, to provide the means
wherewith the late cruel war was brought to so hasty a close. There is
no traffic problem in a community which is dead or dormant.
I wish to express appreciation to all of the officers of the various
Lodges and districts which I attended throughout the year for the uniform courtesy extended to me, and in some instances to members of my
family who accompanied me.
For the great friendships which I have made as your presiding officer,
I am truly thankful. I trust I have justified your confidence in me, and
that in so'me humble manner I may have contributed something toward
the erection of that great structure which we so fondly refer to as Masonry.

Population
In spite of predictions to the contrary, based on prosperity, pensions
and socia1 security legislation that there would be no need for such homes
as ours in the near future, the present trend does not confirm this outlook.
Applications are coming in at an increased rate for Covina and while
there is still ample room available, there are indications that the coming
year's population will probably be the largest since the outbreak of World
War II.
The number of residents at Decato remains about on a level as far as
the reports show, but there has been a marked acceleration in applications
during the past few months. Accommodations for women are now occupied to capacity and the same will soon be true relative to married
couples.

Extending the Fraternal Hand
Among the prisoners of war returned to this country in the spring of
1945, was Past Grand Master Harry E. Stafford of the Philippine Islands
and Mrs. Stafford. After a brief stay at th.e Marine Hospital in San Francisco, they faced a loQ.g; period of convalescence from injuries and mistreatment suffered at the. bands of the Japanese.
It was our pleasure, at the direction of the Grand Master, to have them
as our guests at the Decoto Home from September 8, 1945 to June 26,
1946, at which time we assisted them in going to the Mayo Clinic at
Rochester, Minnesota, for further medical care.
The dire situation of a Brother, a member of a Lodge of the Philippine

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
The year of 1946 having drawn to a close, I shall endeavor to submit
to you,. in this my sixth annual report, a short summary of the activities
of the Home which are not recorded elsewhe~e in our report.
At the beginning of the year there were 149 women and 113 men being
cared for in "the Home. During the year 28 women were admitted at an
average age of 77.07; 39 men, average age 75,72. . During the same period
we have lost by death 16 women at an average age of 78.25; -32 men,
a verage age 78.66, and 3 women and 3,men were withdrawn, leaving us
at the end of the year 158 women and 117 men, including 12 married
couples.

74

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The average age groups are as follows:
4 between 50 and 60 years,
31 between 60 and 76 years,
133 between 70 and 80 years,
90 between 80 and 90 years,
17 between 90 and 100 years.
The average age for women is 78.8 and for men 77.41 years.
Advancing years bring with them ever increasing demands for greater
service. ThE above table, as you will observe, indicates that a large number of our members' ages range between 80 and 100, which necessarily
means that the demand for service is growing greater each year.
I am pleased to say that our Hospital Department is rendering that
service very efficiently under the supervision of Miss Esther G. Payne
in a very commendable manner, Dr. W. L. McWhirter directing the
Medical Department.
The care and comfort of the members of the Home are under the
supervision of Mrs. Virgina M. Lord, our Matron, who renders assistance
cheerfully and impartially where needed.
The kitchen and dining room are important departments. At present
. they are well staffed and operating efficiently. The return of some of the
supplies which we have been unable to obtain, is making it possible for us
to provide the members of the Home with a greater variety of food.
Our laundry is well manned and is operating satisfactorily, supplying
the necessary clean clothing for the family, and an abundance of clean
linen throughout the Home and the Hospital. Plans are underway to
install some new equipment in this department.
Du.ring the war years we were unable to secure efficient help to ~are
for the grounds and garden!!; as a result they do not present quite as
pleasing an appearance as they should. Carrying out instructions regarding this matter I have contacted the California Nursery. Their engineer
has made a survey of the grounds for the purpose of determining what is
needed in the way of frees, shrubs and covering for the banks. If the
plans they submit are practical and we can ·have the work done I am
sure it will make a very desirable improvement in the appearance of the
grounds.
Now that we have been able to secure the services of a competent
assistant for our engineer, he is able to operate the heating plant more
efficiently, and give more attention to the maintenance work.
Due 'to labor conditions and our inability to procure material, it has
been impossible to do much the past year regarding the repairs, alterations
and improvements which have been planned. However in addition to the
completion of the sprinkling system and partial completion of the fire
escapes which the State Fire Warden recommended we have painted
25 rooms, .the ramp leading from the east wing to the dining room and
the pantry between the kitchen and dining room. We have iristal1ed a
public address system in the dining room and the Auditorium, installed
a water softener in the laundry, and work is underway to put our deep
well water pump in proper condition.
Most of the farm land is still under lease. The following receipts indicate that the portion retained·• for Home use has made a fairly good
showing.

Report of Superintendent-Covina Home

To the Tri4stees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is our privilege as well as our duty to present to you at this time our
first annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children
at Covina.
Even in normal times a change in administration presents ma1;1y adjustment problems. Ip times of unsettled conditions such as these, the
situations are usually more exaggerated and severe. Although the war
ha; ended, many of the wartime problems have remained with us. We
are experiencing almost, if not worse, the same war-time difficulty in
obtaining .clothing and supplies. The problem of personnel has improved
somewhat. These administrative problems have been met with a minimum
of disturbance to the children and they have suffered no privations.
The children are, without question, better provided with food, clothing,
and shelter than most children in private homes. The adults who are
engaged to live with the children, care for them, and supervise their activities have devoted themselves unselfishly to their work. Those who,
during the past year, have become permanent members of the Staff have
done outstanding work. It has been with regret that we have bid goodbye
to some workers of long standing who, over the years, have contributed
to the building of the Home and its program of child-care.
Release from war service has enabled our doctors to devote more attention to the children's health program. Each child has had a physical
examination and has received attention wherever care was indicated.
Regular dental service not available during the war has been resumed in
part. Aside from the usual children's diseases which are to be expected,
we have been exceedingly fortunate in our health program throughout the
year.
Some work has been done in redecorating the children's rooms and
living quarters. Shortages of material and labor have naturally hindered
this work. Much remains to be accomplished. Insofar as possible, old
furnishings have been reconditioned -that they might be used to fullest advantage.
The downward trend in the population of the Home is apparently;
checked. The intake for the 1946 fiscal year was 10 children. At · this
writing, six weeks after the beginning of the 1947 fiscal year, nine children
have entered the Home and applications are pending for three others. .It.

78

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

appears that the anticipated increased post-war need for the Home is beginning to manifest itself.
Many of the children have participated in community activities throughout the year: 15 boys have been associated with the Boy Scouts of the
town troop in Covina: 10 girls were members of the Girl Scout troop at
their school. Fourteen older boys belong to the De Molay Chapter at
El 'Monte. Several older girls are active in the Christian Endeavor work
at Glendora and many children regularly attend the various churches in
Covina. During the summer most of the children had two weeks at the
"Y" or Scout camps in the mountains. In the public school which they
attend, some made outstanding records in scholarship, sports, dramatics,
and other activities.
During the year many alumni returning from the service . have visited .
the Home. Of 169 who served their country, 52 have reported that they
are now back in civilian life.
It is with deep sorrow and lofty pride that we remember those who
gave their lives for their country. May this Home be a better Home because these twelve lived and died for it :
Walter Anderson
James C. Blair
Fred Burgen
Robert Countrym;m

We have enjoyed the fellowship of the Board of Trustees who have
devoted many hours of labor and thought to the welfare of the Home.
To the many Lodges, allied organizations, and individuals who have visited
during the year, or remembered the .Home in other ways, we are grateful
for their interest and loyal support.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To thl! Most Worshipful Grand Lodge,
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California:
Again it is my privilege to stand before you and, as your Grand Lecturer,
note the passing of time and render unto you my report as required by our
Constitution and Ordinances.
Though more than a year has elapsed since the abject surrender of the .
originally aggressive, but now quite passive, enemies of these United States,
yet peace and tranquil~ty do not pervade the world. We find strife and dis.<;ension among nations seeking territorial power and influence by negotiation rather
·than actual force and even within this country of ours there is confusion of
thought and conflict of ideas and ideologies.
Within the year since the previous brief communication of this Grand Lodge,
many war restrictions have been removed, yet there have been diverting factors
appearing in this transition from actual war to so-called peace which have in
some considerable measure hampered the usual and normal Masonic activities
lying within the province of the Grand Ucturer's office.
During this period of time, however, three regular meetings of the Ritual
Committee have been held and in addition thereto there was an unusual amount
of inter-member correspondence dealing with matters hereinafter refe,rred to.
Your Grand Lecturer has had the privilege of attending Schools of Instruction
conducted in their respective divisions by Assistant Grand Lecturers Sidney K.
Lehman, Arthur M. Warren, and Obed W. Carr, and also, accompanied by the
entire committee membership, has attended a School of Instruction conducted
by Inspectors Miles J. McLellan and Leighton D. Armstrong at Sacramento.
In every instance the work in these several schools was excellently done and
the few noted deviations from absolute perfection were minor and easily and
immediately corrected. We, have every right to be justly proud of all our
Inspectors and the work they are doing, not only on account of their individual
proficiency in the ritual, but also on account of their skill of instruction.
Method of instruction is very important and when skillfully done it materially
reduces the burden of the instructed.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

On my travels about the State on other matters, I have also had the privilege
of conversing with many of the Inspectors of the several districts and with the
Lodge officers of various communities. These contacts with my brethren have
been a source of real pleasure to me for I enjoy friends, both new and old, and
I am rather hopeful that some general Masonic benefit has come from the
subject matter of the conversations. On one particularly interesting occasion I
spent the entire evening with Past Grand Master Gilbert·C. DeForest, Inspector
William C. Grover and all the Lodge officers in District 6 in an informal discussion of Masonic matters as disclosed by and reflected in the formal ritual
of our Order.
In my report to Grand Lodge for the year 1945, I revealed that in a few
places in the State the ritualistic work was not up to what we considered our
minimum requirements and indicated that special attention was being given to
those places. During the past year, in an endeavor to improve that situation,
I recommended to the Most W"Orshipful Grand Master that Division A of the
State be subdivided and placed in the charge of two Assistant Grand Lecturers.
The Grand Master, looking with favor upon this recommendation, exercised
his plenary powers and, on a temporary basis, made the division and appointed
an additional Assistant Grand Lecturer. I beg to report that this action has
been of assistance in improving, but not completely solving, the problem. .However, sufficient has been accomplished by that action to justify the continuance of
the set-up as it now exists and in my recommendations hereafter set forth, I am
requesting legislation to cover the situation.

eliminate reoccurring errors and place authoritative sources of ritualistic information in each of the several ·Lodges there in the shortest possible time. ,
In my report to Grand Lodge under date of October, 1941 (Grand Lodge
Proceedings, Vol. XLVII, page 448), I referred to a form used in the second
section of the Third Degree. Since that date in my travels I have devoted considerable time to the instruction of the brethren in the physical aspects of this
particular ceremony, cautioning them against over-enthusiasm, as well as discoursing upon its antiquity and solemnity. Again it seems desirable to call
these matters to the attention of the craft, for some of the brethren, especially
among our so-called "co-worker teams," still insist on going too far in their
exuberances. Masters of the Lodges have responsibility for the dignity as well
as for the proficiency of the work and they should insist that all degrees be
conferred properly in deed as well as in word.
Since. the previous communication of this Grand Lodge your Ritual Committee has observed that the form of the "Masonic Funeral Service" and also
the form of the "Installation Service of Subordinate Lodges" each varies
greatly from place to place. Accordingly, we have been giving attention to
both the form and the words of these services, having particularly in mind that
the form used for a service should be specific and be the same in all parts of
our Jurisdiction. Uniformity of a ceremony is certainly to be desired.
In relation to the Installation Service. we fo.und that the language of the
text was such that similar ideas were repeated at various places in the work
with a great variation of phraseology. It seems to us that this unnecessarily
increased the labor of memorizing the service without in any material respect
adding to its beauty. \Ve have, therefore, prepared and offer for adoption by
Grand Lodge not only a set of detailed instructions as to the form of the
Installation Service, but also a number of amendments to its wording.
Numerous suggestions have been made to us regarding amendments to the
wording of the Funeral Service. Many of them had considerable merit, but
it is the considered opinion of the Ritual Committee that the present Funeral
Service is in every respect dignified, impressive, beautiful and excellent and
that its language lies well within the limitations of the abilities of the average
Master of a Lodge. We therefore recommend no change in the language, except
in two places where it is desirable to correct technical errors and in two other
places to make the phraseology of certain passages conform to the language
of our ritual. These latter amendments wi·ll eliminate the source of reoccurring
errors in our Lodge room work and are- recommended upon that basis.
It is impractical, in this report, to set forth in detail the proposed amendments to these two services, or to here include the proposed instructions as to
the form of each service. However, we have had a full set o.f the offered
instructions and amendments delivered to each Inspector. We request that you
contact the Inspector of your own Masonic District and obtain from him the
necessary information to enable you to consider these proposals and cast your
ballot when they come before Grand Lodge later in the week.
There is a minor matter in the esoteric work which needs attention. The
remarks of the Senior Deacon to the candidate at the end of the first sectidn
of each degree should be the same. The language now used in the First and
Second Degrees is informal. The present language in the Third Degree at this
point is esoteric, · is not adaptable to the First and Second Degrees and can be
amended only by action of Grand Lodge.

accordance with the general Masonic custom of the country, to the end that
none may go away dissatisfied. Proper honors are a portion of the present
wages of a Master Mason and while none would be offended by errors of placement, some might smile with indulgence at our in.aptitude.

1. Language of the Service is not amended except as follows:
(a) The opening remarks beginning: " Brethren and Friends" are to
be changed to conform to the First Degree demand, and read as follows:
" Brethren and Friends: It has been a custom among the Frat ernity of Free and Accepted Masons from time immemorial, at the
request of a brother," etc.

(b) The references to the lambskin apron are changed to conform as
nearly as possible to the references in the work and in the lecture a-nd
read as follows:
"This lambskin apron is an emblem of innocence and the badge
of a Mason; more ancient than the Golden Fleece or the Roman
Eagle, more honorable than the Star or Garter or any distinction
that can' b.e conferred by king, prince, potentate or any other person.
By it we are continually reminded of that purity of life and conduct
so essentially necessary to gain admission into that celestial lodge
above where the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe forever
presides."
(c) In the commital the words: "earthly bed" are changed to "earthly
resting place" because many burials are now in mausoleums or· columbariums.
( d) The word "cassia," a shrub, has been changed to "acacia," a tree,
for obvious reasons.
2. Directions as to the form of the Lodge room service and the "chapel"
service have been removed to the addendum, clarified and by a system of
key numbers printed in the work, the directed actions are correlated to
the words.
3. All "formal" street processions are eliminated and the "funeral dirge,"
not being used, is omitted from the printing.
4. The person speaking has been indicated by a designation in script at
the beginning of the part.
Because the above amendments are such a small portion of the total
funeral service, the full text of the service is omitted. For convenience,
however, the locatfon of the key numbers in the text which refer to the
instructions in the addendum are here indicated. Page and line rdei ences

Genera! Statement of the Proposed Amendments to the Installation Service
1. All directions have been removed from the text and placed in the
addendum.
2. The Installing Officer is always addressed by his proper salutation.
3. The directions to present an officer for installation so far as possible,
have been made identical in wording.
4. The Masters' of Ceremonies words of presentation so far as possible,
have been made uniform for each officer.
5. The details of the Certificate of Proficiency have ·been omitted so
that a single uniform phrase is appropriate in each case.
6. The directions for investment with the jewel have been made uniform
for each office.
7. The words addressed to the Chaplain have been modified so that
they are appropriate for use whether this individual be an ordained minister of the gospel or a layman.
8. The words addressed to the org;mist have been modified so that one
not unusually skillful in music will not be embarrassed by the present
flowery language of this portion of the service presently used.
9. The sequence of the "Salutes to the Master" and the "Proclamation
of Installation" have been reversed so that the · Master is not formally
saluted until he has been declared to be duly installed. In a closed installation service this avoids the anomoly of giving formal signs at a time when
the Lodge is at refreshment. .

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TWENTY-SEVENTH ANNUAL
OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

To the M. W. Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
For the first time in five years Public Schools Week was observed this
year without the restrictions and handicaps imposed by wartime conditions.
With reference to World War II, this was the first post war observance;
but it will be remembered, of course, that our first observance was a post war
movement brought about by conditions resulting from World War I.
The success of the observance last year was a surprise to the Masters of
some of our Lodges who had complied with the direction of the Grand Master
with only a hope, rather than any expectation, of success. This year throughout the entire State (except in a few instances where the lack of Masonic
leadership was evident) the arrangements were made with the confidence and
enthusiasm-and intelligence-which insured success.
The measure of that success is indicated not merely by the application of
the usual yardstick of popular interest and support, but also by the character
of the programs. Never before was the purpose of Public Schools Week more
effectively made known to the people; and never before were the programs
better calculated to acquaint parents, and the citizens generally, with our public schools-with present teaching methods, the kind of school environment
provided, the character and fitness of school personnel, the organization of the
school, the program of studies and the type of scheol citizenship promoted.
The key-note was sounded in the proclamation issued by the Governor; and
was echoed, and re-echoed in other proclamations and in public addresses and
newspaper editorials calling on the people to join in the observance.
Governor Warren in his proclamation said that it was "more urgent today
than ever before that public awareness of the importance of our public school
system be maintained .at a high level"; and he urged "upon all parents and
adults the joining in programs through which ·they may more thoroughly
acquaint the!I)selves with the educational services, facilities and needs of our
State."
Among other pronouncements in which the thought expressed in the Governor's prnclamation was developed and amplified was an admirable address
by the Assistant Superintendent of a large city school system. Such is its
worth, and so indicative is it of the aims and purposes of Public Schools
Week that we wish it were practicable to quote it in full ; but the following
'
excerpts will indicate its trend :

88

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"It takes time and effort, of course, for members of the public to
visit their schools, but if the people watch their crops with anxious concern about the harvest, so they should watch the growth, development
and maturing of the children under the nurturing leadership of those in
the profession of education. vVe give ourselves vigorously to the development of our material .resources. Shall we not be more concerned about
the development of our human resources?"
''The parent is concerned about what goes on at school because he has
pride in seeing that his offspring has the best possible preparation for
successful living. The adult without children is interested because he has
an investment in the schools and the ~ttern of his own living is determined in a measure by the success of public education in the community
where he lives. The citizen is interes.ted because he knows that the kind
of community is determined in a large measure by the kind of citizenship
that is promoted in the schools. In fact there is no one whose life is not
conditioned in some respect by the work carried on in the public schools."
"It is well for the citizen who obtained his public school training perhaps twenty or twenty-five years ago to .note .the changes that have taken
place since his days at school. Members of the public cannot properly
evaluate ,the work of the school unless they understand the changes since
they went to school and the reasons for them. Twenty-five years ago the
school population was much smaller, children left school earlier, th~ soCial
demands upon the school were much simpler, the courses of study did not
cover so great a range of activity as is demanded today. Many of the
changes brought about by science were not then reflected in the schools.
The program was more severely academic. Rote learning was more in ·
vogue. The connection between education and every day living was less
real. School life was less a part of community life. The social emphasis of education was less pronounced. The heavy demands of a very
complex civilization upon the schools were not so great. In many ways,
indeed, the schools of twenty-five years ago and those of today differ.
It is important for the citizen to know and to understapd the changes
that have taken place. We cannot deny these changes. We cannot set
them aside. All life has changed, not only life in school. We need to
make adjustments to those changes and to evaluate public education in
the light of the situation as we find it today in the world in general."
"The citizen will want to know the skills that are being developed in
the schools, the knowledge that is being gained and whether or not that
knowledge is functional in·the every day life of the pupil. He will want
to have an understanding of standards of conduct maintained in the
schools; habits formed; the moral and spiritual valuc:s that are being
given attention; the interest of the school personnel in the individual's
advancement; the measure of success that the school is gaining in preparing the young people to meet the problems they must solve, not only
in book work, but in life situations and in the task of making headway
in the world today."
Discussing the major problems confronting · the schools, mention was made
of the housing situation and the time and effort that must be given to the
selection of sites and the placing of the buildings-and of the war time restriction which made it impossible to meet the housing needs.
Describing the personnel situation in the schools the speaker said:
"In ordinary times well-prepared, qualified and credentialed teachers
are available. During war years many teachers leave the service, some
for military service, some because of home requirements or the lack of
help in the home and .others to secure more lucrative employment.''

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

89

In connection with the foregoing, it seems to us worth noting that in at
least one particular the situation in our schools today is not unlike that which
existed at the close of World War I. Now, as then, there is a dearth of teachers. As reported by Dr. Willard E. Givens, Executive Secret:fry of the National Education Association, a serious teacher shortage exists throughout the
world; but the most acute lack is in Canada, United States and Great Britain.
, According to· Dr. Givens, teachers are abandoning 'the educational profession at an alarming rate; and there are comparatively few teachers being trained
in the colleges. Instead of showing an improvement during the last year, the
situation has grown steadily worse; and a larger number of poorly trained
teachers will be employed by the school systems in the United States this year
than ever before. In the United States today one out of every ten teachers
holds an emergency sub-standard certificate, compared with one out of two hundred before the war.
Of course, we are primarily concerned with the situation here in California.
As disclosed by a report issued by the State Department pf Education thirteen
rural schools in five counties were forced to close because there were not
enough teachers. The superintendents of forty-seven county schools have reported that at least fifteen teaching positions may go unfilled· and sixteen
counties reported that between ninety and one hundred per cent ~f their teachers hold temporary credentials. There will be 1300 teachers in rural areas
holding only emergency credentials.
The situation is, of course, a deplorable one; and if it is less alarming than
it was before the inauguration of Public Schools Week, it is only because the
people are now closer to their schools. They are now no longer ignorant as
they were then, of the perils confronting them, and will undoubtedly do .what
is necessary to be done. For this, we think, the Masonic Fraternity may with
becoming modesty claim at least a part of the credit.
For one week at least public attention is focused on the schools and their
problems. The newspapers and broadcasting stations during that week join in
publicizing school programs, and in exhorting the people to visit their schools,
and to concern themselves with the problems which confront the school people.
This year ~gain, in spite of the continuance of paper shortage, the newspapers
were especially generous; and never before did the radio play as important a
part as it did this year.
There viere so many fine editorials calling upon the people to avail. themselves of the opportunity presented by Public Schools Week to learn about
their schools,. that it is extremely difficult to single out any for special mention.
One which was typical of many appeared in conjunction with a cartoon
with the caption "Schools for Parents.'' The picture showed two adults (presumably parents) seated at a school desk looking at a book held by the father
opened at a page on which were the words "Public Schools Week"; and on the
blackboard, in script, was the sentence, "What the schools teach ·is your
responsibility!"
From the editorial we quote the following paragraphs :
·" Are you one of those who blame the school system if your child
doesn't read as well or spell as accurately as you think he should?"
"Is your child being taught the A B C's, and reading, writing and
arithmetic?"
"Are you well enough· informed to judge!" (Emphasis supplied.)
"Do you know what your child studies and how he is taught?"
"Why don't you look into the matter for yourself?"
"After all, it is the average citizen who makes the schools what they
are.''

There were many programs in which the social studies were emphasizedprobably with the idea of having the parents understand that this all too
little understood "subject" is nothing more than a term to describe those portions of history, geography, economics, political science and sociology which
most educators, and well informed laymen, too, regard as suitable for study in
elementary and secondary schools in order that our young people may obtain a
complete picture of the development of our own country.
Again this year there was that same variety of programs which has been
noted in past years. We assume that it is now well understood that not only
does each local community determine the nature of the week's programs, but ·
that, generally speaking, there is a lack of uniformity among the schools compri~ing a particular system. . We say "generally speaking" because in some
instances, there is a controlling idea or "theme" adopted, around which all the
schools in that community build their programs. For instance, this year in a
city in which the annual observance is always admirably handled, the theme
adopted was "Safety Education"; and the program in every school from the
kindergarten to the high school, included some treatment of that theme. In
song, playlet, recitation or actual demonstration attention was directed to the
danger of accident.- in traffic, at home., in industry, in school and at play; and
the need for care to assure safety. A notable variation of the theme. was a
program "Safety Through World Friend~hip."
Apparently one of the most popular of the themes was "World Peace,"
with such variations as "Education for Peace" and "Peace Through Knowledge/' The selection was based, of course, on the idea announced by a committee which arranged an especially successful observance that through the schools
will come the development of abilities and meanings which will contribute to
that understanding among the nations of the world which now exists among the
states of our nation. In an illustrated folder entitled "Good Schools Today
Can Help Insure Peace Tomorrow" (and of which 23,000 copies were distributed) it was explained that the theme "Education for Peace" was chosen
especially for this year's observance of Public Schools Week because of the
general emphasis now being placed on achieving the peace.
Notable among the programs built around a central thought was one which
presented a forum on Juvenile Delinquency. And it is notable because the
participants were four students from different schools who had won speaking
contests; and more particularly because the topic as announced was "Juvenile
Delinquency and What I as a Juvenile Can Do About It."
There can be no doubt that the best way to find out just what the schools
are doing, and why they are doing ii in that way, is to visit the classrooms,
and talk with the teachers and administrators. But that is not the only way,
of course, and the forum, or panel discussfon, apparently continues to grow
in favor.
This year there were two variations of the forum idea reported. In one
there was an address over the radio every day by a selected speaker; and then
on Friday evening all the speakers discussed (over the radio) the addresses
which had been delivered during the week.
The other was a forum conducted by a newspaper. Everyone was invited
to send in his opinion of the school system-teachers, pupils, employers and
the public in general. The publishers said they wanted opinions derived from
personal experience only, and not what somebody else said. "Well he asked
for it-and he got it." The lady who was a poor speller was satisfied it was
because she had not been taught to divide the word into syllables, and that
made it,. difficult for her to pronounce words of more than two syllables; there

It would appear from the reports from our Lodges that that is just what
many, many thousands of people in California did during Public Schools Week.
They went to school. Of course there were some who merely visited the
schools. But many literally "went to school" in the ordinary acceptance of
that phrase.
They sat, at night, in the seats in which their children sat during the school
day. They went from class to class as did their children. In some instances
the "lessons" were not dissimilar. Iti others, instead of having a lesson in a
particular subject, the parents were told, in detail, how it was taught, and why
it was taught in that manner. The changes in the methods of instruction, and
the reasons for them were carefully explained. The parents were encouraged
to ask questions; and there developed a sort of round table discussion which
· must have been of great benefit to both teachers and parents.
It is interesting to note that one of these "Back to School" programs carried
out the idea by providing the parents with transportation in the school buses.
So typical of many of these programs was this one, that it seems to us worthwhile to give this excerpt from the invitation extended to the parents :
"The adults will again become students for an evening, ride the school
buses, meet in assemblies, attend classes and enjoy refreshments in the
cafeteria at the close of a studious evening. The purpose of the evening
· is to give parents and others a chance to meet with the teachers and
friends, to talk over the problems of and the accomplishments of the
school. The parents are urged, so far as possible, to attend the same
classes that their youngster normally attends for the regular school day.
In this way the adult can see the workings of the class, talk with the
teacher, evaluate the work being done in each class and form a true
picture of the work the school is doing day by day for the youngsters
of the district. Only a few of the regular day students will be on hand
to assist with directing and in explaining class wqrk."
Even those who were merely visitors, rather than participants in a program, must have learned much about the modern school of which the average
parent is too frequently unaware.
First, and foremost, they must have discovered that the old tools of learning
are not being neglected in ' the modern school; but that modern methods of
teaching have vitalized the 3 R's and made them more attractive to the children.
They must have learned, too, the reasons for the inclusion in the curriculum
of the so-called "frills." They had an opportunity of seeing how girls are

implies. And some of them must have ~een surprised to find boys as well as

was had by all, and it was fine publicity for Public Schools Week.
•
J
This was the first time since the beginning of the war that Public Schools
Week was observed by all ol)r Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands. Relieved of
the war-time restrictions which had precluded the holding of any observance in
Honolulu, the brethren were looking forward with keen expectation to the
opening event on April 7th for which great preparations had been made. And
then on April 1st the tidal wave brought death and destruction. This of course
materially affected the · attendance at the different events. It also lessened the
amount of newspaper publicity expected; because as one Master said in his
very comprehensive report, "The newspapers were overloaded with stories of
the tidal w~e and newspaper personnel was working day and night covering
the disaster. This resulted in lack -qf space to publish articles on Public Schools
Week and most articles published were greatly cut." In spite of 'everything,
however, the observance was a decided success. There was a good editorial,
and there were several news stories published; and one of the local radio stations ·cooperated very fully by allowing time for five broadcasts during the
week. There were also "spot announcements" of visits to the schools, and
exhibits of school work. Special mention was made in one of the reports of the
fine cooperation received from the Department of Public Instruction and from
the Parent Teacher Associations.
The Parent Teacher Associations were wholeheartedly cooperative everywhere thii>. _year, ·as they always are. And fine cooperation was also received
from the service clubs and from the American Legion and from all the
organizations which join with us in the observance of Public Schools Week.
In one comparatively small community where there are two high schools, one
junior high and six elementary schools, there were thirty-five different organizations which cooperated with the Lodge.
The Master of one Lodge reported: "We had the enthusiastic cooperation
of the Parent Teacher Association, the Eastern Star and of every fraternal,
labor, social and civic organization in this community." And another Master
answered the· question,. "What endeavor did you make to obtain the cooperation of the civic organizations in your community?" by saying, "No effort
needed, as the _organizatjons join wholeheartedly with us each yeai: and give
100 per cent cooperation."
A gratifying. feature of our latest observance noted in several reports was
the increase in the active participation by members of the Craft. In one the
Master wrote: "The attendance at all schools was larger than ever before.
The Lodges were dark all week and a great percentage of our membership
took part in the observance"; and another Master reported, "Almost every
member of our Lodge that was in town was present and also assisted in
serving refreshments."
Gratifying as is this increase, it is unfortunately true that there is not, and
there never was, that support by the individual members of our Lodges which
their Masters have a right to expect. Nnd it is unfortunate because it is a
re_flection on the Fraternity. Although the annual observance has become, as
it should be, a community affair,' its Masonic origin, with the continued fostering by Grand ,Lodge, and the official participation of the constituent Lodges,

is well known, and very generally referred to in the press, and by speakers at
public meetings and over the radio, even where the committee of arra.n~e­
ments makes no mention of Masons or Masonry. And in some communities,
it is alwavs called a Masonic observance even where there is a citizens committee making the arrangements. It should be evident therefore that if Masons
are conspicuous by their absence, they furnish reason to doubt that sincerity
of the professions they make with respect to their concern for our public
schools.
lt is {nteresting to contrast two reports which were received the same day.
In one, which was the report of (to quo_te the Master) "one of the most outstanding Open House Observances of Public Schools Week" (and where the
auditorium was "Literally packed to capacity" with an estimated attendance of
5000 at two performances) appears this comment: "The attendance of the
officers was most discouraging. Two officers and one member besides the
Marter attended the performance." (emphasis supplied.)
The other report was of an observance where there was a "community
committee consisting of 40 or more organizations along with the Lodge." In
answer to the question, "Was the observance a success?" the Master wrote,
"Yes, it was a wonderful success because so many people came, particularly
the Masons and the Eastern Star. They attended almost as a body. We had
at least 300 visits from Masons during the week."
Here there was evident close cooperation by the Masons and the members
of the Order of Eastern Star. But in another community the Eastern Star
"stole the show." According to the report from the Lodge, "The committee
failed to get in communication with the school in time, and the Eastern Star
Chapter took over, and enlisted the school children to put on a program which
left the Lodge out on a limb so to speak." It is more than probable that next
year that Lodge will have a committee which will not fail "to get in communication with the school in time."
It too frequently happens that arrangements for an observance are not
started sufficiently early to accomplish the best result. In this connection we
think it well worthwhile to quote the conclusion (omitting the names of
course) of the report of- a very successful observance: "It is the feeling of
the committee that more could have been accomplished if the committee had
been organized at the start of the school year. In this way we could have better
organized our effort and also worked out a more extensive program with the
school. This thought has been 'conveyed to the Wardens of the three Lodges
with the suggestion that a general chairman for the 1947 observance be appointed at this time. They have accordingly selected one of the Masters to
serve as general chairman of next year's observance. The school people have
been advised of our plans and we believe that we can look for a well rounded
program for our next observance."
There are already several communities in which the arrangements for the
next succeeding year are commenced shortly after the conclusion of each
annual observance and before the beginning of the ensuing school year.
Although it is now very generally known that the annual observance commences on the fourth Monday of April in each year, unless the Easter vacation would interfere, there are frequent inquiries, before the beginning of the
new school term, sometimes from the school people, with respect to the date of
the next year's observance. In passing it may be here said that the observance
next year will begin on Monday, April 28th.
Somewhat akin to ·the suggestion with respect to the time for beginning
arrangements for the observance, was a suggestion from the Master of ·one of
the Lodges which might well be generally adopted. In concluding his report
he said: "I believe it would produce a better Public Schools Week if every

Junior Warden in this jurisdiction would automatically become a member of
the Public Schools Week committee in his Lodge, and each Senior Warden
would be chairman. Then when an officer reaches the Master's chair he will
not immediately step into this project with little or no knowledge of what has
been done before, or what could be done to improve this observance. I can see
several things. that could have been done in addition to that which was done.
As it is at present we do the same things over and over."
Mention has been made of the part played by t<he radio this year. Not only
were all the stations, including the large systems, exceedingly helpful in publicizing the observance by calling attention to the school programs, but there
was an unusually large number of radio programs devoted to the work of the
schools. These included addresses and round table discussions by school men
and laymen (and women, too) and also programs presented by school children.
The laity included representatives of the Parent Teacher Association, American
Legion, the service clubs, the local Chamber of Commerce and League of
Women Voters. The range of subjects is indicated ·by mention of the following: "Discipline in the Home," "Teen~age Recreation," "Student Government,"
"How Much Homework is Best," "The School Nurse," and "Juvenile Delinquency." And of course "Public Schools Week" received adequate attention.
There were at least two reports in which special mention was made of the
radio programs :
In one, the Master wrote that they had found that broadcasting over the
local station was a wonderful way to publicize their schools. There was a daily
broadcast. from the station, of a program presented by the pupils of a grammar
school. One of these it would appear from a newspaper clipping attracted a
great deal of attention. It was a skit entitled "Around the World Flight" in
which, in correlation with the social studies, the customs and practices of many
countries were discussed. Incidentally, they had fine newspaper publicity, too;
and the concluding sentence of an editorial devoted to teaching and to teachers
seems worth quoting: "As adults acquire a· better understanding of the school
program, the more cooperation there will be between the public and the teacher."
In the other of the two reports to which we have referred the Master wrote
that he believed his Lodge had "inaugurated a new method of presenting the
activities of the classroom to the public," and gave the following information:
Through the facilities of the local station of one of the large systems, four
grammar schools and two high schools were wired, and a half hour broadcast was made on three different days from each of the schools. The announcer interviewed the principals of the respective schools, and asked questions
which were of interest to the radio listeners. He also visited the various rooms
where classroom work was broadcast, and interviewed six or seven pupils in
each room. In this way it was said that the work of the classroom was brought
directly into the home. In addition to the school broadcast, citizens were asked
on the regular radio program "The Man on the Street" what they thought of
Public Schools Week and of the school system, and if they had any suggestions for improving them.
The special arrangements for radio participation in the programs are made
by the local committees. But at the beginning of each year a personally signed
letter goes from our committee to every station in the State asking its cooperation; and so cordial was the tone of the responses received this year from
the managers and program directors that it would seem as though they were
receiving, and not extending, a courtesy. There were many who expressed
themselves as "very glad" or "very happy" or "greatly pleased" to (quoting
one of them) "have this opportunity to help make Public Schools Week an
occasion of importance."

And it is cooperation of that sort, received also from the newspapers, and
of course from the school people, and from the Parent Teacher Association,
and the American Legion, and the service clubs and all other fraternal, social,
labor and civic organizations, too numerous to mention, which accounts for the
twenty-seventh successful observance of Public Schools Week.
