ANNUAL ORATION
By MORRIS GOLDSTEIN, Grand Orator

OCTOBER 15, 1946

"HOW SHOULD MASONS ACT?"
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Past Grand Masters,
Officers and Brethren of Grand Lodge:
It is with humility that I stand before you this day of our communication,
for I am cognizant of the high standard established by the illustrious brothers
who have preceded me in the office of Grand Orator. By a strange concatenation of circumstance I find myself obligated for this honor by a debt of gratitude to three Grand Masters, to the Most Worshipful Gilbert C. DeForest
who graciously appointed me in 1944, to the Most Worshipful Lawrence C.
Kelley of sacred memory who under war-time conditions reappointed me in
1945, and to our Most Worshipful Grand Master Arthur W. Brouillet who
with remarkable tolerance so characteristic of him and an exemplary sense of
brotherly love permitted me to continue in that office. Tracing the origins of
this moment, may I also thank our dynamic, likeable and consecrated Grand
Secretary, the Very Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson, who five years ago as
Grand Master, introduced me to Grand Lodge with the appointment as Grand
Chaplain.
In preparation for this day I have searched within myself and asked,
"What can I · say to this impressive assembly of leaders in California Masonry,
men who know their Masonry; what message can I give in the thirty allotted
minutes that would be a true contribution to the work we seek to do, that would
be quintessential in nature?"
One might deal with the history of our fraternity, and interesting indeed it
would be. Or--<>ne might draw up a roster of distinguished Masons of the
past and· the present, and thrilling indeed it would be. Or-one might give a
recital of the ideals and principles of Masonry, and refreshing indeed it
would be.
But is there not something more important to tell, something more vital?

96

.

.

PROCEEDINGS 01'' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

To me it seems that the most important consideration is: How should
Masons act?. How does Masonry affect your life and mine?
It is an accepted fact, is it not, that Masonry-while it teaches men to be
religious is yet not a religion, while it stresses democracy and responsibilities
of citizenship is yet not a political organization, while it practices charity is
yet not a charity institution, while it indulges in esoterics is yet not a philosophy
only.
Masonry, above all, is a way of life. Do we not teach brotherly love,
relief, truth, temperance, fortitude, prudence, justice?
Do we not pray: "Grant that the sublime principles of Freemasonry may
subdue every discordant passion within us"?
Masonry is definitely a way to live. It impresses and perpetuates its teachings by way of symbols-the square, the level, the plumb, the trowel, the
compass, the acacia, the common gavel, and so on.
These symbols, of course, need interpreting. Thus, for example, we are
taught that the common gavel refers to the necessity of divesting our hearts
and consciences of the vices and superfluities of life; or that the plumb admonishes us to walk uprightly in our several stations before God and man.
So far I have said nothing new or startling. But now-here is 'the basic
proposition I would present in this message. It is, that these teachings revealed
through the symbolism of Masonry are themselves mere word-symbols; they
themselves need interpreting.
The plumb, we have noticed, symbolically admonishes us to walk uprightly,
namely, to act correctly, to do the right _thing·. But what is the right thing?
"To walk uprightly"-that phrase is a word-symbol. It is a generality.
Is it enough to admonish Masons to walk uprightly, to do the right thing
... "you must do the right thing"? How far will that get anyone? No one
will debate the generality : certainly we all want to .do the right thing. Who
doesn't? Have you ever come across anyone-a normal person, that is-who
will say "I want to do the wrong thing"?
Bro'therly love, relief, truth: these are our three principal tenets.
It is fairly well defined in detailed terms what we mean by relief. We
mean a Widows' and Orphans' Fund to be administered in specified circumstances ; we mean the Masonic Homes, the War Service Fund, the Board of
Relief, the Employment Service.
Is it sufficiently defined what we mean by truth? Scientific truth is one
thing; moral truth is another; and esthetic truth is still another. Moreover,
much that was thought true one hundred years ago is not regarded as true
today. There is a process of evolution in our knowledge or discovery of truth.
It is wrong to "tell a lie." What about a "white lie"? Suppose that someone whom you loved dearly was afflicted with an incurable disease, but did not
know it and remained hopeful. Should you tell that brother, or father, or
mother, the truth? How answer that? What is truth? "On this theme we
contemplate," says our ritual regarding truth. This is indeed a theme on ·which
to contemplate.
Justice-one of the four cardinal virtues-"is that standard or boundary
of right which enables us to render ' unto every man. his just due, without
distipction." Splendid ! But in a specific situation, where there are two alternatives, which shall it be, which is just? Listen in. to any one of these radio
programs of domestic wrangling a,nd arbitration. Bdth sides of the controversy invariably think they are right, both believe that what they demand
is justice. How much can it accomplish to instruct them not to deviate from
justice? What they need to know is-what is just i1,1 this particular dilemma?

l f Freemasonry is a way of life, and if we take Freemasonry seriously and
we desire to live that way of life, is it not highly important that we interpret
our principal tenets and cardinal virtues and general obligations in terms of
day-to-day living-in each situation in which we find ourselves to know how
should Masons act !
This is a tremendous challenge. It would require a full-sized book for real
analysis-many volumes perhaps.
For the purpose of this half-hour message, however, I would like to convey
~ome of the thinking I have done regarding this during recent months.
With the objective 6f translating our word-symbols-the generalities of our
teachings-into specific and detailed guidance for Masonic conduct, I would
recommend at least five definite ways of knowing how Masons should act:
1. Make use of the best knowledge which we inherit from those who have
preceded us. This is not to say former generations were any more brilliant
than we. It is to say that a single lifetime is of short duration and that
common sense will dictate that we take advantage of all that was learned before
our entrance upon the stage of human existence, that we might begin where
our predecessors left off instead of goillg through the tedious process of relearning what they have already learned, of what is readily available to us.
A suitable analogy is that of a young lad trying to watch a parade. He
cannot see any too well over the heads of those standing in his way. He asks
his father to raise him upon his shoulders. The father does this and now the
boy can see remarkably well-farther in fact than his own father, for he has
the advantage of his father's height in addition to ·his own. So we may climb
upon the shoulders of the generations that preceded us and begin with the
knowledge that was already theirs;
It is for this reason that our Ancient Landmarks in Masonry are so important. These are, in a sense, the shorthand of Masonry, summing . up much
of the wisdom of that which has gone before.
The Holy Bible is given to us as a rule and guide, that we may consult the
very best that we have inheri~ed from ages gone by. The Holy Bible is a guide
for all mankind but it has its special importance in Freemasonry.
The history of Freemasonry is worth knowing. Valuable books have been
written. Hdw many Lodges possess an adequate Masonic 11brary? It would be
well for each Lodge to have its own five-foot bookshelf, on display and
accessible.
Would it be too outlandish a suggestion for me to pass along the recommendation that wherever possible a candidate for the degrees of Masonry be
not only instructed in the memory work required but in addition be encouraged
to read an authoritative and inspiring book on the fuller significance of those
-degrees ? Or the coach may discuss this matter with the candidate. Why be
in such a hurry to move the candidate along from the first to the second to
the third degree?
As it is true that we live by the light of the stars which shone centuries
ago, whose light reaches us only now, so it is true that we receive a good share
of our enlightenment today from the human great lights of the past.
2. We each have some one whom we admire--before whom we wish to
.appear at our best. It may be a parent, a friend, a brother. What would he
think of this act I contemplate? If he were in my place, how would he decide?
What example would he set for me?
Masonry provides us with magnificent exemplars of conduct, We have our
choice. Do we wish to emulate wisdom: there is the ever-available example
·of King Solomon. Do we wish to emulate courage, fortitude, fidelity; there
is the superb example of one illustrious in Masonic tradition. Do we wish to

97

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

emulate pa!~iotism: there is the undying example of George Washington and
his Mason,i,c ,<;a-founders of democracy.
Within the Circumference of our own lifetime we have men of stature,
men of character, men of accomplishment, men known as Masons__,,some in
this very room-who stir our admiration and create within us the desire to be
as they are. Walter Damrosch spoke truly indeed when he advised: ''It is
easy to be different from the masters-see how like them you can be."
3. Am I willing that my behavior be in the open, for others to know? The
moment that I hesitate to permit public knowledge of a planned course of
action the moment it is clandestine, that very moment I may be fairly certain
that 1' should abandon such procedure. It is not accidental that a volume telling
of .subversive conduct in American life should have the title "Under Cover."
Those who write anonymous letters know that they are doing wrong, otherwise they would identify themselves with their proper signature.
A man's reputation is of paramount value. It is the result of his known
acts and attitudes. How truly this is expressed in the charge of the second
degree which reads :
"Your general good. reputation affords satisfactory assurance that you
will not suffer any consideration to induce you to act in a manner unworthy of the respectable character which you now sustain; but that,
on the contrary, you will ever display the discretion, the virtue, and
the dignity which become a worthy and exemplary Mason."

This fourth guide for conduct is indicated in my judgment in the phrase
which we Masons use so often: "together, brethren."
5. What will my deeds do to me as an individual? In the ultimate analysis
we ourselves determine in great measure the character that we shall have, the
happiness that we shall find in life. It has been observed with wisdom that
when we violate standards of conduct we do not break the Ten Commandments; rather, the violation of the Ten Commandments breaks us. We have
the power to determine whether we shall be integrated useful personalities or
walking wrecks. In other words reward al).d punishment come not to a person
so much as within a person.
Is not this the thought of the charge of the first degree which reads:
"And to yourself, by such a prudent and well-regulated course of
discipline as may best conduce to the preservation of your corporeal and
mental' faculties in their fullest energy; thereby enabling you to exert
the talents wherewith God has blest you.''
Masonry stresses the responsibility of the individual: the candidate knocks
on the door himself, he is individually received, he prays for himself, he travels
the road alone; he is individually obligated.
The emphasis in Masonry upon the individual is especially pronounced in
the regulations regarding balloting. One black ball-the judgment of one
individual-may prevent a candidate from becoming a Mason. The use of the
ballot box is a sacred trust in which each individual must search his own
conscience that he err not. On his sole responsibility, a man good and true,
may be deprived of that which Masonry coulq give to him and likewise that
which he might bring to Masonry. Still, the individual Mason stands on his
own grounds and follows the dictates of his own conscience.
This stress upon individual responsibility carries with it the meaning that
it is not sufficient for a Mason to be a good fellow, pleasant and acceptable
though that may be. It is rather that he be able and ready to stand up and be
counted where it counts. It is, for example, that when he finds himself iln a
group that is running down some one person or category of persons, in whatever regard it be, that he express his own true judgment and if need be risk
whatever popularity he might lose, so long as he makes a stand for the sake
of truth and justice. We in Masonry know that it is often necessary to face
ruffians and to be prepared to say "I will not." If we have not learned this
lesson, then we have indeed learned little in Masonry.
Unlike the times of King Solomon, peace and tranquility do not pervade the
world of 1946. A sort of peace-but no tranquility. I am speaking of something
real, immediate, here and now. There is crying need for the influence of one
who acts as a Mason. The world needs desperately men of virtue and courage:
Each one has a station in life to fulfill. Each one has a purpose to accomplish on earth. Though sacrifice be part of the plan, though fortitude be demanded, let each one recognize his individual obligation and with vigor exert
that influence for good which is expected of a Mason.
Can a Mason be indifferent? All the darkness in the world cannot put out
the light of a single. candle.
I have tried to bring to you a realization of the most vital phase of all of
Masonry-namely, how should Masons act? These five guides to Masonic conduct are only a beginning; much more remains to be said. But within the
limitation of time allotted to this· address it may possibly indicate the' avenue
of approach that must be followed.
It is possible to live without being a· Mason. It may not be as complete a
life, though. Likewise, it is possible for one to become a Mason without it
greatly influencing his life. But if one take to heart the lessons of Masonry,

98

When in doubt, ask: Would I, a Ma~on, object to having my contemplated
act known? Ask: Am I creating by my conduct a favorable opinion of Freemasonry-so that the candidate may honestly answer "yes," when the question
is put to him: "Do you seriously declare, . upon your honor, that you are
prompted to solicit the privileges of Masonry by a favorable opinion conceived of the Institution?"
4. Am I seeking to be arr exception, or would it be proper for everyone to
act as I would choose to do in a certain set of circumstances. This is the wellknowii Categorical Imperative as enunciated by the philosopher Immanuel Kant.
It does not take much persuading to convince you of the error in the judgment of the driver Gf an automobile who, rolling up to the crest of the hill on a
two-lane highway' divided by a double line, regards himself as superior to the
requirement to stay on his own side of the highway; that this is a requirement
for others but not for himself. We recognize the inevitability of an accident
sooner or ·later if this mistaken notion be followed long enough.
Equally foolish though not as recognizable is the folly of one who believes
that there is a double ~tandard of values in life: "What is right for me; what
is right for the other fellow."
r I wonder whether vou heard of the man who came to, his physician, complaining of constant headaches. The doctor asked whether he smoked too
much. ''No.'' Did he keep late hours, and sleep insufficiently? "No.'' Was
he stepping. out on too many dates? "No.'' Whereupon the doctor gave his
diagnosis.: "If that's· the case, the only thing I can say is: your headache must
be caused by your halo fitting too tightly· on your head." Who is so selfrighteous as to claim that he goes through life with a halo on his head!
Standards we demand for others we must demand of ourselves. Long ago , this
was called "The Golden Rule.''
, . In a; aemucracy this same guide of conduct gives rise to the guardianship.
of minori.~x. rights. Each individual is in a true sense a minority. If I desire
-freei spe~.c,h. ;for myself· I must desire it for everyone. If I desire freedom of
,r~l~giqp. for myself I must desire it for everyone.

and interpret them in terms of action-interpret not only the symbols but the
word-symbols as well-this can lead to a release of energy not unlike the
mighty power of atomic energy. What a force for good might emanate from
the two and one-half million Masons in the United States of America!
You who are here, try it out in the Lodge, set up a chain reaction, like that
which sets off atomic power, from one Mason to the other. Devote some meeting, not to routine business or conferring degrees or social planning-all necessary and worthY-but, for a change, try to inaugurate discussion of how
specifically we may apply to our daily deeds and the problems of our generation
some of our principal tenets and cardinal virtues.
Let me put the question that we put to the candidate, "Are you willing to
proceed?"
Bring to your members the slogan I once heard, which caught plY fancy:
"So live that when you die-some preacher won't. have to lie."
Closing this oration, I ask that Masons take to heart the words of the
closing prayer: "May each one of us practice out of the Lodge those great
moral duties inculcated in it." May they so conduct themselves that they will
be easily distinguished as Masons, not by an emblem worn, nor by a grip, or
secret word, but by what they are and do. . Beholding the unmistakable
standards of Masonic conduct it will be said, "That man must be a Mason."

One Lodge words the amendment as follows: "and for affiliation the
sum of no dollars, except that the affiliation fee shall be the sum of $25.00,
if the <limit accompanying the application is issued by a Lodge in another
jurisdiction other than California." Another Lodge uses this language:
"and for affiliation the sum of $25.00, except that the affiliation fee shall be
no dollars if the <limit accompanying the application is issued by a Lodge
of this jurisdiction." Quoting from the amendment of still another Lodge
it reads as follows: "and for affiliation the sum of $25.00, except that the
affiliation fee shall be $50.00 if the <limit accompanying the application is
issued by a Lodge of any jurisdiction other than .that of California."
· To make the matter entirely clear one Lodge inserted a paragraph using
these words: "and for affiliation the sum of $1.00. This amendment • • •
does not change the affiliating fee, and does not include the $25.00 Homes
tax."
If the purpose of the Lodge in the wording of the amendment. is clear
or it is clearly defined in the minutes of the Lodge or in the resolution
amending the By-Laws that the affiliation fee does or does not include the
Masonic Hemes contribution of $25.00, probably no difficulty would arise.
If it is not clear, a question might later develop.
In this report, as I stated, we are approving all of these amendments to
By-Laws as being in proper form, certified and in accordance with Masonic
law. They have received the approval of the Grand Master.
We recommend the adoption of this report approving the amendments
set forth herein.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTION
MONTH OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance is pleased to submit herewith the report of its activities for the year.
We are pleased to advise you that much interest has been created
throughout the entire jurisdiction in the matter of this observance and information received from every portion of the jurisdiction indicates that the
observance of the natal day of our Constitution throughout the month of
September was the most successful in the history of such observances.
Activities incident to the observance were outstanding and ambitious programs of merit and unusual interest were presented by the variotts subordinate Lodges.
Your committee has been particularly gratified that in so many instances
the observance on the part of the subordinate Lodges was open to the
general public. Statistics gathered from other quarters indicate the most
universal recognition of the Constitution this year of any previous time.
This is a wholesome and compelling sigh, and our fraternity may well take

108

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

unto itself a considerable portion of .the credit for such a state of affairs.
In these troublesome times which try the very souls of men it is reassuring to all of us who believe in the American· way..of life and are so firmly
committed to the American philosophy of government that our efforts have
impressed upon the body politic generally·: the greatness of this immortal
charter. We are thus not only playing an important part in fulfilling our
obligation to the fraternity but at the same time we are assisting in the
creation of a finer citizenship.
The committee recommends that a suitable appropriation be set aside
for the activities of the committee, including the printing of a brochure
setting forth with particularity the Constitution of the United States, the
Declaration of Independence, and other patriotic documents. There has
been a general demand throughout the jurisdiction for some such information.
We also wish to express our apprecfation to the many members of the
fraternity who gave unstintingly of their time in addressing numerous subordinate Lodges throughout the jurisdiction. In view of the fact that we
have ·had many distractions this year which have had a tendency to divert
our attention from other important tasks, the unusuaJ interest and success
attending the current observance of the Constitution month has been most
heartening, and the members throughout the jurisdiction are to be commended for their every effort expended towards acquainting our fellow-men
with the many blessings conferred upon us through the medium of this
immortal do~ument.
In conclusion we wish to express to the Most Worshipful Grand
Master our deep appreciation of his many communications addressed to
us throughout the year and his great interest in the success of the observance. We also likewise extend our deep appreciation for the interest
and cooperation of our Grand Secretary whose prompt and ready response
to our every demand played an important part in the success which has
attended our efforts during the year just terminated.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM

REPO'.R.T OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC
CLUB HOUSE, U. C., AT BERKELEY
To ·the Most W orshipful Gmnd Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club House of the University
of California presents this report covering the past Masonic year.
Financial Condition
Extensive repairs and replacements, together with increased cost in
operation of every department, amounted to a total expenditure of $10,175.90, being $2,675.90 in excess of the ordinary appropriation of $7,50B
made by the Grand Lodge last year for maintenance. Out of the extraordinary appropriations of $6,000 made by the Grand Lodge for replacements of furnishings, $2,041.49 has been turned over to the Club by the
Grand Officers and requisition is being made by the president and secretary
of the Club upon the Grand Officers on this fund for an additional $821.92.
The new budget adopted by the Board of Trustees at its meeting of
October 1, 1946, calls for the expenditure of $8,741.40 in ordinary operation
and an additional fund of $4,166.43 for reserves to meet accrued and
accruing depreciation of the building and its furnishings. For this 'purpose
the life of the building has been set up as 100 years, and since this is the
beginning of this form of depreciation and the building is 23 years old, the
total building cost is allotted on a 77-year basis. The present furnishings
are eight years old and it is deemed that they should be entirely replaced
in seven years more, which is the basis of th~ depreciation of these items
for furnishings; These matters have been submitted to the Finance Committee and if approved by them the result will be that the trustees should
be able to carry on, not only next year but in the years to come, feeling
secure in their ability to maintain the building and premises in suitable
fashion for the purposes for which the same were constructed and acquired
and have now so long been maintained, as against all forseeable hazards.
I asked Mrs. "Morton, our hostess, and Mr. Luis G. Ireland, student
president during the last semester, to each report on the matters which had
come within their supervision. Their reports follow:
Report of Resident Hostess
It is gratifying to be able to report that we have completed a very successful year, a year in which we saw our expectations realized. With the
university enrollment exceeding pre-war levels, we are looking forward to
an even more varied program of activities than in the past. The return of
so many members, away during .the war, expresses better than words
could do what this Club means to tl:10se students who are privileged to
use it.
However, with an increase in membership will come problems as well .
as benefits., The kitchen and banquet facilities are inadequate for the large
numbers of people for whom it will be necessary to provide. The problem
of a lounge for the men is still unsolved and will be accentuated as more
men return.
In the president's repoi:t is an account of the year's activities. The
events 1'1p1e been well supported and daily attendance has been more than
gratifying. Your support of this "home on campus" for Masonically·
affiliated students ·is truly a thing of which you may be justly pro.ud.

110

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Student President
By the end of the school year 1945-1946 the membership of our Club
reached 378, a tremendous increase over the wartime figures, but far below
the probable total for the semester now commencing. More important;
though, is the fact that a larger percentage of the members than formerly
found the Club the chief factor in their extra-curricular life.
The environment and opportunities offered by the Club-friendships,
self-government, recreational and study facilities, restful and inspiring surroundings-are deeply appreciated by all who come in contact with the
organization. The respect for Masonry and the gratitude to it engendered
by its maintenance of the University Masonic Club are very great.

*

*

*

*

*

A new and unprecedently busy semester has cpmmenced at Berkeley.
Activity at the Club House is vastly increased over what we had come to
think of during the war years as normal. New problems-some of them
vexatious-are continuously presented. We believe that the · resident
hostess, with such assistance as the trustees can give her, will lead the
young men and women who attend upon this building, to wise and conservative solutions thereof. It is recognized that youth is not the time of
life, nor the winding up of a war with its attendant world revolutions, the
atmosphere of conservatism. But Masonry and the Masonic influence must
lend aid to the protection of the noble .edifice of our civilization from the
ravages of the maelstrom. This we think the Masonic Club at the university within the range of its influence will in considerable pad serve to
accomplish.
Resp~ctfully submitted,
, MILTON T. FARMER, President,
Masonic Club, University of California.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC
CLUB HOUSE AT U. C. L. A.
The Board of Directors of the Masonic Club House adjacent to the
Los Angeles campus of the University of California herewith presents its
annual report.
You will recall from our annual reports to the last three communications of this Grand Lodge that the Masonic Club House at Los Angeles
was closed to the normal activities therein on .May 1, 1943, and was thereafter used by the university as a mess hall for the army trainees stationed
on the campus for one year and then by the American Red Cross for its
activities during the past two years. It had been our intention to reopen
to the students for the semester which coip.menced in February, 1946, but
actual possession was not secured until July, 1946, and the club house was
made available with the commencement of classes on September 23, three
weeks ago.
We have reemnloyed as director of_ activities Mrs. Faith C. Sheldon,
who was serving as hostess at the time of closing in 1943. When we closed
the building Mrs. Sheldon went into the U. S. 0. and for three years
served with that organization in Honolulu. The valuable experience she

' GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

111

acquired during that period should be a distinct asset and your board is
pleased that it was able to secure her services again.
We regret to report that her only son, who was in the Army Air Corps,
was killed in action in the Pacific during the war.
The admissions office at U. C. L. A. has announced that there are now
14,000 undergraduates enrolled for the present semester,. nearly double
the pre-war figure. We estimate that there should be approximately 1,000
of these who have the necessary Masonic affiliation to make them eligible
to use the club house. These large pot.e ntials, coupled with our earnest
desire to enlarge the program and increase the use of the club house, have
led us to employ an assistant direCtor of activities for the first time.
As assistant to Mrs. Sheldon we have secured Miss Shirley M. Ander~
son. She attended U. C. L. A. for four years and ,;.as graduated in 1941.
Miss Anderson majored in physical education and went on to Teachers'
College, Columbia University, where she received her master's degree. She
then served on the faculties at Hollins College in Virginia and Scripps
College, Claremont, California, and also gained valuable experience with
the municipal recreation departments of Roanoke, Virginia, and Los Angeles. It has been necessary for her to return to her mother's home just
two blocks from our club house and we deem it fortunate that we have
thus been able to secure her services.
We desire to report one modification of policy since the reopening of
the club house. It had been our .policy that the use of the building, particularly the lounges and study halls, was open to Masonically affiliated
students regardless whether they joined the student group and paid the
nominal dues for admission to the weekly dances, suppers and other social
affairs. This year the students themselves requested a modification to
limit the use of the facilities to those who joined in the full program. We
have consented subject to the condition that any instance in which the
modest dues seem to work a hardship shall be reported to us for action.
Incidentally, this modification will make our policy conform to that which,
we understand, has always prevailed at the club house at Berkeley.
During the summer months we authorized the expenditure of $9,330.06
for repairs, repainting and renovating of the interior of the structure. This
is the first major work done on the building since its construction in 1929.
No additional appropriation from the Grand Lodge will be necessary for
this expense. It has been paid.
We respectfully request an appropriation for operating and maintain1ng the club house for the ensuing year in the amount of $10,750.00 and
present the proposed budget as follows:

In conclusion, may we call your attention to a regrettable situation and
make a suggestion? It is a fact to be regretted that apparently a very large
number of our brethren do not know of the existence of the Berkeley and
Los. Angeles club houses. Our suggestion is that the Masters of our
Lodges at least annually, -0ftener if they will, call attention to the club
houses in their bulletins and by other appropriate means. No donations are
ever requested from the members of Lodges, but we do want the brethren
to know that they are in existence, especially those who might have relatives
about to enter the university. It is, at best, a difficult task to locate in the
ranks of such large student bodies those who come from Masonic families.
The task would be lighter if it was understood that students do · not have
to wait for a bid or invitation to avail themselves of the finest~structure
on either campus.
On October 6 Hollywood Lodge paid a Sunday afternoon visit to our
club house. The brethren toured the building, the students served light
refreshments and members of the board explained the purposes and organization of the institution. Liberal Arts Lodge has scheduled such a visit
during November and other Lodges will be most welcome.
It may not be amiss to call your attention to the pictures displayed in
the Black R.oom on this floor. You will derive greater pride in your Grand
Lodge from scanning them and perchance you will be inspired to give both
club houses the attention they merit.
Respectfully submitted,
ELLSWORTH MEYER, Vice-Chairman,
Board of Directors.

REPORT - OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RITUAL
Funeral Service
Your committee has carefully analyzed the proposed amendments to
the Funeral Service of Subordinate Lodges as presented by the Ritual
Committee. We find that these proposed amendments have been most
thoroughly discussed and considered by the Ritual Committee; that they
have also been reviewed and considered in conjunction with officers of the
California Funeral Directors' Association who are Masons, and find them
to be in full accord. This, your sp-e.cial committee, has given very careful
thought to the proposals and heartily recommends them with two slight
~odifications, namely:

a. On page 5, Section 5, and page 6, Section 5, of the report that
the words "Urn and earth are not to be used" be changed to read
"Urn and earth may be used if preferred."
We movt:: the adoption of this recommended change in the report.
b. On page 8 of the Funeral Service Ritual, paragraph 2, on line
6, starting with "thereby demonstrating the sincerity of our past
esteem for him and our steady attachment to the principles of our
beloved institution" be omitted.
We make this recommendation because we believe that it is poor "taste
to announce before ·the bereaved family and friends that we are making a
public demonstration of "our sincerity." Is it necessary to publicly announce our sincerity? Your committee thinks not.
We, therefore, move the adoption of this modification of the report.
Installation Service
Your committee heartily approved the adoption of the changes in the
installation service as proposed by the Ritual Committee and as presented
by the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer.
We, therefore, move the adoption of the proposed revision both as to
form and language.
Your special committee moves the adoption of the Ritual Committee's
proposed amendments to the Funeral Service Ritual as amended both as
to form and language.

J. CLARK BENSON,
HARVEY M. STULL,
HERBERT R. HARGRAVE,

Committee.

Each portion of the report was acted upon separately artd
ad9pted, and the entire report was adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS
San Francisco, California, September 28, 1946.
To the Most Worshipful Grand L odge of California:
Yo~r committee is charged with the responsibility of auditing and
approvmg for payme.nt, all bills, claims and demands presented to it b the
Grandd SLecdretary, which are found to be in order and proper charges ag~inst
Gran
o ge funds.

that the committee is now able to report that the negotiations with the
California Unemployment Commission and the representatives of the Federal Insurance Contributions Act and Federal Unemployment Tax Act have
resulted in an unofficial settlement of our entire tax problem. The public
representatives have been very cooperative and as a result of audits now completed, it is agreed that the tax will not amount to more than $275.00, with
possible penalties and interest of not more .than $75.00.
On our part we have waived a r efund for the years 1944 and 1945, and
by reason thereof, are granted and retain a merit rating credit of 1.7 per
cent of the e111ployer's tax obligation. This in itself will result in the next
, few years in a saving to Grand Lodge of a great deal more than the refund
which we might have claimed for the years in question.
It is expected that official approval will be given to the settlement witnin
ninety days. This happy settlement of a vexatious problem has been made
possible by the cooperative work of the Past Grand Masters, the Grand
Secretary's office, the members of the committee and the representatives of
the government.
Under date of July 30, 1946, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue
issued a ruling that the secretary of a Blue Lodge, in collecting dues, is
exempt from the term "employment" under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act and Federal Unemployment Tax Acts. Inquiry at the Commissioner's office in Washington indicates that such holding is a technical
one and applies only to that portion of the secretary's duties. It is the
opinion of the committee that as the collection of dues is much less than
50 per cent of the duties of a Blue Lodge secretary, that he would be held
to be entirely under the act. The committee therefore recommends t hat
Blue Lodges continue to pay the tax on the secretaries. In due course we
will attempt to get a clarifying ruling from the Commissioner of Internal
R evenue· and if the status of a secretary is in anywise changed, the Blue
Lodges will be notified by special bulletin.
In view of these unsettled problems, it is recommended that a tax
committee be continued.
Respectfully submitted,
WALTER PERRY J OH N SON,
J.E. H AMMOND,
R. P. WISECARVER,

to us.

programs were'in some cases delayed, hqwever, by rules and r egulations

Larchmont Lodge No. 614-Los Angeles:
An opportunity was presented to this Lodge to purchase the building
in which they had been meeting since the issuance of their charter in

Improvements consisted of a three story brick building containing approximately 13,000 square feet, with two rented business shops on the

of indebtedness provided for the retirement of the entire debt in 129 and
two-third mont~s or practically eleven years.

'
During the past year several Quiz programs were prepared and distributed to the Worshipful Masters throughout the Grand Jurisdiction.

expressing appreciation and telling of the use in the Lodges. Despite the
crowded condition of the Lodge calendars by reason of the great number
of petitioners time has been found for these programs designed to enlighten the Craft on Masonic subjects. In fact, many of the Masters asserted that the influx of multitudes of candidates made some sort of
Masonic education imperative. Simply to confer the ritualistic Degrees
upo~ the candidates and leave them uninformed as to the meaning and
significance of Masonic allegory and symbolism with which Masonic teaching and principles are clothed is to render only part of the servke the
Lodge is under obligation to give them. A well-informed and well-instructed Mason is more likely to become a loyal, enthusiastic, earnest
member of the Fraternity than one who is ignorant of the deeper meanings
of Masonic tradition, history and philosophy. Many of the Masters have
been using the refreshment table and intervals in the Lodge routine to
interject the Quiz programs in whole or in part wil:h gratifying results.
. A much app.reciated cont~ibution of the committee was the publication of a bulletm on Masomc books, with brief information as to their
contents, price and where they might be obtained. This information is of
help to a Lodge projecting the formation of a Lodge library for circulation

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Ypur committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report, together with its recommendations.
During the past year, your committee has answered numerous communications from Lodges and members of the fraternity in the different
states; requesting information as to membership of individuals in the early
days. Some of these communications have come from history committee~
endeavoring to trace the personal and Masonic activities of their membership while living in California. We have been pleased to render assistance
to these committees although, in some instances, our research has involved long and tiresome investigation.
Your committee has obtained additional information with respect to
the history of such colorful characters as John Bidwell, Lansford Warren
Hastings, John W. Geary and E. 0. Crosby. Crosby was a member of
the <;:onstitution Convention of 1849 and, as a delegate, he rendered
yeoman service in the formation and adoption of the several sections of
that ·constitution. During the hearings of the Commission to settle private
land claims ,in California, he handled, as attorney for the claimants, a
large number of claims and was instrumental in protecting the rights of

128

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the native Californians during the seven years these highly controversial
cases were heard by the Commission, and also during the appeals to the
Federal Courts. He was appointed by President Lincoln as United States
Minister to Guatemala, where he so ably represented his Government during the troublesome Civil War period.

At the last session of the State Legislature, the old mu~mg tow.n of
Columbia, in Tuolumne County, was chosen as the i:nosttyp1cal ;tnd best
preserved of the early California gold cam~s, and 1t was proposed that
the business sectio·n be purchased and constituted. a. State park under the
jurisdiction and control of the State Parks Co~m1ss~on.
. ..
The sum of $50,000 was appropriated and set aside for the acqu1s1hon
and restoration of that portion of Columbia to be chosen as a Stat~ park.
It was further provided that an additional sum of $50,000 b_e ra1.sed. to•
match the $50,000 of State appropriation. In furtherance of. t~1s ~b1echve,
there was formed "The Columbia Historical Park Association, 1 a corporation for the purpose of raising the matching $50,000 to me~t the .requirements set forth in the act. The Association has. completed th1_s portion
of its work. The Park Commission is· now preparing ~aps settmg forth
the several pieces of property to be purchased and set aside as a par~.
Within the proposed park is a lot on which was locate? t~e Mason~c
Temple of Columbia Lodge No. 28. This temple was bm_It m the 50 s
and was occupied by the Lodge until its consolidation with Tuolumne
Lodge No. 8 at Sonora in the early 90's, at which time the temple was
sold. The purchasers tore it down and mined the ground under~eath.
As a member of the History Committee, your chairman is vitally interested in rebuilding and maintaining the Columbia Tem~le. I a~ assured by th<! Park Commission that they will lease the ..lot .m questlo'? to
this Grand Lodge, or tQ a committee, trustees or org'amzatlon au~honzed
by Grand Lodge to erect and maintain a tei;nple of the same kmd and
-character as the old temple.
The State Parks Commission intends to repair old structures and restore them as nearly as possible to the same str~ctural appeara~ce as
they were in the SO's. They will also urge the erection and restoration of
buildings as they were in the early days.
Columbia will be the Williamsburg of the west. When fully repaired
and rebuilt it will be a Mother Lode show place-a revived mining town
of the 50's of which the entire state may well be proud. The old temple
should be rebuilt a·nd a Lodge room maintaine? so that _Lodg_e~ ~ay, u'?der proper authority, meet therein and en~age. m Masom~ activities. This
will stimulate interest not only. in Masomc history but m Masonry generally. The lower sto;y could be used as a Masonic mu.seum which would
forther stimulate interest in the members of the fraternity and others.
Your committee has obtained much information as to the size and
appearance of the old temple and we hope very soon to have a well
authenticated photograph of the old building. We understand th.at the
original bricks which were taken from the building are still in existence
and may eventually be obtained.

We have also found several well authenticated instances, during the
gold rush period, where our sign of distress was answered and respected
by Indians on the plains and in the mountains, en route to California.
We are pleased to report that, during the past year, your committee
has received much additional data on the activities of Homer Lea, who
played a leading part in the Chinese revolution which resulted in the
overthrow of the Manchu dynasty and the establishment of the Chinese
Republic. You will remember that Lea was a member of Pentalpha Lodge
No. 202. In 1905, Past Grand Master James Block Gist conferred upon
him the Third Degree of Masonry.
Many of our constitutent Lodges have upon their roster the names
of brothers who have distinguished themselves either in the armed forces
or on the home front, during World War II. The interesting stories of
these members of the craft should be fully written up by competent members of the Lodges and filed with the History Committee, so that posterity
may know, the war-time achievements of these members of Masonry. We,
therefore, respectfully urge the .several Lodges to have this information
properly prepared and forwarded to our committee at the earliest possible
moment.
For several years your committee has endeavored to obtain information
a$ to any Mason who was present at Sutter's mill at Coloma when gold
was discovered. In a recent issue of a Masonic publication entitled "The
Oregon Mason," there appeared an article by Brother Donegan R. Wiggins, a member of Salem Lodge No. 4, to the effect that Charles Bennett,
a member of Salem Lodge, was present at Coloma . on January 24, 1848,
when gold was discovered. Several years prior to 1848, Bennett was in
charge of the pack train for General Fremont on one of his exploration
trips to California.
Bennett claimed that, while watering the mules on a fork of the
American River, he picked up a small nugget of what he recognized as
gold. This fact was verified by Fremont. No further search for additional
nuggets was made. In 1847 Bennett returned to California and was hired
by Sutter to work with Marshall on the Mill at Coloma, and was presept
at the mill when the water was shut off on January 24th, 1848, and, as
he and Marshall walked along the race below the mill, Bennett noticed
a small particle of gold in the millrace, picked it up and handed it to
Marshall with the statement, "This is gold." This he claimed was the
accurate story of the much-publicized discovery of gold by Marshall.
Bancroft, in his history of California, verifies the fact that Charles
Bennett was present on this occasion and that Sutter sent him to Monterey
to seek from the Mexican Government an official confirmation of the
three-year lease to the land surrounding Coloma, purchased by Sutter
from .the Indians, claiming rights to the said lands. However, the Mexican
Government refused to confirm Sutter's lease.
During the rest of his life, Bennett publicly and otherwise claimed
that his story of the real discovery of gold was the truth. He was buried
in a cemetery at Salem, Oregon, and the monument erected at his grave
carries the legend to the effect that Bennett was the original discoverer
of gold at Coloma.

In 1934 the chairman of your History Committee strenuously en·deavored t~ bring about the final preparation and publication of the

·we were authorized by action of this Grand Lodge to enter mto a contract

·
·
In 1950 the Grand Lodge will celebrate its lOOth Anniversat.y;• Jn our

our history. Since 1928 this committee has been engaged in collecting
probably the greatest mass of historical data ever acquired by any Grand
Lodge in the United States, if not the world. We are anxious to see the
final culmination of these efforts in the publication of this valuable data.
For the past several months many members of Grand Lodge have
urged upon this committee the advisability of recommending to Grand
Lodge the a:ppointment of a committee to devise ways and means of
•preparing and publishing our history. To this end we urge Grand Lodge
to authorize the incoming Grand Master to appoint a committee, empowered to fully investigate the most feasible and economical method of
the final preparation and publication of said history and to report their
findings at the next session of Grand Lodge.
We respectfully urge and submit the following recommendations:

2. That the sum of $200 be appropriated and set aside for the use of
said committee.
3. That the in~oming Grand Master appoint a committee to -investigate

Temple at Columbia, and the most economic ~ethod of maintaining same.
4. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to fully
investigate the most feasible and economic method for the final preparation
and publication of the History of Masonry in California, and to report
their findings and recommendations at the next session of Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
Chairman Frank Belcher presented the general report of the
committee and also the omnibus report as follows:
To the Most Woi·shipful Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Grievances there has been referred a total of
53 trial records. This unusual number is due to the fact that unde.r the
exigencies of last year, none of such matters were disposed of and hence
we have an accumulation of two years.
Your committee has found a large majority of these records and the
proceedings referring thereto to be quite regular and consequently will
recommend by this report the approval of those hereafter enumerated.
Many of these matters have been disposed of under the Automatic
Expulsion Provisions of Section 332 of our Constitution and Ordinances,
which may be availed of where the accused has been convicted of a crime
classified as a felony, imprisoned as a result thereof, and after notice fails
to demand a Masonic trial.
We urge the use of the prescribed forms where this procedure is employed; again emphasizing the necessity of mailing the required notice
to the proper address of the accused, which is the prison when he is still
confined. We also point out the absolute necessity of furnishing Grand
Lodge with a copy of all forms used, together with a certificate of service.

covered ~nder section 332 appear, for the most part, such crimes as grand
theft.' bribery, sex offenses, false government claims, manslaughter, bartendmg, and operation of gambling games.

~nte;ed Apprei:itic~s or Fellowcrafts. Two of these involye misrepresentation m the application for degrees. In one instance it developed that an applicant who had been elected to receive the degrees had suffered two prior

Trial Record No. 258
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Report of Grievance Committee-Case No. 2S8, F. L. E., Claiborne Lodge
No. 18S.
.Your committee, to which was referred the petition for restoration of ·
F. L. E., expelled by Claiborne Lodge No. 18S, in July, 1919, has taken the
same under advisement and reports as follows :
The petitioner had been convicted of embezzling public funds in the sum
of $1,282, and had been granted probation by the Superior Court, on certain
conditions, one of which was that he repay his bonding company the amount
taken.
From the record it appears that he removed to another state, and strictly
complied with all the terms of his probation with the result that after thirteen
years had elapsed he had made complete restitution to the bonding company.
He was then permitted, under the humane provisions of the probation laws
of this state, to change the plea which he had formerly entered of "guilty" to
that of "not guilty." The public files were then expunged of all reference to
his transgression.
Attached to his petition are supporting letters from the probation officer
expressing complete approbation for the manner in which the terms of the
probation ·had been complied with.
It therefore can be concluded from the record furnished that petitioner has
accomplished a complete rehabilitation in the eyes of the civil law, and one
which could well afford the favorable consideration of this Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge. Although your committee favors, as a general rule, a more
comprehensive and detailed petition in matters of restoration, than the one here
presented, it nevertheless is of the opinion that such a record of atonement
persevered in for such a long period of time deserves commendation and
reward.
Resolved that the petition of F. L . E. to be. restored to all the rights and
privileges· of Masonry be granted.

Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to which was referred the petition for the restoration of
the accused in Trial Record No. 396, respectfully reports as follows:
M. L.•A. was expelled from Highland Park Lodge No. 382 on May 5,
1924. He was brought to trial on a charge of un-Masonic conduct preferred
·by a member of that Lodge. The specific charge upon which he was convicted
and for which he was expelled was that he had wilfully and maliciously contrived to win the affections of the accusor's wife by taking her to dinner and
theater parties and on auto rides, by writing endearing letters to her and by
giving her presents of money and articles of value.
No appeal was taken by the accused and the trial record was approved by
the Grievance Committee of Grand Lodge in its Omnibus Report. Mention of
this is made for the reason that your committee doubts that the judgment of
expulsion would have been sustained had an appeal been taken. The trial
record does not contain the contents of the alleged endearing letters, nor does it
contain clear and convincing evidence of any wilful or malicious attempts to
alienate the affections of the accusor's wife. There was no charge nor any
evidence of any illicit relations between the accused and the accusor's wife.
While the committee does not approve or condone the accused's actions, it
makes these comments in order that its recommendations herein may be fully
evaluated.
The petition for restoration is supported by letters from numerous Masons,
including a Past Grand Master, a Past Master of Highland Park Lodge, who
was the stenographer at the trial of petitioner, a Master of a neighboring
• Lodge, and petitioner's business associates, all of whom vouch for his reputation, character, and integrity. Due and proper notice of his petition for restoration was served upon Highland Park Lodge and no action in opposition thereto
was taken by it.
Your committee is convinced that full atonement has been made by the
petitioner, that he is fully rehabilitated, and it recommends the petition be
granted. It, therefore, offers the following resolution and respectfully recommends its adoption.
Resolved that the petition of M. L. A. for restoration to the rights and
privileges of Masonry be and the same is hereby granted.

Adopted.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is to be noted in passing that the failure of this trial commission in 1943
to vote upon specifications 2 and 3 charging respectively that the accused (1)
had been convicted of bookmaking, and (2) that he had been committed to the
county jail for a term of six months, was entirely proper. These two specifications were not statements of Masonic offenses. The Masonic offense is the
conduct which results in the conviction of the accused ; and this conduct is that
described in the first specification. Therefore, when the trial commission voted
on the first specification they had voted upon the only Masonic offense described.
Of course, if the proceeding had been for autoqiatic expulsion under Secti?n
322 Constitution and Ordinances, the record of the conviction and comnutme~t of the accused for a felony would 6e sufficient to support automatic
expulsion if the accused f~iled to demand ti:ial, but in this case a. trial was
demanded.
This Grand Lodge at its communication in 1944, by reason of the failure
of the trial commission of 1943 to ballot upon the question of un-Masonic
conduct, set the conviction aside and remanded the case for retrial.
The .record now comes before Grand Lodge following the retrial of the
accused on April 19, 1945, upon exactly the same specifications as had 'been
filed against him in 1943.
At the time of retrial the accused was present and pleaded not guilty.
Evidence was presented on behalf of the accused showing t!:iat he had not
been adjudged to be a felon, and that his imprisonment of 105 days had fixed
the character of his offense as a misdemeanor.
No witnesses were produced against the accused; but, in response t? questions propounded to him by counsel for the accuser, the accused testified as
follows:
That he had first leased the storeroom in question in November, 1941,
intending to operate in it a cigar and magazine store, and marble machines,
then legal; that he had previously operated a similar store in another. location;
that he ceased to operate the place in person in March of 1942; because of
injuries sustained in an automobile accident, resulting in his being confined for
a long period of time in a hospital and at home; that during his a!>$ence the
place was operated by his partner, C. J. S.; that the lease was in the name of
the accused: that the net income from the store .was about $60 to $70 per
month· that he wanted to discontinue the· business, but his. partner felt it
would 'pick up in income ; that he, the accused, was not familiar with the
bookmaking business ; that he occasionally would bet on horse races for fun;
that he had visited Santa Anita track twice, Hollywood Park; once, and
Tiajuana once or twice; that he had no knowledge of his partner making or
collecting bets, before his arrest; that he . only visited the store qn Saturday
nights; that his partner never gave him an accou?t~ng; that h~ went to t~e
store on Saturday nights for the purpose of rece1vmg from ~1s partner his
share of the profits; that his partner pleaded guilty in court, was placed on
probation and paid a fine; that his partne_r testified in court th~t he, the
accused 1 had known nothing of the bookmakmg at the store; that his partner,
since th e trial operates a cafe elsewhere; that his partner had no prior crimi~al
record; that since being released from jail, he, the accused, worked for a wh1~e
in the Silver Dollar Cafe, and now manages a cafe at 138 Locust ~tre:t m
Long Beach; that he has nothing to do with the handling of alcoholic liquor
at such cafe.
No further testimony was received. We submit that there is nothing in
the evidence to prove the allegation o'f specification number one.

Trial Record No. 1035
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which has been referred Trial Record
No. 1035,' begs I.eave to report as follows:
This is the second time that this record has been before the committee.
H. L. R., a member of Stanislaus Lodge No. 206, was convicted of a felony
in the state courts, sentenced and committed to prison. Proceedings for his
automatic expulsion were had and he was declared expelled but, because of the
insufficient notice to the accused, Grand Lodge reversed the action and remanded the proceedings to the Lodge.
By this time accused had been released from prison on parole. Charges
were filed against him alleging the conviction of a felony, commissioners were
elected 11nd the charge was tried by them. Accused was found guilty and
ordered expelled.
The summons and certified copy of the charges were sent to the accused
at his home address within the jurisdiction of the Lodge by registered mail instead of being served personally by the Tiler or being left at his ordinary
residence or place of business as required by Section 308, Constitution and
Ordinances. While the efficacy of registered mail as a means of service is
recognized by your committee and by Grand Lodge, as shown by provisions
for its use in cases of non-resident accused persons and in the case of automatic expulsion under Section 332, Constitution and Ordinances, Section 308
does not provide for such service by registered mail where accused lives within
the jurisdiction of the Lodge but definitely states that the summons and certified copy of the charges "shall be served personally by the Tiler or some other
member of the Lodge authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall be
left at his ordinary residence or place of business.'' Until Grand Lodge sees
fit to amend this provision to provide for possible service by mail we feel that
the manner of service prescribed s,hould be followed.
We also recommend that the proceeding for automatic expulsion be followed
(Section 332, Constitution and Ordinances) . Although the accused had been
released from state prlson on parole his conviction of a felony still stood and
will stand even though his parole term has expired, and Section 332 is available for use in this case.
It has never been held that the proceeding for automatic expulsion is mandatory but it is an expeditious procedure and is advantageous to both the
Lodge and to the accused. The latter may always demand a trial if he wants it.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the action of Stanislaus Lodge No. 206 in expelling
H. L. R. from all the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same is
hereby reversed and set aside, and the matter remanded to said Lodge for
further action in compliance with the provisions of Section 332, Constitution
and Ordinances.

Adopted.

To the Mast Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Report of Grievance Committee-Case No, 1047, H. S., Bay View
Lodge No. 401.
The accused was convicted in the United States. District Court Ort July 28,
1944, of having made a false claim upon the United States Treasury, and was
sentenced to imprisonment for three years in a Federal penitentiary. Thereafter proceedings were taken in his Lodge 'to expel him under the provisions
of Section 332 of our Constitution artd Ordinances. on· August 21, 1944, the
required summons was sent by registered mail prepaid to the accused at his
address in Oakland. No appearance having been made by him, nor request
for a trial within the sixty day period after the mailing of the said summons,
he was on November 4, 1944, declared to stand automatically expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.
One of the fundamental requirements of due process in any judicial proceeding is that of notice. Where the method of giving notice is prescribed by
law, there must be affirmative proof that it has been complied with, or else
all subseq.uent proceedings will be vitiated.
The recqrd here shows that almost a month after the accused had been
convicted and sentenced to imprisonment, the required notice was sent to his
Oakland address, rather than 'to · the prison. This committee has heretofore
given its opinion that such an attempted service fails to comply not only with
the plain import of our own laws but also with those time-honored principles
of jurisdiction above set forth.
The automatic eii.plusion method is summary, and in effect deprives an
accused of all the rights and privileges of Masonry without a trial. There.fore all of its proceedings must be strictly complied with, and in particuiar
those that prescribed the method of givi1'g notice.

I.

Resolved, that the action of Bayview Lodge No. 401 in the case of H s
be reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for proceedings. d~
novo under Section 332 of our Constitution and Ordinances.

Adopted.
Trial Record No 1048

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Calif~rnia:
Case No. 1048. H. B. C., Jr., Pentalpha Lodge No. 202. Expelled 11-7-44.
The accused ~leaded guilty in the state court to the crime of violation of
Pen~! Code Sec~1on 288a. He was sentenced to 15 years in the state peni:-te~t1ary. The trial _court suspended_ the judgment for 15 years, apd put the
defendant on ~robat10~ f~r that period of time, upon condition that he spend
the first year m a samtanum to be chosen by the probation officer.
The accused was brought to Masonic trial under the provisions of Section
332 of_ our Constitution and Ordinances, which section provides for automatic
exp,uls_10n of a member upon (a) conviction of a felony, and -(b) imprisonment m pursu:ince thereof. Grand Lodge has determined that confinement in
a .count~,. roa~ camp o,; a .co~nty jail as part of the terms of probation constitutes · imprisonment w1thm the meaning of this section.
The only question here involved is whether. or not the · confinement of the
ac_cused_ in a sanitarium brings his case within said Section 332. Your com~mttee is. of the. opinion !hat it does. The gravamen of the Masonic offense
is. the ~nme agamst public law and morals, of which the accused stands convicted m our cou:t.s. The ~ta~e . of California through its probation system
may seek to rehab1htate ,the md1v1d~1al and with this State policy Masonry has
the utmost ~ympat?y and gD?d will. ~ut a Mason who pleads guilty to a
felony sets m motion Masomc proceedings to expel him. If no confinement
of any kind is adju~ged by the state court, he may not be automatically expelled. Or he may mterpose a defense on the merits under Section 332 · or
even though he be acquitted in the state court, he may be tried and convicted
of a Masonic offense involving the same facts and circumstances.
. In this case and the £_act that confinement in a sanitarium was prescribed
~n an effort to cure the diseased mentality which was responsible for it makes
it apparent that ~he confi~em~nt in a sanitarium is equivalent to imprisonment
and that automatic expulsion 1s the proper remedy. Perhaps under the circums~ances some other ca~e in which sanitarium treatment as a condition of probation may be for physical reasons only, Section 332 would not be applicable.
Your committee proposes the following resolution :
Resolved, that the _action of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 in expelling H. B. C.
Jr. from all of the rights and privileges of Freemasonry be and the same is
hereby confirmed.

Adopted.

and found gmlty of indecent exposure rather than charging the offense itself
as should have been done. It is the offense itself which constitutes un:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

143

Masonic conduct and not the fact that the accused may have been found guilty
thereof. However, as the accused was apprised . of the nature of the charge
against him, we attach no particular importance to this error.
By a vote of 6· to 3, the co~mission found the accused guilty of the specification; by a vote of 8 to 1, the accused was found guilty of un-Masonic conduct; by a vote of 6 to 3, the penalty was fixed at e;xpulsion.
From this finding of the commissioners, the accused has appealed.
Your committee is unable to concur in the finding of the trial commission
:and at the conclusion of this report will recommend that such finding be reversed and the proceediqgs dismissed.
At the time of the Masonic trial, the accuser introduced the record of
conviction in the Municipal Court without 'any further evidence. Under our
law, this is sufficient to establish a prima facie case on the part of the accuser.
It does not, however, change the rule that the presumption of innocence
attaches to the accused nor the necessity that the accused's guilt must be
-established by proof, not beyond a reasonable doubt, but which should at least
Tise to the dignity of being clear and convincing. The record shows that the
Teporter's transcript was present at the trial and examined by the trial commissioners pursuant to stipulation between the parties. Your committee has
obtained and reviewed in detail this 161 page record. At the Masonic trial,
the accused testified at considerable length and in "great detail concerning the
<:harge against him. He also introduced a number of other witnesses.
Considering the transcript of the testimony in the Municipal Court and the
evidence introduced at the Masonic trial, the following fads may be said to
a ppear:
Undisputed evidence by a reputable doctor, whose qualifications were stipulated in the criminal trial, shows that for a number of years and arising out
·of an injury in World War No. 1, the accused had been affiicted with an
inflammation of the genito-urinary tract. This condition is quite painful in
character and on occasions requires frequent urination, which is accompanied
by some considerable difficulty and pain.

• • • • •

The accused in this case is married and has a daughter of his own of the
.a pproximate age of the complaining witnesses in the criminal cause. He has
occupied for many years a position of great responsibility in the educational
·system of the State. At the criminal trial and at the Masonic trial, a number
<>f highly reputable citizens, both men and women, testified to his excellent
·character. This testimony was unchallenged.
The accused complains of the manner in which the criminal trial was conducted and of the fact that many leading questions were employed in the
-examination in court of the three girl witnesses. There is much justification
for this complaint.
It will probably serve no useful purpose to further extend this report.
Your committee feels that the evidence produced against the accused does not
·warrant a finding of wilful indecent exposure on the part of the accused. The
-proof, in our judgment, is wholly insuffici.ent to meet the test of being clear
and ·convincing which should exist in cases of this kind. The fact that the
Judge of the Municipal Court only imposed a fine of $100 indicates to us that
be, too, did not take a very serious view of the occurrence, for, if it can
be justly said that the accused was guilty of wilful indecent exposure, Such a
-punishment would be wholly inapequate. The testimony of the two fathers
weighs heavily with us. If the accused is guilty, and who should know the
truth from their daughters better than they, then they should ·he the fi.rst to
•Complain. Yet we find both of them feeling that a great injustice had been

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

dorie the accused. The former excellent reputation of the accused and the
manner in which his friends have stood with him in this trying ordeal is.likewise of convincing force.
Because of all the circumstances and a careful review of this record we
feel that this conviction should not be permitted to stand. Accordingly: we
offer and move the adoption of the following resolution :
Resolved, that the conviction of un-Masonic conduct and sentence of expulsion of W . E. M .. in Trial Record No. 1067 be and th,e same hereby is set aside

To the ifost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Case ~o. 1068. R. M. Three Pillars Lodge No. 613. Suspended 6-8-45.
· The accused: was charged with un-Masonic conduct, in that he had been
tending bar in a saloon in the city of -Sacramento. He appeared before the
trial commission with his attorney. His attorney stated that the accused was
an employee of an establishment cailed the " Cotton Club" ; that he. had been
under the impression and had been advised that such a place was not a saloon
within the meaning of our Section 210, Constitution and Ordinances. Counsel
further stated that if what the accused had been doing was a violation of
Masonic law, he would desire to quit and seek other employment.
'
From the transcript of the proceedings of the trial commission which your
committee has carefully read, it appears that the accused and his counsel the
accuser, and the commissioners discussed nothing except whether or not dnderthe present liquor laws of the State there are any saloons in California. Thereafter, .w ithout calling upon the accused to make any answer to the accusation,
and without taking any testimony, a vote was taken, the accused found guilty
of un-Masonic conduct and suspended.
It will thus be seen that there is no evidence in the record showing what
sort of an establishment the Cotton Club was, or in what capacity the accused
was there employed. Therefore, your committee must recommend that the
matter be retried. Th~ following resolution is proposed:
That tl:ie action of Three Pillars Lodge No. 613 in the case ·of M. be
reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for a new trial.

Adopted.

T?~ .accused, C. A. P., a member of San Bernardino Lodge No. 348, and a

a felqny. The -conviction on two o( these counts was reversed by the Appellat~·

felony conviction, found guilty of the specification and sentenced to suspension.
On· th_e . Masonic trfal the accused admitted that he had been convicted of
th~ . felony ~harge but claimed that he was innocent and desired to bring in
w1trtesses. The Master · apparently had in mind that proof of the conviction in

during which the accused maintained that he had performed no. abortion as

Such is not the case. It is not the conviction of the felony that is unMasonic conduct but the commission of the acts constituting the ~elony. _The
conviction in the State court, duly proved by documentary evidence is a
prima facie case, and unless contradicted, will be sufficiefl_t proof that 0e
accused did do the criminal acts charged. But he has the right to rebut th~s
by putting on evidence of his own, and the trial commissioners on the Masomc
trial might find differently from the court or jury in the State court. That has
happened several times.
.
In this case, therefore, we feel that the accused s~ou_ld be given an ~p­
portunity to present all his evidence and th.en the comm1ss.10ners should decide
the question, not of whether he was convicted of the cnme, b.u t whether or
not he did perform the abortion as charged.
It is noted also that the commissioners in this. matter ~id not vote separately on the specification and on the charge of un-Masoruc .conduct. as prescribed bv Section 322, Constitution and Ordinances. The r_eqm~ement is that a
vote shali be taken first of guilty or not guilty on the specifications, a vote for
each separate specification when there are more than one, a~d t~en a vote of
guilty or not guilty on the charge of un-Masonic conduct, as it. might be f~und
that. the accused was guilty of the acts specified but that. the". did _not constitute
un-Masonic conduct. Such result would hardly be possible m this case.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the action of San Bernardino Lodge N~. 348 in suspending
c. A. P . be and the same is hereby reversed and set aside, ~nd the mat~er
remanded to said Lodge with instructions to retry the case in accord with
the views expressed in this report.

Adopted.

· Many inquiries have been sent in concerning Chinese Masonry in California. There is no need to be exercised about it for investigation has disclosed that they have no properties or. paraphenalia of a Masonic character.
They confer no degrees and their meetings are purely social. They operate
under the name "Chinese Freemasons," but that is the extent of their holding
out.
The investigations of this committee have been carried on continuously
since 1929. For the first time the conditions seem to warrant a recommendation that may result in the healing of a substantial group of Mexican clandestine and irregular Masons. This, we have been assured, will result practically
in the elimination of this phase of the problem. These nationals do not understand English. To confer upon them a Masonic degree in English is time
wasted and would · give them nothing. Neither can a degree be conferred
through an interpreter. (Proceedings 1898, p. 852.) The work must be in
conformity to the ritual adopted by this Grand Lodge (Constitution, Section

247).
In California there are far more Mexican nationals than French, German
or Italian. There is far more reason to have Spanish speaking Lodges than
Lodges in any other foreign tongue. The committee is informed that the
failure to understand English is the primary, and sometimes the only reason,
for good men affiliating with this branch of clandestine Masonry. Our investigations of the personnel of some of these groups lead us to believe that many
of their members are of good Masonic material. One group in Los Angeles has
indicated its willingness to surrender its present charter and take all necessary
steps to be healed. There may be some who have been made Masons in regular
Masonic Lodges. These brethren could be healed by the method previously
approved by this Grand Lodge. · Others, if found worthy, could become regular
Masons upon their signed petitions the same as any other profane.
The committee, therefore, recommends that this Grand Lodge approve as a
policy the issuance of dispensations to confer degrees in the Spanish language.
In order to alert the constituent Lodges of this jurisdiction to the existence
of clandestinism in California and to secure from them the information they
have on the subject, the committee desires to send out a letter upon this subject.
Appropriation for this to the amount of $300 was made two years ago by the
Committee on Finance, but has not been used because of war conditions. In
view of the possible added activity of the committee, depending upon the
approval of the policy recommended, a further expenditure may be need~ of
not to exceed $200. The committee, therefore, asks for a bud~et of $500.
Respectfully submitted,
WARREN E. LIBBY,
