REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Wor_shipful Grand Lodge of California:

!s.

Yo~r. ~oard o~ Control
pleased. t.o sub~t the following brief report of
the acttv1t1es commg under its superv1s1on durmg the past Masonic year.
In doing so it desires to again express its appreciation of information and
assistance given to it by the Grand Officers, particularly the Grand Secretary
and his courteous assistants.
The complete harmony and fine cooperation which has existed between the
Board of Control and the Boards of Relief and individual ·Lodges still con~
tinues with ever-growing beneficial results. New post-war problems are continuing to develop but there has been built up such a very able and experienced
personnel in the Boards of Relief and Employment Services, that in the
opinion of the Board of Control, they are fully able to cope ':Vith any contingency.
Relief
.The Board of Control continues its strong advocacy, that all justifiable
relief be freely extended and this policy is carried out by all Boards of Relief·
in fact, relief in the amount of $27,327.50 was advanced during the year.
is ·noteworthy that due to the high efficiency of the Boards of Relief in handling
the many cases represented in this $27,327.50 that the Grand Lodge is not
called upon to make any reimbursements whatever.

It

Meetings .
The ~oar~ of Control held a meeting on February 9, 10, 11, 1946, in Los
Angeles, 1t bemg necessary to have three day sessions, and one night conference
meeting between the Board of Control and local Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus in order to complete the work. A meeting was held on
May 26, in Berkeley. Members of Board of Control also attended Board of
Relief breakfasts at various cities. There were several conferences by mail
and mail voting on various matters requiring determination. Four day and one
night meeting during this Grand Lodge communication.
Employment Service
D.uring the ye~r ended July 31, 1946, the seven Masonic Employment
Ser;1ce offices .re.ce1ved a total of 11,131 applications for employment, this being
art 111c~ease of slightly over 10 per cent above the 10,041 applications during the
precedmg year, 9,555 (86 per cent) of these applicants were placed in jobs
compared to 9,048 (90 per cent) for the previous year.
'
During ~his per~od over $500,000 in fees was saved applicants, averaging
$53.60 per Job, while the average cost per placement to the fraternity was
$3.89, of which $1.77 .( 46 per cent) was borne by Grand Lodge. The total
.expense of the Employment Service showed an increase of $2,885.
Many services were rendered by these offices of which no tangible record
was made but are none the less valuable to members of the craft and their
families.
Further Information
The Board of Cont~ol believes that the following information would
be desired by those attending Grand Lodge who are not familiar with the
workings of the Board of Control and Boards of Relief.
As the Boards of Relief grew in number and size it was believed to be
necessarr 'to incre~se their efficiency, standar,d ization and for purposes of
economy to establish a Board of Control. This Board was created and
·consists of five (5) members appointed by the Grand Master.

Powers of Supervision
Section 92 reads:
"The Board of Control shall have control and supervise the activities of
Boards of Relief and Employment B.ureaus now existin~ or .'1~;eafter to
be created under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Cahforma.
Power to Make Rules
Section 93 reads:
"The Board of Control shall make such rules and regulations as it
shall de.e m necessary for the effectual operation of the several Boards
of Relief and Employment Bureaus within this State, and shall endeavor
so to standardize the work that the operations of the several Boards of
Relief and Employment Bureaus may be conducted economically and
efficiently."
The Boards of Relief are self-governing and self-supporting. Minor
rules and reg~lations may differ in various localities due to size of Bo<1-rd,
location and other varying conditions. The Board of C.ontrol feel~ tl:F;lt
differences are permissible just so long as they do not mterfere with or
run contrary to the rules and regulations of Grand Lodge or compacts
with Grand Lodge under which Boards of Relief operate. Many Boards
of Relief have an Employment Service and contributions are made by
Grand Lodge to assist in the development and improvement of such services.
To give Grand Lodge some idea of employment s~rvic.e performedprior to the war period when there were many seekmg Jobs, our Employment Services found jobs at around the peak of unemployment for
over 19,000 in a single year, approximately 1600 per month.
Notwithstanding conditions during the years of 1940 to 1946 inclusive,
applications for jobs were made by 111,894, and jobs were actually secured
by Employment Bureaus for 88,268.

Tenor and Organ
As far into the dim past as the records of man go we find that he has
considered it a duty, and a privilege, at some season of the year to pause
in his workaday life to render honor and tribute to the memory of those
near and dear to him whom, during the past year, the Creator of all things
has in His infinite wisdom seen fit to call from this transitory life to that
celestial abode where peace and happiness reign supreme.
Today this Grand Lodge pauses in its deliberations that its love,
affection and admiration may be extended to the memory of our brethren
whom, since our last communication, have laid aside the cares and responsibilities of this troubled world.
If our departed brethren could speak to us now they would tell us
not to weep o'er their passing, but admonish us to heed the symbols
which God places before every man. Those manifestations of nature which
through the seasons tell us so clearly that death is "not the end. The sun,
the greatest manifestation of Diety on this earth, gives us daily assurance
that beyond the darkness is light. The changing seasons eternally prove
that with winter's passing comes the spring. Every great religion the
world has known emphasizes the immortality of the soul. Surely God
would not destroy his greatest handiwork with no more compunction
than He destroys the weeds of the fields. Philosophers have written and
poets have sung of the beauty of the passing of the soul from its earthly
to its spiritual glory, and in so doing have taught men better how to live.
The lips of the dead speak eloquently to the living, if only the living
would but hear. They tell us of the folly of the pomp and glory of this
world, and give us the secret of a successful life. Men in all times and in
all ages have tried to properly express these lessons, but none have come
nearer than the unknown author who centuries past, writing in the
Sanskrit, said :

"

"Listen to the exhortation of the dawn!
Look to this day!
For it is life, the very life of lifeIn its brief course lie all the verities and realities o.f your existence;
The gloi:y of action,
The bliss of growth,
The splendor of beauty.

And tomorrow is only a vision,
But today well-lived makes every yesterday a
dream of happiness, and every tomorrow
a vision of hope.
Look well, therefore, to this day!
Such is the admonition of the dawn."

LA WREN CE CARLYLE KELLEY
Seldom in the history of our Grand Lodge has the final call come to
so many in one short year. Only once before in the 97 years of its existence has it · suffered the loss of its highest officer. In 1910 G. M. Pierce
died 8 days before the convening of Grand Lodge. October 24, . l945,
Most Worshipful Laurence Carlyle Kelley, elected and installed Grand
Master of Masons in California only 12 days previously, died at his home
in Los Angdes. The committee, as do you all, feels deeply the loss of
this beloved man; this devoted husband and father; this good citizen, this
outstanding Mason. Brother Kelley was a member of Pentalpha Lodge
No. 202, in which he was initiated December 13, 1921, passed January 17,
1922, and raised March 17, 1922. He served as Master of his Lodge in
1930, and at the expiration of this tei:m was appointed Inspector of the
84th Masonic bistrict, serving unfil · Oc.to!>ei: 1941, when he was appointed Grand Orator by Grand Master Frank M. Smith. He was elected
.Junior Grand Warden in 1942; Senior Grand Warden in 1943; Deputy
Grand Master in 1944, and Grand Master October 12, 1945. A special
eulogy with appropriate expressions of our grief will be given by Myron
E. Smith, Pa&t Master of University Lodge No. 394, who was a law
partner oi Brother Kelley for many yea.rs, and who was ·probably closer
to him than any other man in Masonry.

April 28, 1946, Dr. James Lynn Goode was called from his earthly
labors. Jimmy, as he was most affectionately know~, was bor.n at Los
Angeles, California, August 3, 1890. He was educated. m the pubhc schools
of that city, and following his graduation from Me?1ca~ College he practiced his . profession of physician and surgeon until his death. Brother
Goode was initiated in South Gate Lodge No. 320, April 9, 1913; passed
May 23, 1913; and raised June 14, 1913. He ?emitted from South Gate
Lodge in 1922 to assist in the forming of Euchd Lodge No. 519, and became a Charter Member and. first Secretary of that Lodge. In 1924 he
demitted from Euclid Lodge to assist in the forming of Melrose Lodge
No. 602 and served as first Master of that Lodge in 1925-26. He was
appoint;d Inspector of the 8lst District in 1929, and served ~n t~at high
office until death terminated his labors. He was equally active m other
branches of Masonry. He was 32nd degree in the Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite, and served for many years as a member of the Personnel
Committee. He was a Past High Priest, South Gate Chapter No. 98, Royal
Arch Masons· Past Illustrious Master, Southern California Council No.
35, Royal and' Select Masters. He was Past President, Southern California
Past Masters Association, and his unique and original manner in presenting the work of that organization will ever be a joyful memory to those
who received their instructions from him. His love· for the Fraternity,
his constant efforts in its behalf, and his devotion to duty, endeared him
to ;i.11 who knew him, and placed him among Masonry's great.

of our Fraternity, a Past Master of Lincoln Lodge No. 470. He was ever
willing to give of his time and substance that Masonry might prosper.
Brother Leonard T. Pockman, a Charter Member and Past Master by ·
affiliation of Lincoln ·L odge, will give a special eulogy to the memory of
this great Mason.

Gus Blanchard died at his home in Los Angeles, August 31, 1946, after
a long illness and a series of tragedies such as come to few men. He
was born April 9, 1891, on Aliso Street, which at that time was the center
of the French Colony in Los Angeles. That section was then devoted to
vineyards, bringing forth the finest grapes, and the finest wine produced
in Southern California. Brother Blanchard was initiated in Vallee de ·France
Lodge· No. 329-the French language Lodge-October 31, 1917; passed
November 7, 1917, and one week later was raised to the Sublime Degre~.
He was appointed Inspector of Special District No. 116, ana: served until
his death. Endowed with a marvelous sense of humor, a keen wit, and
an unquenchable desire to be of service to his fellowman made Gus one
of the most beloved Masons in this Jurisdiction.

DR. ARTHUR HUNTER WURTELE
.Past Grand Chaplain
Our Reverend Brother was called from his earthly labors August 1,
1945. He was a member of John Marshall Lodge No. 636, F. & A. M.,
Beverly Hills, California. Brother Wurtele was born at Actonville, Canada.
He was graduated from Bishop's College at Lennoxville, Canada, and
completed his divinity course at Columbia University, New York. He
also held an honorary D. D. degree from King's College at Halifax,
Canada. Before coming to Los Angeles he had been Rector of Calvary
Church at Rochester, Minnesota. or. the past 21 years he was Rector of
St. Thomas Episcopal Church, Hollywood. It was through his efforts

LEO VALTUS YOUNGWORTH
Hist~ry Committee
Leo V. Youngworth served this Grand Lodge as a member of the
Charter Committee in 1934-35; a member of the Pay of Members Committee 1940-41; and a member of the History Committee at the time of
his death, May 16, 1946. He was initiated August 19, 1895; passed August
28, 1895, and raised September 2, 1895, in Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319.
Served his Lodge as Master in 1905-06. It was during his term as Master
that the first Temple of Hollenbeck Lodge was built at 1960 East First
Street, Los Angeles. In other branches of Masonry he was equally active, occupying the office of High Priest, Signet Chapter, Royal Arch
Masons, 1906; Grand High Priest, California, 1912; Eminent Commander,
Los Angeles Commandery No. 9, 1913. He was a 32nd degree Mason in the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite. He was Potentate of Al Malaikah
Temple, Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, for
three terms, 1912 through 1915. In 1929 he was elected Imperial Potentate.
Leo was active in other fraternal organizations, serving as Exalted Ruler
of the Los Angeles ·Lodge No. 99 B. P. 0 . E . in 1909-10. Brother Youngworth was born in San Francisco, California in 1873; moved to Los Angeles 1876; educated in the public schools of that city, and graduated in
law at the University of Southern California. He practiced his profession through a long and successful career, and served as United States
Marshal under President Theodore Roosevelt. Leo Youngworth was a
kind man, a gentle man, and a friendly man; his friends were legion. He
was the type of man Masonry could ill afford to lose.

FRANK FLINT PORTER
A pioneer of the City of Oaklan~ and Past Master of Sequoia Lodge,
No. 349, F. & A. M. was called to his heavenly home September 29, 1946.
Brother Porter, who was affectionately known as "F. F.," received
the degrees of Masonry in Fort Winnebago Lodge No. 33 in September
1885. In 1902 he demitted from Fort Winnebago Lodge to assist in the
forming of Sequoia Lodge, becoming a Charter Member. He served as
Master in 1910. He was appointed Chairman of the Finance Committee
in 1911, and by successive appointments served in that -capacity until his
death. He was a member of the first class to be initiated in Aahmes
Temple of the Shrine in 1904, and a member of Oakland Commandery in
the same year. He was a life member of the Athenian Nile Club. He
received many honors in Masonry, among them the presenting of a
Fifty-year Emblem by the then Grand Master Earl Warren.
Brother Porter was born · in Portage, Wisconsin, October 31, 1862.
Had he lived to October 31st of this year he would have been 84 years
old, and an active member of the Masonic fraternity for 61 years. Of such
men is Masonry made!

erful smile and ready handclasp. His was truly a genius for

· We like to think of him as a great and good man who believed with

Everything he achieved in life came from his own efforts. He was a~

A Presbyterian, he was 'd eeply religious and always interested in
spiritual values. His Bible-the rule and guide of his faith-was at his
side constantly, at home by his favorite chair and in the office on his
desk. It is significant that after he was gone these quotations were found
on his desk, inscribed in his own hand:
"FAITH"
"Faith in ourselves, for the sanctuary of God can only be found within
the individual."
"Inherent in each is the urge to know God, and were there no God
there would be no such urge. We know love exists because of this in~
herency of God and were there no God there would be no such love."
"Unless we find love within aJl the prayers and demeaning likeness
are useless."
Such, mY brethren, was the great and inspiring faith by which our
brother lived and which he imparted to others.
..
Our hearts go out to his family with whom we share their sense of
loss. With them we know that his memory will abide, for througout his
life he built a temple of friendship and service that will long endure as a
monument to his character and an inspiration to his br·e thren. As a perpetual memorial to him may all generations ever be reminded of the imperishable message he left us in his Grand Oration:
Masonry, he said, "teaches us to lift the burden fro~ another's heart,
to wipe the tear from an eye of sorrow and that instead of trying to get
into some imaginary place beyond the stars to try to get more heaven
into us while here on earth. Masonry does not follow the practice pursued
by many religious and other organizations which spend much time in
trying to teach a man how to die. Masonry is life. Masonry is a way of
life. Masonry teaches us how to live and having lived by that standard
set up, we welcome d'eath, 'Not as a grim tyrant but as a kind messenger
sent to translate us from this imperfect to that all perfect, glorious, and
celestial Lodge above where the Supreme Grand Master of the universe
forever presides.' "

EULOGY
BY L. T. PoCKMAN
Past Master, Lincoln Lodge No. 470

JAMES CHASE WILDER
Grand Bible Bearer
The life of our late brother, Past Master James Chase Wilder exemplifies in every way the teachings and precepts of Freemasonry.
Brother Wilder spent a busy Masonic life of some fifty years. He received his degrees of Masonry in Durant Lodge No. 268, Berkeley, California, and later ser ved McCloud Lodge No. 430 as Master and for seven
years its secretary. He was a charter member of Lincoln Lodge No. 470
and served as its first Master. In. 1920 he was elected secretary, a position he held until shortly before his passing, May 7, 1946, at .the age of
89 years. In 1945 he was appointed Grand Bible Bearer by our late beloved Past Grand Mast~r Kelley.
His kindly smile, his genial nature and firm hand clasp were known to
his legion of friend s, and his sage advice was sought by a!L .Jlis devotion

158

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to Masonry was unchallenged and outstanding, and as a ritualist, he was
numbered among the best. He gave freely of his time and talents in
coaching his less informed brethren and his helping hand was always
extended.
No monument is needed to keep alive the memory and good deeds. of
James Chase Wilder in the hearts of his br ctthren, but literally, in the loss
of the Temple of Yolo Lodge No. 81 has been found the site on which to
place a memorial.
For the second time in its long existence fire has destroyed the temple
of historic Yolo Lodge No. 81. We of Lincoln Lodge feel that it is imperative to preserve these pioneer Lodges, and knowing that Jim Wilder
would have like to assist in its rebuilding, Lincoln Lodge No. 470 presents
to Yolo Lodge No. 81, a memorial to Past Master James Chase Wilder,
the Three Great Lights of Masonry, the Holy Bible, Square and Compass,
together with a suitable Altar.
May these endure for time immemorial to the glory of Masonry and
the loving memory of James Chase Wilder.

TO THE APPLICANT
Having expressed a desire to become a Freemason, we presume you are
willing to consider thoroughly the step you propose to take. The exact nature
of our Institution being unknown to you, we deem it advisable that you should
be informed on certain points, the knowledge of which may affect your decision
to apply for membership:
Freemasonry interferes neither with religion nor politics, but has for its
foundation the great basic principles of the Fatherhood of God and the
Brotherhood of Man. No Atheist can be a Freemason. Freemasonry strives
to teach a man the duty he owes to God, his neighbor, and himself. It inculcates the practice of virtue, and makes extensive use of symbolism in its
teachings.
It cannot be too strongly emphasized that Freemasonry is not to be entered
in the hope of .personal gain or advancement. Anyone so actuated will be
bitterly disappointed. The ai~ of the true Freemason is to cultivate a brotherly
feeling among men, and to help whomsoeve.r he can.
Freemasonry is not a Benefit Society. This fact also cannot be too strongly
emphasized. We do' not subscribe so much a year to entitle us to draw sick
pay or ether provision for those who survi:ve us. There are other excellent
Societies founded for this purpose. No man · should enter the ranks of Freemasonry in hope or expectation that he will derive any financial benefit from it.
Loyalty to one's co.untry is an essential qualification in Freemasonry, and
only those are acceptable who cheerfully render obedience to every lawful
authority. Disloyalty in any form is abhorrent to a Freemason, a·nd is regarded
as a serious Masonic offense.
Your admission to the Craft will entail certain financial obligations which
you should be able to discharge without detriment to yourself or those dependent
upon you. In addition to the fees payable on your entrance, there will be an
annual subscription for the support of your Lodge and occasionally you may
be asked to contribute to the relief work of the Craft.
Freemasonry has in all ages insisted that men should come to its doors
entirely of their own free will, and not as the result of solicitations, or from
'feelings of curiosity, but simply from a favorable opinion of the Institution,
and a desire to be ranked among its members.
vVe have no authority at the present time to give you further information
regarding the Brotherhood, but we have imparted sufficient to enable you to
conclude that Freemasonry is not contrary to the principles which mark a
man of upright heart and mind, and has nothing in it inconsistent with one's
civil, moral or religious duties. If you are willing to prove your worthiness
to become a Freemason in accordance ·with these pri11ciples, your application
will be received subiect to acceptance as provided by our Laws and Regulations.

RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
Past Grand Master Hervey reported on requests for recognition as follows :
To the Most Worshipfi4l Grand Lodge of California:
For several years, because of war conditions and the uncertain conditions and unfortunate circumstances in Mexican Masonry, the final determination of requests by Masonic Grand Lodges for recognition were postponed and due in~estigations have now been made. At prcrsent your
committee is prepared to make recommendations on the applications of Vallee
Valle de Mexico, Tamaulipas and Cosmos Grand Lodges.
In Mexico there is a Federal District analogous to our District of
Columbia and more than twenty states analogous to our states. In many
of these states are Grand Lodges and in the Federal District a Grand
Lodge. These Grand Lodges are worthy of consideration and some, if not
all, are worthy of recognition for they each claim exclusive jurisdiction in
their state, or states, are truly Masonic in character• complying with the
fundamentals and landmarks of Masonry, and in most cases constitute the
only Masonry in the respective states.
In addition to these Grand Lodges there is a York Grand Lodge, recognized by the California Grand Lodge, which formerly claimed jurisdiction
over the whole of the Republic of Mexico, but now, we are informed,
claims jurisdiction only over the English speaking Masonry of the Republic.
Our recognition of the York Grand Lodge was right and proper and
we have 'heretofore thought that it precluded us from recognizing any of
these State Grand Lodges without withdrawing our recognition of the
York Grand Lodge. It seemed inconsistent to recognize two Bodies in
Mexico which did not recognize each other. When the application of
Grand Lodge Pacifico was granted several years ago we had the gracious
. and tacit approval of York Grand Lodge for •such action. Since that time
the chaotic conditions then existing have been brought into some order
and a kinder and more fraternal spirit prevails. Visitations are permitted
and in the long run these portend a true amity and concord. York Grand
Lodge is leading the way by its conciliatory attitude and fraternal helpfulness and justifies its position of Masonic and moral leadership. But, as it

180

PROCEEDIN°GS OF THE

has been well said, the Nationals of any country are entitled to rule and
govern their own Freemasonry. Foreigners are not entitled to claim the
right to hold exclusive control of Freemasonry in the hands of persons who
are not citizens and who conduct the affairs of Masonry not in the native
but in a foreign tongue. The York Grand Lodge uses the. English Ian~
guage exclusively and is composed of English speaking Masons. It is not,
and can never become, a natiohal institution of Mexico.
In order to stabilize Freemasonry in Mexico the Mexican Freemasons
established a confederation and admitted only those Grand Lodges which
acc~pte.d the following canons for recognition: (1) Regularity of origin, (2)
Belief m the Great Architect of the Universe, (3) Admission of men exclusively, ( 4) Sovereignty of Grand Lodges, (5) Recognition of the Three
Great Lights, (6) That Masonry is not sectarian and that it does not admit
discussions of religion or politics, (7) Exclusive territorial jurisdiction.
This Confederation is not a Super-Grand Lodge. It merely makes recommendations subject to ratification by its constituent members; which do not
surrender any of their sovereignty.
We find the leaders of the Grand Lodges_ which we recommend for
recognition to be men of character and standing in their respective communities. We think every encouragement should be given to our brethren
in Mexico. It is not a casual or easy matter to profess and practice Freemasoncy in a land when religious and political liberty is· under constant and
bitter attack. It requires courage and devotion to avow oneself a Mason in
the face of religious, social and business opposition.

COSMOS
The Grand Logia Independiente Cosmos of the State of Chihauhua
has applied for recognition by the Grand Lodge 0f California and your
committee has carefully considered the application and reports thereon as
follows:
The Grand Lpdge Cosmos is duly and regularly constituted, havi1:1g
nineteen Lodges of its obedience, which Lodges are in all the considerable
towns of the State. The Grand Lodge ahd its subordinates acknowledge
the Great Architect of the Universe and the immortality of the soul. They
have the three great lights displayed on the altar while at labor they
maintain secrecy and the symbolism of the Craft. The work is divid~d into
three degrees and they follow the legend of the Third Degree. It makes
Masons of men only. It is nonsectarian and nonpolitical. It is not controlled by any Supreme Council or other body. It has governmental and
administrative authority throughout the State of Chihauhau; the official
language is Spanish and it numbers in its membership many of the leading
men of the State and is held in high regard.
'it is a member of the Confederation and conforms to the ideals for
which it stands and is recognized by the Grand Lodges in Arizona Colorado; Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Oklahoma, and Texas.
· Your committee is of the opinion that the application should be granted
and; therefore, recommends that the Grand Lodge of California recognize
the Grand Lodge of Cosmos.
TAMAULIPAS
The Grand Lodl?'.e of Tamaulipas, with its seat at Tampico, was duly

VALLE DE MEXICO
.
The Grand Lodge of California for many years recognized the Grand
Lodge Valle de Mexico and upon the disturbance in that Grand Lodge it
withdrew its recognition of Valle de Mexico and recognized the York
Grand Lodge, which was composed of that segment of the old Lodge from
which the Valle de Mexico seceded. The York Grand Lodge was legitimately a continuance of Valle de Mexico with a change· of name and
language. We continue, and will continue, to recognize York Grand Lodge,
but are constrained to consider the recognition of Valle de Mexico because
o f the rights of intervisitation accorded to the members of the York
Grand Lodge and the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico.
T.hese harmonious relations between the two Masonic powers, and the
acquiescence of the York Grand Lodge to our recognition of Valle de
· Mexico, lead us to favorably consider the recognition of the V alle de Mexico because it is the strongest Spanish speaking Masonic Lodge in Mexico
and has within its membership some of the most distinguish ed citizens of
that country. Our recognition of it formerly was withdrawn because of an
apparent violation of Masonic law but the passage of the years has largely
obliterated the animosities of former days.
,
The Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico has merged with the Grand Lodge
Independiente Mexicana, the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico providing 77
and the lrtdependiente Mexicana providing 40 Lodges to the augmented
Valle de Mexico.
This Grand Lodge has jurisdiction over the Federal District and over the
States of Mexico which have no regular Grand. Lodges. We have been kept
advised from time to time of the work that was being done by the Valle
de Mexico and know that it follows the landmarks, the temple legend
secrecy, the division of symbolic Masonry into three degrees, the recogni~
tion of the Great Architect of the Universe, and the admission of none but
men. It prohibits religious or political discussions in the Lodges, is the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

largest and most important of the State Grand Lodges working in the
Spanish language, which is the language of the country.
It is now recognized by the Grand Lodges of the States of .Colora40,
Indiana, Kansas, Ke~tucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New
Mexico, North Carolina, and Texas.
We feel that for the interests of Masonry, and for the assistance of the
Masonic Bodies who are placed on the defensive by the hostilities of the
strong instit~tions which are predominant in Mexico, that we should extend to .them the assurance of our fraternal cooperation and amity ; and
for the foregoing reasons your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
recommends that the Grand Lodge of California recognize the Grand Lodge
Valle de Mexico.

NICARAGUA
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was referred the application for recognition of the Grand Lodge of Nicaragua
(Gran Logia Simbolica de Nicaragua) has examined into the merits of
the application and reports as follows:
That the Grand Lodge of Nicaragua occupies exclusively its territorial
jurisdiction, was lawfully formed on November 27, 1907, and has eight
Lodges and about 370 members. It is a responsible, self-governing organization and is not connected with or controlled by any Supreme Council.
Its legal standing has been recognized and chartered by the Nicaraguan
Government. The membership is composed exclusively of men, it adheres
to the ancient landmarks, traditions and usages of the Craft as set forth in
the Constitutions of the Grand Lodge of England. It acknowledges a
belief in God, it recognizes the Great Architect of the Universe, believes
in immortality, requires the presence of the three great lights in Masonry
and obligates its candidates on the Bible, is non-political and non-sectarian,
requires an adherence to the symbolism of operative Masonry and its
division into three degrees. It uses the legend of the third degree and its
dominant purposes are fraternal, charitable, benevolent and educational.
It is recognized by· Arizona, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Texas,
Vermon.t, Washington, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New York, North
Carolina, Louisiana, and Ohio.
Your committee is of the opinion that the Grand Lodge of Nicaragua
is a regular Grand Lodge and entitled to favorable action on its application
and, therefore; recommends that the Grand Lodge of California recognize
the Grand Lodge of Nicaragua.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee has carefully considered the application of the Grand
Lodge of Venezuela (Gran Logia de Los Estados Unidos de Venezuela)
for recognition, and reports thereon as follows:
The · Grand Lodge of Venezuela with its seat at Caracas is a regular
Lodge and has exclusive territorial jurisdiction over the United States of
Venezuela and permits no other Masonic Power in its territory nor desires to extend its jurisdiction to territory of ~ther Grand Lodges. It was
founded in 1824 and reorganized in September of 1838. It has a Lodge
under its jurisdiction in practically every town of importance in Venezuela.
It makes Masons only of men. It requires a belief in the Great Architect
of the Universe. ·It holds that secrecy is the main principle in Masonry and
its work ·is through symbolism. It only confers three degrees-Entered
Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason. It believes and is practicing
the legend of the third degree. The purposes are charitable, benevolent,
educational and for the worship of God. Politics and religion are excluded
from all activities of Grand Lodge and its subordinates. It holds that the
three great lights are indispensable in the Lodges while at work and follows the landmarks as laid down by the Grand Lodge of England. It has
no connection with any Supreme Council or other Bodies. It is composed
of the finest type of men in Venezuela and enjoys a high standing. It is
recognized by the United Grand Lodge of England, Scotland, New York,
Louisiana, Kentucky, and the District of Columbia.
Because of our acquaintanceship with members of the Grand Lodge
and the representations made to us to which we give full credence, we are
of the opinion that the application should be favorably acted upon and,
therefore, recommend that the Grand Lodge of California recognize the
Grand Lodge of Venezuela.

Pohona Lodge in Yosemite Valley has 30 members and after outstanding indebtedness is taken care of, they will have approximately $465 in
cash. They are particularly fortunate, not only in obtaining quarters at
the npminal rental of $1 per year, but also in having among their members
Master craftsmen who have been able to remodel their Lodge room and
construct much of the necessary Masonic furniture.
The committee has been favorably impressed with the perseverance of
the brethren in Yosemite Valley in obtaining their dispensation. They
have worked hard for three years, and the peace and harmony existing
between them and their neighboring Lodges is evidenced by the assistance
given them by these Lodges and their officers.
While Yosemite is usually thought of as strictly a vacation spot, the
fact that it has a year around population of over one thousand permanent
residents, should justify the establishment of a Lodge. The unique location of a Lodge in this area with nearly three-fourths of a million visitors
this year has resulted in an extremely interesting Tyler's register, showing
visitors from 87 different Lodges and 12 different Grand Jurisdictions.
The committee believes that in the years to come this Lodge will render a
valuable service to Masonry by affording a meeting place for brethren of
every country and every clime.
The committee, therefore, recommends that a charter be granted to
Pohona ~odge No. 689, Yosemite Valley.

Lodge is located in close proximity to other Lodges, the assistance rendered
by these Lodges is ample evidence of the close harmony existing between

Relating to Investments by Lodges
The Grand Master, in his message, referred to a letter received from
Cyril W . McClean, Secretary of Sequoia Lodge No. 349, asking for a ruling
respecting the type of investments which a Lodge may make. Brother
McClean referred to the prudent man rule which has recently been adopted
as a part of the law of California.
The Grand Master calls attention to the fact that the adoption of this
rule through its uncertainty as to whether or not the investment of funds
has been broadened by the civil law. To avoid any broadening of the
powers of investment, the Grand Master recommends that the words "or
trustees,'' Section 152 of the Constitution, be s~ricken out, which would
leave the requirement that all in".'estments be legal by the laws of the State
of California or the Territory of Hawaii for investments by savings banks.
This would very properly forbid the investment in common or preferred
stocks.
Your committee recommends that the words "or trustees" be eliminated ·
from said Section 152. The Jurisprudence Committee concurs.

Adopted by a five-sixth vote.

The Grand Master, in his message, recommends that the second and
last sentence of Section 248 of the Constitution and Ordinances be eliminated. The two sentences of the section are antithetical and the contradiction should be corrected.
The first sentence of the section is :
"The Grand Lodge alone has power tq authorize any changes in

And the second sentt.nce of the section provides:
"All propositions looking to any. :change in the Ritual will be

Minimum Annual Dues
The Grand Master recommends that Section 251 of the Constitution
and Ordinances, relative to the dues of members, be amended by striking
out the word "nine" and substituting "twelve" in lieu thereof, so that when
amended, the sentence ~hall read:
"The minimum annual dues for members shall be twelve dollars."
Your committee appreciates the desirability of a greater fee than nine
dollars in many of the Lodges, but in the case of other Lodges it feels that
a fee of nine dollars is ample because of the conditions and circumstances
of the Lodges.
It is impossible to establish a fair rule to apply to all the
1
Lodges of the State because of the differences in their needs and the ability
of their members to' pay. Many years ago the minimum dues was raised
from six dollars to nine dollars with results that many of the Lodges can
carry on all their activities, charitable and otherwise, with dues of nine
dollars. There is no maximum limit placed on dues and Lodges requiring
more than nine dollars will very properly raise the dues to the amount
necessary to maintain a creditable Lodge.
Your committee is of the opinion that the amendment to Section 251
be not ·adopted and so recommends.

Adopted.
Fees for the Degrees
The Grand Master, in his message, recommended that the fees for the
three degrees be amended and recommended that the second sentence of
Section 245 of our Constitut.i on and Ordinances be amended by striking
out the word "thirty" and substituting the word "fifty" in lieu thereof, so
that when amended the sentence shall read as follows :
" The Lodge shall not confer the three degrees for a fee less than
fifty dollars."
He also recommended that the third sentence of Section 245 be amended
by striking out the word "fifty" and substituting the word "seventy-five"
so that when amended the sentence shall read:
"Where Lodges have concurrent jurisdiction, the fee for the
three degrees shall be at least seventy-five dollars, except by consent
of all such Lodges."
The economic situation makes it desirable that the fees be raised in
California to meet rising costs. Your committee recommends the adoption
of these am~ndments to Section 245 of the Constitution and Ordinances.
The Committee on Jurisprudence concurs.

Adopted by a five-sixth vote.

Boards of Relief and Employment Offices
A resolution has been introduced by the Masters of several Lodges
proposing that the name of the E~st Bay Masonic Board of Relief and
Employment be changed to eliminate the word "relief.'' The principle
tenets of our Order are Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth and we think
that a body charged with dispensing Masonic relief,' as is the East Bay
Board of Relief, should continue to use the word "relief" in its title.
The Employment Bureau is a subsidiary and distinctive organization
operating under the Board of· Relief and its name, so far as we are informed, is the East Bay Masonic Employment Bureau. This Employment
Bureau is a service organization and should not have the word " relief" in
its na.me, while the Board of Relief should not dispense with the word
"relief," nor should it add to its title except the name of the place where it
· operates. The Board of Control .concurs in this opinion.
'
We are of the opinion that the resolution should not be adopted and so
recom,mend.

Adopted.
Information on Current Events
Paul W. Adler, Worshipful Master of Burbank Lodge No. 406, has
introduced a resolution for the appointment of a committee to study and
determine suitable means whereby our m embership may be kept informed
of the scientific discoveries and swiftly moving events of a social, economic
and religious nature of world-wide importance and because tpe continued
growth, maintenance and prosperity of Freemasonry as a worfd-wide institution is dependent on a vigorous and well-informed membership. The
members would be happy indeed to be informed of such events and their
relationship and implication to Freemasonry; but we ·have no means of
accomplishing results. There is no man or body of men known to us
who are so wise and infallible th~t they possess such information or who
have the power of disseminating it to the California Masons.
Our Education Committee is supposed to afford Masonic instruction
and our laws, proceedings and other literature contain· much matter that
is available to the Craft.

Nominating Committee
Chas. L. W. Wocke, Past Master at Valley Forge Lodge No.. 587, has
presented a resolution that a recognized committee representing this Grand
Lodge for each section of this Grand Jurisdiction whose duty it shall be to
consider the qualifications of all brethren selected for an elected office in
this Grand Lodge and to make necessary recommendations to this Grand
Lodge before each annual election of Grand Lodge officers.
Your committee is of the opinion that Grand Lodge does not need a
committee of Grand Lodge for each section of this Grand Jurisdiction to
consider the qualifications of all brethren suggested for elective office in
this Grand Lodge. Such a committee would be a super-political organization and would contribute to confusion and more or less bitterness if it
presumed to recommend one or more out of h,undreds of members of
Grand Lodge for election. The existence of such a committee, with the
power of nomination vested in them, would present an almost insuperable
barrier to a brother desiring or seeking a place who had received the
frown rather than the smile of this politic<il committee.
For 97 years the Grand Lodge has teen able to function without the
aid of such a committee and in our opinion the time has not come, and
may never come, when such a committee would be desirable, wherefore,
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.
Grand Lodge Office Hours
Our law now requires that "for the transaction of Masonic business''
the Grand Secretary keep his office open "at least 6 hours each day except
Sundays and legal holidays."
·'
The Most Worshipful Grand Master recommends that paragraph 9,
Section 44 of our laws be amended to require the Grand Secretary to keep
his off).ce open "at least 8 hours each day except Saturdays, Sundays and
legal holidays."
The Grand Master cites that "the 5-day week has come to be an
accepted part of our b~siness life" and also cites "the increased inability
to employ help for Saturday morning work."
Your committee believes the Grand ·Master's proposal is sound and in
line with widely pre~alent practice. It notes, however, that under this
amendment the Grand Secretary's office would be open 40 hours instead
of 36 hours per week.
We recommend the adoption of the amendment.

Adopted.

Liability Insurance
The Most Worshipful Grand · Master in his annual message included
the following recommendation : "That the incoming Grand Master be
authorized to appoint some well-qualified member or committee of our
fraternity to investigate the ·:probable cost and benefit to be derived by
the constituent Lodges by insuring our Lodges from claims arising out of
any injury received by candidates, members or visitors through accident
and that said member or committee report to the next annual communication of Grand Lodge:" •
Your Committe~ ·o n Policy and General Purposes has had the foregoing under consider;i.tion and herewith reports as follows:
Incidents of injury to candidates, members of, or visitors to, Masonic
Lodges in this Grand furisdiction have been so rare of occurrence as not
to require or, .justify, in our opinion, the suggested measure.
The insurance proposed would add substantially to the operating exp ense of Lodges, and your committee is advised that from an underwriting
point of view it would present a complex and difficult problem.
It :goes without saying that Masonic Lodges should always exercise
care not only during the conferring of degrees but also in the accommodation and entertainment of mepibers and visitors to guard against the
infliction of even the slightest injury, and we have no. doubt that they are
fully conscious of this obligation and responsibility.
We, therefore, r ecommend that the proposal herein referred to be not
adopted.

Adopted.

Committee on Lodge Financing
Worshipful Brother Herbert C. Goldman, Past Master of Los Cerritos
Lodge No. 674, submitted the following resolution: "That Section 70 of
the Ordinances of the Grand Lodge of California be amended to include
the Committee on Lodge Financing."
· Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels that the Committee on Lodge Financing has rendered and will continue to render highly
valuable service to many of the Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction. The
counsel and advice given to numerous Lodges in connection with financial •
problems arising out of building activities and re-financing of obligations
has saved a number of Lodges from loss and serious embarrassment. We
feel that, to. use an old expression, "this committee has won it s spurs,''
and should become a Standing Committee of Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of Brother Goldman's resolution.

Brotherhood Week
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was referred that portion of the Grand Master's message, relative to "Brotherhood Week,'' and the resolution of Center Lodge No. 465 and concurring
Lodges, has had the same under consideration and respectfully and fraternany reports as follows:
In the opini~n· of your committee every· week among Masons should
be a brotherhood week, just as it should be a truth week, a relief week,
and a week for the practice of each of all the other tenets of Masonry.
We do not believe anything would be gained for Masonry or the· welfare
of mankind by singling out any one or more of our teachings and making
a public display of such.
The Grand Master has made no recommendation and your committee
concurs in this, and recommends that Grand Lodge do not take any action

Gift of Fees
The Grand Master, in his annual report, stated that Liberty Lodge
No. 299 inquired as to whether it would be permissible for a Lodge to
accept as a gift the amount of the fees returned to a rejected applicant
and that he replied that it was his opinion that the Lodge should not
accept any such gift. He thought that in the event the candidate should reapply after the expiration of the statutory period it might appear in an
unfavorable light because of the gift.
Your committee is of the opinion that it would not be right for the
Lodge to put itself in a questionable position by receiving such a gift if the
applicant again petitioned for the degrees and we, therefore, recommend
that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.'

History Publication
In 1934, the chairman of your History Committee strenuously endeavored to bring about the final preparation and publication of the History
of Masonry in California. Many of you will doubtless remember we were
authorized by action 6f this Grand Lodge to enter into a contract to this
end with H. S. Crocker Company, Inc., which we ·did, but not enough
subscriptions were obtained to warrant publication and the project, for the
time being, was abandoned.
In 1950 the Grand Lodge will celebrate its lOOth anniversary. In our
judgment, this will be a most appropriate time to perfect and publish our
history. Since 1928 this committee has been engaged in collecting probably
the greatest mass of historical data ·e ver acquired by any Grand Lodge in
the United States, if not the world. We are anxious to see the final culmination of these efforts in the publication of this valuable data.
For the past several months many members of Grand Lodge have urged
· upon this committee the advisability of·recommending to Grand Lodge the
appointment of a committee to devise ways and means of preparing and
publishing our history. To this end we urge Grand Lodge to authorize the
incoming Grand Master to appoint a committee, empowered to fully investigate the most feasible and economical method of the final preparation
and publication of said history and to report their findings at the next
session of Grand Lodge.
We respectfully urge and submit the following recommendatfons:
1. That the History Committee be continued for the following year.
2. That the sum of $200 be appropriated and set aside for the use of
said committee.
3. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to investigate
the most advisable method of financing· the rebuilding of the Masonic·
Temple at Columbia, and the most economic method of maintaining same.'
4. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to fully inves-·
tigate the most feasible and economic method for the final preparation and
publication of the History of Masonry in California, and to report their·
findings and recommendations at the next session of Grand. Lodge.

Adopted.
Physical Qualifications
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was re-ferred the recommendation of the Grand Master embraced within that por-·
tion of his message entitled "Physical Qualifications," and certain resolu-·
tions proposed by W. Brother Ludley H. Nebeker, Past Master, Yerba
Buena Lodge No.· 403, and others, has given the same its earnest, careful:
and fraternal consideration and begs leave to report:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

195

We are not unappreciative of the'feeling of sympathy and concern given
by the Grand Master and these brethren to our sick and maimed youth,
veterans of this second World War, who may be interested in taking the
degrees of Masonry but who because of their misfortunes in battle are not
now possessed of the physical qualifications required of a candidate for
the degr.ees. There have been other wars, practically one every twenty-five
years since. we attained our independence, and other sons and brothers have
returned maimed and sick or returned not again. Always after one of these
holocausts our brethren in their sympathy have sought ways of receiving
some of these into our midst without violating the laws of the institution.
Some would knock at our door for whom we would like to make an
exception, for whom perhaps we have great admiration, who would perhaps bring great credit to the Craft. But even though physically qualified,
our membership has not embraced all the great and good men of our, or
past times, nor can we ever expect to do so. Masonry has traveled its
road, possibly a lonely one, at least a singular way owing to its peculiarities,
and, remember, if Masonry by reason of its peculiarities does not appeal
to any man, or disqualifies a man to take its degrees, remember, no man
has a vested right to take the degrees of Masonry, or to. request us to alter
our ways of life to include him.
Masonry is a peculiar institution, perhaps the most peculiar of all the
organizations in which men are accustomed to associate. For instance, by
the unwritten law of the fraternity no Mason will solicit anyone to take
the degrees of Masonry. There are no organizations, societies, clubs or
associations, whether of the laity or religious, in which the contrary is not
the practice; thus they seek by annual, or more or less frequent intervals,
membership drives to keep up their membership rolls. Few organizations
require unanimous ballot in the election of members; while it is religious
in its nature, it is not a religion; while it annually spends millions in relief,
it is not a chai;itable institution; while it will make a good man a better
man, it is not a reformatory, and its purpose is not to reform men. You,
perhaps, can point to other peculiarities wherein it differs from other
organizations of a similar nature.
·
In family and community relations we do not select our intimates because they .resemble the great mass of hu.manity, but, on the c<;>ntrary,
because they are different from their fellowmen.
'
We do not choose our wives, or our intimate friends, because they bear
a close resemqlance to the people about them, but because they are differ'ent. We lov~ them for their peculiarities, and we love Masonry not because it is like other societies and organizations, but because it is different.
We love Masonry for its traditions and legends unequaled in romance and
interest by any organization existent in these times; we love it for its
traditional history of centuries of service to man and mankind; we love it
for the legendary connection with the ancient mysteries, the 'firsf endeavors
of men to raise themselves..above the animal by the erection of a moral
philosophy. We love Masonry for what it is; we love it because so far as
we know, it has always been what it is today; we love it because it is a
rock of ages to ·which we may cling when all else is at sixes and sevens;
when other faiths and beliefs are tossed .upon the waves of the storm of
prejudice and confusion, in affairs of State or church, we can step into the
temple .of Masonry confident that there we shall find a· ·surcease from the
fires of political and religious debate; and it is easy to see why this is so.
It is so because from time immemorial (from a time whereof the
memory of man runneth not to the contrary) the course of the fraternity

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

has been guided by certain unalterable landmarks. Among the matters
controlled by the landmarks is the matter of ·the qualifications of candidates
for initiation.
As far back as our written record goes the qualifications of a candidate
has been a part of our landmarks and as you will note from what follows,
had in its inception, or in its later history, no connection with the occupation of the operative Mason.
This Grand Lodge has recognized and is committed to twenty-five
landmarks of which the eighteenth is ·"The qualifications of candidates for
admission" (Appendix, Ross. Digest, p. 547).
Section 6 of our Constitution reads as follows:
"Sec. 6. The Grand Lodge is the supreme Masonic power and authority
in this jurisdiction, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government-legislative, executive and judicial-limited only by a strict adherence to
the Ancient Landmarks of the Order .. ·· ."
The eleventh of the Ancient Charges and Regulations to which a Master
must submit before installation reads as follows:
"You admit that it is not within the power of any man or body of men
to make innovations in the body of Masonry."
We find the subject of physical qualifications of a candidate to receive
the degrees of Masonry considered in the proceedings of many of the
Grand Lodges in America, both before and after the formation of the
Grand Lodge of California.
In the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of New York, 1848, p. 57, appears the following:
"The rationale of the law excluding persons physically imperfect and
deformed ... is grounded on a principle recognized in the earliest ages
of the world, and will be found identical with that which obtained. among
the ancient Je.ws." Note that the sacrificial lamb must be one without
blemish.
In the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Georgia fqr the year 1852,
the Committee on Correspondence discusses the question of the admission
of maimed candidates. After tracing the existence of this law to remote
antiquity and finding it in the Egyptian and Mosaic rites, the r'e port discusses its symbolic meaning and concludes:
"Enough has been said to show at how remote a period in the history
of Masonry this important Landmark was erected. Can Man, in his shortsighted notions of convenience, vary its meaning? Can a Mason, the
solemnly installed Master of a Lodge of his brethren and equals, consistent
with the obligations he has voluntarily imposed upon himself, remove it
from its place?"
After an exhaustive examination of the above and other authorities,
Mackey, in his text book on Masonic Jurisprudence, enumerates as Landmark Eighteen-The qualification of a candidate for initiation. (Ross
Digest, 1943 Edition, p. 547).
As to this Landmark, Mackey states in his text book:
"Statutes, it is true, have from time to time, been enacted, enforcing
or explaining these principles; but the qualifications really arise from the
very nature of the Masonic institution, and from its symbolic teachings,
and have always existed as Landmarks."
The Landmarks being unrepeatable must ever continue in force and
constitute the unwritten law of Masonry.

The ritual constitutes binding law regarding the matters contained in it.
As to these matters the office of the Constitution and Regulations is substanti:illy to construe the ritual.
· ·
The first written law that we find explaining this Landmark is contained
in the fifth artide of the Old York Constitution of 926, and is in these
words:
"A candidate must be without blemish, and have the full and proper
use of his limbs; for a maimed man can do the Craft no gqod." (Digest,
p. 548.)
The next enactment is to be found in the Regulations of 1663 and is in
these words:
"No person hereafter shall be accepted a Freemason but such as are of
able body.'' (Digest, p. · 549.)
The next regulation in order of time is that contained in '~The Ancient
Charges of Makings," adopted about the year 1686 in ·the following language:
"3. That he that be made able in all degrees; that is, free born of good
kindred~ true, and no bondsman, and that he have his right limbs as a man ·
ought to have.'' (Digest, p. 550.)
'
And lastly, similar declarations, with respect to physical ability, are
made in Charges approved in 1772, at which time Masonry had long ceased
to be operative, which are as follows:
"No M;,ster should take an Apprentice unless he has sufficient employment for him, and unless he be a perfect youth, having no maim or defect
in his body that may render him uncapable of learning the art of serving
his Master's lord, and of being a Brother," etc. (Digest, p. 552.)
Such is the law as it stands today. The question then is shall we depart
from traditions, history, law and landmarks to meet a transitory demand
for loosening up on approaches. Shall we depart from our age old rules
under which this fraternity has become and now is greatest and most
universal of all fr~ternal orders.
If so, where shall we stop. Our friends who urge this departure will
readily claim no other changes ought to be made. But some one at next
Grand Lodge will propose to abandon the rule that prevents electioneering
in Lodges or that the Holy Bible shall be displayed on the Altar whenever
a Lodge is in session. 1'here could be found readily acceptable reasons for
these and many other changes in our Masonic ways.
But when the start is made to alter the body of Masonry the decline
will be speedy and the end riotous; no longer will we have that institution
to fly to as a rock of re~uge; no longer the- institution that has been and
now is the pride of the great body of Masons; no longer shall we have the
thing we loved and in our youth gave of our strength and very lives to
upbuild, maintain and perpetuate.
We, therefore, recommend that the r~commendation of the Grand
Master under the head of "Physical Qualifications" and the several proposed resolutions having for their purpose a change in the language of
Sections 208 and 209 of the Constitution and Ordinances be not adopted.

Relationship to Masonry
The Order of De Molay was conceived by Masons who saw a need for
a youth organization among the young men of America. Its ritual, particularly the Initiatory Degree, was written by an inspired Mason who put
into writing some of the .noblest sentiments ever expressed by man.
Sh.o rtly after its organization leading Masons who were interested in
young people brought De Molay to California and it was here that it had
a phenomenal growth. The need for s·uch an institution was proven by its
rapid increase in membership. In the early days of organization some overzealous Masons referred to them as Junior Masons, but this was quickly
suppressed by the De Molay leaders. In fact, the De Molay organization
has never claimed any Masonic affiliation and it). its ritual makes several
references to the fact that it is not such .a body.
However, the aims and purposes of De Molay are completely in line
with the philosophy of Masonry. It was conceived and nurtured by Masons
and in every jurisdiction its work has been so universally ac~laimed that
it has attracted more and more interested Masons to its support.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In California our 1922 Resolution urged the membership of the Fraternity fo give its moral and personal support to De Molay.
At least five of our Past Grand Masters in their annual messages have
seen fit to comment favorably upon the work of De Molay, particutarly the
late M. W. Albert E. Boynton, who said:
"In 1922 this Grand Lodge placed itself on record regarding the Order
of De Molay, and again reaffirmed its position in 1924. In its inception,
the organization was an experiment, but the numerical growth of this
wonderful movement and the results of its efforts among the young men
of our land has justified its existence and warranted the confidence that
we reposed in those who were inspired to found the Order and have governed it to the present time.
"White it is not a Masonic organization, its .importance in the future
of the Craft is one that we cannot overlook. I bespeak for the Order of
De Molay a continued interest by the Masons of this jurisdiction along
the lines embodied in the resolutions above referred to. Our future membership must come from the young man of today. If he is thoroughly conversant with the principles and teachings ·of the Masonic Fraternity, even
though taught to firm in an organization that is not Masonic but labors
under its shadow, just so far will our future strength and efficiency be
multiplied.
"There is a time in the life of every boy when some man or older boy
is taken as an ideal. That exemplar may be a good one or an evil one,
but in the initial instance that is not considered. Only after years can
det~rmine whether his mind has turned in the proper direction. I believe
that every man and Mason should continually carry this idea and ask
himself the question: 'Am I the. kind of man I would like to see my own
son or the young man of today become?' Individually and collectively,
Masonry owes a duty to the coming generation. An interest in an organization that has for its object the building of character and good citizenship
is one that will produce splendid dividends."
We feel that Brother Boynton's words completely outline the relationship which exists between Masonry and De Molay. Further De Molay is
an institution conceived by Masons, directed by Masons, and morally and
spiritually supported by Masons. In turn, by this support the members of
De Molay and the world at large have come to look upon the Order of
De Molay as an institution allied with, if not affiliated with Masonry.
For · these reasons we feel that a definite relationship exists between
Masonry and D e Molay and we cannot escape .that fact.

who know nothing but hate, racial and religious persecution. It is our duty
as Americans to see that these conditions shall not plague our country.
The need today is for an institution that will inculcate in the mind of
the American boy, love of country, respect for family, consideration for
others, toleration of all religious creeds and above all a sound theory of the
American way of life.
Our Masonic ritual is- full of references to our duty, as citizens, to
preserve and defend our country. We hold annual celebrations honoring
the Constitution of the United States. California Masonry has taken the
lead in support of the Public School System. We have even gone so far as
to establish and maintain Club Houses at our State University for students
of Masonic affiliations. Yet all of these efforts would be in vain if our
young people who take part in these activities were to fall under the spell
of subversive influences.
We have a real obligation to our youth, particularly our boys of teen
age, who will be the citizens and leaders of tomorrow. Masonry cannot
afford to stay in the background and watch the world go by. We have a
real opportunity to serve our young men and our country by supporting
an institution such as De Molay. For that reason we feel that the program
which we are to offer should deserve and receive the unanimous support of
this Grand Lodge.
The correspondence with the Grand Lodges of the United States has
disclosed much interesting information.
The Grand Lodge of Michigan has taken over the complete operation
and sponsorship of De' Molay in that state. Other states permit Lodges
to directly sponsor -Chapters, others allow De Molay Chapters to meet in
Masonic Temples but prohibit' sponsorship. A negligible number prohibit
any support of De Molay. By and large most Grand Jurisdictions have
approved De Molay and have commended it to its members to foster and
support.
·
In analyzing these methods we have determined that De Molay in
California is more in need of advisors and direction rather than sponsorship. The Grand Council of De Molay has the mea,.ns to charter Chapters
without direct sponsorship. The real need in California is for able and
willing advisors. Men who are capable of working and counseling with
young people.
If sponsorship was permitted we are afraid that enthusiastic Lodges would
sponsor Chapters and then after the novelty wore off would allow them
to drift. We feel that the De Molay leaders can handle matters better if
sponsorship were kept under their control. Further, sponsorship would
entail financial support and there is no reason why the Order of De Molay
cannot stand on its own feet. We do not feel that Masonry should in any
way become obligated to the financial support of any institution that is
. non-Masonic in character.
We do, however, have a plan that we feel would solve the matter in
California. It is a plan of education and coordination rather than one of
sponsorship. Our plan would create a group of men who would act as coordinators between De Molay and Masonry in our state. From time to
time they would be authorized to bring to our Lodges the message and
needs of De Molay, to enlist the aid of men who would be willing to assist
in the work and to keep a watchful eye on the activities of De Molay.
Finally they would report annually. to Grand Lodge the progress of that
Order in California. Accordingly we recommend · the following plan.

Conclusion

for such an organization as De Molay. The upheaval of war, the shifting
of population and the change in habits of the American family have
caused a serious condition in our National social structure. Ali' over our.
country authorities are making a serious effort to combat this situation.
All agree that a breakdown in the outlook of our young people will seriously undermine the future . of our country. Further we have all seen the
result of the regimentation of the youth of Europe by the Nazi Youth
Movement in Germany, by the Fascists in Italy and in Asia by the fanatic
Japanese mi,litarists. E~ch grotip captured the fancy of their youth and
developed them to follow blindly the teachjngs which have brought the
world to misery and bloodshed and have created a group of young people

be adopted and the recommendation was adopted.

"that no member shall be appointed on more than one committee" be held over for consideration at the next Annual Communication and the recommendation was adopted.

Report of Grand Secretary
Your attention is directed to the Grand Secretary's Annual Report
which indicates many interesting developments. Membership of 161,752 is
an all-.time high. Previous top was in 1945, 150,368.
The following is a comparison of the five years, 1937 to 1941 inclusive,
with the five years 1942 to 1946 inclusive. Sales of supplies have almost
doubled in the past five years. It is likewise true of Proficiency Certificates
issued. The receipts from dues, endowments, legacies, -etc., have more than
doubled. Income for the year just closed was three-fourths of the entire
income for the five years 1937 to 1941. These gains are gratifying.
The establishment of Monthly Membership Returns has made it possible to keep Grand Lodge membership records up-to-date besides correcting innumerable errors in membership records. It also makes possible a
current membership analysis and report. Lo<lge and Grand Lodge membership records are in the ,best condition they have ever been.
Collections from various sources have , been centralized and better
accounting has resulted. Financial records_ are now current.
Establishment and encouragement of Secretaries' Associations in various parts of the Jurisdiction h'as resulted in much benefit to all. One hundred and six secretaries spent last Sunday afternoon considering their problems and exchanging ideas.
The general appearance of Grand Lodge_ offices has been greatly improved by the installation of modern furnishings, and the new equipment
with adegu'ate staff has greatly increased the efficiency and effectiveness
of Grand Lodge office.
Audit reports indicate good management and accounting. All monies
have been properly accounted for and records are in good condition.
The Grand Secretary and staff are commended for the good work they
are doing.

Portrait of Lawrence C. Kelley
Within ten days of his installation as Grand Master . at our last Annual
Communication, Grand Lodge suffered the loss of its new Grand Master
the Most Worshipful Lawrence C. Kelley, by death.
·
'
In his passing the Jurisdiction underwent a genuine tragedy. Brother
Ke1ley had carefully planned to devote the entire year to the service of
Masonry. It was indeed a misfortune that the Masons of this Jurisdiction
could not have had the benefits of a year's service as Grand Master of this
able and devoted Mason. However, the Fates decreed otherwise.
While Brother Kelley was denied the opportunity of serving his year
as Grand Master and yet, it seems to this committee that his portrait
should be included in our gallery of portraits. There are already in that
gallery at least two portraits of other than Past Grand Masters.

be painted from portraits and descriptions that may be supplied of him.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that the Grand Secretary be

Lawrence C. Kelley, at a cost not to exceed $300 and when completed to
include it in the gallery of portraits.

Report of Masonic Homes
The report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes and the report of the
certified public accountant concerning the Masonic Homes have been reviewed by your Committee on Finance.
The reports as usual are very complete and indicate that the finances
of the Homes are in excellent condition.
During the last four years the income of the Homes has exceeded the
expenses by $1,040,034.60, including the sum of $290,673.39 for the year
1946.
It is to be remembered that no special per capita tax has been raised
for the operation of the Homes since 1944 and none is requested this year.
The trustees have recommended that in view of the excellent financial
condition of the Homes the portion of Section 99 of the Constitution, providing for a 50 cent per capita tax for a building fund for the Homes, be
repealed.
This committee desires to compliment the trustees of the Masonic
Homes on their excellent financial condition and heartily concurs in their
recommendation that the per capita tax be repealed.
We, therefore, recommend that the matter· be referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for the preparation of the needed legislation.

"Let me do my work from day to day
In field or forest, at the desk or loom,
In roaring market-place, or tranquil room;
Let me but find it in my heart to say,
When vagrant wishes beckon me astray,
'This is my work, my blessing, not my doom;
Of all who live, I am the one by whom
This work can best be done in my own way.'
Then shall I see it not too great nor small,
To suit my spirit and to prove my powers;
Then shall I cheerfully greet the working hours,
And cheerful turn when the long shadows fall,
At eventide, to play and love, and rest,
Because I know for me my work is best.''

Retirement Allowance
Your commi.ttee _is in accord with the recommendations made by the
Grand Master m his message that an appropriate retirement allowance
should be made by Grand Lodge, upon the retirement of her whom so
many Masons in ~he Jurisdiction affectionately know as Miss Van. This
year sees the completion. of thirty years service by her. Her services
have been long and faithful and were performed with a very great devotion to the interests of Masonry. Many have been the brethren of the
Jurisdiction who are indebted to Miss Van for favors. rendered. No matter
wh?t ~~e may have beei:i called upon to do," either through the request
?f md1v1dual Masons or in the performance of the duties required of her,
1t has always been performed graciously and gladly.
. Some years ago o~e who prefers anonymity for his good deed, paid
Miss Van a great tribute by presenting her with a framed copy of a
verse b:y Henry Van Dyke_. Because of the beauty of the wording, the
appropriateness of the sentiment and that she is so eminently deserving
of the tribute, it is fitting that it should have a place in the annals of Grand
Lodge. We therefore quote:

215

This Sonnet, by Henry Van Dyke, so aptly expresses the philosophy
of the life of her to whom it is sent; the happy faculty of doing, with
pleasure, whatever comes to her hand to do and constantly and with
graciousness and with ease doing those thoughtful daily acts which makes
life sweet for those with whom she associates, it is being printed and
framed and sent to Miss Van.
Knowing that the question of retirement allowance for the employees
of Grand Lodge was being discussed, the members of this committee have,
during the past year, done considerable research work on the problem.
This research discloses that retirement allowances are largely based on
the average salary received during the last ten years of employment and
that the amount paid ranges from 30 per cent to 60 per cent of the salary,
the lower percentage representing much more nearly the amount allowed.
The salary paid to Miss Van by Grand Lodge for the past six years
has been $2,400 annually and for the four years prior thereto $2,200 annually . .
This committee has decided to recommend to Grand Lodge that it
allow Miss Van an annual retirement allowance of $900. This will be
38.6 per cent of the average salary received by her for the past ten years.
Your committee feels that this retirement allowance must not be regarded as a pension, or as granted because of need, but that it has been
richly earned by her in thirty years of faithful service. This committee
therefore offers the following resolution and rec.o mmends its adoption:
Resolved, That upon her retirement there be allowed Marian Van
Buskirk, during the remainder of her life, the sum of $900 annually, payable monthly, the allowances to commence November 1, 1946.

REPORT OF RITUAL COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grani:l Lodge of California:
The Ritual Committee has had referred to it the resolution of Abell
Lodge No. 146 F. & M., requesting that the ballot box be not placed upon
the Holy Bible during the voting.
The Ritual Committee does not 'approve of the suggested change.
The Holy Bible is sacred not because it is an assemblage of paper, cardboard, and leather but because of the divinely inspired thoughts that are
recorded in it. It is the human thoughts associated with the book and
arising from its words not the physical aspects of the book itself that entitles it to a position upon our altar.
No one has eyer suggested the removal of the Square and Compass
from the book on our altar because of the symbolism of those working
tools to one skilled in our craft.
The hand upon the Bible during the obligation is proper because of
the human ideas associated with the act.
The ballot box is not pieces of fashioned wood, balls and cubes but
is the guardian key to the doors of the temple. The full appreciation of
its proper symbolism to the craft and an understanding that it is thus
placed upon .our Bible as a reminder to each voting member of his duties
and responsibilities to our order to see that none but good ·men and true
enter our doors, thus preserving the integrity of our institution will remove from the mind of the Mason any suggestion of sacrile~e · in its
placeme~t. We, therefore, recommend that the resolution of Abell Lodge
No. 146 ' be not adopted.

Respectfully submitted,
OBED

w. CARR,

A . M . w ARREN'

G. c. DEFORREST,
CHAS. SCHWARTZ,
CHESTER

H. WARLOW,

D ecision ( e)
There hc.s been referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence Decision (e) of the Grand Master.
The facts in this decision are as follows:
A resident within the concurrent jurisdiction of Santa Barbara Lodge
No. 192, Magnolia Lodge No. 142 and La Cumbre Lodge No. 642 addressed a letter to each of said Lodges to authorize Carpenteria Lodge
No. 444 to receive and act upon his application for degrees.
La Cumbre Longe .No. 642 granted the waiver of jurisdiction, but
Magnolia Lodge which met on the following evening refused to waive
jurisdiction.
The Grand Master ruled the waiver of jurisdiction by the Lodge whose
Stated Meeting preceded by one night the meeting of the Lodge that on
its meeting night refused the waiver bound all the other Lodges having
concurrent jurisdiction.
·
Section 220 of the Ordinances provides that if any Lodge having concurrent jurisdiction shall refuse the waiver, no other can, within twelve
months, act upon the request of the same person.
It is the opinion of your committee that applicant having requested the
three Lodges to act and one of them having refused to grant the request
brings the case within the provisions of Section 220.
We, therefore, recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be not
approved.

Adopted.
