In 1944, the Master of Truth Lodge No. 628 was cai!ed ·for induction
into the Armed Forces of. the United States. He declared himself to be a
"conscientious objector" and was assigned to non-combatant service with
the result that he was unable to perform the duties of his office during .
the remainder of his term. In September 1944 Truth Lodge requested the
then Grand Master to declare the office of Master vacant and to grant a
dispensation to elect a new Master. The reque.st was denied. In November.
1944 Truth Lodge adopted a resolution declaring that said Master "has
~10t served the Lodge as Master since July 1,· 1944, owing to his removal
from the Jurisdiction, ;md . : . that he shall not be considered and is
hereby declared not to be considered the Past Master of this Lodge."
Decision of the legal questions involved in this case goes far beyond
its effects upon one who was a "conscientious objector" and might, under
certain circumstances, determine the rights of. several hundred of our
brethren who now carry the title and status of Past Masters. It might
well challenge the right of many here today to sit as members of this
Grand Lodge. After long and earnest consideration of the problems involved the committee has reached the conclusion:
1. That it should have further time to consider the need for new legislation on the subjects under discussion and
2. That there are insufficient facts before us to serve as the basis for a
just decision.
We, therefore, recommend that the case be· referred back for an investigation and finding by the Grand Master on the facts that gave rise
to the original resolutions.

therein."

of the conferring of."

First: Resolved: That Section 50 as it now reads be stricken and that
a new section numbered 50 be enacted in words and figures as follows:
Sec. 50. It shall be the duty of the Grand Lecturer:
1st. To supervise and direct the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the
Inspectors in the performance of their duties, and 'to require conformity
with the adopted ritual and work.
2nd. To examine the Assistant Grand Lecturers and issue certificates
of proficiency to such as are duly qualified, on receiving notice of their
appointment by the Grand Master.
3rd. To see that the Inspectors examine all Officers who are required
to produce certificates of proficiency at their installation in accordance
with these ordinances.
4th. To render to Grand Lodge at each Annual Communication a full
and detailed account of his services during the year, and to set forth
therein a report of the condition of the Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction.
5th. To cause to be held Lodges of Instruction for the Inspectors at
each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge; and at his convenience
· to attend Schools of Instruction held by Assistant Grand Lecturers or
Inspectors.
6th. To call and preside at meetings of the Ritual Committee whenever
in his judgment it is necessary or advisable for such committee to convene.
He shall receive such compensation for his services as the Grand
Lodge may direct.
Sec?nd : Resolve.cl : That Section 51 be.. amended by striking the words
Appo1nt four Assistant Grand Lecturers, each of whom" in lines one
and two, and in lieu thereof insert the following after the word shall in
line one: " divide the Jurisdiction into four general divisions and shall
.appoint for each of such division an Assistant Grand Lecturer'. who shall
be a Past Master and member of a Lodge in such division and who shall
be considered an appointed officer of Grand Lodge and who."

and figures as follows:
Section 53: The Grand Master shall divide the jurisdiction into districts, and shall appoint for each district an Inspector, who shall be a
Past Master of the jurisdiction and a resident of the district for which
he is appointed, and who shall, before entering upon his duties, produce
a certificate from the Grand Lecturer or an Assistant Grand Lecturer
that he is proficient in the work and lectures adopted by the Grand Lodge,
and is qualified to act as Inspector.
It shall be the duty of the Inspector:
1st. To hold Schools of Instruction in his district and instruct . the
officers of the Lodges in the ritual.
2nd. To require any Master of a Lodge in his distriet to convene his
Lodge for inspection, and shall report to the Grand Master the failure
of any Master to do so.
3rd. To cause to be organized within his district an Officers' Association and to supervise meetings of such association for the purpose of
instruction in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations of the
Grand Lodge which relate to the government of the Lodge, for instruction
in the proper administration of the affairs of the Lodges, and such other
matters as may be for the welfare of the craft. It shall be the duty of
the officers of his district to at.tend such meetings .
.4th. To issue certificates, where required by law, to the officers of
the Lodges when they are qualified to give the work and lectures required o_f them respectively, and are thoroughly proficient in those porti~ris <;>f the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge which relat~ fo. the government of the Lodge.

of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1946, and present herewith the

$163,571.00

The revenue from per capita dues and other sources exceeded the expenses
and appropriations by $56,451.27, as shown by Exhibit E. A bequest from
Reuben Lloyd of $5,000.00, made the total increase to capital $61,451.27.
All per capita dues, as reported on the 1945 annual returns from constituent
Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Schedules 1 and 2 show proof of the revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1945 returns and the $25.00

The total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total cash received from the
Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts ·Were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries.
Distributions welle made by checks and supported by vouchers properly approved by the Committee on Accounts. All bank balances were verified by
correspondence with the depositaries. Certified lists of the securities .were
received from the Anglo California National Bank which holds the securities
for safe keeping. The securities as recorded in the books of account were
checked to these lists. All interest and dividends due thereon were received and
accounted for. Government bonds purchased during the year amounted to
$80,270.00. No securities were sold.
The two special funds, the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands Dues
Fund and the Philippine Relief Fund, were closed out by sending the entire
·funds to the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands.
We certify that, in our opinion, 'the attached statements set forth the financial condition of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of · California, as at July 31,
1946, and the result of its operations for the fiscal year 1945-46.

We have audited the accounts and records of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1946, and present herewith the

Comments
Cash :
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest due was received and turned over to the Masonic Homes. The
total income received by the Homes from the Endowment and Luckenbach
Funds amoun~ed to $54,797.53.
S ernrities:
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed at
market valu~ when received, or "at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual value
is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment Fund
were received from the Anglo California National Bank. The · records were
checked to these lists and those not listed were found in the office of the Grand
Secretary, and were inspected by us.

following increase for the current year :

MASONIC HOMES AUDIT
September 28, 1946.
Masonic Homes of California,
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:
We have audited the books and records of the Masonic Homes of California
for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1946, and present herewith the following
statements :
Statements of Funds and Properties
Exhibit A: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1945,'
to July 31, 1946.
Exhibit B: Balance sheet, July 31, 1946.
Schedule B-1: Statement of securities owned, July 31, 1946.
Schedule B-2: Statement of Entertainment Fund.
Schedule B-3 : Statement of Stud~nts' Loan and Scholarship Fund.
Schedule B-4 : Statement of Summer Camp Fund.
Schedule B-5 : Statement of Post-War Reserve Fund.
Schedule B-6: Statement of Charles L. Patton Fund.
Schedule B-7 : Statement of C. N. Flint Trust Fund.
Schedule B-8 : Statement of C. N. F lint Annuity F und.
Schedule B-9 : Statement of C. N. Flint Annuity "Morgan" Fund.
Schedule B-10 : Statement of George and Harriet Wadleigh Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-11 : Statement of Harriet Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-12 : Statement of Verbarg Fund.
Schedule B-13: Statement of Decotci Monthly Grant Fund.

Exhibit C : Statement of Revenue and Expense, 1945-46.

Exhibit E: Statement of Direct Operating Expense-Covina~
Schedule D-1: Detailed Operating Expense-Decoto.
Schedule E-1: Detailed Operating Expense-Covina.
Comments
Cash:
All recorded receipts were properly accounted for and deposited in the proper
funds bank account. All interest due on securities and notes was received and
~c~ounted for,· except those marked with . an ';asterisk on the securities statement, Sche<lule B-1. Disbursements were made by checks and supported by
proper vouchers. Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the
depositaries, and reconciled to the books.
·

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

253

The .1945 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the amounts
due to the Homes thereon, plus the $25.00 contributions received for the first
three quarters of the current year, agreed with the amount turned over to the
Treasurer of the Homes by the Grand Secretary.
Securities:
A detailed list of all securities owned by the Masonic Homes is shown on
our Schedule B-1. Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost, all other securities
were received by donation and are listed at market value at the time donated.
When market value is unknown, a nominal value of $1.00 is used for purpose
of record.
Life insurance policies are recorded at the amount due at the death of the
insured, if determinable, otherwise at a value of $1.00.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as at July
31, 1946. Three notes were paid in full during the year. Principal and interest
payments were received on all the others except one, on which no payments
were received.
The older real estate is recorded at the assessed value at the time of donation. Real estate donated during the past several years has been recorded at
a value of $1.00.
All securities were accounted for as held by the Anglo California National
Bank, or in the office of the Grand Secretary. Those held by the bank were
verified by a certification from the bank. Those in the office of the Grand
Secretary were inspected.Other Funds:
The Masonic Homes has numerous separate funds which have been created
for definite or special purposes. Full details of these funds are shown on the
attached statements, Schedules B-2 to B-13, inclusive. Payments due from the
annuity funds in accordance with the contracts and agreements, were made.
All in't erest due on the securities in these funds were received and deposited
in the proper bank accounts. All bank balances were verified by correspondence
with the depositaries. T he securities were verified by certification from the
Anglo California National Bank which holds them for safe-keeping.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
FOREWORD
A New Yor)c jurist once said of a certain lawyer that in trying to be
tediously clear, he was clearly tedious. Your Committee on Correspond~nce
has sought to avoid that fault in our review this year of some 53 sister
jurisdictions. By a winnowing, screening process we have s~lected th.e excerpts which follow as items of information which we feel .will be of interest and value.
We searched diligently for those things of moment to the California
craft. But, though we had our eyes cocked for that four-leaf clover which
is the object of those who browse in the pastures of research-the discovery~the item overlooked · by others-we were not so fortunate as we
had hoped. This was because the jurisdictions were unable to function
with customary, peacetime activities. Only a comparatively few could produce other than brief or statistical items at abridged sessions. Fortunately,
this handicap imposed by wartime conditions has now been removed, so the
harvest next year will be more plentiful.
Most grand juri.s dictions have had an abundance of new members.
Those on the higher watchtowers of Masonry seem satisfied with the increase, although some have read the handwriting on the wall. They have
sounded warnings against the inevitable let-down. War years w ere a n incentive to membership growth. Peace years present an opportunity to
cultivate a continuance of the original zest and enthusiasm.
The membership increase has been matched by the problem of deciding whether physical impairment, occasioned in many instances by
wounds on battlefields, are such as disqualify an otherwise worthy applicant.
·
· Some jurisdictions have ventured into a discussion of the inherent
necessity of preserving our form of government in these post war days.
It is not hard to assert that we may be beset by attempts to change our
established framework. But, we are cautioned not to intrude as Masons
into a political arena. Debate on these subjects can often descend into
a duel. Adherents become overzealous, dogmatize and dispute. In times
past; for expressions of views on these .subjects, men have been thrown
into dungeons, stretched upon . racks and burned at stakes. T he cardinal
Masonic principle-charity-forbids such discussion.
But, thert· are certain closely allied questions so basic in nature that on
these our grand jurisdictions do speak. Thus, it has been said that we
1
should recall why our Masonic minded countries stand as a bulwark
against communism. They are the. nations which have produced the
Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, the Declaration . of Independence, the
Constitution of the United States, the Anglo-Saxon common · law, the
ideals and practices of human rights and justice. These political concepts are in tune with the basic tenets of our craft.
The fundamental need stressed in the reviews appears to be the translation of our agreed ideals into reality in our daily lives. We know that

405

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

we should pr«ctice all the virtues of temperance, sobriety, chastity, fortitude, prudence, justice and charity. Our ears have heard the eloquent
and oft repeated affirmation of the brotherhood of man. Only by our
actions will we make our ideals reality. Prattle of principles without action is a rimless zero. We must breathe life into these ideals by a positive
enthusiasm for them, for good, for justice and for decency. Our activities must match our beliefs and professions. An unparalleled opportunity
is now offered whereby we can help our brethren in the devastated
countries. Following is an excerpt of a letter ·to your chairman just received from the Grand Master, Michael Goldenberg, of the Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands.

It is ·well that we remember, however, speaking of Masonry's entry
into a new era, that similar changes have oCCt!rred since the dawn of
man's experience. But the principles of Masonry are everlasting. As
Froude truly said, "The moral law is written upon the Tablets of Eternity."
Albert Einstein aptly remarked, "What the world needs is not more
physics, but more ethics." Even so eminent a scientist as Nobel Prize
winner Professor Miliken recently stated, "The most important thing in
the Universe is moral and spiritual values." Let us have the courage to
realize he expressed in · that statement, not only the sound future of Freemasonry, but ·the future of civilization itself.

404

"Our greatest problem now is to .organize some means to secure
enough funds on a long range loan in order to assist our eighty
odd Lodges to house themselves in adequate small temples in the
various provinces. On my last visit to the distant provinc~s, I
found nothing left of the beautiful little temples, all destroyed.
They met in the homes of brethren or in shell-torn school houses.
Our first urgent concern now is to build on the ruins of the Grand
Lodge "Plaridel" Temple which would cost us around $50,000.
The next large item is to loan on a long term plan to about fifty
of our Lodges in the, provinces in order to enable them to build
their small temples. It is my idea to have them build wooden
frame buildings, uniformly made, located in the commercial center
of each town. Rent the ground floor for stores, the second floor
for offioes and the third for Masonic purposes. This will enable
them to have an income to pay off the loan. The cost would be
· about $8,000 each. It has been suggested that a voluntary donation
of 3 cents or the cost of a postage stamp by members of th e
fraternity in America would probably be enough to cover the bill. "
During his wartime assignment in the Philippines, your chairman visited
the then Acting Grand Master, Michael Goldenberg and his co"- workers in
Masonic re~abil\tation. If ever the finger . of Masonry pointed to courageous
and true brethren, and to a place where help is needed now, it is to the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands.
Masonry is now entering a new era. Social orders that existed for
centuries are being changed. Scientific developments astound the imagination. Masons have recognized these events.
This new era has called forth comments of criticism that our offices
are not conducted with .modern methods. We have been admonished to
promote eff,iciency, economy and effectiveness in our administrative affairs.
One Grand' Master said:
"I found that we were clinging to ancient methods ~f administration of Lodge and Grand Lodge affairs under the misapprehension that everything in Masonry is unchangeable. There appeared to be vital need for the application of sound business practice to Lodge and Grand Lodge affairs. Waste and inefficiency are
often apparent, particularly in the smaller Lodges. I attempted,
therefore, to separate the functional from the philosophical, to
urge Masons everywhere to bring the administration of the Lodge
in step with the times."

SUGGESTIONS FOR POST-WAR PROCEDURE
Freemasonry today especially speaks to the world a message of universality. It has been the one force which has a common ground whereon
men may meet religiously, socially and morally. Thus, it can offer that
patterrt of human conduct which is the one great hope of man. The precepts of Freemasonry are simple things, yet they co~e "out of the genius
of that fraternity which has drawn upon the riches of the whole world
and the best and finest ideals of all ages."
Arkansas, 1945 (Grand Master):
Even though the roaring of guns and blasting of bombs has stopped,
we certainly cannot afford at any time to relax our efforts in promoting
the ideals for which Masonry stands, guarding against over-confidence
and· slackening of efforts; for dissention still exists among people the
world over and this is true even in our own nation. New ideas and
philosophies are being offered on every hand as to what man peeds in order to live, and it is my sincere belief that no people can long maintain
their rights or independence when they are divided against themselves.
Arkansas, 1945 (Grand Orator):
In addressing you on the Obligations of a Master Mason, I lrefer not
only to those ritualistic vows assumed at the altar, but to those larger
and just as binding obligations which are implied and of necessity encompassed within the specifically repeated obligation. Merely repeating a part
of a r;itual does not in itself make a man a Mason, and the man who does
no more for Masonry than is demanded. of him by the obligation he repeats
is in no wise a true Mason. Masonry begins in the heart, and unless the
beginning is there the assuming of all the obligations contained in the
entire ')VOrk will do very little towards making the man a Mason. The

410

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

man who joins a Masonic Lodge becomes a point of. contact between the
world and the brotherhood, and the world no less 'thart the fraternity has
a right to demand of him that he be a living embodiment of the creed
which he professes. The wearing of the emblem of the fraternity should
mean more than a method of recognition between members, and until
it does Masonry cannot function as it should.
A most important obligation to which I wish to call attention is the
obligation to our country. If there is any one class on earth to which this
obligation should carry an especial appeal, it is to Masons. Emphasizing
as we do, religious liberty and freedom of thought and speech, and because of the very prominent part which Masonry has played in the building of this great commonwealth of ours. When our forefathers, in search
of religious liberty turned their faces toward the new land of promise, they
brought with them their Masonic Altars and set them up in the wilderness.
They placed upon them the Book of Holy Writ, symbolic of God's law
for the government of man and upon the Book they placed the· Square,
symbol of equality before the law, and the Compasses, symbol of that due
restraint of personal liberty which is necesssary for the protection of the ·
rights of others. Then as the American colonies grew and prospered in
this land of "Milk and Honey," the Masonic lodges grew and prospered
with them: The history of the two being inseparably linked together.
The Green Dragon Tavern, where the plans for the famous Boston
Tea Party were formed was not only owned by, but was the meeting
place of St. Andrews Masonic Lodge, and the Secretary's record closes
with a line of Capital T's across the bottom of the page, which to say
the least is rather significant. Paul Revere, who spread the news of the
arrival of the British was a Mason and a junior officer of this Lodge.
Robert Newman who hung the lantern in the belfry of Old North Church,
was a Mason, as was William Dawes who rode in the opposite direction
· to Paul Revere, and spread the same tidings. Patrick Eenry, regardless
of the sound of his name, was a Mason. General Joseph Warren, the first
General to fall in Freedom's cause was a Past Grand Master of Masons in
Massachusetts. J ohri Hancock, the first signer of the Declaration of Independence, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton and
James Madison were Masons. There were fifty-six signers of the Declaration of Independence, and all but six were Masons. Of the fifty-five
members of the Constitutional Convention, fifty were Masons, and it was presided over by our Masonic Brother George Washington. General Lafayette
was a Mason, and out of the twenty-nine Major Generals serving under
Washington. twenty were Masons. Of over sixty Brigadier Generals' under him all but one were Masons. Of the nine Major Generals who were
not Masons, one was Lee, who failed at Monmouth; Gates, who continually plotted to overthrow his Chief; the Infamous Conway and General·
Mifflin who were dismissed from the service for negligence of duty. Our
predecessors in Masonry builded well and it is our duty as their successors to see to it that the principles for which they fought are preserved.
It is our duty to see to it that we do not interfere with the right of
any man to worship God in any way that he chooses. On the other hand,
it is equally our duty to see to it that no man interfere with . our right to
worship God as we choose, whether he be in authority, civil or ecclesiastical, whether he live in America or Rome. There can be no merging of
state and church. Neither can we allow any one, ecclesiastical or otherwise
to interfere with the greatest institution on this continent next to the .•
home and church-the free sch.Pol, as the perpetuation of American ideals
rests almost wholly with our schools.

Our predecessors in Masonry builded well and we as their successorsas true Masons, and real Americans must see that the principles for which

By far the greatest danger confronting America today is the menace
to our civil institutions brought about by those on the inside of America,
not on the outside, and it is high time that we as Masons awake to the
perils that confront us and learn to work and earn Master's wages. We
must arouse in the hearts of our countrymen a love for our country,

In this generation, when the peoples of our world have so flippantly
traded faith, peace and brotherly love for war, hatred and evil, more and
more does it become apparent that the oracles of God do not speak only
through the pulpit, that dogmatic religion is not sufficient; that not only
must we have faith in God and also understanding among men; that not
only must we have a religion of faith, but a religion of human fellowship.
To that understanding and fellowship Freemasonry points the way.
But our institution has been fashioned to a formula so old that it is
new; so orthodox that it is radical; so traditional through the years that
unless it is daily implemented upon the lives o{ men in these days of discord and chaos, it may still be forgotten.
Never before in its long history has Freemasonry had a greater opportunity to translate human rights for themselves into human rights for all
mankind; to transmute Masonic ideals into universal realities and to bring
victory to the hearts of men rather than the armies of men.
This accomplishment can never be achieved through its spirit but only
through its action. Its moving and compelling force for good is not found
in the Lodge room, but only in the hearts of its members.
Freemasonry today as never before speaks to the world a message of
universality. It has been the one force which has found a common ground
whereon men may meet religiously, socially and morally, and thus it can offer
. that pattern of human conduct which is the one great hope of man. The
precepts of Freemasonry are simple things, yet 't hey come " out of the
genius of that Fraternity which has drawn upon the riches of the whole
world and the best and finest ideals of all ages."

Georgia, 1945 (Grand Master):
I have said we are living in a new world. It does not necessarily follow that it is to be a good world. Before it can be a better world, we

To me, one of the most interesting revelations of Masonic history lies
in the fact that it was the gentlemen of this fraternity, more largely than
all other contributing factors combined, who brought this great nation
into being; nurtured it; developed it and, through posterity, have handed
down to us-you and me-not only the responsibility but the high privilege
of maintaining and perpetuating what they had achieved through so much
heroic sacrifice and effort.
In contemplating .the task that lies ahead, we can draw courage and
inspiration from the lives of the men who made this nation great. For,
if they, guided as they were by an unfaltering faith in the fatherhood of
God and the brotherhood of man, could penetrate the wilderness that once
enveloped America and overcame the many obstacles that lay in their
pathway and place in our hands this nation with its untold wealth, its ·
unlimited natural resources, with a government organized by and for the
people- then surely we, the descendants of those men guided by that same
principle and inspired by their loyalty and devotion and sacrifice, can, without disturbing the fundamentals, adjust our lives to the changed conditions
and, through our government, make a liberal contribution to world stabilization.
·

who to my mind has always watched over and guided this nation in its
hours of peril, be with us · now and show us the way. May He give us
courage and fortitude that looks beyond the ever-crowding problems and

M aryland, 1945 ( Grand Master):
Freemasonry is a charitable, benevolent, educatio~al and religious
society, adhering to its own landmarks. Its principles are proclaimed as
widely as men will hear. Its only secrets are in its methods of recognition
and of symbolic instruction.
It is charitable in that it is not organized for profit and none of its
income inures to the benefit 'of any individual, but all is devoted to the
promotion of the welfare and happiness of mankind.
It is benevolent in that it teaches and exe~plifies altruism as a duty.
It is educational in that it teaches by prescribed ceremonials a sy'stem
of morality and brotherhood based upon the Sacred Law.
It is religious in that it teaches monotheism, the Volume of the Sacred
Law is opened upon its altars · whenever a Lodge is in session, reverence
for God is ever present in its ceremonial, and to its brethren are constantly
addressed lessons of morality; yet it is not sectarian or theological.
It is a social organization only so far as it furnishes additional inducement that men may foregather in numbers, thereby providing more material for its primary work of fducation, or worship, and of charity.
Through the improvements and strengthening of the character of the
individual rr.an, Freemasonry seeks to improve . the community. Thus it
impresses upon its members the principles of personal righteousness and
personal •responsibility; enlightens them as to those things which make .
for human welfare, and .inspires them with that feeling of charity, or good
will, toward all mankind which will move them to translate principles and
conviction into action.
To that end, it teaches and stands for the worship of God; for truth
and justice; for fraternity and philanthropy; for enlightenment a~d orderly liberty, civil, religious and intellectual. It charges each of its members to be true and loyal to the lawful government of the country to which
he owes allegiance and to the obediency of the laws of any state in which
he may be.
It believes that the attainment of these objectives is best accomplished
by laying a broad basis of principle upon which men of every race, country,
sect and opinion may unite rather than by setting up a restricted platform
upon which only those of certain races, creeds and opinions can assemble.
Oregon , 1945 (Grand O rator):
Heretofore the major races of the world have been separated by space,
by protective oceans, and by barriers of tongue. Their comparatively
small attempts to intermingle met with mutual aversion. The oriental
wanted to keep the white man out of Asia. In turn we built legislative
walls against the oriental. Only this year did our own state legislature
take steps to repeal the Chinese exclusion act. Neither the white nor the
oriental indicated any brotherly attitude toward the black. But this is
changing. Our men have gone to war. They have fought and lived with
the oriental, the black man, the Polynesian, and others about the world.
Their experience has opened our eyes .to the reality that all men of all
races are possessed of souls. Some have simple minds and lack a formal
education, some are irresponsible and uncouth, but one can readily sense
the breaking down of racial barriers. One further hopefol sign is evident.

thought mto practice. We do not recognize negro Masonry in our own
country, although about the world we recognize many regular lodges
among whose membership are those of red, yellow, or black skin. I fully
realize that this bold suggestion will not meet with favor among all the
grand jurisdictions of the United States, nor even with all the members
of our own Grand Lodge. But I feel that Masonry should look at a very
practical problem in a very practical way. If we mean what we say, we
would willingly, admit to our lodges men of all races who are found worthy
under our moral and religious standards. To act otherwise is to become
dogmatic. We will find ourselves, not among the leaders of great world
movements, but left behind among those who could not progress with a
progressing world.
Wisconsin, 1945 (Grand Master):
In all of my written and spoken · messages, I have endeavored to emphasize the supreme importance and high value of Masonic philosophy
and particularly the application of that philosophy to modern times and
conditions. Our Masonic philosophy in the abstract is a beautiful system
of morality but it is quite commonly retained in mental moth balls for
use only in the lodge room. I have often said that too many Masons deposit their idealism upon the tiler's desk with their aprons upon leaving
the Temple. Too many of us are satisfied to give lip service to those ideals
and fail to recognize in our everyday transactions and in our social and
business relationships the situations to which those ideals were and are
intend~d to apply. We like to speak solemnly of brotherhood . but do
noth~ng about the hates and grudges we continue to nurse through life;
we hke to talk about toleration but often join quickly in any campaign
against races and creeds not our own. Perhaps it is true that human nature
being what it is, w·e must expect that there will never be a man virtuous
enough to m easure up to the perfection of Masonry. Perhaps this ex-·
plains the hold of the Masonic philosophy upon its members because an
ideal that is easily attainable is soon lost sight of.
~t is an easy matter to pledge allegiance to abstract ideals but it takes
courage to live up to those ideals when one's personal interest is involved.
Many of us speak feelingly of charity, human justice, freedom and the
rights of the individual man, but when these fundamental prin~iples run
counter to a carefully cultivated prejudice, that prejudice which is the
product of the emotion will triumph over the ideal which is the product
of the mind. Hypocrisy is the greatest enemy of Masonic progress and
what Masons need most is to be called more frequently to the practice
of their profession.

Before closing these remarks I want to comment on one example
which illustrates better than all of my words the point I have tried to

make. I read with pride and great satisfaction the address of Brother
Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander of the United States armed
forces in the Pacific, a native son of Wisconsin, on the occasion of the
historic Japanese surrender. Here is a man steeped in militarism, a professional soldier all of his life, acc11stomed to violence, hardened to the
brutality and hatreds of war, from whom one might expect an attitude of

"It is my earnest hope and indeed the hope of all mankind that fro~
this solemn occasion a better world shall emerge out of the blood and

will synchronize with our almost matchless aqvance in science, art, literature, and all material and cultural developments of the past 2,000 years.
It must be of the spirit if we are to save the flesh."

individual, political, and international relationships. The great self-evident
truths of Freemasonry offer light to lead the way. The responsibility of

and fulfill our manifest destiny.

Delaware, 1S45 (Grand Master):
Serious thought should be given to the physical requirements of applicants. Our ancient brethren who were operative Masons needed good
and whole arms and legs, good sight and good hearing to construct or
build structures such as cathedrals, etc. It was really c;.xternal fitness that
was needed in ancient times. But now we as speculative Masons teach
our candidates that Masonry does not judge men externally, but internally. Now that we have sold the good work of our beloved order to the
men of our armed forces in providing for their pleasure and welfare
through the Masonic Service Association and in other ways for which we
have given of our funds, they on returning after fighting our battles to
keep us a free country in which to practice the teachings of Freemasonry
are thinking of making application for the Masonic degrees. Some may
not be sound in all of their limbs and members, but internally they may
be just the type of men who would be assets to our organizations. About
75 per cent of the grand lodges in the United States have modified their
requirements and we should give this matter due consideration. Therefore; I recommend that a committee of five be appointed to consider this
matter and report at the next annual communication.
.
The recommendation was adopted.

Maine, 1945 (Grand Master):
One of the most troublesome of all Masonic questions is that of physical requirement for eligibility. Section 100 of our Grand Lodge Constitution reads in part as follows: " .. . when the deformity of the petitioner
is n.ot such as to prevent him from being instructed in the arts or mysteries
of Freemasonry, and does not amount to an inability honestly to acquire
a means of subsistence, the admission will not be an infringement upon the
ancient landmarks but will be perfectly consistent with the spirit of our
Institution." This is a negativ~ definition. The Text Book states the facts
positivc;ly. "A man to be eligible for the degrees must be able to conform to the ceremonies in the practice of Masonry, to receive the work
and impart it to another. The substitution of limbs or parts shall not be a
bar, provided such are under the practical control of the petitfoner."
My answer to the question is that if such applicants can meet all other
qualifications, then he should be eligible to become a Mason. I believe
that the majority of the brethren will be in agreement with this principle.
I recommend to this Grand Lodge that Section 100 of our Grand
Lodge Constitution be rescinded and a new section be substituted. An
amendment will be presented at this communication to accomplish that
purpose.
The amendment was duly presented and under the constitution it must
lay over for one year.

Virginia, 1945 (Grand Master):
The physical qualifications for Masonry are being subjected to attack.
Our own standards have always seemed to me to be eminently sound.
They represent a departure from the rigid qualifications of operative
Masonry but prescribe certain essentials t't> the practice of the speculative
art. After all they do no more than require a man to have the physical
requirements necessary to prove himself a Mason. Yet there are those
who would throw aside these minimum standards on the theory that
Masonry has outgrown what is inaccurately ·termed "the doctrine of perfect youth."
If my time and your patience would permit, this list could be indefinitely extended. The addresses of some of my brother Grand Masters
in other jurisdictions reflect a feeling th;i.t Masonry has political duties.
I refrain from pointing out ' any examples, but a careful reading of our
foreign correspondence for some years will give you expressions of opinion that could only spring from minds that have forgotten that Masonry
is non-sectarian and non-political.
Do not misunderstand me. I do not question either the sincerity or
devotion of those who urge these views. I have purposely refrained from
the mention of names. My opposition is directed to the principles and
practices and not to the persons. Nor are my remarks to be taken as
implying any belief. of mine that Virginia alone clings to orthodox Masonry
and that our brethren elsewhere are alone in following after false gods.
'These views have infected Virginia also but I am grateful that none of them
have achieved dominance.

It 'was Freemasonry which first practiced the principle of self-government under constitutional restraint. You as the chosen representatives of

each other's views and ideas. Thus only can each make a real contribution
to the advancement of Freemasonry in Connecticut. Frankly, it is not

to confine his discussions to side-line whisperings or wash-room &roadcasts.

Freemasonry's security can be maintained only as all its constituent
and appendant organizations present. a united front before the world. It
is composed of many branches, in each of which some people find the
·keenest satisfaction of their Masonic cravings. This is as it should be,
unless these groups enter into a competition with each ·other which causes
divisio·n and discord rather than "that noble contention" as to which best
can serve and be·s t agree. The former must inevitably result in division
and destruction, while the latter will make our beloved fraternity a con-·
stantly more potent force in the service of God and man. The Symbolic
Lodge is the foundation of all Masonry, it is the source from which all
other groups draw their material. The Symbolic Lodges united in Grand
Lodges offer a common meeting ground and rallying point. In furthering
this objective I have given my fullest cooperation to all Masonic and appendant organizations in our own jurisdiction and beyond its borders. The
enthu&iastic reciprocation has been both pleasing and inspiring. I am so
bold as to think that these activities and experiences have been for the
good of the Masonic institution.

I like to think of ·F reemasonry as a g4eat, sturdy tree whose roots
drive ever deeper into the great mass of humanity while its spreading
branches extended toward heaven constantly shelter more and more · people from the hot rays of the meridian sun as well as from the tempests
and the cold rains. The great sturdy trunk represents Symbolic Masonry,
while the branches represent the collateral and appendant orders. Each
branch is dependent upon that great, strong trunk which converts the lifegiving elements derived through ,the deep roots into the fiber .which
strengthens, the flower and leaves which ornament, and the fruit which
jus~fies our place on the great highway of history. True enough, the
trunk may indefinitely endure the loss of one or more of its branches, but
usually at the ptice of being perpetually deformed and suffering a loss in
usefulness to the world. But the branch itself, torn loose from its source
of strength and health, must inevitably wither and die. Let us therefore
dedicate ourselves to the proposition of strengthening and supporting each
pther ·· to the limit of our talents and strength to the end that all may
flourish and produce good fruit plenteously.

WHAT DO I OWE TO MASONRY?
What do I owe to Masonry?
Well, brother, that depends
On if you joined for other's good
Or just for selfish ends.
For if you joined for others' good
For good that you could do,
Why then, my friend, you owe a lot
And it owes lots to you.
But if you joined for selfish ends
So honors would accrue,
Why then; my friend, you owe it naught
And it owes naught to you."
-T. M. Read.
Nevada, 1945 (Grand Master):
I would feel remiss in my duties, and indeed recreant, if ·I did
not call your attention to an evil, which, if permitted to assume proportions of greater magnitude, might undermine the foundations upon
which Freemasonry has been erected. "It is fundamental in Masonry to
place our order above any personal consideration in our relations with
each· other, to the end that no gri_evance, real or imaginary, be permitted
to threaten the spirit of brotherhood which cement us." There is a place
for the discussion of Masonic controversies, but it is not in public places
and in the sight and hearing of the profane. It is deplorable to learn
that our Lodge business becomes general information in a community, by
virtue of the fact that some of the membership did not use proper discretion in what may have seemed to them trivial or at least of little importance. Speaking derogatorily ·or disparagingly of another Mason is
truly a Masonic offense. We as individual Masons are not clothed with
the authority to pronounce judgment as to the guilt of another; we can
only charge him by accusation. Few instances of this kind have been
manifested in our jurisdiction, but these old scores have been permitted
to fester long enough, and should be lanced; and if then they do not heal,
amputation of the affected part is recommended within the next year.

Pennsylvania, 1945 (Grand Master):
·In the wake of every war, Freemasonry has experienced periods o f
phenomenal growth in membership.
But our history has also taught us that such rapid growth has not
necessarily been sound growth. For with the coming of financial adversity those . who had flocked into our lodges in such great numbers were
the first to give up their membership. I need not again remind you of th!!
events of the 1930's.
Now we have been wont to explain the defection of those members
by saying that Masonry had not been deep ly rooted in their lives. When
pressed for a reason for that fact, we have usually blamed it on their
fundamental lack of interest in, and appreciation for the deeper meaning
and significance of Freemasonry.
But I feel that is only part of the truth. We ourselves were in large
measure to blame for that lack of interest and appreciation. We were too
busy obligating great numbers of new brethren; we had no time for any
further personal interest, and as far as we were concerned, they became
just so many more names on the secretary's rolls. Oft en enough we killed
their interest at the very outset by the perfunctory, hurried and slipshod
way in which we conferred the degrees. It was we who failed in our
task of trying to make them Masons in fact as well as in name.
And now the wheel is come full circle. Again we are receiving large
numbers of new members in our lodges. Let us then realize our responsibility toward them.
Wisconsin, 1945 (Grand Master):
Fifteen years of active participation in the affairs of the Blue Lodge
and the Grand Lodge inevitably produce in a man certain profound and
fundamental convictions. When I undertook the honor and respqnsibility
of serving as Grand Master of this Grand Lodge, I resolved that those
convictions should guide my official actions.
First of all, I was convinced that the traditional conservatism of Freemasonry, which as to its philosophy and landmarks has been its greatest
source of strength and stability, had penetrated deeply into the administrative phases of the institution, where I felt it was doing harm. In other
words, I found that we were clinging to ancient methods of administration
of lodge and Grand Lodge affairs under the misapprehension that everything in Masonry is unchangeable. There appeared to be vital need for
the application of sound modern business practice to lodge and Grand
Lodge affairs. Waste and inefficiency are often apparent particularly in
the smaller lodges. I attempted therefore to separate the functional from
the philosophical; to urge Masons everywhere to modernize their lodge
machinery to bring the administration of the lodge in step with t.he times.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALI~ORNIA

Secondly,' i observed a vital need for greater unity among the lodges
comprising this Grand Lodge and likewise among those appendant bodies
whose membership is predicated upon Symbolic Masonry. I understand
and appreciate the feeling of those who maintain that there is no Masortry
except in the Blue Lodge and that Masonry cannot therefore .be charged
with the errors or omissions of other so-called Masonic bodies. But to be
realistic one must understand the viewpoint of the general public to whom
all Masonic bodies, by whatever name they may be called, are one. The
enemies of Freemasonry will never let us escape responsibility for the
a'c ts of our brethren in these· appendant bodies on the technical plea that
they are not in fact Masonic. Consequently I hold to the view that we
must face the future with a united front; that all appendant bodies calling
themselves Masonic should realize their responsibility for the good name
of Freemasonry and guaql the reputation of the fraternity on every occasion. To this end I have b.e en actively interested in many other Masonic
organizations and endeavored to spread .the gospel of Masonic unity and
~armony throughout Wisconsin. •
Thirdly, I have long felt that Masonic charity and relief is more of an
abstraction than an actuality. Here again our traditional conservatism has
blinded us to the realities of modern life and we have attempted to practice
our charity as it was in the beginning of organized Masonry. Consequently I have endeavored to convince my . brethren of Wisconsin of the·
realities of their obligations and of the necessity for discharging those obligations · in a more efficient and adequate manner.

SANCTITY OF THE TEMPLE

District of Columbia, 1945 (Grand Master):
On February 15, 1945, my attention wa's called to the operation and
maintenance of so-called "slot machines" in a Club conducted by one of
the Bodies, the organization of which is predicated on Masonic member- ·
ship.
The head of this body was immediately contacted and, he having' verified the truth of the report, stated that these machines were used to prevent a loss in operating expenses covering the dining room of the Club,
and that without this revenue it would be impossible to provide meals for
members anc. their guests.
He was informed that "slot machines" would not be tolerated in a
building in which Masonic meeti~gs were held; that the machines must be
removed not later than midnight on February 28th, and that if the dining
room could not be operated without the assistance of funds made available
through the operation and maintenance of these machines, it would be
necessary to close the dining room.
·'
The head 'of the body in question promised prompt compliance with the
order of the Grand Master, and the machines were removed as directed.
Ohio, 1945 (Grand Master):
On April 2, 1945, I received a letter from the Master of a Lodge in the
city of Cleveland, which contained a resolution of indignant protest by his

427 .

I immediately wrote the temple board, and urged that the lease be
canceled, even if it should involve a suit for damage, which to me appeared
unlikely, and saying that any possible damage that might be incurred would
not compare with the damage which would result to the fraternity if the
meeting were held. Upon receipt of my letter, a member of the temple
board .called me by long distance telephone, and tried to justify the meeting by saying that the portion of the building in which the meeting was
to be held had never been dedicated to Masonry. He further stated t hat
policemen would be at the meeting to see that nothing untoward happened.
My answer was that the public did not know that the room where the
meeting was to be held was not dedicated. All they would know was ' that
it was in the Masonic temple, and that I could not go on record as sanctioning ;,.ny such use of the temple. I should also have objected if it had
been rented to Democrats or Republicans.
Later I was informed that the same room was rented to Jehovah's
Witnesses, another organization whose members will not salute the flag
or serve in the military forces.
Both of these organizations stand for things diametrically opposed to
our fundamental principles, and M asonry cannot afford to be identified
with them by permitting the use of its halls by such organizations.
Soi;ne time in the late winter, in walking to the Masonic temple in Cincinnati, arriving at what I thought was the entrance, I saw a large circular
metal sign bearing the word "Unity," with a hand pointing to the door,
which I discovered was the entrance to the Temple. Upon my return to
Columbus, I immediately wrote the Temple board in protest against the
placing of signs by this organization, which indicated there must be some
connection between it and Masonry. I should likewise have objected if
the sign had borne the words "Epworth League" or "Christian Endeavor."
Shortly after this a schism occurred in the organization and "Unity" became "Disunity." The matter got into the courts and the temple was
picketed, all to the· scandal of our order.
·
Such incidents can do the fraternity no good and must be very confusing to new Masons. Some of these temple boards seem to feel that
they are beyond the reach of Masonic law, but they are mistaken.
I recommend the adoption of legislation which will make illegal the
renting of temples or any portion of them, to either political or sectarian
religious organizations, whether the premises be dedicated to Masonry or
not. The non-Masonic public cannot differentiate. All it knows i~· what it
sees, and it judges the fraternity accordingly, and Masonry cannot afford
to be identified in the public mind with any political or sectarian organization.

In connection with this ma"tter I held:

I also published the following opinion:
There have been a number of recent instances in which Masonic lodges
and other organizations composed exclusively of Masons have conducted
affairs in violation of the above cited regulations. The e~use has been.
offered that since all of the proceeds went to a worthy cause the violation
was regarded as of no consequence. Others felt that because the enterprise
was conducted by an organization other than the Lodge itself, no violation
of the code occurred. Still others point to the frequent money-raising
promotions of non-Masonic fraternal groups as justification. Of course,
none of these excuses are tenable.

Ohio, 1945 (Grand Master):
On May 29, 1945, the foll9wing was sent the Secretaries of the Lodges:
My dear Brother Secretary:
The response which met the plea of Bro. A. A. Stephens last year when
he urged our secretaries to labor diligently to obtain "reinstatements" and
avoid "suspensions for nonpayment of dues," was perhaps the most gratifying experience of his year as Grand Master.

1

The ancient fallacy that the end justifies the means will be rejected by
every thinking person. No Masonic cause, however worthy, can justify
the violation of our code in order to achieve success.
.
Ne.i ther is it sound logic to hold that a Lodge should be permitted to do
indirectly that which it is prohibited from doing directly. It cannot hide
behind a "Booster Club" or "Ladies Auxiliary" to operate games of chance.
And to seek to imit;ate or compete with any other fraternal society, organized solely for the purpose of providing pleasure and · entertainment
for its members, is to undermine the hi.gh moral character of our institution and render us defenseless before our enemies.
Moreover, I am convinced that the code provisions above quoted were'
intended to apply and do apply to every "body of Masons" by whatever
· name they may be called, under whatever circumstances they may meet,
and by whatever authority they purport to act.
·
It must never be forgotten th~t in the eyes of the general public all
so-'called "Masonic Bodies" are one; that justifiable criticism, censure or
reprobation directed at one such "Masonic Body" adversely affects all.
Conseqqently all Master Masons, however they may be labeled for the
time being, must always conduct themselves in public as Master Masons
should. On this basis alone can the Masonic system survive. We cannot
do as Companions. or Templars or Shriners that which we ought not do as
Master Masons. We must at all costs have unity, and to insure the perpetuation of our craft that unity must rest upon the solid bed rock of
Ancient Symoblic Masonry.

A well-done task of a secretary here and there would not have made
possible such an outstanding accomplishment. It required the combined
co-operation and united effort of all of our secretaries. That this was had
is evident, for here are the figures-2,542 reinstatements and 988 indefinitely susp~nded for nonpayment of dues. The same interest and enthusiasm in this work by all of our secretaries this year will be even more
impressive.
Here are our objectives. Show a larger increase in reinstatements than
last year. There are still thousands among brethren who have been suspended heretofore that would be a credit to our membership, and would in
addition be contributors to the funds of th e Lodge. You may also know of
those among the 988 who were suspended last year that you would like to
see enlisted again as active members. Such work is constructive and builds
up. It is highly gratifying to those who participate in such a laudable undertaking. The requirements for reinstatement are greatly to the advantage of the brother. In fact, they show a decidedly generous attitude
toward him.
Happily the number of members suspended for nonpayment of dues has
been decreasing for a number of years. T h e rate of decrease will continu.e
if, without fail, in every Lodge, no member is suspended unless he has been
personally interviewed by one or more of his fellow members, and importuned to keep himself in good standing for his own welfare and that of his
family and for the influence of his standing as a Mason in the community.
The amount of one's dues is a highly profitable investment. There have been
some pathetic cases during the past year because some of o ur members
permitted their dues to lapse, or took out their dimits and did not reaffiliate.
May the goal of your Lodge be "no suspensions for nonpayment of
dues." As it is almost time to close your membership list for your annual
return, keep that fact before your Master, officers, and members and enlist
all in your efforts to attain your goal.
While it is impossible to determine exactly the effect of tms appeal
and that of Bro. Stephens last year, we do know that there were a large
number of restorations last year and also this, and the number of suspensions for nonpayment of dues was cortsiderably less this year than last.
The results have been such as to encourage strenuous efforts to induce
suspended . Brethren to seek restoration, and as pointed out in the letter
of May 29, there is yet a large field ripe fo r the harvest.

Saskatchewan.• 1945 (Proceedings):
Bro. Roosevelt was a member of Holland Lodg~ No. 8 on the Grand
Register of New York. His life reflected the teachi.ngs of the lodge room;
his statesmanship was touched with the flame of his Masonic faith; his
countenance was redolent with the light of one who never sank beneath the
influence of terror when the hour of trial approached.
That his interest in Freemasonry was deep and his faith in the efficacy
of its teachings profound we have many evidences. Let us take ·ourselves
'back to that night of November 7th, 1935, and journey with him to New
York. Masonic history was made that night. He raised his two sons,
James and Franklin Jr., to the sublime degree of Master Masons. He had
performed a similar duty for his son Elliot in 1933. What a thrill must
have been his as on that memorable night father and sons clasped hands
across a Masonic altar. We may well ask ourselves why was this high
man-high in so many respects-'-so anxious that his sons should be Master
Masons, should fix their gaze on the morning star before beginning the
long journey on life's highway whose destination no man knows. Let us
reverently and resolutely seek the answer by following in his Masonic
footsteps.
"Here dr hereafter-we shall see it ended,
This mighty work to which our sails are set;
If from beyond-then, with the vision splendid
We shall sink back and never know regret."

Extract from oration, delivered in 1822 by Brother R. P. Spalding,

To the females in this assembly, I feel bound to offer a reason why
they are not allowed to participate in the privileges of this ancient and
honorable Institution, agreeably to the tenets of our Order, "no woman can
be made a Mason," and this for very substantial reasons. It is not, as some
have imagined, because we distrust their power of preserving a secret.
It is not that our deeds are evil and would call forth the blush of modesty
upon their cheeks. It is not that the "tools of the craft are too ponderous
for them to wield." Neither is it because they are destitute of any of the
heavenly virtues which we profess to practice. But it is through a con- .
sciousness of our own weakness that the fairer portion of creati9n is excluded from our meetings.

I ruled that the election of February 13, 1945, was null and void,' and
further that ·another ballot be held for the three candidates involved at

Another question was involved in this situation as to whether the
Senior Warden or the Acting Master was in authority in the absence of
the Master.
Answer: Ordinarily the Senior Warden would be in charge. However,
according to Sec. 72 of our Code, "If a Warden, in the absence of the·
Master, through courtesy, place . a Past Master in the chair, such Past
Master becomes, 'pro hac vice,' Worshipful Master, and his rulings are
the law of the Lodge." Therefore, when this Past Master took the chair
at the request of the Senior Warden all powers properly belonging to the
Worshipful Master devolved upon him.

The suggestion of the Grand Master will strike a responsive chord in
the heart of every true Mason because it proposes, in a practical manner,
to exemplify the fraternal principles and ideals which we are · con~tantly
preaching. In order to be a Mason for fifty years or more, a man mus t of
necessity be more than seventy-one years of age. At that time of life many
men have retired from their usual fields of activity and their period of
productiveness is past; and many of them, by reason of reduced income,
find it difficult, if not impossible, to pay their dues, and relieving them from
this obligation, after so many years of membership in our fraternity, will, in
a small measure, evidence the appreciation of Masonry for their many
years of service.

Prince Edward Island, 1945 (Proceedings):
In this jurisdiction after 35 years of continuous membership, Masons
become exempt from dues.
A resolution has been introduced that the fees for life memberships . in
the different lodges shall be a certain sum for the full 35 years, depending
upon the rate of dues in the particular Lodge. If the applicant has already
been a member for a number of years, then the fee for life membership
shall be a proportion of the total fee equal to the difference between the
elapsed membership and the maximum, 35 years. Thus if the full fee were
$150 and the Mason had already, at the time of application, been seven
years•a member, as seven is one-fifth of 35, he would save one-fifth of the
total sum, or $30.

433

The loss in revenue to both the Grand Lodge and our subordinate
Lodges will be small, for the number of fifty year veterans is comparatively small, but whether the loss be large or small, these brethren who
have worn the square and compass for half a century or more, are entitled to this consideration.
~ome of the other Masonic bodies, or so-called Masonic bodies, relieve
their members from the payment of dues after 30, 35 and 40 years of membership, and your committee feels that Ancient Craft Masonry should fall
irt line by showing this fraternal consideration to its fifty year members,
in accordance with the recommendations of our Grand Master, and that
our laws should be amended accordingly.

The amendment was seconded by the representatives of more than
twenty lodges, a vote was taken and the report was unanimously adopted,
to beco·m e effective at once.

Illinois, 1945 (Grand Master):
For many years it has been the custom to award any brother who
has been Mason for fifty years a suitable pin in recognition of his long
and faithful service to Freemasonry. It has seemed to me that more than
just that should be done. Many times after a brother has served the craft
for fifty years he finds himself unable to continue payment of dues because
of his inability at that age to continue his usual business activities.
Many feel that after a brother has become entitled to a fifty-year
emblem he should also be relieved from the payment of dues both to his
own Lodge and to the Grand Lodge. This would be a far greater favor
than receiving an emblem in token of his long contin.ued membership.
. Why should we not do this? There are not so many who acquire this
distinction, and the loss in revenue would be very slight, while the favor
to the brother might be very great. I trust that favorable legislation may
be had at this session to carry out this recommendation.

MASONIC EDUCATION
This subject continues to inter~st the serious thinking members in
almost every jurisdiction. An analysis of the various committee reports
seems to demonstrate that where the candidate has been carefully coached
in the ritual, and has had explained to him the esoteric meanings of the
symbols and of the drama, he himself has then delved further on his own
account. But, where his interest in· the preliminary lessons has not been
attracted, very little benefit has accrued from further lectures. In short,
it is the serious duty of Lodge officers. to impress the candidate deeply at
the beginning.
Indiana,' 1945 (Grand Master):
The second step in the making of a Mason is to make him who would
become a true Mason acquainted with the meaning of its symbols and
philosophies, things which are not always apparent, but require much
study and reflection. And this is exactly what Masonic education seeks
to do-to teach him who would be a Mason the meanings of Masonry's
symbo'ls and t4e deep significances of her various philosophies. In time,
after study and reflection, the true Mason will come to the understanding
that there is a fundamental purpose underlying all Masonry, which underlying purpose is to teach the kind of existence a true Mason should live,
so that he might obtain the utmost of perfection in his life presently lived,
and his life to be lived hereafter. The third step naturally follows, for
after a true Mason realizes that Masonry is a way of life, then all th at
remains is to live it.

Kansas, 1946 (Grand Orator):
Masonry, because of the vastness of its scope and antiquity of its roots,
has too often in the minds of some men, come to suggest tradition, forms
and symbols. We rightly cherish tradition, forms and symbols, for the
"system of the order is veiled in allegory and illustrated by symbols."
But just because we keep them in the forefront of our minds by repetition,
secrecy, and vi's ible evidence, we ought not let them hide the great principles our ancient brethren intended them to reveal.
Traditions that are not grafted on principles can grow sterile and
bear no fruit. Any student of history knows that scores of secret mysteries
and cults akin to our order once flourished in the Oriental and Mediterranean world that are now only name.s. The principles they embodied
that wae true and worthy have remained, the rest has been lost .
Forms can change. The record of the change from operative to speculative Masonry in the 16th and 17th centuries is profitable for every Mason
to read. It is striking to discover our brethren in the early 18th century
period of revival knew but one degree, one initiation and one catechism,
and the Master's degree was first given only to those who had occupied
the Master's chair and then only by a Grand Lodge. But the principles
these forms embodied have been handed down with faithfulness and we
have kept the forms our brethren of the 18th century developed, fresh and
alive.
Even symbols can lose their meaning. A symbol carries only the meanin?" with which men invest it. For example, the hammer that meant one
thing to the Norseman and another to the Jews in the day of Judas Maccabaeus, means another to the present day Russian whose flag carries it
as a symbol and another and very different thing to a Freemason.
Symbols, even when conservatively guarded live because of principles that
fill them with the meaning of which they are emblematic.
. T?erefore, today, I want to call your minds to certain great abiding
principles of Masonry that have enlivened tradition, that give forms meaning and use symbols for their illustration. For in the recognition of these
principles and in their exemplification Masonry and Masons have a
.message and a witness for our day.
At least four principles stand out as fundamental in all Masonic. teach~ng. They are: (1) Trust in God. (2) .The dignity of man. (3) The authority of law and order. ( 4) The ultimate triumph of truth. Masonry has
n;any other great ideas embedded in its structure and exemplified in its
ritual, but almost all of them depend on the four just mentioned. They
control the perspective of Masonry even as a building is delineated by the
location of its corners. These principles ought to be the message and
witness of every Lodge and of every true Mason.
Maryland, 1945 (Grand Master):
I find one great deficiency in our present system of advancement from
degree to degree. and to membership in a Lodge. We develop excellent
Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts, but fail to give our new brethren
a satisfact~ry knowledge of ~he Master Mason degree. This degree and
the truths 1t develops are all-important to every Mason. He has little ln"
sight into the t.eachings of the craft until he has a fair knowledge of the
thought-provoking lessons emphasized in this degree. There is a tendency
upon. the part of many of our applicants, to use the Blue Lodge as a
stepping stone to other dependent bodies. This should be discouraged.
He who knocks should tarry to ask and receive. We are not primarily. in- .

terested in bringing more men into Masonry. Our main interest is to
develop more Masonry in men. This cannot be accomplished if our applicant hastens through the Lodge intent only upon qualifying himself to
wear the emblem of this, or some coordinate body. The member of a
Lodge should be so fully informed he could gain admittance to any Lodge,
anywhere. Yet many Masons are deprived of this privilege as they are
not sufficier.tly enlightened upon the Master Mason's ritual to pass a
satisfactory examination before a Lodge committee. To study the catechism of th€: Master Mason degree and to pass an acceptable examination
before an open Lodge is as essential, and perhaps more so, than our customary examination in the catechism of the Entered Apprentice and
Fellowcraft degrees. Therefore, Lodge membership should be dependent
upon proficiency in the ritual of the Master Mason degree as is the case
in twenty-seven of the forty-nine grand jurisdictions in the United States.
Some extensive study will be necessary to properly incorporate such a requirement into. our constitutional law,, but I see no reason that the law
cannot be developed from the experiment. I, tperefore, recommend that
beginning January 1, 1946, all newly obligated Master ·Masons be required
to stand an examination in open Lodge as to their proficiency in the
catechism of the Master Mason degree . before being enrolled as members
of the subordinate Lodge, that proficiency be determined by ballot as in

·
From time immemorial, man has been gregarious. At first it was
necessary for survival but eventually he formed various ill-defined tribes,
societies, creeds or organizations for his mutual protection, advancement
and social intercourse. All Masonic authorities agree that Masonry is a
moral ii;istitution, teaching and fostering a spirit of loyalty to God, our
country, our neighbor and ourselves. It has long championed the principles of liberty, equality and fraternity. Our Masonic pilgrimage begins
with our confession of a Supreme Being and the rites and ceremonies are
of such a nature as to dispel doubt and ignorance and encourage obedience
to the Supreme Law. The superstructure of Masonry rests upon the
foundation of the moral law.
Even though the exact origin of the fraternity is somewhat clouded
and even eminent authorities are not agreed as to e~act time or place,
yet the principles are quite discernible in the time of Moses and the
Israelites. The ten commandments which Moses received on Mt. Sinai
were designed as moral code to govern the people and may be. regarded
like our present laws as the sum of human experience up to that time.
Probably no assemblage of mortals has ever designed anything bett~r.
The building of King Solomon's temple was an exemplification of
builders working under a code of moral laws. At this point, operative
Masonry working under certain rules of workmanship and pe·r sonal conduct may have had its origin. This may be true only in the same degree
that civil and religious liberty had its birth at the momeni the Declaration
of Independence was formulated. Masonry has appropriated the circumstances attendant to building of the temple to impress upon the mind the
beauty of a system of moral instruction and conduct which have come
down to us through the centuries, unallied to secretarian creeds or political
philosophies that obtained momentary power. Even though a large group
of craftsmen demonstrated that they could work harmoniously in Solomon's time, the secret order fell upon evil days and virtually disbanded.
The evidence of their labor disintegrated under the influence of barbarian
forces and those of nature only to be built again. However, secret societies
were maintained in concealment for purposes of moral and scientific instruction. Pythagoras, the Greek philosopher and mathematician in the
fifth century B. C., was the founder of one of these secret societies which
became very successful in the promotion of the arts. Unfortunately,
Pythagoras was ambitious and attempted to convert it into a political institution and the society dissolved in discord. Contemporaneously with the
last effort at the rebuilding of Solomon's temple, a new civilization was
springing up with Athens as its center. The secret orders for instruction
in the moral and building arts continued to thrive in the heyday of Greece.
Some of our basic designs in architecture requiring skill and ingenuity to
construct resulted from training of Masters in the builders' art. The
beauty of their design and details of contruction have never been surpassed.
That operative or craft Masonry in ·guild form must have endured
through ten centuries is, apparent and there is quite definite evidence of

MASONIC HISTORY
The history of Masonry prior to 1700 remains · shrouded in mystery,
even though many authorities bring evidence of a decidedly convincing
nature. It is always interesting reading, especially the influence exerted
by the craft on world affairs since 1700, and of which very definite records
do exist.
Missouri, 1945 (Grand Master):
Those who came to our shores as colonists brought with them, in large
measure, these ideals which men had long learned to love and practice
in the Masonic fraternity. Thus it was that these ideals came to be introduced into the very foundations of our government by those who had
learned them so well in our order. The leadership in that turbulent period·
of our history was furnished in large measure by the Freemasonry of that
day. The army, the continental congress and all qther agencies and instrumentaiities of government were profoundly influenced by leaders who
were Freemasons. Conservative historians tell us that about SS per cent
of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were Masons, while 59
per cent of the signers of the constitution were members of our fraternity.
Of all of our presidents about 45.5 per cent have been Masons, . while 40
per cent of the .justices of the U . S~ Supreme Court (as of 1937) were Freemasons. George Washington, and most of his generals, as well as a large
number of the junior officers and enlisted men of the colonial army were
Masons. John Marshall, father of the supreme court, Peyton Randolph,
president of the continental congress, himself a Grand Master, Alexander
Hamilton, founder of our financial system, and· first Secretary of the
Treasury, and many other leaders, including Thomas Jefferson, the distinguished author of the Declaration of Independence, were Masons.
Thus did the Masonic fraternity have much to do with the establishment
in this continent of a nation dedicated to the proposition that all men are
created free and equal, and having certain inalienable rights, among which
are life, liberty and the pursuit of hi!.ppiness.
