the existence of secret orders of craftsmen in the early Germanic era.
Some historians ~redit these secret guilds bound together by some moral
as well as working code with giving aid and comfort to the Crusaders.
The motivating influence behind the Crusades was the church. The Crusades will ever remain an astonishing act in the drama of life. They
brought forth acts of daring and devotion even though blemished in
places with abysmal shame, self-interest and commercialism. Yet no one can
deny that in the Crusades men strove for righteousness and to extend
Christendom on earth and return the flag of its faith to the cradle of
Christianity. In the Crusades 1 we may detect some of the incipient influences that led to two incidents of far reaching effect on the civilization
of western nations and ultimately on Masonry-the Renaissance and the
Reformation. Even though often regarded as separate incidents, in many
respects they are closely related and...inseparable, the Renaissance contributing and adding momentum to the Reformation.
In the tenth century the fraternity of "Operative Stone Builders" was
established in Europe and claimed the right under Papal privilege of
exercising building craft over all Christendom. The old stone builders left
much of their history in symbols and chronicles of stone and all documents
that remain attest to their morality, piety and honesty. They became
established in England about the tim.e of the Conquest having connection
with the main body in continental Europe. They kept the rules and manual
arts of their craft secret to preserve monopoly. They were always engaged in construction of ecclesiastical edifices and were protected and supported by the most talented and influential tnen. The ecclesiastics being
the learned m~n of the time, it appears that certain instruction in the
arts, religion, and architecture was impartedtby them to the Operative
Masons in their employ and it is intimated t at there were some among
them who were regarded as Master Masons.
~ abbots or superiors designed the plans for· the buildings. The lay brothers dwelling, within the
circle of the monastic establishments having assisted in the construction
of religious houses, in the course of time formed similar societies among
themselves outside of the monasteries. From this source sprang the independent ledges such as German " Ston~ Masons," which preserved their
Christian character to modern times. These craft lodges sponsored in a
sense by the monastic orders might be regarded as early manifestations of
our present day labor unions.
With the Reformation and following it, the zeal for extensive church
structures and cathedrals began to wane, the Society of Stone Masons degenerated to the level of mere operative craftsmen. The decline of the
monastic influence and activities entailed the decay of the operative craft
lodges attached to them. The ceremonial forms and usages gradually lost
their significance. Yet some of .the ancient ceremonies were retained and
preserved so that at the establishment of the modern symbolic system,
many of the customs and usages were still in existence required only a
new and different explanation. We have no authentic documents which ·
refer to the operative fraternity during the flourishing period of its existence, even though there may be unverified allusion to Freemasonry in the
time of Pythagoras between 500 and 600 B. C.
The name "Freemason" appears for the first time in Statute 25 of
Edward I of England 1350 A. D. and from the French text signifies "a
Free-Stone Mason," one who works in free-stone as distinguished from
one who built walls of rough stone. About 1600 A. D . persons who were
not operative Masons began to unite with Freemasons and were dis-

tinguished from regular working Masons by the term "Accepted" or
"Speculative" Masons. Noblemen, military officers, clergymen and others,
attracted by the moral principles of the Fraternity joined existing lodges
and brought about the radical changes which took place in the reconstruction of the order. Many of the learned "speculative" members were
inclined to push abstract theories and get involved in philosophical matters. Had it not been for the induction of speculative or accept ed members,
those having no connection with operative Freemasons and no intention
of becoming such for livelihood during the seventeenth century, it would
appear that the ancient fraternity of Free and Accepte.d Masons would
have ceased to exist and its history forgotten. By the year 1702, the
speculative lodges in England began to decay and became so degenerate
as to be used for purposes of self-interest and gain. They appealed only
to the credulous and superstitious as a mysterious sect useful to travelers
and mariners as a safe introduction. Signs over the doors of ale houses
along the docks in London and Liverpool read: "Masons Made Here for
12s."

Search for oral traditions to establish a history of Freemasonry prior
to 1717 has not been very fruitful. The early craftsmen usually did not
record their customs and usages on paper but if they did so all such
documents of essential value have disappeared or were destroyed. It is
quite possible that, even though many were master craftsmen, they were
unlettered men unable to keep any permanent written records. Furthermore, with the advent of the art of printing, the demand for paper exceeded the supply and many libraries were ransacked for paper, manuscripts were consumed by book binders without regard for their value.
Such may have been the fate of early records now of value to Masonry.
Reference is made to old charges and constitutions, but the validity of
them has not been verified. There is reference to the Book of Constitutions as far back as 926 A. D. as well as the Cook and Regius manuscripts
but their authenticity has been questioned by Masonic scholars. Unfortunately, there are no written records of actual lodge meetings prior to
1599, so that the relation and proportion that the. speculative bore to the
operative is more or less conjectural. W hen the ancient forms had begun to decay and the true meaning of the ceremonials, usages and discipline was dying out, the fraternity realized the necessity of preventing
its extinction by reestablishing the ancient Landmarks and reorganizing
the order. Four " Old Lodges" and possibly more took part in that eventful gathering in L<;>ndon in June 1717 and formed the first Grand Lodge
of tl:ie Craft "of Free and Accepted Masons. Sir Christopher Wren, the
architect for St. Paul's Cathedral in London, was elected the first Grand
Master. From that body so formed has sprung directly or indirectly every
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons working the three degrees
throughout the world. Unfortunately, the transactions of the premier
Grand Lodge in London in 1717 were not duly recorded at the time. The
Book cif Constitutions, 1723 A. D., and the minutes of the meeting in
that year, together with Reverend Brother Anderson' s account in the second .edition of the Books of Constitutions, are about the only records of
this memorable event.
To the Reverend James Anderson, D . D ., a Scotch Presbyterian minister in London, assisted by Reverend Brother Theophilus Desaguliars,
L. L. D., of Christ Church, Oxford, goes the credit for assisting the old
members who had some knowledge of the fraternity in its reorganization.
Actuated ..bY a spirit of religious toleration, they eradicated the sectarian

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

elements of Christianity and introduced what we know as the legend of
Hiram and the symbolism of King Solomon's Temple. According to
Brother Albert Pike, we cannot assume that the symbolism used in the
body of Freemasonry is of an earlier date than 1717, but he admits, however, that among Freemasons of a certain class in limited number, the
same symbolism or a large part of the same· afterward placed in the degrees did exist long before and perhaps some centuries before 1717.
Unity of the Grand Lodges claiming jurisdiction in England, the "Ancients" and the "Moderns," was not attained until 1813. Until this ' time,
they used different rituals and did not recognize each other as Masons
even though each had subordinate. lodges all over the world. In 1813, by
agreement the new work of the "Moderns" became the standard of English
Freemasonry.
While transition was occurring in England, it is evident that Freemasonry was active in France and Germany, possibly arising from a similar
reorganization such as occurred in England. In the early. part of the
nineteenth century, the craft was quite active in Germany. Included in
the ranks were intelligent, educated men. Karl Christian Kvause is widely
recognized as an outstanding scholar of Masonry and Masonic philosophy
at that tim<-, even though he was severely criticized and misunderstood.
He propounded a simple and understandable philosophy emphasizing Religion, Law and Morals as the three pillars of . the social order. Had the
Germans as a nation followed the philbsophy of Krause instead of the
ideology of the Junkers symbolized by th~ God of War atop the Brandenburg Gate, the world .might have been spared this present holocaust.
There is ample evidence that Masons were among the early colonists
of North America. A burial stone with a square and compass bearing the
date 1606, was uncovered in Nova Scotia and presumably dates from
French occupation. Prior to any constituted. authority, there is a record
of meetings of Freemasons officered by Masters and Wardens, and the
language used to describe their work and ceremonies is as Masonic as at
the present time. They held correspondence and intercourse with lodges
and brethren wherever they found any regarded as legitimate as themselves.
The first authority for assembling Freemasons in America was issued
June 5, 1730, by the Duke of Norfc;ilk, Grand Master of Free and Accepted Masons of England, to Daniel Coxe of New Jersey, appointed as
Provincial Grand Master of New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
On April 30, 1733, Lord Montague. issued a deputation to Henry Price, of
Boston, designating him as Provincial Grand Master of New England.
The deputation of Henry Price created an ambiguous situation and his
authority was questioned in some quarters. Benjamin Franklin was
elected as Grand Master of Pennsylvania in 1734. The colonists friends
were most numerous in the lodges under the "Ancients," of the Grand
Lodges of Scotland and Ireland, while many of the Tories or Royalists
were found in the old Grand Lodge of "Moderns" of London. The adherence of the four Grand Lodges of England brought unrest and discord
in the colonies. The craft was divided between their loyalty to the King
and their sympathy for the colonies. The plan of Grand Master Coxe, of
New York, for union of the colonies, later advocated by Benjamin Franklin, led to the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
The Revolutionary War with its sorrows, bloodshed and bitterness
pitted brothe.r against brother; yet amid strife, the to1.1ch of Masonry
penetrated the picket lines and guards to the tents of the officers. The

exemplification of the teachings of Masonry was a redeeming feature of
the war. At the ~nd of the war came the longing for independence as in
other matters and several states established independent jurisdictions.
Later an attempt was made to fuse them into a union of Grand Lodges
but without success. To this date . the state jurisdiction of a Grand Lodge
prevails.
The spread of Masonry through the colonies and to frontier settlements from the Atlantic to the Pacific is generally familiar to all and need
not be dealt with in any qetail. However, several incidents occurred with
which Masons were concerned and they caused considerable excitement
among Masons al)d others at the moment.

The Morgan episode at Batavia, New York, in 1827, had far reaching
fraternal and political repercussions. It apparently arose from the announced intention ~f one William Morgan to expose the secrets of Freemasonry. His Masonic connections were never established, he being a
shiftless, unreliable drunkard, it is hinted that his threat may have been
for purposes of blackmail. He disappeared and Masons were immediately
charged with his disapp;arance and foul play. This episode caused a
violent political reaction with the formation· of the anti-Masonic party
which caused considerable discussion and commotion in fraternal and
political circles for a decade or more, then died out. However, some unscrupulous mendicants, together with a few who were alleged to have
seceded from bona fide lodges, attempted to capitalize this issue for personal gain by giving public demonstrations of degree work. Their efforts
fell flat because of the moral turpitude and shady character of the imposters. It is intimated that from this group of mendicants and renegades
sprang some of the few clandestine lodges not recognized by any jurisdiction. Study of the incident by Reverend Brother S. U . Mock of Batavia
1
Lodge No. 475, Batavia, New York, published in 1930, indicates that '
Masons had no connection with the disappearance of Morgan, nor was
tHere ever established any evidence of foul play on the part of anyone.
Morgan just disappeared without track, trace or remembrance.

The dispensation granted to a lodge at Nauvoo, Illinois, in 1842, ultimately involved two or more jurisdictions. The Mormons originally
sprang up as a religious sect in New York about 1830. But their religious
views and radical departure from monogamous marital status was violently opposed among staid upstate New Yorkers and they migrated to
Nauvoo, Illinois. lrt 1842, a dispensation was granted by the Grand Master of Illinois to several brethren to organize a lodge at Nauvoo. In a
period of 149 days this lodge h.a d initiated, passed and raised 286 candidates, averaging six degrees per day during that time. Soon thereafter,
dispensations were issued for two other lodges, Helm and Nye in the
vicinity of Nauvoo, which also behaved in a similar fashion. From the
records, it appears that these three lodges in or about Nauvoo made 1500
Masons in one year. If this same ratio prevailed during the two years of
their existence under dispensation, they must have made an army of 3000
or more. When called to account for un-Masonic conduct, they had the
effrontery to Fefuse to present the records of their work for inspection.
The dispensations of t!.e Nauvoo, Helm and Nye Lodges were abruptly
revoked and charters refused in 1844. After some · disturbance and alleged bloodshed at Nauvoo, the Mormons migrated from Illinois and
Missouri and sought asylum near Great Salt Lake which was then still a
part of Mexico. For a period of twenty years they lived in open defiance
against the United States. In addition to polygamy, armed defiance and

During the bitter, turbulent days prior to and during the Civil War,
an attempt was made to divide Masonry into opposing sides on the issues
at hand. Fortunately, wisdom and judgment prevailed in our fraternal
circles and the spirit of fraterna~ fellowship undoubtedly helped to heal the
scars and dampen the animosities arising from this internal conflict.
To our state in territorial days came men of all creeds and from many
lands. Among them were many of sterling character, untiring diligence
and unblemished integrity. Carson Lodge No. 1 has the honor of being
the first lodge to be established between ·the Rocky Mountains and the
Sierra . Nevada. As you all know, the lodges in Nevada first operated under dispensation or charter from the Grand Lodge of California until the
Grand Lodge of Nevada was formed in January, 1865. We today in
grand assembly enjoy the fruits of their labor.
Concurrently, with the spread and development of the fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons have arisen the related concordant orders with
individual ceremonies also based on Masonic philosophy and traditions.
Among all these peace, harmony and unity of purpose prevails.
The history of the Nevada jurisdiction as set forth by our late esteemed
Brother Torrence abounds with the prominent part the fraternity has taken
in the development of this state, a record unblemished of which we are all
proud.
To the illustrious brethren who carried the standards of the fraternity
through the centuries, it can be truthfully said "The good they did has
lived after th-em."

Masonic history in Utah territory began in 1859 when the Gr~nd Lodge
of Missouri issued a dispensation to open a lodge composed of army officers and men stationed at Camp Floyd. This lodge was bona fide and
conducted itself creditably later surrendering the dispensation when this
army unit was removed to another post. In 1863 the state of affairs became so rebellious that two regiments of soldiers under General Connor
marched in and established Camp Douglas and restored some ·semblance
of order. With some security· of life and property assured, business men
and miners . migrated to Utah, some of them being Masons. They petitioned the Gr.a.nd Lodge of Nevada in 1865 for a dispensation. Lander
Lodge No. 8 . at Austin recommended the petition.
The Grand Master of Masons in Nevada issued a d1spensation for Mt.
Moriah' Lodge to be located in Salt Lake City. But remembering the
treachery and conduct of the Mormon Masons at Nauvoo, he attached an
edict to the dispensation to "exclude all who were of Morman faith." Soon
after the first meeting of Mt. Moriah Lodge, the question was directed to
Grand Master De Bell "how to treat Mormons who claim to be Masons
who present themselves for examination and request the privilege of
visiting."
The reply of Grand Master De Bell testified to his knowledge of
Masonic tradition and jurisprudence. In substance, he ruled that as a
people, Mormons were then living in direct contempt of the moral laws
as given in the Decalogue as well as the laws of the land and therefore not
good Masons and ·should be excluded from our assemblies. At the meeting of the Grand Lodge of Nevada in 1867, Mt. Moriah Lodge again ap'Plied for a charter. The committee. found the records satisfactory and
possibly would hl!ve granted the petition had it not been for the effrontery
and spirit of insubordination manifested in petition wherein they attempted
to dictate the terms to the Grand Lodge by declining a charter unless the
edict of the last grand communication concerning Mormons be repealed
and the petitioner be allowed to judge for itself who shall or shall not be
admitted. The edict of Grand Master De Bell was upheld forbidding the
admission of Mormons to the Lodge. The petition was denied and the
Grand Secretary was· directed to deliver to the Master of Mt. Moriah
Lodge. certificates of membership for all members and furthermore donated
the jewels and furniture of the late Mt. Moriah Lodge recently under dispensation. Few instances are known where a subordinate Lodge needing
discipline for their contempt and insubordination were so leniently dealt
with. Later bona fide lodges were opened under dispensations from Montana, Kansas and Colorado, the Utah Grand Lodge being duly organized
in 1872.
From a turbulent infancy, we have witnessed the development of a
great commonwealth in ·which all creeds have come to live in harmony
and where the fraternity has become a potent influence.
Masonry migrated with the earliest immigrant trains to our region,
the first Lodge under dispensation on the Pacific -Coast bieing Multnomah
Lodge at Portland in 1848. The turbulent days of the gold rush found
lodges being opened in the Bay region and elsewhere in 1848 and 1850.

At the close of the 16th Century the English, that nation of shopkeepers, were eager to share in these big profits in Indian commerce.
Small ventures were embarked upon with some success and 'reports of these
spurred on the merchants of London to enter the trade on a scale that
' might freeze out the Portuguese, who at that time exercised a virtual
monopoly. A Royal Charter was granted by Queen Elizabeth and the
London East India Company was incorporated. There were 2'17 subscribers to the venture, their capital amounting to the modest sum of
$340,000. The Portuguese resisted these new competitors and several stubborn engagements took place.. In 1639 the English acquired a strip of land
on the East Coast, built a factory tliere, fortified it and named it Ft. St ..
George. This was · Madras, which after some 14 years became Madras
Presidency.
Most naturally the first Masonic Lodge was held in India within this
Fort St. George, but more of this later.
In 1797 there landed in Calcutta a Colonel in Command of the 33rd
Reg. of Foot named Arthur Wesley, an Irishman who had been initiated
into the Lodge 494 of Trim Co:, Meath, Ireland, in the year 1790. There
was some question about this gallant gentleman's return as a member of
Parliament for Ireland that same year. A petition was made to unseat him
as being scarcely of age and seeing his Initiation preceded his election,
one wonders how he answered a vital questio? on first en~~~ing a Lodge.
Full age of 21. This Colonel Wesley was a fairly regular vrs1tor at Lodge
Humility with Fortitude, and later when he was transferred to Fort St.
· George, Madras, he regularly attended Lodge there, though he never
affiliated with the English Lodges in India.
A few years later when his brother went to Calcutta as Gov~nor-Gen­
eral in addition to his Irish Earldom of Mornington, he was created a
Pee~ of England, taking the title, Lord Wellesley, using a more. glorified
and medieval spelling, by the addition of two ll's. Then this Colonel
Wesley changed the spelling of his name and as perhaps you have identified him already, he afterwards became Duke of Wellington. ·
I have introduced these scraps of history in order to link up the story of
Freemasonry, for the earlier years the history of the craft in India is indissolubly bound up with the Army of Occupation there. I have no records
here in Canada from which to refresh my memory, but I have the circulars
from my Calcutta Lodge which show how the work of the Lodge was
suspended by wars, and I will follow that.
The premier or Mother Grand Lodge of the World, the Grand- Lodge of
England was founded in 1717 and during the succeeding 50 years over 200
Lodges were established under its banner. No. 229 Lodge, Humility with
Fortitude, was constituted in 1773, one hundred and seventy-one years ago.
As I have said, it was not the first Lodge to be established in India, but it
was the first to become a real territorial Lodge. I say this because as you
are probably aware some of the earliest of our overseas Lodges were held
under Travelling Warrants granted to Regiments of the British Army. It
is understood that 229 was originally a Travelling Charter Lodge.
The Lodge next reopened in the cold weather of 1785 and a new Master,
Ge~rge Nelson, was installed and reigned for three years. I? 1789-99 the
Lodge met only occasionally. Wars and rumors of wars disrupted continuity, despite an accretion of new members.
The Lodge in Calcutta settled down again to regular meetings and a
Robert Evans became Master occupying the Chair for.rather more than a
year, from 1800 to 1801.

After the close of the 18th Century a period of peace was vouchsafed to
India and Freemasonry rapidly spread throughout its borders. Very
naturally Indians themselves sought membership and certain Lodges
opened their doors to all and sundry. Now there are Lodges exclusively
Indian even as other Lodges have remained exclusively European. The
Scotch' Constitutio·n is well represented, though they have no District
Grand Lodge there. There is a Superintendent of all Scottish Freemasons in India. The Irish Constitution too, is represented there by six or
eight Lodges, but the English Constitution is by right pre-eminent.
Lodge Himalayan Brotherhood, the oldest and largest in the Punjab
was founded in 1838. On St. John's Day, June 24, 1839, the members assembled at the Royal Hotel in Simla and marched in procession in full
regalia to Church, were a sermon was preached and a collection taken for
charity, which amounted to $837.00. The Governor-General, the Earl of
Auckland lent his• band for the occasion and quoting from a newspaper
of that d~y, "the music offered great eclat to this novel scene in the hills."
The natives and others thronged in numbers to witness it. Some called
the Brethren Jadoogurs or Magicians and others with equal wisdom and
sagacity said they were people who had dealings wittl the devil.
As you have all heard, Freemasonry is of great antiquity, evidence considered conclusive pointing to its existence thousands of years ago. The
greater part of thls evidence consists of marks upon stones and buildings
and for what they are worth, India can supply plenty. I have only seen
one building on which clearly visible are still seen marks in common use in
the craft.
In old Delhi there is a' fort which is claimed to be 5,000 years old. It is
built of red sandstone and is called the Pararyuilla. There are triangles,
triangles interwoven, squares, crosses, swastikas and composite hiero- ·
glyphics of various Masonic signs. India's buildings were chiefly of stone
and even to this day the workman is required· to place his mark upon
every stone he ;vorks. When . a dome is to be constructed the· Master
builder.. distributes small lengths of sticks· and the workman must make
all his 1stones to the dimensions of the sticks received. There is a family
which s.l?ecializes in domes and there is a workman for every ring of stone

in the dome, and upon each stone will be found clearly marked on <the

were pieceworkers, they were paid for what they produced, not for the

Particular parts of buildings, porches, arches, buttresses and domes
were often the subject of separate contracts and construction by different
classes of stonemasons. Not infrequently such structures would have the
master builder's mark prominently carved upon it and such are the marks
now visible upon buildings of greatest antiquity. The mark of the workman was necessary only to ensure payment for. the accomplished.

On August 9, 1944, a cyclone struck the town of Kamsack and vicinity.
Many buildings were wrecked and a great amount of damage was done.
King Solomon Lodge No. 58 was the possessor of an up-to-date Masonic
Temple. This building was almost completely wrecked, with no financial
protection against windstorm. Feeling that the brethren of Saskatchewan
would wish to assist our stricken brethren of Kamsack and help enable
them to resume the practice of Masonry, as soon as possible, I directed
that a fund be established, to be known as the Kamsack Masonic Relief
Fund, and issued an appeal to the brethren throughout the Grand Jurisdic~
tion, to assist the brethren of King Solomon Lodge to the fullest extent.
This appeal was responded to most generously, for not only the brethren
in Saskatchewan, but brethren from· far distant points, contributed wholeheartedly. As a result King Solomon Lodge is again meeting in surroundings conducive to the practice of Freemasonry.

FOREIGN JURISDICTIONS
Experienced newspaper writers try to avoid making positive statements.
But even one of those seasoned scribes would be inclined to break thEl
rules and set forth some definitely positive statements as to the universality
of Masonry after reviewing the Proceedings of some 17 foreign jurisdictions.
Naturally, racial habits, customs and modes of living tend to set up different sets of values on many subjects, but in none of the countries reviewed
is there a suggestion to depart even in the slightest degree from the basic
fundamentals and landmarks of Masonry. The unanimity is startling, as
is the zest with which those same principles are upheld and promulgated.
Many of the following reviews are from the pen of Brother W . M.
Martin, chairman of the Correspondence Committee of the Grand Lodge
of Saskatchewan. Our opinion of the work and progress in the various
English provinces is one of pure admiration. We feel, however, that a review by one of their own members conveys a truer picture.
Saskatchewan, 1945 (Grand Master):
I declined to grant a dispensation to elect 'a Brother to the Master's
chair who had not previously served as Warden. In considering the case
the question ~f whether it was an emergency or neces.sity was fully considered. The Lodge in question has among its membership a considerable
number of experienced and capable Past Masters from whom a suitable
selection could have been made and I felt that an em,e rgency did not exist.
In my opinion the :filrother on whose behalf the request was made, would
be much better fitted for the highest position in the Lodge after a year's
experience as Warden.
I also declined to grant a dispensation for the initiation of a class of
more than five candidates. Five is the maximum set by the Constitution,
and I question whether, in a class of even this number, the individual candidate can receive the fullest benefit from the lessons taught. Every candidate for Masonry is. eager to receive a full impression of the ceremony and
the lessons imparted. In my opinion this is not possible with a mass
initiation such as was requested.
I received a request for dispensation to receive a petition and, if favorable, to initiate a candidate who was totally blind. Mention was made of
this at last Grand Lodge by the Committee on Grand Master's Address
and Jurisprudence. The committee expressed the opinion that blindness .
itself was no bar. I have the same opinion and feel that under present
conditions spiritual, moral and mental conditions should rank above physical

British Columbia, 1944 (Proceedings):
In referring to the war, the Grand Master said that dark clouds were
still hadging over the whole · earth and that life everywhere is affected by
the world conflict. Speaking of the effect of the war on the daily lives of
men, he said:
"Beyond question, too, our minds are dominated by the necessities of
this conflict. All our affairs and procedures are altered and every pla?'.i
every expectation, every hope must be re-focused to meet the needs of th~
dominant concern. We carry it in our thoughts every hour of the day.
Perhaps the ~ost intense part of the· struggle lies ahead of us. The one
supreme demand of the hour is to win the war and roll back the fierce
onslaught of tyranny and paganism that has threatened the liberties of all
mankind. What is needful we must furnish. The spirit of grim determina~ion takes firmer hold as greater trials may await us."
Referring to the theme of citizenship as the great and supreme interest
of Freemas0nry, he said:
"The great major concern of Freemasonry is the man himself, the citizen. Its procedures and its programs must of necessity accord with its
supreme aim. No man passing through our ceremonies can do oth~r t?an
realize that Freemasonry has an aim above that offered by other institutions and that it addresses itself immediately and directly to the considerations which determine character and human happiness."

Mexico, 1945 (Grand Master):
We are gathered here, primarily, because deeply and sincerely we are
inspired by the same reasons which induced us to join the order, and as a
sign that W{; are still striving to be worthy members of a great institution.
While nominally we are Master Masons, in a wider sense we are yet mere
apprentices governing and disciplining ourselves to the task of building our
lives agreeable to the design of the Great Architect of the Universe. Secondly, we have assembled for the purpose of conforming to the requirements of perfect organization, to review the steps during the past year and
so voice our opinions freely thereon, to consider the advisability of enacting new legislation which may be deemed essential for the further good of
the order, and to elect (or appoint) and install a Grand Master and officers
to serve for the ensuing· year. In all these duties we must remember that
ours is a trust which should be discharged with perfect fairness to all,
and we must therefore be prepared to meet with gentleness and forbearance any opposition to our own wishes, whatever they may be.
As the end of the war draws in sight there is bound to arise a common
desire to get back into one's own little corner· of God's creation, and to
forget the events of recent years. But both the present and the future are
so deeply rooted in the past that there will be no way of escaping the after
effects of a long war. One thing is already apparent: Victory and the laying down of arms will leave the world with far greater problems than
before. Millions of people will have to be fed, clothed and rehabilitated.
There have been and will be many more disappointments.
Already we have witnessed the sad spectacle of liberated people rising
against ea:ch other. The world has suffered the consequences of the various
"isms" which used their power in an evil manner, and we are now haunted
by the dread prospect of other equally potent forces developing and spreading among long suffering and tortured people if they are not provided with
an early means of regaining their rightful place in society. In seeking to
find the origins and the cause of these social systems we cannot escape the
feeling that they are to a great extent brought about through the misuse
of human wills. The "greed, selfishness and indifference of some peopl~
have been responsible for the delusion, dissatisfaction and, finally, intolerance of others. Our peace of mind, too, has been disturbed by the unfortunate arguments in higher places over the spoils of war, spheres of influ.ence trade and economic advantages. In these days moreover it is hard to
find 'a refuge from the flood of controversial topics fostered and encouraged
by pressmen and radio news commentators alike, o~ to see~ a haven from·
·commercialized effort calculated to confuse and to stir up strife among those

I would point out that there is a heavy responsibility on b~ethren who

Complants have been made to me that Lodges and brethren are r.eceiving ·
requests for donations for Masonic objects which are not recognized by this
Grand Lodge. One of these objects is known as "The Aged and Distressed
Brethren Comforts Fund," which is seeking funds, and which is endeavoring
to establish Masonic homes for aged and distressed Masons.
. T~e fund was started some years ago by a few brethren who were interested in some old Masons who were confined to the homes controlled by
the state goyernment. This object was before this Grand Lodge some years
ago when it was decided by Grand Lodge that such a scheme could not be
approved. It was agreed ultimately to subsidize beds in the home for incurables at Ryde to the amount of £480 per annum to meet cases that were ,
entitled to consideration. The starting of such a scheme by brethren on a
basis of voluntary contribution would be a liability, as the cost of erection
and maintenance of such an institution would soon be beyond the revenue
that could be obtained from such contributions.
I have to point out that aged and distressed brethren who have the
necessary qualifications can be best cared for by that excellent institution
"The Freemasons' Benevolent Institution," which is doing splendid work
in this direction by the maintenance of 193 brethren and 271 widows, at an
annual cost of £13,000.
··
There is also the Fund of Benevolence of this Grand Lodge, and the
board of the fund is always ready and willing to disburse benevolence to
any case brought before it having the· necessary constitutional qualifications. The president and the members of the Board of Benevolence are,
I· trust, vigilant in watching the interests of brethren in this regard. Any
other appeals made to brethren in Lodges must necessarily diminish the
contributions to these worthy and approved objects.
If brethren feel that there are cases requiring Masonic ass,istance that
are not covered by these funds, they have the right to approach this
Grand Lodge, and ask for any modification or alteration of the regtilations governing them, or they may take the matter up with the F. B. I.·
itself, where I am sure they will receive a sympathetic hearing.

neighbor Lodge on account of so many members moving away, He also
reported many requests for the conferring of Degrees by courtesy and
that similar requests had been made of other jurisdictions.,

seas, particularly from the· United States. He expressed the opm10n that
the real tragedy of the world lies in the fact that men are strangers, and
that the path of friendship should be cultivated.
Quarterly communications were held on September 1 and December
1, 1943, and on March 1 and June 1, 1944. The assets, including the value
of the Masonic Temple at Brisbane, are placed at £ 190,000. There is a
Benevolent Fulfd of about £67,000. The receipts for the Benevolent Fund
for the year were £4,846, and grants paid' amounted to £ 1,880, much less
. than in the previous year.
The Board of General Purposes, supported by the Grand Master, ruled
that it was undesirable to issue invitations to the wives of members or
other lady friends to attend the festive board after Lodge meetings.
At the quarterly communication in March, 1944, it was announced that
the Grand Master, at the request of the Board of General Purposes, had
consented to accept nomination as Grand Master for the following year.
M. W. Bro. W. H. Green, the Pro Grand Master, in making the announcement, said he felt sure that the request of the board would be
endorsed by eve.ry Mason in the jurisdiction.
At the quarterly communication in June, 1944, the Grand Master asked
the chaplain to invoke the blessing of Divine Providence for the Allied
Nations in the momentous happenings on the new front in the war in
Europe. He stated he felt sure all would wish him to place on record the
feelings of pride and gratitude to the soldiers, sailors and airmen who had
embarked in the greatest adventure the world had ever known.
The only nomination for the position of Grand Master for 1944-45 was
that of the present Grand Master, and delight was expressed that he was
again able to accept the office.
'
The annual gathering of brethren to pay tribute to the members of t~
fraternity who lost their lives in the last and the present war was held on
April 25, 1944, at the Masonic Memorial Temple on Anzac Day. Over
100 Lodges were represented. The Grand Master was present and delivered an address, and wreaths were placed around the Urn of Remembrance on behalf of the Grand Lodge and many of the Lodges.

Prince Edward Island, 1944 (Proceedings):
The Grar.d Master referred to the war, stating that the Allied Nations
are still engaged in total war but under more encouraging circumstances
than at any time since the struggle began. He said .that June 6, 1944,
will always be remembered by reason of the invasion of Western Europe
for the liberation of the dominated countries of Europe.
The Grand Master granted a number of dispensations to confer degrees
1n less than the time required and then only to members of the armed
forces on the eve of embarkation for overseas service.
The Grand Master, accompanied on each occasion by some of the
officers, visited every Lodge in the jurisdiction. He was impressed by the
activities of the variou·s Lodges. On his visitations he tried to stress the
1mportance of practicing the tenets of Masonry in every-day life so that
·e very act would be characterized by lofty ideals and right and justice.
There was s'urplus in the General Fund as a result of the year's operations. There is a Benevolent Fund of $23,000. Only three cases were
assisted during the year. There is also an Orphans' Fund of about $5,000.
Queensland, 1943 (Proceedings):
In addressing the brethren, the Grand Master said that he had now for
the tenth successive year to endeavor to thank the brethren for electing
him Grand Master; ten years is a long space in a lifetime, and he said it
was difficult for him to say how highly he appreciated the continued confidence. He stated that Freemasonry in Queensland has been passing
through an experie.nce neve'r before faced; many brethren are away on·
.active service but the Lodges have been reinforced by many from over-

South Australia, 1944 (Proceedings):
Grand Master His Excellency Sir Malcolm Barclay-Harvey. Lodges
153. Members 14,046. Gain 493. This Grand Lodge was formed in 1884
with a total membership of 2,241. From that year forward there were
gains each year until in 1930 when the membership reached 15,341. From
1931 to 1937 inclusive there were losses, but from · 1937 to 1943, with the
exception of the year 1941, there have been gains.
The half-yearly communication was held on October 20, 1943, at
Adelaide. The Board of General Purposes reported that in order to supplement the War Re.lief Fund letters were sent to all Lodges asking for
proposals in order to secure the success of the fund. Many replies were
received, some advising that a certain amount be contributed by each
member. All former appeals 'have been voluntary and excellent results
have been achieved, but it appears now that an effort is being made to
secure a contribution of 10s. from each member.
From the annual returns, it appears that the dues of 1,143 members
who enlisted for service have been remitted by the Lodges.
The Master of Darwin Lodge, now resident in Adelaide, expressed his
appreciation of the contribution of £383 made by 103 Lodges to assist the

The annual communication was held on March 2, 1944, at Adelaide.
The Grand Master presided.· The Board of General Purposes reported
that the Wai- Relief Fund had reached the sum of £7,350, which amount
they felt was inadequate. The brethren were urged to keep the fund constantly before the Lodges.
It was with deep regret that the Masons of the state learned of the
approaching departure of the Grand Master. On account of ill health he
asked to be relieved of his office before the end of his term. He arrived
in Australia in August in 1939 and had presided over the affairs . of the
state during a difficult and strenuous period of nearly five years when the
cares of office have been increased by the anxieties through which the
empire has passed. A resolution was moved by M. W. Bro. Sir Mellis
Napier expressing appreciation of the Grand Master for his services to
Masonry and also for his services to the state, and as a token of esteem
conferring upon him honorary membership in the Grand Lodge.
There is a Widows' and Orphans' Fund of ~'bout £23,000, and grants
of £ 1,246 were made from the fund. There is also a Benevolent Fund of
about £24,000, out· of which grants were made totaling £847.
Tasmania, 1945 (Report of Board of General Purposes):
During the period under review, regular monthly meetings have been
held and the attendance has been most satisfactory.
The board agreed to purchase, when material is available, a full dress
set of Grand Masters' regalia for presentation to M. W . Bro. H. U.
Wilkinson, P . G. M.
A letter was received from a country Lodge asking for a remission
(for a period) or a reduction in amount of dues payable by Lodges to the
Board of Benevolence. After full and careful consideration a reply was
forwarded that the board could not entertain the proposal.
The board arranged for "'Farewell" gatherings of Masons, at Launceston and Hobart, on 16th and 30th June last, respectively, to bid "Farewell" to His Excellency M. W. Bro. Sir Ernest Clark, P. G. M., prior to
his departure from Tasmania, for Great Britain, after a sojourn amongst
us for a period of some twelve years, during which time he took a keen .
and active interest in Freemasonry, and held the office of Grand Master.
The board arranged for "Masonic Thanksgiving Services" on the cessation of the war in Eur-0pe, in May last. The services were held at St.
John's Church, Launceston, on Sunday, 13th May, and at Town Hall,
Hobart, on S_u nday, 20th May, when large numbers of Masons, their wives
and families attended. Many of the Lodges in country districts also
arranged for similar services for the convenience of their brethren.
In response to a request to modify the Grand Master's instructions for
the due governance of Lodges regarding what is called "Pas~ ..Masters'
Nights" in the direction of allowing the Master to vacate the chair pro
tern., the board, without dissent, decided that except where the O:mstitu-

Victoria, 1943 (Proceedings):
In its report at the quarterly communication in March, the Board of
G~ner~I Purposes referred to the subject of American soldiers joining
V1ctona Lodges, and expressed the hope that prior to the admission of
any American citizen there should be a · previous communication by the
Lodge of all the circumstances to the Grand Secretary, so that a waiver
of jurisdiction may be obtained from the jurisdiction located at the place
of the legal residence of the candidate.
,
The Grand Master at the commencement of his second year thanked
the bret?ren for the. renewal of confidence, and referred to the loyal support which had been accorded to him during his first year of office. He
spoke of the many who are preven_ted from attending the Lodges because
they are now serving their king and country in the great cause for which
the United Nations are fighting. He expressed pride in the fact that
Masonry is so well represented in the forces, and spoke of the added
duties and responsibilities of those at home .. Four months ago the Grand
Master made an appeal for the raising of a fund to be devoted to the
health and comfort of the men on active service, and secondly to assist
them after the war when they may be in· need. He expressed the hope
that every brother would do his share in the support of this fund.
This Grand Lodge has assets valued at approximately £465,000.
At the quarterly communication in September, 1943, reference was
made to rullngs made in 1931 and 1939 with reference to the presence of
non-Masons at festive boards. The Grand Master referred to these rulings
and enjoined each Lodge to take special care that no person except a
Freemason shall take part in entertainments at the festive board.
W. Bro. H. Philip, who had spent much time in the area of the
Aleutians, in Japan, China and the Philippines, delivered an address on Japan
in which he emphasized the fact that the great menace of Japan lies in the
objective of complete world domination.
At the quarterly communication in December, the Board of General
Purposes reported that the Lodge of Research No. 218 was undertaking
to compile a history of Victoria Freemasonry for its first one hundred
years.
M. W. Bro. Book was re-elected Grand Master for the ensuing twelve
months. In thanking the brethren for conferring the honor upon him for
the third time, the Grand Master referred to the many "pleasant meetings
he had ·e xperienced and thanked the officers for their most loyal support.
He expresstd the hope that this would be the last wartime Christmas

and that by next year all the gallant brethren would be at home with

Western Australia, 1944 (Proceedings):
· At the communication in November, 1943, the Grand Master, in addressing the brethren, stated that ever since the dark days of February,
1942, the ·clouds hanging over the world have grown less menacing and
that all might now look forward fo ultimate and decisive victory over the
powers that would take away liberty and freedom. There are 1,818 members on active service.
.
At the communication in February, 1944, M. W. Bro. ]. S. Battye was
again elected Grand Master by acclamation. The year 1944-45 will be his
ninth term as Grand Master, and in thanking the brethren for the honor
he said he had spent eight very happy years marked by harmony throughout the juriE·diction and by progress in every part of the state, which has
been achieved by all working together in peace and harmony.
The annual communication was held in May, 1944. In referring to the
increase in members, the Grand Master said that it was the largest in the
history of the Grand Lodge, the . greatest previous increase having been
jn 1900, when there was a gain of 584. The proceedings contain a statement of the membership in each year· since the formation of Grand Lodge;
this statement indicates a consistent growth, with very few years showing
a decr\!ase in lllembership.
The sum of £4,418 was contributed to the Widows' and Orphans' Fund,
and grants were made amounting to £4,386. The capital of the fund is
£60,828. The Grand Master expressed a desire to see the fund increasei;I.
to £ 100,000,, to take care of
drain. on the fund, which he foresees in
years to come.
A reception was accorded the Grand Representatives, Saskatchewan
being represented by Bro. R.. H. Moore. The Grand Master asked the
representatives to convey to the various jurisdictions the desire on the
part of the Grand Lodge of Western Australia to help bring about a
state of affairs where pea~e should reign and happiness shall be the lot
of all mankind. .

Hn was married to Tekla Bender on October 12, 1922, at Hollywood,
having met Miss Bender when they were .students at the University of Colo1·1do. His son, John Bender Moore, age 22, is a pre-law student at the
l7nlvenity of Southern California. He also has a daughter, Edith M. Bear,
1&Joln 21, who is the mother of John's one grandchild, a boy.
Brother Moore ~as raised in Four Mile Lodge No. 212 at Campbell,
Mluouri, August 29, 1918, and is a charter member of Meridian Lodge
No. 667, Glendale. He was Master of the latter Lodge in 1933. From 1934
t<> 1936 he was a member of Grand Lodge Committee on Charters and
1erved as Inspector of the 86th District from 1936 to October 12, 1944.
On October 12, 1944, he was installed as Junior Grand Warden, was
elected Senior Grand Warden in 1945, and Grand Master on October 18,
1946.
On January 15, 1919, Brother Moore was consecrated 32° in New Mexico Consistory No. 1 and is now a Knight Commander of the Court of
Honor of the Los Angeles Bodies, A. & A. S. R. He is a member of
Royal Arch, Unity Chapter No. 116, Glendale, and also a member of the
Los Angeles Council No. 11, Royal & Select Masters. In 1941 he was
knighted in Glendale Commandery No. 53 and served as Commander in
1946. Brother Moore first became a member of the Shrine in Ballut Abyad
Temple, Albuquerque, New Mexico, January, 1919, and now holds mem·
bership in Al Malaikah, Los Angeles. St. Gabriel Conclave No. 14, Los
Angeles, Red Cross of Constantine installed him a member November
24, 1942.
During World War I, John Moore was a Second Lieutenant, Co. 1,
Second Infantry. He attended the University of Missouri and was gradu. ated from the University of Colorado in 1922. He was admitted to the Bar
of Colorado in 1922 and to the Bar of California in 1923. Since 1930 he
has been Inheritance Tax Appraiser, State of California.

He is a member of the following organizations: Society, Sons of the
Revolution; American Legion; Los Angeles Bar Association; State Bar
of California; Kappa Sigma; Phi Delta Phi; Oakmont Country Club;
and the Los Angeles Club of Rotary International.
John Moore has preserved and perpetuated the finest traditions of the
office of Grand Master during his incumbency in that exalted station.
On matters of policy h~ has steadfastly adhered to the Ancient Landmarks and has found a way to be progressive and modern within their
limits.
On matters of law he stated at the outset of his term that he would
not knowingly violate nor permit to be violatep the law of Grand Lodge
and he has kept his pledge.
He has brought to problems of administration a careful, studious mind
and has been painstaking in his search for the essentials necessary to a
proper solution.
Kindly, considerate, social, and so friendly that all brethren were at
ease in his presence, John will be affectionately remembered as "My
Grand Master" by all who served with him.

ADDRESS BY GRAND CHAPLAIN, EZRA ELLIS

The greatest power in the world is that which holds Masons together.
It is centered symbolically at the altar. Sometimes we neglect the cen·
trality of its meaning or do not transact the divine business there. .
We are at the altar but that is not the important part. What matters
most is that we find G~d there. If we do not, we mock Masonry. God is not
the all-seeing Eye to spy upon us. This last year I heard a nationally
prominent speaker tell a large audience that when he was ~ boy he ~as
taken to a lodge room and when he saw that eye, h~ was fn~htened .mto
numbness. He said it still makes his shudder every time he thmks of it.
Some who enter the hallowed halls of the craft and see that symbol
never think of God. Masons must think! Let us think of God in these
moments. We pay Him no compliment in our devotions, but without Him
nothing done here will be of any importa~ce.
.
. .
God must be in the midst of Masomc meetmgs. This is Masonry.
Masonry is not a Religion, but it is Religious! If God is to be~ our midst
He must be in us. To be in us we must understand that God is a person
who loves. When we have the relationship of love-God to man and man
to man, we have the greatest power in the world.
.
Love is the gift of God. It is true that one must know somethmg about .
God. Dr. Ernest Colwell was rebuked by one of his students who claimed
that the teacher had misrepresented God. "God," said the student, "is

omnipotent, omniscient, the absolute of absolutes." The youngster in·
1isted that the professor must accept that definition. When asked how he
knew that was the final answer about God his reply was, "It is in the
dictionary."
Many would like some short-cut to the Almighty One. They are much
as the young soldier in the first World War who said to the padre just
before going over the top, "What do you know about God? Quick!"
We will know about God when we stand before His altar and accept
His love. As Scott says in the "Lay of the Last Minstrel,"
"True love's the gift which God has given
To man alone beneath the heaven
It is the secret sympathy
The silver link, the silken tie
Which heart to heart, and mind to mind
In body and in soul can bind."
We mean the kind of love a man wrote about in the Bible, "I may speak
with the tongues of men and of Angels, but if I have no love, I am a noisy
gong or a clanging symbol." I may prophecy, fathom all mysteries and
secret love. I may have absolute faith that I can move the hills from their
place but if I have no love I count for nothing.
,
I may distribute all I possess in charity, I may give my body to be
burned, but if I have no love I make nothing of it.
·
Love is· very patient, very kind.
When I was a child I thought like a child, I talked like a child, I argued
like a child. Now that I am a man I am done with childish ways.
At present we see .only the baffiing reflections in a mirror, but then it
will be face to face.
At present I am learning bit by bit, but then I shall understand as all
along I have myself been understood.
Thus faith and hope and love last on, these three, but the greatest of
these is love.
Make love your aim, and set your heart on spiritual gifts. Is this not
the need of the world today? The darkness, desolation and despair which
threaten to engulf us are too much for human beings, no matter how
clever. That which we talk of as God's gift of love will lead us into light.
II

In two of his poems Henry Van Dyke points the way to this light.
"Who looks for heaven alone to save his soul
·May keep the path, but never reach his goal,
· While he who walks in love niay wander far -·.
But God will bring him where the Blessed are."
"Self is the only prison that can ever bind the soul,
And love the only angel that can ever bid the gates unroll,
So when he comes to call thee, arise and follow fast,
His way may lead through darkness, but it leads to light at last."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We are seekers after the light. That is why we are so interested in public
education. Ignorance means superstition, bigotry, hatred, and all of the
fears of darkness. There would be no problems in the world which could
not be adjusted if we had properly educated persons.
Only education which seeks for the light of truth, goodness and beauty
will bring men the good life which God intends for them.
What we mean by education is not required courses, the accumulation
of grade points by methods foul or fair, and the completion of profes·
sional assignments. We think· education is a matter of disciplined intelli·
gence.
One of the hopes of America ought to be the fact that so many of our
young men are on college and university campii. There are two possible
weaknesses however. One is the fact that education might become only
mass production of classified and undigested data. The other is that
young men might become too dependent upon a paternalistic govern·
ment Santa Claus.
There are, however, very definite reasons for being hopeful. One is in
.the responsible educators who are not mere handy men to an entrenched
system either of politics or of a particular brand of educational philoso·
phy. Dr. Francis Pendleton Green, the President of Washington and Lee
University, says "the leaders are in our hands." In commenting upon
them he goes on to point out that "these gifted youth who will shortly
take over the control of our world need: (1) a deep unders~nding of
what we may term the human situation, (2) the discipline adequate for
mental tasks, (3) moral sensitiveness and unwavering moral conviction,
and (4) the grace of human relationships."
If all of our education does this we shall come out into the true light
of which the Psalmist sang, "O send out thy light and thy truth; let them
lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles.
Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy."
You see we cannot get away from the altar. It is there we find light.
III

That light brings God upon whom we can depend. His love never ends
and never fails. Our trust must be in Him.
: There are men who think they can trust their own common sense in all
things. Dr. Le Comte du Nouy in a book called "Human Destiny" gives
a scientific view of God arid reminds us that we cannot trust what we
glibly call common sense.
Co:Ounon sense leads us to thmk the earth is flat; that two pltimb lines
are p*rallel (they are directed toward the center of the earth and conse·
quently form an angle) ; that motion in a straight line exists, which is
absolutely false as we have to take into consideration not only the motion
of the earth and its axis around the sun, and that of the entire orbit of
the earth, but also the motion of the whole solar system toward the
constellation Hercules, etc. As a result, a bullet, oi an airplane, which

11

seems to move in a straight line, with respect to the earth follows a
course more closely resembling a corkscrew when scaled ; 0 a vaster
~ame o~ refe~ence. Common sense tells us that the edge of a razor blade
l~ a straight hne, but examined under a miscroscope it resembles a wavy
hne ~rawn by a child. Common sense tells that steel is solid, but modern
th~~nes of ~atter teach. us that in r~alitr there are trillions of animated,
m1ma~ure universes havmg extraordmanly rapid movements and no contact with each other."
So! .Common sense is not the answer. We listen to those who examine
the evidences for factual
.
. .information about the past for mill"ions 0 f
year~ and . accept t h eir cnt~cal analysis of the scientific capital which is
man s heritage today to bnng us light and truth about God.
And we find !11~t God has not failed, nor changed. Love never ends. As
Shakespeare said m one of his sonnets,
"Lose is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove;
0, no! it is an ever-fixed mark
That looks on tempests and is never shaken·
It is a star to every wandering bark."
'
. We never can define love adequately. Poets can write about it but there
is never complete satisfaction in their lines. Philosophers can speculate
and reason but they tend to leave us cold. Theologians can speak of love
but they generally leave us up in the air. We mortals sometimes are so
bol.d a~ to suppo~e th~t we know something about this greatest power
which Is the mystical gift of God, but our mutterings are vain indeed.
But why talk abo~t love? ~· S. Lewis, th~ Oxford don, is doing a very
great d~al of prea~hmg, albeit unorthodox, m his books. He gives a good
s.uggestion ~egardmg the gre,at c~mmandment on charity. "Don't waste
time bothermg whether you love your neighbor; act as if you did. As
soon as we do this we find one of the great secrets." And the ultimate
secret is the presence of God.
Unless what we do here is done in this consciousness of His mighty
concern, we shall miss the greatest power.
We can have the sense of His undergirding, "the Everlasting arms"
underneath. A short time ago I was returning home from the mid-west
by air. This was my first ride on the Constellation. I had seen one in the
process o.f being made. I had been all through the plane as it was under
construction.
During the trip the Stewardess asked the passengers if they would like ·
to visit the cockpit. When I went forward I saw the familiar surroundings
and ~adgets. How pilots and engineers figure out how to use them is still
baffimg to me. There was the pilot in his seat, the first officer in his place
and o~er at the side was the flight engineer at his controls. They paid no
attention to me, but I ~arvelled at their attention to duty.
Just as I was dreammg about the wonders of air travel in these modern

12

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

days the Stewardess jarred me somewhat with the firm but polite sug·
gestion, "You'd better get back to your seat. Do you see that storm to the
right?"
I made my way back to my chair and obeyed the sign up front which
said "Fasten your safety belt." The plane climbed up and up. It veered
to the left. It bumped a bit, twisted a bit and shook a bit. But somehow
I could not help but think of the pilot and his helpers up front. They were
confident. They were attending to their business. As the plane went along
shifting this way and that, one somehow had the feeling that there was
strength in that plane, in the power of the motors pulling us onward and
that underneath were the everlasting arms.
Is this not as the power of God? Not in a word, not in symbols, not in
an altar, but in us. It is this greatest power in the world that holds Masons
together.
And the greatest power is the presence of the Person who fashioned us,
who breathed life into us, who has set before us--Life.
And the greatest power is--Love!

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
By your sufferance, I now have the honor to bring to your attention the
state and status of the fraternity. It is my good fortune to be privileged
to report to you that the general condition of Masonry in our jurisdiction
is excellent. We now have 590 Lodges-587 under charter and three under
dispensation. As of July 31, 1947, the end of our fiscal year, the record
shows our membership to be 173,917, which is an all-time peak. The
returns for this year show a net increase of 12,165 in our membership,
which has not been exceeded in any year during all the history of this
Grand Lodge. We ought to be stimulated and encouraged by the fact that
so many of these new members are young men.
NEW LODGES

During the year, I granted dispensations to form new Lodges, all of
which were instituted by me under names and at places and dates as
follows:
Palm Springs Lodge (Charter Home Palm Springs) at Banning on
April 2, 1947.
Travelers Lodge at Sacramento on April 18, 1947.
San Antonio Lodge at South Gate on July 30, 1947.
It was deemed advisable and expedient to deny petitions for dispensa·
tions to form new Lodges by a group of brethren in Honolulu, by such a
group in the United States Navy at Yokosuka, Japan, and by a group in
Rosemead, California.
NECROLOGY

During this year the inexorable hand of Death has invaded the ranks of
this Grand Lodge. In January, our very able, devoted and respected Past
Grand Master, Brother Dana R. Weller, was called from labor. Among
them born of women, there has not been a greater Mason in our jurisdiction than Judge Weller. In the language of Past Grand Master William
Rhodes Hervey, "he stood as a flaming sword against innovations in
Masonry and the ritual of Masonry." It is our hope that another will rise
to bear this "flaming sword." In May, Brother Frank W. Mixter, who was
Grand Master in 1932-33, the year I was Master of Meridian Lodge, was
also called. He was one of the kindliest of them all. In addition to these,
Inspectors William L. Hovis, District 79; Hardus Sorkness, District 107,
and Prosper A. Sainges, District 113, and other members of Grand Lodge
have passed to the undiscovered country. Our comfort is that the good
they have done will live after them. With their passing, it is not for us to
quarrel, for only God knows when to call his children home. At a later

INTER·JURISDICTIONAL VISITATIONS

Puerto Rico

En route to the Grand Masters' Conference in Washington, D. C., I
journeyed from Miami, Florida, to the island of Puerto Rico by Pan
American clipper, for the purpose of extending to the Grand Master and
other officers of the Grand Lodge of Puerto Rico my fraternal greetings
and good Wishes and those of this Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge of Puerto Rico was not in session, but I was accepted
and treated with the utmost courtesies by the brethren. On February 15,
Brother Rodolpho Ramirez Pabon (a district judge, Past Grand Master,
and the Grand Representative of the Grand Lodge of California near the
Grand Lodge of Puerto Rico) called together a group of twenty-one officers from Lodges in the city of Mayaguez and held a banquet in my honor
at the Cocoanut Hut by the sea. The historical high points of Masonry
in the island were interestingly presented by Judge Ramirez, as well as
its current practice and procedure. It is hardly necessary to say that all
the brethren were kind and C!onsiderate and the meeting was tho-roughly
enjoyed by me.
On the day of my departure, February 16, the Grand Master, Brother
Jose G. Bloise, called together a group of twenty-four, consisting of
Grand Lodge officers and Past Grand Masters, and tendered a luncheon
in my honor at the Condado Beach Hotel in San Juan. The Grand Master

19

and four others, in short speeches, eloquently testified to their appreciation of my visit and presence. In my response among other things, I introduced the subject of our forthcoming centennial and invited the whole
group to attend it, conditioned, however, to the extent that we would pay
the expenses of only the then Grand Master. All the brothers were cordial,.
attentive, and respectful. After the luncheon, the Grand Master accompanied me about the city and· poi11ted out objects of interest, including a
dormitory which that Grand Lodge maintains, adjacent to the campus of
the University of Puerto Rico, for Masonically affiliated girl students.
It was my pleasure to meet and visit again with Grand Master Bloise
and the Grand Secretary, Brother Angel M. Torres, at the Grand Masters'
Conference in Washington.
Washington

On June 17 and 18, I attended the Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Washington, at Tacoma, and was received with private Grand
honors. The Grand Master, Gustav H. Schultz, assigned to me a Past
Grand Master; the Grand Marshal, Brother Alexander K. Stewart; and
another brother-with a new Cadillac-as my personal attendants. In
addition to my comfortable enjoyment of the interesting and educational
proceedings of the Grand Lodge, I had an opportunity to view at short
distance the beauties of Mt. Rainier and other attractions with which
Nature has blessed the State of Washington.

groups; ex-Inspector J. F. Fenwick; General Wayne Smith; Ray Marston
Allen; Dr. C. E. Fronk; Duke Kahanamoku; and others. Inspector Potts
and Grand Standard Bearer Townsend did not overlook the sick, for they
made it possible for the Grand Master to visit brothers who were illincluding Brother David M. Moncrief - and crippled children at the
Shrine Hospital.
All these contacts afforded the Grand Master an opportunity to become
well acquainted with the condition of the Lodges and the status of
Masonry. I am therefore able to report that the financial condition of the
Lodges is excellent; membership is at an all-time peak; Lodge halls are
adequate and well kept; Masonry is indeed flourishing, and the fraternal
trade winds of harmony prevail.
When World War II came to these islands on December 7, 1941, with
its black-outs, martial law, restrictions on transportation, and limitations
on meetings in time and number, ordinary men and Masons would have
said that Masonry must come to a halt and that the trowel be laid down
during hostilities. Not so with Inspector Alexander Douglas Potts a~d the
brethren who assisted him. The dark hours kindled their spirit and fortified their determination that Masons and Masonry must work and° serve
even in time of war. These brethren, therefore, by their enterprising spirit
and driving devotion above and beyond the call of duty, pulled Masonry
through the havoc and hardships of war to the flourishing, outstanding
position it holds today and for which they are entitled to the grateful
thanks of this Grand Lodge.
Kings, consorts, potentates, and countless brethren have ministered to
Grand Masters in former years, but the courtesies, receptions, and ovations extended to the Grand Master this year must stand as the climax to
all of them and a very definite challenge to the future.

PETTUS BIBLE

This Bible, which is printed in the Chinese language, was accepted in
1940 by this Grand Lodge from the donor, Worshipful William B. Pettus,
on condition "that it would be held each year by the Lodge which has
rendered the best service to Masonic charity." It is not possible to say
which of our 590 Lodges has rendered the best service to Masonic charity,
for this would entail an exacting investigation and examination of the
records and activities of every one of them.
It can be said, however, that Confidence Lodge No. 203 has rendered
outstanding service to Masonic charity. Among many other things chari·
table in nature and unnecessary here to recount, the Master of this Lodge
and the other forty members thereof converted a seeming impossibility
into an objective reality.
The Grand Master was invited to pay an official visit to this Lodge on
March 24, 1947. I agreed to do so on condition that the meeting be made
a district affair, to encompass all the Lodges in District 56. This condition
was imposed, because it was deemed unfair to travel so far to visit only
one Lodge, when districts and even combinations of districts were beseeching a visitation by the Grand Master. The Master of this Lodge informed
me that the foundation of the Lodge Hall was giving way and that its
condition and capacity would not accommodate the entire district; that
materials and labor with which to restore and enlarge the hall were not
obtainable; that the Lodge had not the funds with which to restore or
remodel; and that there was no other building in Castroville which would
serve such a meeting. I told the Master that the condition imposed by me
would, nevertheless, have to stand.
Whereupon, the forty-one members of this old Lodge, under the leadership of the Master, set about their duties. In just thirty-one days, these
brothers, under the driving, charitable, enterprising spirit which should
always characterize Masons and Masonry, somehow found the materials,
money, and labor, restored and remodeled the temple, and doubled its
seating capacity. So the Grand Master, on March 24, 1947, was received
in due and ancient form by Confidence Lodge, as the host Lodge for District 56, in the presence of a full and magnificent audience.
At this meeting, Past Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg-who was
born just across the street from the Lodge Hall-installed the officers.
In passing, I desire to say that I returned to Castroville on March 26, 1947,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Master of this Lodge, who is now serving his second term, is Brother
Fong Q. Jing. He is the first native Chinese ever to serve as Master of a
Masonic Lodge in California. He is also the first naturalized Chinese ever
to be Master of a Masonic Lodge in this jurisdiction.
The Pettus Bible is therefore awarded to Confidence Lodge No. 203 for
the coming year.
INSPECTORS

Having come from the ranks of Inspectors, it was my good fortune to
know many of them personally and well when I assumed this office, and
this year has afforded me an opportunity to know them better and to
meet many more. On several occasions I have called upon Inspectors for
assistance in matters of great importance to the Craft, and they have
always responded eagerly and effectually. It is not my purpose to be
fulsome, but the record must show that these capable and loyal gentlemen
are the teachers and willing servants of Masonry.
However, they are not perfect, and one criticism is in order: The Grand
Master and his nominee, generally, and the Inspector in his own district
are the only members in this jurisdiction who are entitled to be officially
received with private Masonic Grand honors. I have learned that some
Inspectors make no official visits and others make few. Some fear that
Grand honors will make them seem grandiose. This is error. It is the
office which receives the honors, not the man. Maintenance of the dignity
of the office requires that the Inspector make at least one official visit to
each Lodge in his district during each Masonic year.

The record will probably show that the line officers of Grand Lodge this
. year have extended to the Grand Master greater co-operation and assistance and have accompanied him on more official ceremonies and recep·
tions than in any previous year. The brethren in all parts of the jurisdiction
appreciate the personal visits of the Grand Master. I can testify that they
too value an opportunity to meet and talk with the other Grand Lodge
officers. These officers are all able men and Masons. My thanks and the
gratitude of this Grand Lodge must go to every last one of them.
Fairness dictates that I should individualize one of these. From close
contact and observation, I am able to say that our Grand Secretary, Lloyd
E. Wilson, is an efficient executive and an able administrator. The records
and condition of his office affirm this statement. Among other Grand
Secretaries, he is the most popular; among his brethren, compliments to
him are commonplace. It is common knowledge that he is an able and
brilliant speaker, albeit in the presence of the Grand Master he always
contrives to make a poor speech. To put it another way, courtesy and
condescension to the Grand Master are to him fundamental: the comfort
and convenience of the Grand Master are his first concern.
RITUAL

· In the course of this year, I have sat in more than fifty-five Lodges and
have been deeply impressed by the manner in which the Masters and
other officers devoted themselves to the Ritual and by the degree of
perfection in which they administer it. This is complimentary to the
system under which we teach it, to the Committee on Ritual, and to the
Inspectors.
In other Grand Jurisdictions, I have observed a tendency to blame the
Ritual for lack of attendance and other shortcomings. Some have introduced changes--to no avail. Here the brethren seem to abhor changeswhich is a healthy attitude. If our Ritual was good for our Masonic fathers,
it should be good enough for us. It remains an uncontradicted fact that
the Ritual, fortified by the unflinching devotion of the men who were
Masons, has brought Masonry down through the centuries unfettered and
unsullied.
Only once during the year did I encounter absence of avouchment.
At Kilauea Lodge in Hilo on the island of Hawaii, no one could vouch for
the Grand Master, so it was necessary for me to be examined. I call upon
you now to witne~s the smile upon the face of my moderator, Very Worshipful Grand Le'cturer Arthur M. Warren, when I tell you that I passed
the examination.

young men to the sublime degree of Master . Mason, including my only

son, John Bender Moore, at my own Meridian Lodge in Glendale on

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

The members of this Board are charged with the responsibility of
securing an adequate Endowment Fund, by means and methods approved
by the Grand Master, the income from which is to go for the support and
maintenance of our Masonic Homes. The size of the contributions this
year will hear witness to the effectiveness of their endeavors under direction of the chairman, Brother Ernest G. Bashor.
This fund is the guardian of our temple of Masonic charity. It is my
belief that the members of this mighty fraternity, if properly informed,
will ever keep this guardian strong.
In my proclamation on this subject this year, I did not set the dollar
sign on contributions but left the amount to the free will of our brothers.
I expressed the hope, however, that the aggregate would not be less than
for 1946. It is therefore comforting to find that the total contributions
through the Lodges this year, $186,398.55, not only exceeded last year's
figure but established an all-time high yearly record.
BOARD OF CONTROL

Under our law (Secs. 91-%, inc., Ross Digest) the supervision and control of our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus are obligations of
the Board of Control. At the beginning of this Masonic year, I directed the
attention of the chairman of said Board to this law and these obligations
for assurance purposes only, for he was of course already quite· familiar
with them. It is encouraging and satisfying to he able to report that this
Board, under the most able leadership of its chairman, Brother Jack C.
Butler, has shouldered its obligations and discharged its responsibilities
in such a manner that it will redound to the benefit of the whole fraternity.
If confirmation be required, its forthcoming report will suffice.
