PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

For twenty·eight years, this Grand Lodge has sponsored Public Schools
Week. The Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools Week has limited
its activity to urging the people to visit their schools at least once each
year. It is evident and conceded that this activity has caused untold thou·
sands to visit our schools during Public Schools Week, has contributed
to the upbuilding of our schoolhouses, and has probably helped to obtain
more teachers when badly needed.
·
If this is all we have done, we are not in a position to boast, for we can
only say that we have drawn the multitudes, while others have swayed
them. If we have drawn the multitudes, we should at least urge our own
brethren to look inside the schoolhouses and find out the type of teachers
we have and what they are teaching our children. We should he industrious enough to obtain some facts concerning our schools, including the
curriculums and the teachers, and disseminate such facts among the
brethren.
Our government was founded as a representative or republican form
of government, and by and large it has been traditionally representative
and democratic. For half a century in this country, the teaching of some
of its political and legal philosophers in our institutions of higher learning
has been essentially totalitarian, anti-democratic, and, perforce, subversive. The results have not been too encouraging to these philosophers; so
they or the un-American forces sharing their philosophy and purpose
have dropped this type of teaching down to the public schools in the age
bracket of eleven to thirteen years. They recognize, as did Hitler, that it
is easier and more effectual to indoctrinate students of tender years. These
things ought to be called to the attention of every member of thisfraternity.

DECISIONS

1. The Master may lawfully permit a group of Master Masons, belonging to any Body, Order, or Organization, the prerequisite of membership
wherein is that a member be a Master Mason, to confer one or more of
the three degrees of Masonry in his Lodge as a degree team under the
name of said Body, Order, or Organization, provided that the dress of
such team be such as is customarily worn on such occasions by members
or officers of the Lodge and provided, further, that the Master is assured
of the ritualistic proficiency of said team. (This decision is based upon
Sections 506 and 507 of Ross Digest.)
2. It is not lawful for a Lodge to confer or to begin to confer any
degree of Masonry prior to the time fixed for convening a special meeting
therefor, as directed by the Lodge or the presiding officer thereof.
3. A bequest to a Lodge under the will of a decedent is not revenue
within the purview of Section 159 of Ross Digest.
4. The Charter of Santa Cruz Lodge, dated May 6, 1854, reads in part
as follows: " ... to be called Santa Cruz Lodge F. & A. M. number 38,
to be held in Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz County, California, or within five
miles of the same." This is called by some a roving charter.
It is held that such charter does not grant the Lodge unlimited latitude. Such a charter contemplates that meetings will be held in regular
meeting places, i.e., Lodge halls, and not in parks, valleys, or on hills.

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

!n .order for such a Lodge to hold a meeting outside a regular Lodge hall,
it is necessary for the Lodge to obtain a dispensation from the Grand
·
Master under Section 121 of Ross Digest.
5. Under Section 227 of Ross Digest, if the applicant removes from
the jurisdiction of the Lodge after filing his application and before the
beginning of initiation in the first degree, the application may be withdrawn if the applicant so desires and if the Lodge consents.
6. I~ the trial of an indiv:idual Mason under Section 287, et seq., of
Ross Digest, where a qualified Master talces jurisdiction and begins the
trial under Section 299 of Ross Digest, said Master maintains jurisdiction
and power to complete the trial as the trial Master, unless he becomes
subsequently disqualified, notwithstanding the fact that during the trial
he becomes a Past Master by the installation of his successor. Such duly
installed successor has no jurisdiction or control whatever over the trial
proceedings in his capacity as Master.
7. Hermosa Lodge No. 557, pursuant to Section 180 of Ross Digest,
requested approval of a resolution of its Lodge changing the time for the
election of its officers from the stated meeting in December to the stated
meeting in November. Approval was refused.
In 1936, brethren from certain Lodges located in the northeast section
of this jurisdiction appeared before the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes and sought permission to elect officers of said Lodges at the
stated meeting in November instead of the stated meeting in December.
They represented that said Lodges were located in the mountainous areas
where travel in December was dangerous or impossible because of heavy
snows; that many of the brethren were virtually snowed in during the
month of December; that many members resided at a considerable distance from their Lodges and, because of that fact and the heavy snows, were
prohibited from attending the meetings at which officers were elected in
December. Said Committee on Policy and General purposes recommended
legislation which would. permit Lodges so circumstanced to elect officers
in November (1936 Proceedings, p. 226).
/
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported as follows:
"We can readily understand that climatic conditions in December in
some parts of the jurisdiction render it practically impossible to hold
Lodge meetings in December, but it will be impossible to make exceptions
in behalf of any particular Lodge." ( 1936 Proceedings, p. 235.)
Thereupon, Grand Lodge, upon recommendation of the Committee on
Jurisprudence, enacted the law as it now stands in Ross Digest, Section 180.
The approval of a proper resolution is within the discretion of the
Grand Master, but necessity- not convenience--of the Lodge should be
the test. It would be an unwarranted exercise of discretion for the Grand
Master to bring Hermosa Lodge No. 557, with its soothing and balmy
climate, within the exception by approval of its resolution.

29

8. The Ninety-seventh Annual Communication, by amendment to
Section 245 of Ross Digest, increased the minimum fee for the three
degrees from $30.00 to $50.00; and where Lodges had concurrent juris·
diction, the fee for the three degrees was increased from $50.00 to $75.00
except by consent of all such Lodges.
Under this amendment, it was held that it was mandatory upon the
constituent Lodges affected by this amendment to initiate proceedings to
amend their bylaws, pursuant to Section 1 of Article 13 of the Uniform
Code of Bylaws under Section 133 of Ross Digest, to conform to the
provisions of said Section 245 as amended, at the next stated meeting
following the close of Grand Lodge, and that said amendment would
become effective on the date of the amendment to the bylaws of said
constituent Lodges.
9. From information furnished me by Brother John L. Cox, present
Master of Gardens Lodge No. 621, it appears that an application for the
degrees was received by said Lodge from a candidate on September 6,
1944; that he was elected to receive the degrees on October 4, 1944; that
he was initiated on October 11, 1944, and passed to the degree of Fellow
Craft on May 11, 1946; that said candidate, now brother, was and is
crippled in his left foot and leg, caused from infantile paralysis; and
that he cannot conform to what the several degrees require of him unless
he is supported by two men. It also appears that Question 12 of the
application pertaining to physical deformity, signed by said candidate,
is unanswered.
It further appears that Brother George T. Slater was Master of said
Lodge at the time said application was received and at the time said
candidate was initiated; that Brother Eugene Wayne Collins was Master
at the time he was passed; and that Brother John L. Cox, the present
Master, refused to raise, and submitted the matter for decision.
In the foregoing circumstances, it was manifest at all times that the
candidate could not substantially or at all conform to what the several
degrees, respectively, required of him. It will be observed too that the
candidate himself failed to answer Question 12 in the application, relat·
ing to physical deformity, and that Brother George T. Slater, the Master
at the time, apparently considered the answer nonessential, when in fact
it was vital.
Therefore, in the initiating and passing of said candidate, it muet be
held that Brother George T. Slater and Brother Eugene Wayne Collins
and Gardens Lodge No. 621 fouled the charter and violated the laws,
edicts, and regulations of Grand Lodge, set forth in Sections 208, 879,
880, and 880(a) of Ross Digest.
The unlawful actions of these two brothers and the Lodge have been
partially redeemed by the refusal of the present Master, Brother John
L. Cox, to raise said candidate to the degree of Master Mason. His attitude
in the premises is commendable and shows attention to duty and a respect

10. The provisions of Section 332 of Ross Digest may be invoked,
even after the accused has served his term and is no longer incarcerated.
11. The purchase price paid by a Lodge for an organ for its own use
falls within the category of "necessary expenses" under Section 157 of
Ross Digest.
12. On December 28, 1946, Gravel Range Lodge Hall was destroyed by
fire. Fortunately the records and Charter of the Lodge were not destroyed,
for they were in the Secretary's vault. The Lodge carried fire insurance
in the amount of $4,200.00 and had a building fund of $188.00 and cash
in the sum of $865.00, all of which was not sufficient to erect a new hall.
The Lodge therefore sought permission to solicit contributions from
the other Lodges in this jurisdiction to enable it to rebuild its temple.
This request was denied for the following reasons:
a. One of the cardinal conditions for granting a dispensation to form
a new Lodge is that the petitioners must be able to provide a proper
meeting place. So if the brethren of a community cannot financially
support a chartered Lodge and provide a proper meeting place, said
Lodge should not exist.
b. A candidate who is likely to become a charge upon the Lodge
should not be accepted. A new Lodge which is likely to become a charge
upon the other Lodges should not come into existence. Therefore, a
chartered Lodge which can exist only by becoming a charge upon the
other Lodges ought not to continue.
c. Section 155, Ross Digest, provides that a Lodge shall not divide its
funds with a new Lodge formed by its own withdrawing members. It
must therefore be held that a Lodge cannot divide its funds with an
existing Lodge.
d. Sections 157, 158, and 159, Ross Digest, set forth the sole purposes
for which the funds of a Lodge may be used, and a contribution to another
Lodge is not among them.
Therefore, should the Grand Master grant the request of Gravel Range
Lodge to solicit contributions from other Lodges, he would do violence
to the Ordinances of this Grand Lodge.
When denying this request, I stated in effect that the early builders of
Gravel Range Lodge did not let Masonry suffer for want of a Lodge Hall;
that the great Mason, William Bull Meek, was Master of this Lodge for
twenty-eight years; and that the enterprising spirit of the Masons of other

31

days somehow found a way. I stated too that I did not want old Gravel
Range to die and that I had the faith to believe that the brothers of this
day would by their own efforts find a way.
On my trip through the northeastern part of this state, I stopped at
Camptonville, viewed the spot where the temple formerly stood, and
discussed this subject with Acton M. Cleveland, Secretary of the Lodge
and grandson of William Bull Meek. At Sierra City, I also discussed the
subject with Inspector Frederick J. Joubert, who is a member of said
Lodge, and with very able Senior Warden Erle Pauly. I am therefore
able to report that my faith in the members of this day was confirmed and
that the temple of Gravel Range will rise again.
If Gravel Range Lodge should seek temporary assistance from this, its
mother Gland Lodge, I do not believe it should lend an unhearing ear.
13. In response to 8. question submitted by Brother R. P. Wisecarver
requiring an answer to comply with regulation of the United States Treas·
ury Department anent Exemption Affidavit-Form 1023, I held that the
Grand Lodge of California-not the Masonic Homes of California-is
the owner of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
The historical and legal authority for this decision is as follows:
1. The Grand Lodge, on October 16, 1891 (Proceedings, 1891, p.
228) adopted the following resolution:
" ... Resolved, That a committee of nine be appointed by the Grand
Master, whose duty it shall be to organize a Masonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home Association, or Incorporation, in manner as to that
committee may seem best; and which association or incorporation, when
so formed, shall have full power to purchase, receive, use and appropriate for the purpose of erecting and maintaining a Masonic Widows'
and Orphans' Home, all necessary property, real and personal, or
moneys which can be obtained by the said incorporation or association,
by purchase, donation or otherwise; and to that end, and for these
objects, to receive donations from all Masons or Masonic Lodges within
this jurisdiction, and to select, receive as a gift, or purchase a site for said
Home; and, finally, to do and perform all needful acts necessary to carry
into successful operation the said enterprise."
Such committee was appointed by the Grand Master, and the following
year (Proceedings 1892, p. 721) the Grand Lodge adopted the report of
the Committee on Jurisprudence, reading in part as follows:
"The committee, to which the preparation of a plan for the organization
of a Widows' and Orphans' Home was referred last year, with directions
to report to the Grand Master, completed its work in December,' and the
plan proposed meeting the approval of the Grand Master, he proceeded
to carry it into effect by appointing a Board of nine Trustees, 'to receive,
hold and administer, as joint tenants, with right of survivorship during
their term of office and until their successors are appointed, all property,
real and personal, and all rights of action belonging to said charity or
to which it may, in any manner become entitled.'

RECOMMENDATIONS

During the interval since our Annual Communication last year, I have
given much thought to certain important subjects concerning our fraternity and have discussed most of them with countless brethren in different
parts of this jurisdiction. It is my belief that these subjects ought to have
your serious consideration, and I herewith submit them to you with
recommendations as follows:
A. War Relief and War Activities Committee.
On December 30, 1946, I issued a proclamation which read:
"On February 14, 1942, the then Grand Master, Frank M. Smith, issued
a proclamation establishing the Masonic War Relief Fund, which proclamation, among other things, provided for issuance of War Service
• Certificates to California Masons in the service of our country in World
War II.
"Acknowledging that this war came to a successful conclusion on
September 2, 1945, I do now proclaim World War II ended for our
purposes, and hereby order that the issuance of War Service Certificates
be henceforth discontinued."
It is interesting, if not significant, that the President of the United
States on the very next day, December 31, 1946, proclaimed World War II
ended for all the people.
I therefore recommend:
1. That the foregoing proclamation be approved.
.2. That the War Relief Fund, amounting to approximately
$155,574.94, be transferred to the General Fund, earmarked, and held
subject to further orders of this Grand Lodge.
3. That the War Activities Committee be abolished.
B. Lodge of Research Committee.
The Lodge of Research Committee has not functioned in several years
and there appears to be no need for it. I therefore recommend that said
committee be abolished.
C. Committee on Cl,andestine Masonry.
It is my opinion, based upon knowledge and experience, that our Committee on Clandestine Masonry does not assist but disturbs this Grand
Lodge. Grand Masters of other Grand Jurisdictions have said that California has the question of Clandestine Masonry solved, because it has a
committee which maintains contact or collaborates with the clandestine

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

deployed throughout the great Pacific Basin look upon us as the gateway
to the American Republic.
The Grand Lodge of California and the Golden State have paralleled
each other in age, in growth, and in progress. Masonry must continue to
keep the pace, for it is destined to exert a p-otent influence for the good
of mankind in the yet more marvelous future which obtains in California.
In keeping with the spirit of California, our centennial ought to be-must be--"stupendous and colossal." To it will come delegates and dignitaries from most of the Grand Jurisdictions on earth.
This temple is not a fit or proper place in which to hold our centennial
celebrations. We ought to have a new Grand Lodge temple erected in San
Francisco as a memorial to the Masons from California Lodges who served
and died in World War II, in which to celebrate our centennial. Voices
will contend that this can't be done; that the time is too short and the cost
too great. The enterprising spirit of Masonry abhors the word "can't."
The value of the dollar is relative. It is easier to raise two dollars today
than it will be to raise one when deflation comes.
Our brothers in previous years set a precedent which we ought to be
able to emulate: On October 11, 1911, Grand Master Weller laid the
cornerstone of this temple; on October 13, 1913, Grand Master Filmer
adjourned the meeting in this place and dedicated this temple.
In addition to serving as a memorial to our brothers who served and
died in World War II, a new temple would furnish a comfortable meeting
place for the delegates to our communications in the years to come and
would provide a fitting place in which to pause and acknowledge our
debt to the early builders of Masonry in California whose consummate
wisdom, fidelity, and courage have placed in our hands this magnificent
heritage.
I therefore suggest:
1. That a committee of nine members of this Grand Lodge be appointed
by the incoming Grand Master, to be known as the Committee on Me·
morial Temple; that said committee be empowered to purchase
and acquire land for a temple site in the nanie of this Grand Lodge in
the city of San Francisco and to erect a Grand Lodge Temple thereon of
such size and type as it shall decide; that said committee be further
empowered to make, sign, and enter into all documents, contracts, and
agreements in the name of this Grand Lodge, which may be required
or necessary to erect and complete said temple; that said committee be
definitely enjoined to complete said temple and have it ready for occupancy on or before September 1, 1950; and that said temple, when completed, be called "Masonic Memorial Temple" and bear an appropriate
inscription to the memory of the Masons from California Lodges who
served and died in World War II, as determined by said committee.
2. That the War Relief Fund, amounting to approximately Sl 55,574.94,
be transferred to, and set up as, a special account and entitled "Memorial
Temple Fund."

E. Grand Lodge of Philippine Islands.
A letter, dated April 17, 1947, came to me from M. W. Emilio P. Virata,
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, reading in
part as follows:
"Last year the former Grand Master issued a dispensation to brethren
of the U. S. armed forces, residing at Okinawa, to form and organize
a blue lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of F. & A. M. of
the Philippines. A charter was requested in our last Annual Communication, but action was deferred because the brethren felt that the island
still was a part of Japan, and as such came under the Grand Lodge of
England.
"Now we have before us a request to permit some brethren to organize
a lodge on Saipan, an Island very close to Guam--our Masonic territory
for more than twenty years. The Marianas Islands are now about to
come under the trusteeship of the United States of America, and no longer
will they be mandated islands of the Japanese. Guam being an integral
part of the Marianas group we considered this group as masonic territory
of the Philippines. In fact this group used to belong to Spain along with
the Philippines. It is hoped that your Grand Lodge will not interpose
any objection for our Grand Lodge to establish Lodges in Okinawa and
in the Marianas group inasmuch as our jurisdiction has extended over
Guam for many years."
Under date of June 20, 1947, I responded to this letter in part, to wit :
"This responds to your letter of April 17 anent the Marianas and other
islands.
"The Grand Lodge of California takes the position that the territory
embraced by the Island of Okinawa and the Marianas group, including
the Islands of Guam and Saipan, is 'open' Masonic Territory and will
remain such unless and until a regular Grand ~dge is legally estab-

38

lished in said islands, respectively. This Grand Lodge further considers
the Country of Japan 'open' Masonic Territory.
"It follows, therefore, that this Grand Lodge has no present intention
to interpose objections to the establishment of Lodges in the areas above
referred to by the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands.
"The Grand Lodge of California is not presently disposed to establish
Lodges in the areas above described, but this position is without prejudice
to future action."

G. Legislation Requiring and Defining "Notice."
I recommend that sections of Ross Digest be amended as follows:
1. Section 255, by striking the words "and who either" in line six
and inserting in lieu thereof "provided he".
2. Section 296, by striking the whole and inserting in lieu thereof
the following: "A separate and distinct notice of such meeting shall be
given to every member of said Lodge whose residence is known and is
within such distance as may reasonably permit him to attend; which
notice shall state that the purpose of the meeting is to elect Commissioners to try a brother (using no name) upon a charge of un-Masonic
conduct."
3. Section 298, by striking the whole and inserting in lieu thereof
the following: "A notice, whenever or wherever used in the regulations
of Grand Lodge, is a call i~sued by the Secretary by order of the Lodge
or Master or by other competent authority, to attend for some specific
purpose at the time and place therein indicated, or to perform some
specific duty therein set forth; and it is the duty of every Mason to
comply with its direction if he can do so without great inconvenience.
Said notice shall be written or printed and shall, when practicable, be
personally served upon the brother to be notified by a Tiler or some
other Mason properly deputed for the purpose. If this cannot conveniently be done, it shall be left at the residence or usual place of
business of such brother, or be sent by first-class or registered mail to
him at his usual address in a sealed envelope."

H. Lodge Birthdays.
Western Star Lodge No. 2 submitted a request for permission to form
a Centennial Club, the members of which are to be Masons and nonMasons and a fee set for membership therein; the club then to engage
in activities, such as holding banquets similar to those held by one of
our political parties, where excessive prices per plate would be charged
and the net receipts, including membership fees, used for defraying
the expenses of the hundred-year anniversary of said Lodge, beginning
May 10, 1948.
This request was denied for the following reasons :
Throughout the centuries, Masonry has been able to conduct its affairs
and its business through its own Lodges and without the benefit of collateral clubs and groups. A Lodge and its members within the framework
of its own organization ought to be able to provide funds in a regular,
legal way, with which to celebrate its birthday, be it one hundred or ·
otherwise.
It is commendable indeed for a Lodge to plan for and to celebrate
its own centennial, but the celebration should be geared to the financial
ability of the Lodge and its members without collateral clubs and certainly without solicitations from the profane. I therefore recommend
that the Grand Lodge pass upon this subject.
I. Masonic Clubs.
In the past several years Masonic clubs have been in numerous instances
irksome and a source of trouble to the constituent Lodges and to Grand
Lodge. In my travels and visitations this year I have heard and received
much criticism of them, some of which is as follows:
1. They draw the attention of Masons from their Lodges and interfere
with the attendance of Masons upon their Lodges or other Lodges in the
vicinity.
2. In their meetings a sense of freedom from Lodge·room decorum
sometimes prevails, and liberties are indulged which are not consonant
with the dignity of Masonry and which sometimes cast umbrage upon the
great institution of Masonry.
3. Some charge. and collect fees and dues and expend part thereof for
purposes not authorized by the laws or rules of this Grand Lodge.
4. Some of these clubs are beholden by charter and bylaws to a national organization with headquarters outside this jurisdiction, to which
a part of the funds of the club is sent; that the national or parent organization, by its governing rules and regulations, by its bulletins and its
publications, is influencing or endeavoring to influence the members of
the club Masonically.
5. Some of these clubs, by their solicitations and drives for membership, enlist numbers of what we call sojourning Masons; that these
brethren then consider that they belong to a Masordc organization and

40

PROCEEDINGS. OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

probably partly for this reason do not concern themselves about dimit·
ting to a regular Lodge; that this is a definite interference with the
processes of Masonry.
From my observation all such clubs are not subject to this criticism.
Many adhere to Masonic regulations and principles, and co-operation
with the Lodges is their primary concern. I therefore recommend that
the Grand Lodge explore this subject for proper determination.
J. Masonic Publications. .
.
Magazines, newspapers, bulletins, and other publications using the
words "Masonic," "Masonry," or phrases indicating Masonic connections
in their titles or headings and posing as official Masonic publications of
this jurisdiction or some part thereof, or using our Masonic emblem
(the square and compass) have caused embarrassment to and embitter·
ment of some of our brethren, our Lodges, and the Grand Lodge. These
· results have been effected by the methods used in soliciting advertising
and subscriptions and by the nature of the published contents, including
advertisements, some of which have proved odious to the fraternity of
Masonry.
It is therefore necessary for me to hold that there is now no official
Masonic magazine, newspaper, bulletin, or similar publication in this
jurisdiction, and that this Grand Lodge, by virtue of the provisions of
its Constitution, has and holds the vested and exclusive right to the use
of the words "Masonic" and "Masonry" and the square-and-compass
emblem, and that the unauthorized use of them or any of them by any
publication or otherwise ought to be appropriately challenged.
I therefore recommend that the Grand Lodge pass upon this matter.

he carries and performs. I therefore recommend that consideration be

L. Courtesy Degrees.
On January 11, 1947, I issued an Edict concerning courtesy degrees,
to become effective February 1, 1947, reading as follows:

(a) Certifying that his legal residence is in the Jurisdiction of California,
(b) Giving his exact legal address, and
( c) Stating that he is residing temporarily in said other jurisdiction,
·
and then only in exceptional circumstances.
3. The request of a Lodge in another jurisdiction to have the degrees,
or any of them, conferred upon its applicant or candidate by a California
Lodg~ will not be approved unless said applicant or candidate presents •
a statement in writing signed by him:
(a) Certifying that his legal residence is in said other jurisdiction,
(b) Giving his exact legal address, and
(c) Stating that he is residing temporarily in the Jurisdiction of California, and then only in exceptional circumstances.
This Edict conforms to the policy of this Grand Lodge which was
adopted at the 78th Annual Communication in 1927, reading as follows:
"We, therefore, recommend that no degree be conferred by courtesy
upon men whose actual legal residence is within our jurisdiction, except
when good cause be shown why the candidate should remain a member
of the requesting Lodge. (Adopted)" (Sec. 886, Ross Digest, p. 416.)
A Masonic Lodge is or should be a part of the community life, and
its members should be residents of the community or area in which the
Lodge is located. Men who earnestly desire to become Master Masons
should obtain the necessary dimits or waivers of jurisdiction and seek
the degrees, or remaining degrees or degree, in the jurisdiction in which
they hold legal residence. California bas enabling laws to effect these
purposes, as follows:
" ... If the applicant shall have removed from the juri~diction of the
Lodge after filing his application, the application may be withdrawn
if the applicant so desires and the Lodge consents ..." (Sec. 227 Ross
Digest.) The law here quoted applies up to but not beyond the beginning
of initiation in the first degree.
" . . . An entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may, ·after receiving
a waiver of jurisdiction from his Lodge, apply to another Lodge for the
remaining degrees or degree, accompaning it with the fees required
therefor." (&,c. 243 Ross Digest.)

M. Ross Digest.
The supply of this compilation of our Masonic Law is almost exhausted.
The fourth edition was printed in 1943 and many changes in our law
have since occurred. For this great work, we are of course indebted to
Past Grand Master John Stewart Ross. The Ross Digest has been of inestimable value to me, but, best of all, my fortune has been the privilege and
benefit of his wisdom and personal counsel. The records of this Grand
Lodge ought to reflect its grateful thanks and appreciation to him.
I therefore recommend that Most Worshipful John Stewart Ross be
requested to bring the Ro~ Digest up-to-date and that a fifth edition be
printed, the number of copies thereof to be determined by the Grand
Secretary.
N. Massachusetts and Negro Freemasonry.
.
· According to its Proceedings for the year 1876, the Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts approved the report of its committee which had extensively
investigated and explored the subject of the so·called Prince Hall (Negro)
Freemasonry and which had reported that the said so·called Prince Hall
(Negro) Freemasonry was clandestine and irregular.
In 1899, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts appealed earnestly to the
Grand Lodge of Washington to reconsider its action in holding so-called
Prince Hall (Negro) Freemasonry to be valid and regular.
In spite of the foregoing commitments, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, at its regular Quarterly Communication, held on March 12,
1947, accepted, approved, and recorded a report of its Committee on ·
Negro Freemasonry, holding:
.
" ... that ... it is advisable for the official and organized activities
of white and colored Freemasons to proceed in parallel lines, but organ·
ically separate. and without mutually embarrassing demands or commit·
ments," and " ... that, within these limitations, informal cooperation
and mutual helpfulness between the two groups upon appropriate occasions are desirable," and further " ... that ... the origin, early procedures
and subsequent development of the so-called Prince Hall (Negro) Free·
masonry in this Commonwealth have been, and are, regular and legiti·
mate."
In the pamphlet issued by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts ahnounc·
ing the approved report above quoted, the Grand Secretary annexed
a statement reading in part as follows:
"The Committee did not recommend, and the Grand Lodge did not
vote, what is Masonically known as 'recognition.' "
This is a matter of construction and interpretation. The very words of
the report itself above quoted compel the conclusion that so-called
Prince Hall (Negro) Freemasonry was held to be regular and legitimate,
which is tantamount to recognition. In fact, it has been reported that
a member of the so-called Grand Lodge of Prince Hall (Negro) Free·
masonry stated that the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts had recognized
his Grand Lodge.

Regarding this subject, the law and policy of the Grand Lodge of
California are as follows:
1. This Grand Lodge has always adhered to the doctrine of exclusive
territorial jurisdiction. Since the date of its organization, April 19, 1850,
it has been, and is, the supreme Masonic power in this State, and recognizes no authority, except in itself, to grant any charter or dispensation
for a Masonic Lodge therein. Authority: Sec. 6, Ross Digest ( Constitution) :
"The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Masonic Power and Authority in
this jurisdiction, possessing all the attributes of sovereign,ty and govern·
ment-legislative, executive, and judicial-limited only by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the Order, and by the provisions
of its own Constitution and Regulations.''
2. This Grand Lodge in 1872 declared:
.
" ... We have established a rule recognized throughout the United
States and British America, that only one Grand Lodge shall he established
in any State or Territory, and that, whenever one is established, it has
the absolute control and government of all Masons and all Lodges of the
first three degrees; and that no other Grand Lodge can in any way interfere with its jurisdiction, to establish new Lodges therein, or even to
maintain those already established. The territory is absolutely, exclusively, and perpetually the territory of the Grand Lodge established
over it; and the Grand Lodge of any State not only has exclusive jurisdiction within the limits of the State, but it has full, original, and exclusive legislative, judicial, and executive power within that territory, subject only to the great landmarks of the Order. If any Grand Lodge of
the United States or Europe should seek to establish in California a new
Lodge, or should recognize any spurious and clandestine Lodge or Lodges
already therein established, this Grand Lodge would consider it an invasion of its rights and would suspend all friendly relations with the Grand
Lodge so offending.'' (Sec. 584, Ross Digest 4th Ed. )
3. This Grand Lodge as jealously protects the sovereignty of every
other American Grand Lodge by providing in its Ordinances:
"A Lodge shall not recognize any Body, purporting to be a Masonic
Lodge, which shall be holden within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of any State or Territory of the Unit~d States without authority from
such Grand Lodge; nor shall any Lodge, or any member thereof, admit
or hold Masonic intercourse with a member of any such Body, with an
expelled or suspended Mason, with an illegal Lodge, with any person
who has received degrees therein or is a member thereof, nor with any
Mason not acknowledged as such by this Grand Lodge.'' (Sec. 116, Ross
Digest 4th Ed.)
Every American Grand Lodge up to this time (with one exception,
which was later revoked) has acquiesced in the doctrine, set forth in
Paragraphs 1, 2, and 3 above, as protecting, rather than attacking, its

44

45

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sovereignty, and as enabling the various Grand Lodges to live together,
in peace and harmony. Disregard thereof can only result in hopeless strife
and confusion.
This Grand Lodge, by its rules for admission to membership, does
not draw the color line (Sec. 208, Ross Digest 4th Ed.), but it does
claim that no one--be he red, white, black, or tan--can be made a Mason
in California except in a Lodge existing by the authority of the Grand
Lodge of California; that all Lodges existing in this State without the
authority of this Grand Lodge are spurious, clandestine, and illegitimate;
and that a recognition of any such Lodge or the members thereof, by any
other Grand Lodge, is an invasion of the rights of the Grand Lodge of
California.
It is conceded that there are so-called Prince Hall (Negro) Free·
masonry Lodges and members thereof located in the State of California.
It must therefore be concluded that the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, by
its action of March 12, 1947, in recognizing as regular and legitimate
the so-called Prince Hall (Negro) Freemasonry, did violence to and
invaded the rights and sovereignty of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of California and that the comity and friendly relations
heretofore existing with the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts have been
severely strained, and it is incumbent upon me to present the matter to
the Grand Lodge for such action as it deems necessary and wise.
Dated August 1, 1947.
JoHN R. MOORE, Grand Master.
The foregoing brief and the following letter were sent to Grand Master
Samuel H. Wragg of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts on August 16,
1947:
A copy of your report entitled, "Massachusetts and Negro Freemasonry," which was accepted, approved, and recorded by your Grand
Lodge on or about March 12, 1947, reached me in the latter part of June.
I have given much consideration to your action on this subject and
have prepared a brief on our Masonic law with respect thereto, which is
enclosed.
I am mindful of the statement, appended to said report by your Grand
Secretary, to the effect that your Grand Lodge did not vote what is
Masonically known as recognition. With this statement I disagree. The
word recognition implies formal acknowledgment, as of a fact or a claim.
Your Grand Lodge, in formal session, acknowledged the Prince Hall
institution to be regular and legitimate--which is recognition. Masonic
recognition admits only that the body recognized is a regular Masonic
one. A regular Masonic Lodge cannot lawfully engage in "official and
organized activities" nor indulge in "informal co-operation and mutual
helpfulness" with any body or organization which is not recognized by it.
In this jurisdiction we have so-called Prince Hall Masonry. Your
report has already caused confusion in our jurisdiction and promises to
cause more. It has been said that if the Institution of Masonry is de-

1troyed, destruction will come from within. Your action is considered
as an internal explosion, with confusing consequences.
It is therefore earnestly hoped that you and your Grand Lodge will
give further consideration to this vital subject, with a view to restoring
harmony.
JoHNR. MOORE, Grand Master.

Page 7:
"Members of this Committee have inspected the original charter of

Dear Brother Wragg:
In your letter of September 24, 1947, you state that only one of the
paragraphs quoted in my letter of September 12 was actually from the
report of the committee. I consider the whole pamphlet which your Grand
Lodge issued germane to the subject and the provisions thereof as constituting reasons for its action. A conclusion is no stronger than tlre
reasons upon which it ia based.

You state that I did not suggest any way in which you could have more
explicitly or emphatically restricted your findings to yout own jurisdiction. On the last page of my letter of September 12 I stated: "This is
a serious matter, and its effects cannot be limited by statements defining
boundary." ·
In the third paragraph of your letter of September 24, you state: "I do
not detect in your correspondence any indication that you differ with the
factual findings of the committee. . . ." Heretofore I have limited my
attention to the effects on California which your actions have caused and
deemed it presumptuous to speak about the logic of your actions. ! 'consider your statement an invitation to do so. I have differed and do now
differ completely with your factual findings, for the reasons set forth
below:
So-called Negro Masons generally claim descent from the "Prince Hall"
organization. The latter has been repeatedly investigated by various of
the Masonic Grand Lodges in the United States, including the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts. That Grand Lodge, in 1876, as a result of an
exhaustive investigation, referring to the Prince Hall organization, said:
"It professed to grant Charters, and did make some clandestine Bodies
in other places. No Masonic power, domestic or foreign, stood its sponsor,
and no known Mason belonged to it * * *. The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts never authorized any Lodge or recognized any person claiming
Masonic rights from this source."
Also:
"Th~ existing Prince Hall Grand Lodge organization is supposed to
dr~w· its. power from this National Grand Lodge" and, referring to the
latter, "It is understood that this Body claims jurisdiction in and over
Masonry in all the States of this Union, but no official intercourse has ever
been sought by that Body with this Grand Lodge, or those who pertain to .
it, and we are ignorant of all that concerns it.''
The Massachusetts Grand Lodge referred to its proceedings of 1869 and
1870 "for a fuller statement o~ the history * * * of these bogus Masons

(Questions obviously present themselves as to how it is possible for a
regular Masonic Lodge or Mason to recognize or treat any activities of a
clandestine organization as "official," or for the activities of such a Lodge
or Mason to proceed on parallel lines with the activities of clandestine
Lodges or Masons, or how there can be even "informal" cooperation
between legitimate and clandestine Masons. As to these questions Massachusetts offers no reply, and, it is believed, they are Masonicallyinsoluble.)
The report was accepted and its recommendations adopted without
qualification by the Grand Lodge. Referring thereto the Grand Secretary
says:
"The Committee did not recommend, and the Grand Lodge did not
vote, what is Masonically known as 'recognition.' Neither was any action
taken concerning intervisitation."
The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, like every other Grand Lodge,
may, of course, determine for itself who shall be recognized by it as
regular and legitimate Masons and Masonic Bodies. Its determinations
in this respect are of concern to the Masons of other jurisdictions, how·
ever, to the extent that they may affect Masonic communications and intervisitation. By comity a Mason, recognized as such by the Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts, is entitled, upon satisfactory showing or identification, to
freely visit California Lodges and to appropriate consideration by California Masons. If Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction recognizes as
legitimate Masons belonging to an organization held by the Grand
Lodge of California to be clandestine, confusion seriously affecting harmony between such Grand Lodges would seem inevitable. While the inter·
pretation of the Grand Secretary of Massachusetts of the action of his
Grand Lodge is to be respected, it would seem that the latter's meaning
must be gathered from its own language, where the latter's words are
clear and specific. The Committee reported that "the early procedures
and subsequent development of so-called Prince Hall Freemasonry * * *
have been, and are, regular and legitimate." Acceptance and approval of a
finding and report that an organization of Freemasons is regular and
legitimate clearly recognizes the Masonic status of the organization referred to, with all the implications incident thereto.
Such a finding concerning an institution universally condemned as
clandestine itself challenges attention. The Grand Secretary's statement
denying the apparently plain effect of the language of the Committee gives
added emphasis to the necessity for careful consideration.
The report, among other things, states:
"On March 6, 1775, a freeman by the name of Prince Hall, and fourteen other free colored men, were initwted in Boston by Army Lodge No.
441, of the Irish Constitution.* * *
"On July 3, 1776, African Lodge No. 1 was organized in Boston by an
assembly of unaffilwted Negro Brethren and authority from that Army
Lodge.***

* • *"
November 25, 1946, a committee appointed by the Grand Lodge of
Massa~husetts "to investigate the subject of Negro Freemasonry" made
its report in which it found that the "early procedures and subsequent
development of the so-called Prince Hall Freemasonry in this Commonwealth have been, and are, regular and legitimate," and concluded:
"* * * that * * * it is advisable for the official and organized activities
of white and colored Freemasons to proceed in parallel lines, but organically separate and without mutually embarrassing demands or commit·
ments.
"* * * within these limitations, informal cooperation and mutual helpfulness between the two groups upon appropriate occasions are desirable."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Official acknowledgment of the legitimacy of African Lodge No. 1 was
almost immediately made by John Rowe of Boston, Provincial Grand
Master for North America, holding authority from" the Grand Lodge of
England. "He issued a permit authorizing the Lodge to appear publicly
as a Masonic Body in procession for the purpose of celebrating the Feast
of St. John and to bury its dead.
"On both March~ and June 30, 1784, African Lodge No.1 applied to
the Grand Lodge of England -for a charter. * * * September 29, 1784, a
charter was executed for African Lodge No. 459 by authority of the Duke
of Cumberland, then Grand Master of * * * England.
"This was not a trespass for an owner cannot trespass upon property
of which he is already in possession."
It would seem obvious that the finding that a Masonic Body is regular
and legitimate entitles it and its members to all of the Masonic rights and
privileges, including visitation and other Masonic intercourse; and
equally obvious that a clandestine body is not and cannot be recognized,
or in any manner or at all treated as, legitimate, nor can any member of ·
such a body be received or otherwise treated as a Mason.
The report states that "for one hundred and seventy years African
Lodge and its successors have been functioning in Massachusetts in good
faith with the justifiable belief that their origin and procedure were as
regular and legitimate as we have thought ours to be." Apparently the
committee's conclusion was influenced by its assumed beliefs of the
members of the organization in question. Not only is the assumption of
good faith inconsistent with the records of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts (see New Age, pp. 146-7) but, manifestly, a counterfeit is no less
so because its holder believes it genuine. The question is: "Is the Prince
Hall organization Masonically regular and legitimate?" An affirmative
answer means recognition, with all that Masonic recognition implies; a
negative answer precludes any relationship whatever by Lodges or Masons
with the clandestine organization or its members.
The motion by the committee chairman appended to the report sets
forth particulars upon which the committee's findings and conclusions are
based. Careful examination of the report, the motion, and admitted historical facts will, it is believed, show the findings to be without warrant
and the conclusions erroneous.
The historical facts include the following:
The quartering of British troops in Massachusetts and other colonies
was for many years prior to the Revolution sorely. resented; it was one of
the grievances of the colonies against England recited in the Declaration
of Independence. Among these troops there were so-called "army" or
"traveling" lodges, apparently functioning under charters from the respective Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland. It is stated,
however, by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts that no member of any
such army or traveling lodge was ever received by or sat in a local
lodge; under the notopously strained relations between the people and

the British troops, fraternization cannot reasonably be assumed. Reflective of these conditions is the fact that on October 1, 1773, the Provincial
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts (of which the patriot Joseph Warren was
then Grand Master) was asserting jurisdiction over the entire Commonwealth and voted that "no tr11velling lodge had the right in this jurisdiction to make Masons of any citizens."
British troops (and presumably the army lodges) evacuated Boston
March 17, 1776. The Massachusetts Grand Lodge in 1876 declared that
"certainly after the evacuation * * * there is no pretense that England
had any control in Massachusetts."
The regularity and legitimacy of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts is,
of course, beyond question. It was formed March 8, 1777, and then declared "the independence of Masons of this Commonwealth whereby the
duties of self-government were assumed by the Masons of this Commonwealth, which they have continued to exercise to the present time."
[St. John's Lodge (English) chartered in 1733, united with the Massachusetts Grand Lodge in 1792; St. Andrew's Lodge (Scottish) chartered
in 1759, did likewise in 1809. Neither is shown to have had any relations
with the Prince Hall organization. Their relations with the Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts up to the times of their union with the latter do not
appear.]
The "initiation" in Boston on March 6, 1775, of Prince Hall "and fourteen other free colored men" by "Army Lodge No. 441 of the Irish Constitution" was plainly irregular. In the first place, Army Lodge No. 441
of the Irish Constitution derived its existence from the Grand Lodge of
Ireland (not England); and neither ·the regularity nor legitimacy of
either said lodge or its connection with the Grand Lodge of Ireland is
apparent. In the next place, such initiation was in violation and defiance
of the asserted jurisdiction of the Massachusetts Grand Lodge indicated
by the latter's vote of 1773 and irregular according to normal conception
of the amenities between any army or traveling lodge and Masons and
Masonic Lodges in occupied areas.
The organization in Boston by Army Lodge No. 441 on July 3, 1776,
"by an assembly of unaffiliated negro brethren" as African Lodge No. 1,
was a flagrant violation of Masonic law and tradition.
July 3, 1776, was, of course, after the evacuation of Boston by the
British troops, and presumably by Army Lodge 441. Even the Grand
Lodge of England was then without authority in Massachusetts, and
there is no indication that the Irish Grand Lodge ever claimed any such
authority.
In addition to the unauthorized invasion of Massachusetts jurisdiction
on July 3, 1776, there are other indicia of irregularity in the organization
of African Lodge No. 1: The characterization of the assembly as "unaffiliated negro brethren" is pure assumption. How "brethren" and what
"affiliation"? A little more than a year before the same army lodge had
initiated fifteen colored men; it is hardly possible that these "novitiates"

54

55

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CAUFORNIA

were "unaffiliated" in July, 1776. Who were the "assembly" of unaffiliated negro brethren; whence did they come; and by what right were they
entitled to recognition? Regularity and legitimacy of individuals as
Masons cannot be predicated on speculation, especially when the title of
their host is not clear.

ity and legitimacy) was not, as assumed by the committee, an occupation
of "property of which he was already in possession," but, on the contrary,
was a flagrant invasion of the territory of an. independent Masonic sov·
ereignty. Manifestly, authority for such invasion must depend on something more th.an the fact that the person purporting to authorize it was
then acting as Provincial Grand Master for North America. Such an act
to be authoritative would seem to require deliberate action by the Masonic
Body itself, rather than by the act of its Grand Master.

The statement that the African Lodge was organized by authority of
the Army Lodge 441 itself shows that the new "lodge" was neither regular
nor legitimate. Army lodges ·are normally confined to particular and
temporary military exigencies and areas and do not encompass authority
to make Masons of civilians, much less to charter Masonic Lodges gen·
erally in occupied areas.
The statements in the motion that African Lodge No. 1 was almost
imniediately acknowledged to be legitimate by John Rowe of Boston,
Provincial Grand Master for North America, and that the latter issued
a permit authorizing said lodge to appear publicly as a Masonic Body
leave much to be desired as muniments of Masonic regularity. Particulars
as to the status or authority of Rowe are lacking; no excuse is offered for
invasion of the jurisdiction of the Provincial Massachusetts Grand Lodge
or violation of its edict forbidding army lodges to mak~ Masons in Massa·
chusetts; the right of Rowe, however exalted his station, to authorize such
an invasion is gravely doubted. Such an infringement of fundamental
Masonic amenities could hardly be sanctioned by action short of the
Grand Lodge itself; the restricted purpose of the permit (to appear publicly as a Masonic Body in a procession for the purpose of celebrating
the Feast of St. John and to bury its dead) would seem to preclude accord·
ing to it the effect of general Masonic recognition.
Masonic independence of Massachusetts was established March 8, 1777,
and Cornwallis surrendered October 19, 1781; the motion says that in
March, 1784, African (army) Lodge No. 1 (set on foot by Irish Army
Lodge No. 441in1775) applied to the Grand Lodge of England for a
charter, and that on September 29, 1784, the charter was executed "for
African Lodge No. 459 by authority of the Duke of Cumberland, then
Grand Master of' England. (In this connection it will be recalled that
the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts has declared that after March 17, 1776,
there could be "no pretense" of English Grand Lodge control in Massa·
chusetts. Hence, the application to the Grand Lodge of England and the
action of the latter thereon were an infringement upon the authority of
the Grand Lodge of Massuchsetts.)
The motion further states that St. John's Grand Lodge functioned by
authority of the Grand Lodge of England under Provincial Grand Master
Rowe until February, 1787; that it "first assumed the authority to act as
an independent Grand Lodge on July 9, 1790." As the Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts had been, probably since 1773, and certainly since 1777,
exercising jurisdiction over the entire Commonwealth, this act of the
Provincial Grand Master for North America (assuming his own regular-

Warrant for the statement that "when the charter for African Lodge
No. 459 was granted (September 29, 1784) as well as when the lodge was
organized on May 6, 1787, the Grand Lodge of England was still exer·
cising its authority over" Massachusetts, is in direct conflict with the
unchallenged declaration made in 1876 by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, heretofore quoted.
Other indicia of irregularity and illegality will, it is believed, be appar·
ent from a critical examination of the pamphlet issued by the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts and the excerpts from the proceedings of the
latter body appearing in the New Age for March, 1947. The foregoing
will, however, be sufficient to show that the findings of the committee
that the Prince Hall organization is an organization of Freemasons, and
that it is not clandestine but Masonically regular and legitimate, are
without support and that acceptance of the report and approval of its
recommendations are tantamount to Masonic recognition of an organiza·
tion generally declared to be clandestine by other jurisdictions, including
California.
As stated at the outset, a clandestine body cannot be recognized or
treated as regular or legitimate, nor can any Masonic intercourse or relationship, however informal, be had with it by any Mason or Masonic
Body. The recommendations of the committee adopted by the Grand
Lodge of Massachusetts cannot be carried out without violating funda·
mental rules as to Masonic regularity. The action of the Grand Lodge
in accepting the committee's report and adopting its recommendations
is quite inconsistent with the statement of the Grand Secretary as to what
the committee and the Grand Lodge intended. If the Grand Secretary is
correct, the records should be modified so as to make it entirely clear
that the Prince Hall organization is not an organization of Freemasons;
that it does not recommend or countenance any relationship with Prince
Hall or any other organization or individual whose claim to Masonic
status is not free from doubt. (All italics herein supplied by me.)
I have discussed this matter at length with our Senior Past Grand
Master, Oscar Lawler, and other Past Grand Masters, and they are in
complete accord with my position.
Fraternally,
JOHN R. MooRE, Grand Master.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

57

I therefore recommend that this Grand Lodge give full consideration
to the subject involved and determine the course it is to take.
CONCLUSION

When I assumed this exalted office-the highest gift in your powerI deemed myself to be a fairly good Mason and the fraternity above the
ordinary. After spending a year in your service, performing the duties of
the office as best I could; af.ter visiting extensively among countless
brethren, whom I found ever willing and eager to lay aside their tools
of livelihood and obey the call of Masonic duty; and after observing the
profound and unstinted zeal and earnestness with which the brethren and
especially the Masters respect Masonry and its tenets, I now find myself a
stimulated and ardent Mason and our fraternity the greatest.
During this year, it has not been my policy or purpose to disturb the
orderly processes of Masonry or to change its course in any fashion.
I have striven earnestly to keep our fraternity on the track prescribed by
our landmarks, our fundamental laws, and our magnificent traditions.
My services have now come to judgment at your hands. I have not the
temerity or the vanity to argue that my acts this year have contributed
to the progress of Masonry, but I shall be compensated and flattered if,
in your wisdom, you find that they have not interrupted or impeded it,
and that it will continue to flow, under God, slowly, serenely, and har·
moniously on into time.

RESOLUTION INTRODUCED BY ARTHUR JOEL
INSPECTOR, 48-A DISTRICT

The Freedom Train is being sent by the Government of our country
over the many miles of our railways and will arrive in California in the
early part of the coming year.
It is an armed train, armed not with atomic bombs, guns, munitions
or the destructive implements of modem warfare, but with the most per·
suasive documents for freedom, peace and toleration. It contains the
original declaration of independence, the bill of rights, the emancipation
proclamation issued by the immortal Lincoln, the two year old United
Nations Charter and numerous other historical documents on which the
very foundations of our Government were laid and by which our Nation
lives.
Masons have been the champions of free gevernment and liberal insti·
tutions, which are so well exemplified by the instruments and documents
the train contains on its journey and which focus the attention of our
people on the liberties and privileges that they enjoy.
Now, therefore, be it Resolved that the Grand Master of Masons in
California be and he is hereby empowered and directed to appoint a
committee of such size as he may deem suitable for the occasion to
welcome the advent of this train to the borders of our State, and to do
such other things in the reception of the train by the Masons of this State
as the committee may in its discretion deem appropriate.

Be it Resolved, That the following plan of balloting be recommended
and referred to the Grand Lodge with recommendations for adoption:
1. Use a ballot box for each 'petitioner and on the front of the box
affix a holder for the lettered name of the petitioner.
2. Conduct each ballot box to its regular place for balloting, separately, and following the ballot reconduct the ballot boxes to the East,
separately, in the same manner as the ballot box is now handled.
3. The member balloting will complete his ballot in each individual
ballot box for so many ballot boxes as are before him.
Be it further Resolved, That Section 233 (Method of Balloting) of
the Constitution be revised to conform to this procedure and that the
following change be referred to the Grand Lodge with recommendation
for adoption:
Insert a new paragraph following Section 233, to read as follows:
"At the option of the Lodge, when more than one applicant is to be
balloted on at the same meeting, a ballot box with a label holder affixed
on the face of the ballot box with the name of the applicant legibly displayed, may be prepared for each applicant and presented separately,
and balloting shall then proceed on the entire group in the same manner
as for individual balloting."

Resolved, That Section No. 153, of the Constitution and Ordinances
be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 153. Only the income from amounts paid for life membership,
whether on deposit in a bank or invested in securities legal for savings
banks, shall be used by the Lodge, the original amounts to be forever
kept and maintained as and for a permanent life membership fund. Provided, nevertheless, that upon the death of a life member, such sum as
he shall have paid into said fund may be withdrawn therefrom and
become a part of the general funds of the Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
E. A. TROXEL,

RESOLUTION RE REFUSAL TO SERVE ON COMMITTEE

Be it Resolved, That refusal of a Master Mason, without good and
sufficient excuse, to serve on a committee of investigation, when appointed
by the Master of his lodge, shall constitute a Masonic offense.
Good and sufficient excuse is defined as absence from the community
of his lodge or confining illness for half or more of the investigation
month.

HARRY L. BUCKALEW,

There was also transferred from the Masonic Homes General Fund to
the Endowment Fund $100,000 face value United States Treasuries 2%'s,
12/15-64-69.
In August, 1946, the Grand Treasurer deemed it advisable not to risk
possible loss by investing in long_term maturities at existing premiums.
The market was unsteady at the time. The opportunity to observe the
market and the possibility of another government issue, purchasable at
par before the end of the year, influenced the recommendation to purchase
U. S. Treasury 7/ B's Certificates of Indebtedness. Accordingly, for that
purpose and establishing a short term position, investments were made in
the certificates.
The Treasury and the Federal Reserve Bank operated to control fluctuations in price within a very limited range and prices did not recede
substantially. Also there was no indication of any issue of the type which
had been previously offered at par in the market. Accordingly in July,
1947, it was determined to dispose of the 7 /B's certificates and shift to
long term issues for increased yield.

Conforming to practice, odd lots of securities accumulated by gift and
otherwise are in the process of listing for sale or transfer for the purpose
of consolidation in larger blocks where that may be possible.
There are two items, namely $10,000 par value Southern Pacific deben·
tures 41h's 5/1/81 Grand Lodge General fund, when purchased (1931)
cost 95. and a fraction, presently quoted at 92% and $9,000 par value
Northern Pacific Railroad General Lien 1/1/ 2047 Luckenbach fund, cost
when purchased (1936) 80% , present quotation 6B. It is not likely under
existing conditions that there will be much improvement. The yield is a
factor. Consideration is being given to sale.
As is customary, the detail of odd lot and unimportant transactions is
not included in this report but may be ascertained by referring to other
financial reports.
We are in stormy times. Inflation in an increasing degree is with us.
What the outcome may be is puzzling the best analysts. Their problems
may be visualized by contemplating the excessive currency in circulation,
excessive purchasing power, scarcity of food items among other commodi·

64

ties, contributing to high prices magnified by government purchases for
European relief and higher wages in a game of see-saw with higher prices.
This is not intended to encompass all the economic problems even were I
competent to make such an analysis. However, there is sufficient to indicate the present difficulties of an investor. The experts range from one
extreme to another and there is confusion. For example: one specified in
detail what conditions must exist if present status is to continue, then he
proceeds to dispose of every required factor as his premises for forecasting an imminent depression.
Some are pessimistically apprehensive of governments dropping below
par which they did after World War I. However, at that time the issues ·
were without government support which presently is geared to protect
the cost of servicing the great national debt against increase. I certainly
am not a prophet but I am not impressed. I confidently look forward to a
satisfactory solution avoiding a run-away inflation or disastrous depression because of the genius of the American. people.
What may happen market-wise is not particularly important to those
who are confining themselves to purchases of governments and who may
hold to maturity, which is the case where investments are for trust funds
such as ours. There are other prime securities which may be safely held.
Conservative dealers in such securities must be keen analysts with exceptional judgment. We may well imagine what may happen to the speculative trader when the market for securities in the least speculative is
unpredictable. However, as we follow the safe course presently pursued,
we are unconcerned.
What must have attention are maturities as related to future investment
problems. Our maturities 72-67 are somewhat heavy. A switch will be
made to shorter maturities if it ·may be accomplished without more than
nominal loss or other disadvantage. We shall take full advantage of the
U.S. Treasury bonds, Series A-1965, 21h% non-transferable, purchasable
at par and accrued interest, announced at the date of this writing. The
subscription will open September 29. The bonds will be dated October 1,
1947, maturing in 18 years, October 1, 1%5. They are similar in type to
the U.S. Savings G bonds in that, if redeemed prior to maturity, the investment yield will be less than the interest rate on the bonds.
I should be remiss if I did not express my appreciation for the cooperative services of Lloyd Wilson, Grand Secretary, and Henry Oliphant,
Assistant Grand Secretary.
Members of the Grand Lodge are urged to review the schedules following this report and the consolidated cash statement which will appear in
the "Special Appendix" with sufficient cross references for detail.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANCIS V. KEESLING, Grarnl, Treasurer.

Report of Special Committee on Taxation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:.
.
Without any change in its membership, this Committ~ has fun.ctioned
during the past year and has given both oral and w~itten advice and
opinions to the officers of Grand Lodge and of the vanous B~ue Lod?es
and to other -Masonic organizations on the constantly recurrmg routme
problems of taxation and on the special problems incident to the sale
of properties held for Masonic purposes.
.
As stated in the report for the year 1946, the taxes due for SoCial
Security and for Unemployment and Disability, have been placed o~ a
firm basis. The problems reported for the years 1944 and 1945, at w~ich
time it was anticipated that back taxes in the amount of $7,500 might
be levied, have been completely settled with the payment .of only a sm8:ll
amount for taxes and penalties. Grand Lodge appropnated $7,500 m
1944 and $5,000 in 1945 to cover these taxes, b~t the total amounts
actually paid in settling the taxes levied and penalties assessed, has been
$856.98. At the same time a merit rating credit of 1.7 percent of our
employer's tax obligation has been granted.
Our recommendation in the 1946 report was that the Blue Lodges
should continue to pay the Federal Insurance Contribution Tax and
Federal Unemployment Tax for the Secret8:ries of the Blue .L~dges in
spite of what appeared to be a contrary rulmg of the Commissioner of
Internal Revenue. Our stand has been vindicated and approved by a new
ruling of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, hol~ing that the Secre·
taries of Masonic Lodges do not collect dues and premmms for the Grand
Lodge, but rather make collections of dues on behalf of local lodges.
It is therefore held that local Masonic Lodges should pay tax on the
remuneration paid to Secretaries.
.
There is at present pending an issue over the payment of mcome taxes
for the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, but as the Grand Master has
ruled that this fund belongs to Grand Lodge, we believe it will be held
that the fund is covered by the general exemption of Grand Lodge.
Because of the constantly changing tax laws and the ever-recurring
tax problems, we recommend continuance of a special tax committee.
Dated October 1, 1947.
Respectfully submitted,
WALTER PERRY JoHNSON,
J.E. HAMMOND,
Adopted.
R. P. WISECARGER, Chairman.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Sixth Annual Report
as your Grand Secretary.
A number of factors, including legislation adopted at the last Com·
munication, have combined to make the year just closed as busy as any in
our experience. Our thanks are due the Secretaries of the Lodges for the
splendid cooperation given by them which has made it possible to keep
the work current and to meet the demands which are made upon us.

LEGISLATIVE PROCEDURES
The meeting of Lodge Secretaries arranged during Grand Lodge has
proved so helpful that it merits continuation. As this report is prepared
in advance, I can only say now that it is my intention to hold such a
meeting this year and to discuss a number of matters personally with the
Secretaries. I trust that by the time the report is formally presented this
will have been accomplished.
Because not all Secretaries can attend Grand Lodge I desire here to
refer to some matters which will be on the agenda of the conference.
A great deal of time and work can he saved for the Secretaries if they
will carefully read the law and particularly the Uniform Code of By-Laws
when an amendment to the By-Laws is considered and finally reported to
the Grand Lodge Office. Special attention is called to Sections 133 and
134, and if they are followed carefully there should he no difficulty in get·
ting an amendment in the proper form and with the proper certification.
There have been a number of cases where an amendment to a life
membership provision or an original life membership proposal have been
referred to as an amendment to the By-Laws. The error of this can be
quickly found by referring to the law and by reading the Uniform Code
of By-Laws, the latter of which makes no provision whatever for life
membership. A Standing Resolution is the proper procedure in such a
matter, and our office will furnish a suggested form of resolution on
request.
From evidence which comes to us from time to time it is quite apparent
that a number of the Lodges have never observed the requirement of the
law relative to the Uniform Code of By-Laws. When the Uniform Code of
By-Laws was adopted, the then Grand Master, Dana R. Weller, ruled
that no action was required except to copy the Uniform Code into thP.
Book of By-Laws and observe it. There can be no question about the

70

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

correctness of that position, but the unfortunate truth is that many of the
Lodges did not actually take the steps suggested.
It seems to me that every Lodge should be required to actually operate
under the Uniform Code of By-Laws, and I recommend this for consideration by the proper committee.
FEES FOR DEGREES

Another matter on which· there seems to be a lack of understanding
relates to the fees for Degrees, the point being that many Lodges seem
to consider that they should include in their fees the amount required
from each initiate for the Masonic Homes. This $25.00 contribution is
provided for in the law of Grand Lodge and has nothing whatever to do
with the amount of the fees set forth in the By-Laws. The amount designated in the By-Laws must be collected in addition to the $25.00 Masonic
Homes Contribution.
If there are any Lodges which are not following this procedure, steps
should be taken to make their practice conform with the law.
GENERAL OFFICES OF GRAND LODCE

The problems of labor, materials, etc., have seemed to make it advisable not to undertake the modernization of the Grand Lodge Offices for
which appropriations have heretofore been made. The action of Grand
Lodge on the proposal made by the Grand Master for the erection of a
new temple would, of course, be a determining factor in any steps which
might be taken to carry out the modernization program.
In the meantime a sufficient appropriation should be made to carry the
work through if Grand Lodge is to remain in its present quarters.
MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the membership figures for the year I have shown comparative statistics for the past six years for the purpose of indicating
trends, if any there be.
During the year the Lodges conferred 41,907 Degrees or 506 more than
the previous year. This is the largest number in our history. It is interesting to note that while there were 990 fewer Candidates initiated, there
were more passed and a mtich greater number raised than in 1946. This
would seem to indicate that applications are decreasing and that the
Lodges are catching up on the backlog of work which developed during
the war.
' The total membership at .the end of the fiscal year was 173,917, the
greatest in our history, and the net gain was likewise the greatest, being
12,165.
