PROCEEDINGS OF THE

THE THIRD · STEP

GRAND ORATION
GRAND LODGE F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
JUDGE WILLIAM

B. McKESSON, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, Grand Lodge Officers, Distinguished Guests and Members of Grand Lodge:

As I stand here where but few are permitted to stand to address you as ·
the Grand Orator, I am mindful that heretofore Grand Orators have been ..
distinguished Masons of rare attainments and abilities. For one so humble
in the labors of the Temple as myself to be permitted to occupy this
honored station, is clear and convincing evidence of a basic belief of our
. Most Worshipful Grand Master. He believes, and by my a~~ointment
wants to demonstrate. to you that Masonry affords opportumhes to the •
low as well as the high. Throughout this year he has endeared himself to
the members of the craft by his warm personality and faithful labor.
If ever there was a man of whom it could truthfully be said that he could
"walk with Kings nor lose the common touch," that man is John Randle
Moore. I have read the thought-provoking and inspiring Grand Orations
of the past. Some of them have dwelt upon the beauties of our phil~sophy;
others have chosen to rhapsodize in poetic-prose on our symbohsm; the
literature and poetry of the ages hav~ been combed for reference~, similes,
metaphors, and examples to illustrate the meaning of our working tools. .
Would that I could couch my poor speech in the diamond-studded phrases
that have sparkled here in by-gone days, or that I could tip my pen with
the gleaming gold of lofty thoughts, ~r even that I could deliver ?1Y
prosaic platitudes in a voice redolent with the lush tones of a great pipe
organ. Those gifts have been denied me, and I must therefo.re speak ~o
you as I am, not as what I'd like to be. What others have. given you m
beauty, learning, philoSQphy and history, I cannot duplicate or .even
imitate-I can only promise you sincerity, humility and I hope a modicum
of brevity.
Masonry is rooted in antiquity, ripened by modernity and harvested in
eternity. Truly it is a growing and progressive science, ever unfolding
new beauties as the men of every generation have explored its most concealed recesses. Someone has aptly said: "The practical object of Masonry

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

83

ie the physical and moral amelioration and the intellectual and spiritual
improvement of individuals and society•.Masonry labors to improve the
social order by enlightening men's minds." It is to our duty as Masons to
improve the social order that I would direct your thinking today under
the subject of the Third Step.
The Three Steps in a Masonic career expressed in the terms of our
beautiful ritual are, initiation, passing, and raising but I choose to denominate them Revelation, Education and Operation. These are the three
progressive steps of a well rounded Masonic career. Some Masons stop
at the first step, initiation, when the meaning of our mysteries is revealed
to them. Others take the second step-Education-by becoming profi. cient and learned in the art of Masonry and then stop. They fail to .put
into practical, daily living the lessons we teach. Important as these two
steps are-and they must be taken before one is ready for the third stepit is the Third Step, Operation, that marks a man a Mason-what you do,
how you live, what you stand for. Revelation, Education, Operationthese three-but the greatest of these is Operation.
Masonry, as I have said, is rooted in antiquity and Masons turn to the
past for teaching and inspiration. Standing on the pinnacle of Today, as
we look backward over the valley of the Masonic past, we see there majestic peaks, broad peaceful meadows, and great forests representing the
giants of Masonry. Let us focus our attention for a moment upon that
segment of Masonic history called American Masonry. There we see men
wearing the Square and Compass, forsaking tradition, comforts and the
security of their homeland to brave a three months' journey across an
unfriendly and tumultuous ocean. In a tiny ship they sail to a savageinhabited land, where daily struggle is the price of existence, that they
might practice the great Masonic principle-the Fatherhood of God and
the Brotherhood of Man.
Like a great epic the history of American Masonry moves onward, its
verses studded with the names of illustrious brothers, whose deeds shine
like stars in the firmament of the future. Masonry is entwined and interwoven with the history of America. As this new land of America grew, so
Masonry grew. Oar brothers of the past labored here to build an edifice
where freedom, equality, justice and opportunity were vouchsafed to
every citizen. Our failure to recount the deeds or call the names of those
ever-honored brothers contained in that thin book ·of the Nation's Great
cannot, nor is it intended to, dim the luster of their achievements for their
fraternity, their country, their neighbors or their Go~. The list is far too
long for enumeration on this or any other one occasion but no Mason can
study the history of the United States without thrilling with pride at the
great part Masons have played in building America. You will find them
in all walks of life, in all fields of endeavor, in all periods of our Nation's
history.

84

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

One glorious decade of our Fraternity's progressive march from the
past to the future is that period between 1847 and 1857. The plains of
America were overrun by ox-teams, covered wagons and trudging brothers
moving westward, ever westward; fording streams, scaling mountains,
penetrating forests and conquering deserts in feats of daring adventure
that beckoned men onward, onward over the rough and rugged road beset
with the ruffians of starvation, hardship and discouragement. It was a
cavalcade of which it has b~en said that "Only the brave arrived; the
cowards never started, and the weaklings died on the way."
Through struggles, privations and sacrifices was ·Masonry brought to
California. The intrepid and rugged brethren who had found in the
teachings of Masonry great solace from the trials of their daily lives
carried it by land and sea to this new country. Like their brethren of the
preceding century who had braved the forbidding Atlantic to plant
Masonry on the eastern shore of this great land of opportunity, those who
brought Masonry to the shores of the Pacific were impelled by an unyielding and indomitable conviction that men are better men where Masonry
flourishes. From all outward appearances they seemed to be rough, uncouth, fighting men but they possessed that "goodness of heart, that •
purity of intention, and that love of virtue" that we know makes a man a
better man because he is a Master Mason.
For ninety-seven years now the Grand Lodge of California has met in
annual communication to hear the reports on the state of the craft in this
jurisdiction, to consider whether any improvement can be made, either
for strength or ornament in our work among the brethren, and to receive
instructions whereby we may pursue our labors. A review of the proceedings of those annual communications reveals the abiding faith, lofty ideals
and great accomplishment of those who have wrought here to "build our
temples in .the hearts of men." Would that time permitted a recital of the
many stirring, inspired and inspiring incidents which have marked our
progress. Would that we might just call the roll of those who have wrought
at the building of Masonry's temple in California, as they planted Masonry ·
on the highest hills and in the lowest vales of our great state. They knew
with Virgil that "Too low they build who build beneath the stars."
Even as our pioneer brethren of 1849 dug the gold from the canyons,
streambeds and mountains of California so can every Mason retrieve the
great treasure buried in the Masonic libraries if he will but dig deep into
the poetry, prose, narration and literature of Masonry.
In each new generation the meanings, attitudes, faiths and works of
Masonry have ripened through the initiation and education of new
members.
,
All of the symbolic ritual of our initiation and all of our learning, are
as naught, however, if we do not take that third step in Masonry-Operation-whereby we put into practice those great truths, texts and principles
which have been laid down as the rule and guide of our faith. We transmit
our teachings to the repository of faithful breasts for one purpose only.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

85

That purpose is the teaching men how to live as Masons. We are not mere
vessels in which to store the rare vintages distilled from the fruits of our
labors; the corn, wine and oil we receive as wages, are not to be hoarded,
they are to be used to nourish, stimulate and strengthen our minds and
bodies for the tasks that lie ahead. Mere proficiency i_n the ritual, learning
in the arts, or study of the precepts, excellent as they are, do not in themselves make a man a Mason. It is what he does that proves that it is the
internal, and not the external qualifications which recommend a man to
be made a Mason. 1£ he does nothing but spend his days in slothful idleness, he becomes a wastrel and Masonry shuns him. 1£ he knows the great
lessons taught at the Masonic Altar but is not impelled to put them into
practice, Masonry has been wasted upon him, and it were better that he
had never been permitted to share in the rich honor of becoming one of
its members. We are an organization of the living, not of the dead!
"Beaten paths are for beaten people." Our glorious history will crumble
into the ashes of the past, unless we each take that third step-Operation.
In our proceedings we frequently hear the phrase "We no longer work
in operative Masonry." I wonder! Some assume that the only "Operative"
Masons are those who build visible structures with stone and brick and
steel, And concrete. Such, however, you know is not the case.
It is by demonstrating that we are operative Masons in the labors of
today, that we take the third step in Masonry - Operation - and thus
improve the social order in which we live.
Brief mention has been made of the brethren who had the vision and
courage to bring Masonry to America; who held aloft the flame of Brotherhood as a beacon glowing in the wilderness in those early days of our
republic; and of those who drained the swamps, bridged the streams and
battled the elements that we might have Masonry in California. Pioneers
they were, blazing new paths that we might follow after them. Did their
matchless courage die with their generation; was the pioneer spirit buried
with them; is their flaming faith now but a dying ember beside the campfire they left along the trails? Are the Masons of 1947 worthy of those of
1847 or 1747? You, my brethren, are the living answer to that question.
They say there are no more frontiers; that the pioneer spirit of yesteryear is gone because there are no new lands to conquer. My brothers: We
are surrounded by ever expanding horizons for those who will but lift
their eyes to see; each new day presents a new frontier. So long as man
remains human, there will always be frontiers, frontiers of social, economic, political, scientific and religious wildernesses to be invaded,
explored and conquered by men of courage who have vision and faith.
All true Masons are "builders" and thus our craft is an "Operative"
organization, each brother building here on earth "that house not made
with hands, eternal in the heavens."
It has been said, "Our past is a poem, our present, a problem, and our
future, a promise." I've indicated to you something of epic of the past,
let us now turn to the problems of the present.

We have on the rolls of the 590 Masonic lodges in California 173,917
members; in the past year there have been 12,165 Master Masons added
to our rolls, a greater number than in any other single year in the history
of this Grand Lodge; our financial, administrative, and procedural practices have been tested, improved and modified until now they require
only our routine attention; our treasury bulges with funds. Our house is
in order-what kind of living shall we have in it?
Some lament the recent unprecedented increase in our membership, in
many quarters we hear the whispered complaint that our lodges have
been too lax in accepting candidates and conferring upon them our cherished degrees. Be reminded, that many of these new brethren knocked at
our portals and sought admission only after they had learned of the
weaknesses of the flesh. They had beheld the stark horror caused by men's
adherence to the philosophy of hate, and greed and brutality in a second
World War. They turned to us with souls awakened to the great spiritual
truths we teach. Their eyes have seen the Glory of the Coming of the Lord.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

87

In some distant shell-spattered battle field they verified the truth we
preach, that divine aesistance is vouchsafed us when human strength and
wisdom fail. From the fox-holes, the beach-heads and the life-rafts they
have come to us, truly seeking the Great Light. The greatest and most
challenging task facing Masonry today, is the drawing of designs upon
the trestle boards of our lodges that will give these new, eager, sincere
brothers tasks to satisfy their yearning and tests to prove their strength!
They came to us of their own free will and accord asking for bread; we
dare not give them a stone!
Masonry today in California finds itself possessed of great resources;
they can be hewn, squared, marked and numbered for the builder's use
even as were the timbers felled in the Forests of Lebanon. Thus will the
hopes, the sacrifices and the faith of our pioneer forebears not have been
in v~in. If, however, we fail to use with wisdom, strength, and beauty for
the improvement and perpetuation of the temple our building materials
of men, minds and money, we shall have squandered our heritage, violated
our vows and betrayed our trust.
What specific duties lie ahead? Just how can our great brotherhood of
f'l~,917 men work shoulder to shoulder? How shall we put our newly
enlightened brothers to work and thus retain their interest and enthusiasm? What needs to be done by Masons today if we would have a Masonry
of tomorrow? The answer to those questions constitutes the problem of
the present; it is the new frontier for the Operative Masonic pioneer of
1947.
Masonry teaches many great truths, has many noble precepts and stirs
many deep emotions, but the quint~ssence of all its teachings and inspiration is to teach the simple art of how men may live together in peace and
harmony. "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell
together in unity. "In unity"-peacefully, cooperatively, helpfully, gloriously! Isn't this the basic, the fundamental task of Masonry today-teaching men to live together in peace? That would truly be an improved
social order.
We read in sacred history that after King Solomon ascended the throne
in Israel, peace and tranquillity pervaded the world. Why did not this
glorious fulfillment of man's most cherished dream- a peaceful worldcontinue? How was it that man left the ways of peace to follow the bloodsoaked pathway of war? Having traveled along that highway of horror
these many centuries, can mankind now be turned aside; must we forever
travel down the road of destruction? Today the pace is ever increasing as
each new generation fashions fiendish instrumentalities more destructive
than the one before? Must civilization commit suicide? A man seen tottering upon the ledge of a building 200 feet above the crowd as he prepares
to leap into eternity excites all within sight to do something to deter him
from taking that fatal plunge. Who will cry out to a tottering world to
turn aside from its headlong pursuit of self-annihilation? Has Masonry
a duty here?

88

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

An organization that is founded upon principles for right living cannot
sit supinely by and let a dying world hurtle itself into oblivion. Here is a
definite task that Masons around the world must assume. There will
never he world peace-in spite of our prating about and for it-until
there is a change in the hearts of the people of the world. So long as men
cheat, lie and steal as individuals, they will continue to do it as nations!
On the other hand, there can he universal peace if the lessons you and I
are taught at the Masonic Altar are universally practiced. Simple acts they
are: Never failing to go out of our way to assist another; remembering in
our prayers to seek aid for others as well as ourselves; being unwilling to
violate a trust reposed in us by our fellowman; helping to raise by our own
hands those who are less fortunate than we; and by using every opportunity
to spread the gospel of good will and wise counsel. These obligations if
faithfully fulfilled by the Masons of the world would make war unthinkable! To those who think that Utopian day will never come when people
will actually live that way, I say that unless such a day does come, we must
surely perish. "One world or one cinder"-is not a mere catch phrase;
it is a cold statement of our only present alternatives.
What has universal peace to do with Masonry? I propose merely that
all Masons forsake the evil companions who have lured them from the
teachings of Masonry and return to the Temple where nobility counts for
more than trickery; integrity supplants intrigue; virtue transcends vengeance; and truth makes men 1:ree. If this Grand Lodge and all the Grand
Lodges would seriously lay out plans by which the more than 2,500,000
Masons in the United States--not to mention the vast number scattered
around the globe-could and would honestly set about to put the philosophical precepts of our order into practice in the world, war would not
have to he outlawed, it would he outlived. Here is a frontier that beckons
as alluringly as did the quest for gold a century ago!
Brother John H. Cowles, Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish
Rite, Southern Jurisdiction of the United States, voiced this thought some
time ago when he said, "The cry is for peace, when there is no peace ...
Clearly the matter has been approached from the wrong angle. There is
hut one way to insure peace among nations and that is putting into practical application of the Masonic ideal-th~ Brotherhood of man and the
Fatherhood of God. Nothing less than this great objective- for which
every true Mason constantly prays, hopes and works--can solve the prob·
lems of war with its ever present threat of civilization."
How can we set about to achieve this great objective? Work of that
kind commences with the individual. Passing resolutions, adopting platforms or issuing manifestos, will not do the task. So long as brother continues to assail brother for llivergent political, economic, social or religious convictions; so long as men seek to gain advantage through violence
rather than through merit; so long as one portion of society seeks to
suppress or handicap another portion merely because of economic status,
the color of the skin or racial origin ; so long as men consort with the vice11

of intolerance, cupidity, bigotry, suspicion, greed, envy and jealousy-

Many controversial issues confront us today ; they seek to rend society
into factions and divide it into competitive groups; they tend to destroy
unity among the people. The Operative Mason of 1947 will recognize that
disn;garding the rights of our fellowmen; failing to honor the dignity of

The late Bishop Bruce Baxter, of the Methodist Church, once said,
"The man who is too busy to serve his God and his community is too busy."
No true Mason will he "too busy." Here is the supreme opportunity of

pursuits and activities Masons propose, sponsor and support? We have

they make, they cannot shirk responsibility for the kind of community in
which they live.

Report of Committee on Twenty-Eighth Annual
Observance of Public Schools Week
To the M. W. Gralld Lodge F. & A . M . of California:
In a report from a· city in which the arrangements for the annual
observance of Public Schools Week are always made with that intelligence, as well as enthusiasm, which ensures success, the Chairman of the
Committee wrote :
"If attendance at the school functions is a criterion, this observance of
Public Schools Week was one of the most successful in the history of
almost three decades of annual programs."
Comment of the same sort appears in a very large number of the
reports from the lodges; and it is, we think, fairly applicable to the
observance generally.
The complete success of any observance of Public Schools Week is,
of course, dependent upon the extent of public interest attracted; and
never before was that public interest so great, and so widespread, as this
year. It was in all probability due to the deplorable plight of our public
schools and the publicity given it.
The teacher shortage and what was referred to as "the salary crisis"
had been widely publicized by the National Education Association; and
there were few people who had not read, or heard, of school systems
which had been demoralized by teacher strikes an~ "walkouts."
For the second time since its inception, Public Schools Week was
observed this year under conditions paralleling those which were responsible for its institution.
In 1933, as in 1919, schools were being closed, or maintained with
shortened terms ; children, particularly in rural districts, were being
denied the education to which they were entitled; and e~ucational service
considered absolutely essential to a modern American school system was
being discontinued or materially curtailed. The crisis was similar to that
which had confronted the public schools fourteen years earlier, but with
a different origin. It was notthe result of a war, except remotely, but because
we were in the throes of an acute social and economic disturbance. Every
governmental activity was being rigidly scrutinized; and the universal
demand for a reduction in public expenditures had naturally affected
school budgets.
This year the situation was almost identical with that which prevailed
at the close of World War I and which had impelled our Grand Lodge
to institute Public Schools Week. Again this year there were thousands of
classrooms for which there were n<;> teachers. It has been authoritatively
stated that for a variety of reasons, principally because of an economic

92

93

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

urge, 350,000 qualified teachers have abandoned the profession; and
according to a report made to the American Association of School Admin·
istrators by a commission of ten leading educators "school rooms are
crowded, buildings are run down, teachers are underpaid, the shortage of
qualified teachers is acute and equipment is often obsolete and meager."
Even now, when steps have been taken to improve the physical condition,
the teacher shortage is such as to constitute a threat to our system of public
education.
The situation is better here in California than it is throughout the
country, generally. But even here in California it is a grave one· and that
in spite of the fact that our people by an overwhelming vote' provided
last November for increased support for our schools, and for a minimum
salary in excess of that for which teachers elsewhere were striking and
staging walkouts.
Heartening as is California's generous support of public education, the
fact remains that the schools of our state are seriously threatened by a
shortage of teachers. And the present shortage is not the most serious
factor in the problem.
California's population is increasing by leaps and bounds; and this
sensational increase will present new problems in the face of a shrinking
teaching force. In this State there are today between 900,000 and a million
children under six years of age all headed for school. Now with teachers
already scarce, with more than ten thousand teaching with only emergency
cr.edentials, and with the impact of the high birth rate of the war years
still to be felt by the schools, the teacher shortage bids fair to become
even more acute.
The only hope for betterment depends upon the success of the campaign
being carried on by the California Teachers Association through its
Recruitment Committee. The most ominous factor in the entire problem
is the decrease in the number of young people being attracted to the
teaching profession.
.
The .threatened danger was briefly set forth in a Bulletin issued by our
Committee, and sent to the master of every lodge with a suggestion that
although, of course, the nature of the program of the observance in his
community would be determined by those in charge there, it might be
well for local committees everywhere to in some way direct the attention
of their people to the teacher shortage; and that the attractions of a
teaching career here in California with its manifold advantages could be
appropriately made the subject of addresses, and of panel and forum
discussions.
Mention of this Bulletin was made in one of the press releases issued
by the California Teachers Association in their very active campaign for
the recruitment of teachers; and it undoubtedly accounted for some of the
publicity given the observance of Public Schools Week. Incidentally, their
Director of ~ecruitment materially assisted our Committee in our own
publicity.

The teacher shortage was, naturally, the subject of a great many edito·
rials during Public Schools Week; and in practically all of them there
was some reference to our observance. There were· also this year an
unusually large number of editorials with Public Schools Week as the
subject, in which the Masonic origin was publicized. They were all
extremely complimentary, and some of them made special mention of its
worth at a time such as this when a crisis again confronts our public
schools. Typical of these was one which after detailing the advantages
of the teaching profession in California concluded as follows:
"These advantages have been written into State law and the Constitu·
tion by virtue of California's popular interest in the welfare of its schools
-an interest in no small measure due to the institution of Public Schools
Week."
There was a time when an occasional report from a lodge on its
observant'e would seem to indicate that there were some of our brethren
who were apparently fearful that the good work being done by the
Fraternity in behalf of our public schools might not be fully credited.
We hope that time has passed forever. But if there be any who do entertain
such fear, they would find reassurance with a perusal of the clippings
this year. Not only in the editorials to which we have referred, but in the
news columns as well, wide publicity is given to Masonry's relationship
to the observance of Public Schools Week.
Appreciation by the school people of what is being done for the schools
by Grand Lodge, and its constituent lodges, is evidenced each year at the
conclusion of the observance by letters to the master of the lodge, or to
the committee in charge of the observance in that community. They come
from classroom teachers and from principals, and from Superintendents.
And sometimes there are resolutions by organized bodies of school people.
This year there was one which we quote because not only were printed
copies of it among the clippings attached to more than one report, but a
signed copy was sent to the Grand Secretary. It was a resolution adopted
by a Principals Association, and reads as follows:
"RESOLUTION

Whereas, Public Schools Week was inaugurated in this state by the
Grand Lodge of Masons in 1920, and
Whereas, this annual observance has brought about a better under·
standing of the problenis, needs and methods of. the public schools, thus
contributing immeasurably to the welfare of the children of the state, and
Whereas, the 28th observance of Public Schools Week will take place
this year from April 28 to May 3, and
.
Whereas, the Public Schools Committee of the Grand Lodge has recom·
mended that special emphasis this year be given to the need for teachers
and the advantages of teaching in California, thus assisting greatly in our
efforts to induce well-qualified young people to plan teaching careers,

In connection with what' we have said with reference to Masonry's
participation in the observance, we feel we should here state, and cheerfully acknowledge, that the great public interest which made the observance such a success this year must have been, in part, the result of the
Proclamations, Resolutions, announcements and endorsements issued by
those organizations which always so enthusiastically cooperate with
Grand Lodge. Included in these, with the co-ordinate bodies of Masonry
(including the Shrine and the Sciots) and the Order of Eastern Star,
were the American Legion, Department of California, American Legion
Auxiliary, American Association of University Women (California State
Division), California C.I.0. Council, California Congress of Parents and
Teachers, California Farm Bureau Federation, California Federation of
Women's Clubs, California League of Women Voters, California State
Chamber of Commerce, California Junior Chamber of Commerce, Northern and Southern California Councils of Churches, California State Federation of Labor and California Teachers Association.
This enumeration of cooperating agencies is made with the hope that
every organization which should be, has been, included. The danger of an
unintentional omission is a reminder of the loss this Committee has suffered in the retirement of Brother Vaughan MacCaughey. The securing of
the announcements from the cooperating agencies, with all the detail,
including at times an extended correspondence, was his responsibility; and
he met it with that zeal and fidelity with which he discharged all his duties
as Secretary in a service extending over more than twenty years. As the
Editor of Sierra Educational News, the official organ of the California
Teachers Association, and himself by -profession an educator, he furnished an extremely valuable contact for this Committee of laymen with
the school people throughout the State. With the preparation of "The
Story of Public Schools Week," copies of which were sent to all the lodges
this year, he brought to an end his official connection with the Committee.
With a knowledge of the splendid service he has rendered, we deem it not
inappropriate to here make this mention of it.
As evidencing the development of the observance of Public Schools
Week from a Masonic event into a community affair, mention has been
made, from time to time, in these reports, of Proclamations issued by the
Governor of the State and by Mayors of cities, or other heads of local
governments. The first of these was by Govern<;>r Young in which he
stated that although he had theretofore steadfastly declined to issue proc-

lamations with respect to all celebrations or observances of special days
or weeks except for such nationally observed holidays as Thanksgiving
Day, Armistice Day, and the like, he felt constrained to call public
attention to the Eleventh Annual Observance of Public Schools Week;
and commending its purpose, he urged the people of the State to avail
themselves of the opportunity that would be afforded during that week to
obtain first hand information of the methods, aims, purposes and achieve·
ments of the modern school.
This year there were some especially fine proclamations issued by
Mayors of cities and which must have been very effective in arousing
public interest. Limitation of space precludes further reference to them
as it does also to similar announcements by the State heads of the agencies
cooperating with us-some of which would also be well worth quoting.
There are, however, two proclamations of which we make special
mention because considered together they seem to us to define, as could
not perhaps be otherwise better done, the character of the annual observ·
ance of Public Schools Week in its development from a purely Masonic
event into a community affair.
One of these was signed by a man who is now Grand Master of Masons
in California; and his title as such followed his name. It was addressed to
his brethren of the Craft and bore the seal of Grand Lodge.
The other was signed by a man who once had been Grand Master of
Masons. He is now the Governor of California; and his title as such
followed his name. His proclamation was addressed to all the citizens of
California; and to that document was affixed the Great Seal of the State
of California. Nowhere did there appear the word "Mason" or "Masonry,"
but it breathed the spirit of our Fraternity.
Governor Warren's proclamation so clearly indicates Masonry's attitude toward public education that we believe it should be, through this
medium, incorporated in the Proceedings of Grand Lodge. We therefore
here quote it in full:
"PROCLAMATION

One of our greatest hopes for restoring balance to an unsettled world
lies in the field of public education. It is through the broader education
of all peoples that there can best be nurtured the virtues of tolerance and
understanding which are needed in the world today.
It is part and parcel of the American tradition that every child, no
matter where he lives or what may be the economic or social situation of
his parents, has the birthright to a sound education. Government's respon·
sibility for making this education available to our young people is met
through a public school system which has contributed greatly to the
strength of our democratic way of life.
·
Training for good citizenship must continue to be the concern of the
public schools, not only in providing academic and vocational preparation for life but in stimulating character-building activities that supplement the moral instruction for which ·p arents are responsible in the home.

97

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Standards of education must be constantly raised and adapted to the
changing needs of the day, and these standards must recognize the ever·
increasing importance of the homely virtues as a basis for good citizenship
in the highly complex age in which we live. The public schools are constantly seeking new ways and means of expanding and improving educational opportunities for our children, and if their continued efforts are to
meet with success, they must be backed by the conscientious interest of all
the citizens of the State.
With this thought in mind, I, Earl Warren, Governor of California, do
hereby proclaim the week of April 28 to May 4, 1947, as PUBLIC
SCHOOLS WEEK, and I urge that all of our citizens set aside time during
this week to better acquaint themselves with ways in which they may take
a part in the further development of our local public schools.
In Witness Whereof, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Great
Seal of the State of California to be affixed this 4th day of April, A. D.,
One Thousand Nine Hundred and Forty-seven.

Among the editorials included with the clippings received from the
lodges, there were some from which it would appear that the teacher
shortage was not, in the minds of the writers, the only impending threat
to public education. Typical of these was an exceedingly well written
one in which, after referring at length to the existing conditions, and to
the need for watchful care upon the part of parents and all who believe
in public education, the writer continued as follows:
"The public school system was not established without a struggle, for
there are interests which are continually at work toward the effort to
defeat this democratic system. The methods used are many times not
open and abovebo~d, but are hidden in many innocent looking efforts,
su~h as transpo~tahon on public school busses for children attending
private or sectarian schools. The public school was established and has
continued throughout the years as an institution for all children of all the
people and not for any particular sect or creed."
. The ne~s columns of both the urban and the rural press were replete
with stones of school events; and there were many reports received of
newspapers publishing the time and place of the day-to-day programs.
And not only were there extended news reports of the happenings of the
week, profusely illustrated by photographs, but there were also special
articles on educational topics. Some of these were contributed by students
and others by faculty members, and by laymen and women including,
among others, representatives of the Parent-Teacher Association; and
there was an entire issue of a newspaper with a "banner" reading "Public
Schools Week issue of local newspaper edited by school staff."
As its contribution to Public Schools Week, a newspaper in a community which reported an especially successful observance published
a series of articles on education. In one of these articles the writer, who
had been educated in England, sounded that ever recurrent note of criticism with respect to the alleged neglect of the fundamentals, and compared our system of public education with the English and German
systems which he regarded as superior.
A reply to that article was made by the City Superintendent of Schools
who pointed out that the educational programs of the European nations
are on a class-intellectual basis; and that the American program aims at
training everyone for citizenship and for participation at the highest
possible level in our social and economic life. As an endorsement of the
views he was expressing, he quoted another ·English writer who had used
these words:
.·
"If t~e million~ of boys a~d girls in American schools are .judged solely
by their academic accomplishments, they will be judged harshly. But
!11ey are not to be so judged; for their schools are doing far more than
mstruct them along academic lines; they are letting them instruct each
other in how to live in America."

The President of the California Teachers Association issued an espe·
cially effective announcement to the teachers. After reviewing some of
the problems with which school boards, administrators and teachers had
been battling, he pointed out that the observance of Public Schools Week
would afford 1¥1 excellent opportunity to acquaint the general public
with the seriousness of the situation; that in a general way most citizens
knew about it, but that unless they were given an opportunity to visit the
schools and get first hand information they could not really know how
serious conditions were. He closed his announcement by asking the
teachers to make a special effort this year to bring the schools to the
public by bringing the public to their schools. And loyally indeed did
they respond to that appeal.
Mention should also be here made of the fine cooperation received
from the State Department of Education through the Bulletin issued to
the school people; and from the Superintendent of Public Instruction,
personally, who, in every position he has occupied, has always enthusiastically supported the observance of Public Schools Week.
It seemed last year as though never again would an observance of
Public Schools Week receive the publicity given that one. But it was
exceeded this year in both extent and character.
Not only were there more, and longer, editorials this year, but their
tone evidenced a real concern for public education. In more than one
there was a plain indication of a belief that danger threatened our public
schools. While the subjects of most of them were the teacher shortage,
crowded classrooms and the need for new buildings and the remodeling
and repair of old ones, it would seem that every phase of education
received attention.

What has been said of the extent of newspaper publicity this year is

views of the editor, or publisher. It is now apparently also applied to
broadcasting. Included with other material accompanying a report from
one of the lodges, was what was entitled "copy of the radio editorial
broadcast during Public Schools Week."
For the same reason that no mention is made in these reports of

this year from the broadcasting stations, large and small, and from all the
net-work systems. Merely as an indication of the willingness and enthusiasm with which that co-operation was given, we may say that there were
program and production managers who planned campaigns for publicizing our observance just as they would an advertising campaign for
a commercial sponsor; and who carried out that plan by the same
methods.

Although there were an unusually large number of lodges which reported that ou~ latest meeting was the most successful ever held, there

The Master of one of these lodges reported that he had appointed
a committee but because they felt that there was a lack of interest in the

so there was no observance.
The other Master gave as a reason for his lodge not joining in the

fishing season.
In startling contrast to what was said by the Masters of those lodges

endeavor he had made to obtain the co-operation of the civic organizations in the community :
"Public Schools Week is as much a part of our community life as is
Fourth of July and Christmas. No special endeavor is therefore needed
to obtain the hearty co-operation of every civic organization."
This was only one of the very many, and increasing number of, communities in which the observance of Public Schools Week apparently
engages the interest and the active support of all the people.

This year there seemed to be an unusual. number of these pre-week

presentation of awards to the winners of a high school flower show.
Many of these "pre-week" affairs were regular meetings of organizations scheduled for a date prior to the beginning of the observance. At
these meetings there were presented programs designed to awaken interest
in the observance of Public Schools Week . . In some instances it was an
address by a school administrator, or perhaps a high school student, in
others an entertainment by school children.
There are communities where the annual observance is always inaugurated with a church service on the preceding Sunday. The nature of the
service is not always the same. Sometimes the only departure from the
regular church service is in a change in the character of the sermon. The
minister selects a text appropriate to the occasion, and the discourse is
on some such subject as "Church, School and Home." But there is always
some reference to our public schools and to the beginning of the observance; and there is frequently an admonition of the duty of parents to
support the observance.

This year there were some decided variations reported. One report was
of an evening service to which parents and teachers were especially
invited and at which three school men discussed the topics "Manners and
Morals," "Relationship to the Home," and "Relationship to the Community."
All the co-operating agencies, together with the service clubs, appear
to have been very active this year; and without any invidious comparison
it would seem that especially so were the women's organizations, including, of course, the Parent-Teacher Associations everywhere.
It is not our purpose this year to make even brief reference to the
many individual observances which are well worthy of commendable
mention. Indeed all that we think may be said without unduly extending
this perhaps already too long report is that as was the case last year, and
perhaps in an even greater degree this year, the programs arranged for
the observance were designed (and very properly) to be informative and
inspirational rather than merely entertaining.
In this connection, however, and for obvious reasons, we do make
mention of the fact that a feature of several auditorium programs which
was both informative and entertaining was a spelling match or "spelling
bee" as it was frequently termed. In some instances the only contestants
were the school children-sometimes of the same grade, and at others of
different grades, with the words suited to the respective grades. There
were, however, more than one reported where both children and adults
participated.
·
These contests were informative as tending to show that notwithstanding the frequent assertions to the contrary, there are children in our
modem schools who can spell not only "easy words," but hard ones, too;
and they must have been decidedly entertaining to the parents of the
children when the adults were "spelled down." We can mention (and
that very briefly) only two of these.
In one the contestants were three pupils from an elementary school,
three from a high school, and three adults. The scoring was on the point
plan and the final result showed the elementary school first with 59 points,
the high school second with 57 points and the adults third with 49 points.
The other was a children-adult contest between six students and six
members of the local Rotary Club. According to the newspaper report
five of the six Rotarians "went down in quick order, but Judge - - was
very scholarly in his spelling ability until the word 'epiphyllum' drove
him from the stage as one of the school children spelled it very quickly."
In view of the repeated references in this report to the State of California, we feel that it should not be closed without our reporting to Grand
Lodge that the constituent lodges in the Hawaiian Islands joined in the
observance with that same enthusiasm with which they always so loyally
support every undertaking of Grand Lodge; and that it appears from the
reports that the school people there are as appreciative of what Masonry
is doing for the sc~ools as they are here.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Complying with Section 50 of the Constitution, I submit herewith my
report as Grand Lecturer together with the report of the Committee on
Ritual, of which the Grand Lecturer is.Chairman.
·
The Masonic Year just passed has been a busy one. The Lodges of the
jurisdiction are working hard, are prosperous, and are actively engaged
in the process of initiating, passing, and raising good men and true. By
all standards, the officers of the Constituent Lodges are of high calibre
and are carrying out the mission of Masonry in accordance with the high
ideals and traditions of California Masonry. This information is gathered
from the reports filed by the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts,
and by personal observation.
While we are actively engaged in the busy process of conferring degrees,
let us not forget that there are other Lodge activities besides degree work.
We must not forget that while our ritual has profound beauty and deep
significance, yet constant ·repetition under pressure, without relief, becomes a bore and has a tendency to drive away our members from our
meetings. We must attain a true sense of balance and proportion if we
are to attract our membership to good attendance. As Masons, we are
taught that we should divide our day into three equal parts. Likewise, we
should divide our Lodge activities into three equal parts, whereby we find
a part for the business of the Lodge, a part for our ritualistic endeavors,
and a part for refreshment and repose. This may sound peculiar coming
from an officer charged with the responsibility of supervising the ritual of
Masonry. Nevertheless, I am convinced that care should he exercised,

BOOK OF CEREMONIES

It is also necessary and desirable to make certain corrections in the
Book of Miscellaneous Ceremonies containing the rituals for Laying
Cornerstones, Instituting New Lodges, Constituting Lodges, Dedicating
Masonic Halls and Burial Plots, and Presentation of Buttons to the Veteran Masons. This book has not been published since 1937 and the supply
is running low. Due to the revision of the Constitution, certain references
to sections of the law must be corrected. In addition, the Ceremonies
should be modified and brought up to present day practice. In most
instances, specific musical selections or odes are prescribed, in other cases
certain processions are mandatory. In the light of present day practice,
the Ritual Committee feels that some of these requirements should be
made optional. It is not our purpose to change any of the wording of the
particular ceremonies except in one or two instances. Our main suggestions cover methods of opening, conducting processions, eliminating from
the book the required odes, and permitting the substitution of appropriate
music to be selected by the musicians or vocalists who are to perform. Our

point in suggesting a change in the procession is that we should ha~e
a uniform method of assembling in line for all occasions. One of the mam
reasons why these ceremonies have not been discussed, is that for _many
years the problem of constituting Lodges, dedicating Halls, and laymg of

9 Lodges were constituted. The charterin_g of four ~o~~es in 19~ and

In examining the ceremonies, it provides that Grand Lodge should be
opened in a convenient room and that only members of Grand Lodge
should be present. In most cases, in a town in which the new Lodge occupies the only hall, it is impossible to. comply w~th this re.quirement. This
regulation has been violated many times. For mstance, m 1945, Albany
Lodge was constituted at the evening session of Grand Lodge with members of the Lodge, their guests, and Grand Lodge members present. At the
conclusion of the ceremony, Grand Lodge was closed in their presence.
At the constitution of San Carlos Lodge, Oildale Lodge; Indian Wells
Valley Lodge, and Pohona Lodge in 1946, Grand Lodge was o~ened with
the entire group as above present, and the Lodges were constituted, and
then Grand Lodge was closed in each case. The Hall of Pohona Lodge was
dedicated under similar circumstances.
Our Ritual Committee feels that it would be highly desirable to revise
the ceremonies so that it would be proper for all interested Masons to be
present at the ~pening and closing ceremonies, as well as at the consti~u­
tion or other ceremonies. It would add much dignity, color, and solemmty
to the work and all who have witnessed it in the past have been greatly
impressed. We feel also that these ceremonies are of interest only to
Masons, and that the Institution, Constitution, and Hall Dedication Ceremonies be conducted in a closed tiled Masonic Lodge, and that the public
be not admitted. We also call your attention to a part of the Ritual for the
Presentation of Fifty Year Buttons. At a certain juncture the Presiding
Officer orders the Secretary to "read the Masonic record of our distinguished brother." In many cases the Secretary is ab.le only t.o read ~e
year in which the brother has been raised, all other mformahon havmg

brother. It is a record of honor, loyalty, and service, the brief summmg

SEPARATE SCHEDULE PRESENTED

Throughout the year, several of the brethren have offered many suggestions for improving our Ritual. We have discussed most of them in
committee, and have made a record of those matters which we feel have
merit. However, we feel that the time is not ripe for any further changes
in our work. During the thirteen and one-half years of the present system
of operation, the following record has been accomplished:
•
1. The Esoteric Work has been clarified, and the Floor Work has
been improved and developed to the present standards.
2. The Monitor and Officers Manual, Installation Service, and Funeral
Service have been corrected, improved, and adopted by Grand Lodge.
3. This report presents a proposed revision and recommendation for
adoption of corrections or additions in the balance of our rituals, namely:
Book of Ceremonies, Installation Ceremonies for Grand Lodge Officers,
and Opening and Closing Ceremonies of Grand Lodge.
We feel that it will be some time before these modifications can be
digested, and we, therefore, advise strongly against any further changes.
It is gratifying to note the extreme interest of our brethren in ritualistic
matters, and we shall make every effort to be alert to their suggestions.
OFFICERS' COACHES

During the course of the year certain points of administration have
come to my attention, among them being the matter of Officers' Coaches
in Lodges. In 1942 Grand Lecturer Chester H. Warlow recommended the
following in his report:
"That in each Lodge, a Past Master, selected by the Inspector of the District, be
especially trained in the ritual and be used by the Lodge as an Officers' Conch and
a source of ritualistic authority in the absence of the Inspector. In the larger Lodges
it is suggested that three such brethren be chosen, severally assigned a separate
degree and especially trained in their particular portion of the ritual. This semiofficial officer should be more or less permanent, hold office at the pleasure of the
Inspector of the District, and be regularly invited to attend all Inspectors' Schools
of Instruction. The Master of the Lodge should make use of this brother's profi·
ciency by holding frequent Schools of Instruction for the officers of his own Lodge, as
well as using this Past Master as the Coach in preparing the individual officers ·to
qualify for advancement. By this means, persistent and frequently reocc.u ring errors
will be eliminated in the degree work." (This report was adopted by Grand Lodge.)

During the hectic years of the war, this system proved itself to be most
valuable. The inability of the Inspector to get around, due to travel
conditions and gas shortages and other causes, made the work of the
Officer's Coach indispensable. During the time that I served as Assistant
Grand Lecturer, I found the Coaches to be most helpful, and I know that
our Inspectors are 100 percent for this system of operation. However, in

many cases, the Inspector has allowed the Master to make the selection
in order to promote harmony or good will. Most Masters have co-oper·

Inspectors' schools. In other cases, he feels that he is more competent
than the lnapector of the District. When the Inspector steps in to correct

we would alleviate some of the misunderstandings which have arisen. It
should be definitely understood, however, that in making this recom·
mendation, the Officers' Coach is to be a coach only, and the Inspector
is not to delegate any of his powers in any manner or form. In other
words, the Officers' Coach is not an Assistant Inspector.

cases, is far below the standard required for the qualification of officers.
In addition, the use of theatrical novelties, and their efforts to improvise
upon the adopted work, has caused considerable consternation among
those who are charged with maintaining the dignity of our degrees. Lodge
officers ask why they are not permitted to add the colorful devices
employed by some of our imaginative degree team brethren.
This problem has been discussed with Inspectors, Masters, Past Masters,
and many of our Grand Lodge Officers. All agree that the unrestricted
growth of these groups has placed a problem in our path that must be
solved, if the stability of our ritualistic system is to be preserved. Several
brethren, who have given this matter serious thought, have requested
legislation, either to prohibit these groups from operating, or in some
manner restricting their functions. A certification system has been suggested, whereby these teams would be required to submit to examination
before being permitted to operate. We point out that this would not be
practical, as there are at least a hundred or more such teams in existence.
It would require the services of at least 25 or more additional Inspectors
to supervise and qualify these teams. In addition, the changing nature
of membership of these groups would add an additional burden to these
Inspectors. We also point out that these teams would then be put into a
preferred class, and placed on an equal basis with Lodge Officers who
form the foundation of our Lodge system. In addition, such a regulation
would be in conflict with Ordinance 506 permitting a Master to invite
any qualified brother to confer or participate in a degree. This ordinance
was adopted in 1917.
In our opinion, the answer to the problem is simple, and is in the hands
of the Masters of our Lodges. I am certain that a review of the Master's
duties and responsibilities will indicate that our laws are sufficiently
strong to enforce what we are seeking. Accordingly, we are not making
any request for additional legislation. Rather, we are setting forth a strong
policy, which we propose to follow.

To appoint in each Lodge within his District an Officers' Coach, who shall be
a qualified Past Master of the Lodge, and who shall serve at the pleasure of the
Inspector. The Officers' Coach shall assist in teaching the ritual to the Officers of
his Lodge, and assist in preparing them to qualify for advancement.
DEGREE TEAMS

Degree Teams have been a source of friction and annoyance to every
Grand Lecturer and Inspector from time immemorial. The growth and
tremendous interest in Masonry today has increased by leaps and bounds
the number of so called Degree Teams operating in our jurisdiction.
Many large firms, public utilities, transportation companies, and em·
ployees of political subdivisions have developed teams. Most of them
have endeavored to cooperate, and are doing a fairly creditable job.
Others are interested only in providing entertainment for the Lodges
who issue invitations to them; their interest in the candidate being only
secondary. Some teams are of a semi-permanent nature, others are will o'
the wisp groups, who appear only now and then, and have no particular
standing. A few of these organized teams have done a good job and have
contributed to the advancement of our Institution. They have produced
good fellowship, and in portraying our ritual in a dignified and impres·
sive manner, have encouraged interest in Masonry, and have demon·
strated the true spirit of Brotherly Love.
During the course of the past year, however, it has been necessary for
the Grand Lecturer to reprimand several groups, and warn them of flag·
rant violations of our adopted ritual, and in many cases good taste. These
traveling teams are composed of brethren who do not have the advantage

DEGREE TEAM P OLICY

Any Master permitting willful violation of our ritual by a degree team
will be cited to the Grand Master for judgment. The team involved will be
barred from further Masonic activity for such time as may be determined
by the Grand Master.
We further recommend, unless otherwise ordered by this Grand Lodge,
that the portion of this report relating to degree teams be sent to each
Master and Inspector in order that they may be fully informed as to this
policy.
We are certain that if the Masters of the Jurisdiction are thoroughly
aware of their strict responsibility, they will, of their own accord, eliminate this evil from our midst.

law to adjust some differences between the Constitution and our Ritual.
Recently, our attention has been called to the following language used
in Section Three.
"The Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master (whose address shall be Most Worshipful), a Deputy Grand Master, a Senior Grand
Warden, and a Junior Grand Warden (whose addresses shall severally
be Right Worshipful), a Grand Treasurer, a Grand Secretary and a Grand
Lecturer (whose addresses shall severally be Very Worshipful), a Grand
Chaplain (whose address shall be Very Reverend) , the Assistant Grand
Lecturers, a Grand Orator, an Assistant Grand Secretary, a Grand Marshal, a Grand Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a Grand Bible
Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior Grand Deacon, two Grand
Stewards, a Grand Pursuivant, a Grand Organist, and a Grand Tiler
(whose addresses shall severally be Worshipful) ; together with all the
Past Grand Officers and Past Masters of this jurisdiction, and the Masters
and Wardens of the several chartered and duly constituted Lodges, or
the representatives thereof duly elected."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

111

We call your attention to the word "addressed."
Definition in Webster: To direct words to anyone. To use a set form
in accosting or greeting.
In our ritual, we use the various titles: M.W., R.W., V.W., V.R., or
W. when we speak of an officer. When speaking to the officer or in giving
an order to him, we omit the title.
This is the revers_e of the correct usage of the word address.
When the Constitution of the Grand Lodge was adopted in 1850, the
following section described the officers of Grand Lodge.
"RANK AND TITLE OF OFFICERS AND MEMBERS

Sec. 1. The Grand Lodge shall consist of a Most Worshipful Grand
Master, a Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, a Right Worshipful
Senior Grand Warden, a Right Worshipful Junior Grand Warden,
a Right Worshipful Grand Treasurer, a Right Worshipful Grand Secretary, a Right Worshipful Grand ·Chaplain, a Grand Marshal, a Grand
Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior
Grand Deacon, two Grand Stewards, a Grand Tyler, and such other subordinate officers as the Grand Lodge, from time to time, may appoint,Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters, Right Worshipful Past Deputy
Grand Masters, Right Worshipful Past Grand Wardens, Right Worshipful Past Grand Treasurers, Right Worshipful Past Grand Secretaries,together with the Worshipful Masters and Wardens, for the time being
of the several chartered and constituted Lodges under the jurisdiction
of this Grand Lodge, or their legally appointed proxies, and the Past
Masters, members of Lodges under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge."
Our Ritual, as presently used, follows this form in detail with some
minor corrections. When the Constitution was revised in 1859, the section of the law governing the composition of Grand Lodge was revised
to the language now in use. At that time, no change was made in the
ritual and we are still using the same work.
In other words, the Constitution says that the Grand Lodge is composed
of the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, etc. The Ritual says the
M.W. Grand Master, the Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, etc.
The same holds true regarding the title of Worshipful Master as used in
the Constituent Lodges.
All of our ceremonies follow the old form of ritual and we are of the
opinion that it would he unwise to make any change in the work for
several reasons:
First: Our present ritual is in harmony with the usage of most of the
American Grand Lodges.
Second: It has been in use since the very beginning of our Grand
Lodge.
Third: It would be a tremendous task to completely revise the ritual
because our Constituent Lodge work would have to be revised in addition
to all of our Grand Lodge Services.

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The simplest way to adjust this difference would be to amend the
Constitution. The use of the word "title" in place of "address" would
cover the situation very easily.
The definition of "title" is as follows:
Webster-Title: An appellation significant of office, dignity, rank, or
distinction.
·
Title may be sub-divided into (I) Titles of honor, (2) of distinction or
merit, and ( 3) of address.
The third embraces prefixed words or phrases attributing rank, office
or disitnction, terms of respect when used either in direct address, or
in mentioning a person; as, his Grace, the Rt. Honorable, his Reverence,
Sir, Madam, Mister, etc.
We therefore recommend the following amendment to Section Three
of the Constitution.
In place of the word "address" to substitute in each case the word
"title."
In place of the word "addresses" to substitute in each case the word
"titles."
Also to Section 22:
Add after the word "Master," the phrase--"whose title shall be
Worshipful."
During a review of the Grand ·Lodge Opening Ceremonies yesterday
another defect in our Ritual became apparent. In the recital of the
duties of the Grand Pursuivant and the Junior Grand Deacon there are
conflicting duties; viz:
G. Pur.-To guard the inner door of the Grand Lodge and .communicate with the Worshipful Grand 'filer without, to announce all applicants
for admission by their names and proper Masonic titles and see that all
who enter wear the jewel and clothing proper to their rank, to allow none
to withdraw who have not obtained permission to do so from the M.W.
G.M., to act as assistant to the Worshipful Grand Marshal in all processions of the Grand Lodge and at all public ceremonies.
J. G. D.-To carry messages from the R.W.S.G.W. in the west to the
R.W.J.G.W. in the south and elsewhere about the Grand Lodge as
directed, attend to all alarms at the door and see the Grand Lodge duly
tiled.
As will be seen, according to the ritual, both of these officers perform
the same duty as far as 'answering the door, etc. When the office of
Grand Pursuivant was added to the line of officers, certain duties of the
Junior Grand Deacon were transferred to him. However no change was
made in the ritualistic functions. In order to clarify the clash of duties
we recommend that the ritualistic duties of the Junior Grand Deacon be
revised to the following:
To carry messages from the R.W.S.G.W. in the west to the R.W.J.G.W.
in the south and elsewhere about the Grand Lodge as directed, and to
perform such other duties as may be requi~ed.

CONDITION OF THE HOMES

The physical properties of our Homes at both Covina and Decoto have
had the careful and unremitting attention of your Trustees.
As has heretofore been repeatedly reported to the Grand Lodge, during
the wa:r we were unable, of course, to secure the labor and materials
necessary to make urgently needed repairs and replacements. This includes furniture and furnishings, modernization of elevators, laundry
equipment, and additional refrigeration. Other long contemplated im·
provements included the completion of the second floor of the Hospital,
a building to house nurses and other women employees, as well as demolition of the old buildings which housed married employees. To house these
latter, the existing brick building will be remodeled foto a number· of
apartments. The installation of an elevator in the Semino:ff Temple as
well as other repairs in that building, including the comfortable chairs
suitable for a lodge room; and the construction of a residence for a
Superintendent, have been included in the post-war plans.
The work contemplated will, of course, involve the expenditure of a
large amount of money, but during the time that labor was unavailable
a post-war reserve fund was set up to which an allocation was made each
year out of our surplus. This reserve with the amount transferred to the
Building Fund, plus other funds available to the Trustees provides a fund
in excess of $500,000 for the above mentioned rehabilitation and construction.
With the end of the war, although there was not yet that flow of labor
and material which may come later, we felt warranted in entering upon
the long deferred program. We have already completed work required to
• be done to comply with demands made by the State Fire Marshal, and
other urgently needed work is now in progress.
A survey of the property at Covina was conducted under the general
direction of the Southern members of the Board of Trustees, and·a firm
of architects · employed for the purpose. The result of this survey was
reported to the entire board and approved. The necessary contracts were
entered into and all work to fully rehabilitate the Home at Coviria has
either been completed or is in process of completion.
The Home for our aged members at Decoto presents, because of its
greater size, a more difficult problem. The Trustees, together with the
Architects engaged for the purpose, made a thorough survey of the prop·
erties at Decoto. The report compiled as a result of this survey listed
sixteen new projects, some of which have been mentioned, looking toward
the complete rehabilitation of these properties and the construction of

POPULATION

The population trend at the Homes continues to present an interesting
situation. Applications for admission have not fallen o~, b.u~ on the. contrary have increased month by month. The aged are findmg 1t mcreasmgly
difficult to support themselves on the State Old Age Grant and consequently are continuing to seek other means of security.
This trend, together with the increase in the average age presents prob·
lems both of administration and housing. It is interesting to note that
recent Federal reports show that the average length of life has increased
twenty-one years since 1900 and this certainly is reflected in the age of
those seeking admission to our Home.
Your Board is now faced with the necessity of denying immediate
admission to women, because no rooms are available. The reason for this
is not only the general_ increase in the average length of life, but also the
undisputed fact that people with security have a greater life expectancy
and actually do live more years, and cases are numerous where pe~s?ns
admitted to the Home and given but a short expectancy by the exammmg
physician, actually live for a great many ye~rs a~ter going to Decoto ..
The first step in the solving of the room situation for women applicants
is being taken in the construction program, for when the new quarteTs
are provided for employees, rooms now occupied by them in the main ·
building will be released, making forty additional beds available.
While our Home at Covina is not being used to capacity, there has been
a noticeable increase in the applications made in behalf of children. Most
agencies concerned with child care th~oughout the country p~edict t~at .
within five to ten years many of the children born of war marnages will,
of necessity, become a charge upon the public, and it is only reasonable
to expect that some of these children will become the wards of your
Trustees in the Home at Covina.

FINANCES

The finances of the Masonic Homes are in excellent shape, but it should
be borne in mind that an amount in excess of one-half million dollars is
being spent in the work heretofore mentioned.
At the present time, both Homes are being maintained without any
contribution from the Lodges, except such payments as are made for
admissions in excess of the Lodge quota.
Last year on the recommendation of the Trustees the provision in the
Constitution for a SO-cent tax for the building fund was repealed; and for
two years now, and also on the recommendation of the Trustees, there has
been no per capita tax levied for maintenance, nor will there be this year.
In this connection, for the information of those not comiersant with the
situation, it should be explained that our funds at present are being
derived from three sources--first, and principally, of course, the contributions of the initiates; second, income from investments (including, of
course, income of the En~owment Fund); and third, gifts and contributions for specific purposes not included in those for, or by the Trustees
allocated to, the Endowment Fund. It is largely from this last mentioned
that the residents at Decoto are provided with "spending money"-at
present $5.00 per month.
·
The matter of the per capita levy is one on which the Trustees must
take action annually, and if conditions in the future require it, they will re·
quest Grand Lodge for a per capita tax for the maintenance of the Homes.

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-DECOTO HOME

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: In submitting this, my seventh annual report of the Masonic
Home at Decoto for the year ending July 31, 1947, I am pleased to report
that the affairs of the Home are quite satisfactory.
A tree is judged by the fruit it bears. By the same measure of judgment
the Masons of California may well be proud of their Home at Decoto.
The fine adjustment made ~y the great majority of our members testifies
to the fact that through the forty-eight years of its existence, the Home
has been developing a technique for the care of the aged. "Does it work?"
This is n.o~ ~o say that we are now, or have been at any time in the past,
above cntlc1sm. If we could reach that perfection in policy, program and
managem~nt, we would still be furnishing a substitute for the happy
homes which most of our members once enjoyed. We on the inside have
been trying to correct our shortcomings, to improve our care, and to.
approach the ideals of real home life, using to the best advantage of the
members the buildings and equipment we have.
Any type of .care for the aged, even the care they receive in the homes
of relatives, can be criticized from without. I am convinced that our type
of care is right in principle and economical in practice, and that the
Masonic Home at Decoto is one of the best homes of this type to be found.
We are pleased to have our tree judged by its fruit.
At the beginning of the year there were 158 women and 117 men enjoying the care and comforts of the Home. During the year 32 women and 42
men were admitted, and we lost by death 17 women and 27 men, and 1
woman and 5 men were withdrawn, leaving at the end of the year 172
women and 127 men, a total of 299. Included in this total are 12 married
couples. The average age for women is 78 and for men 77.97 years.
The health conditions in the Home have been very good during the
year. At present, due to infirmities common to folk in advanced years, 59
are being cared for in the hospital and East Wing. These members are
receiving excellent care under the kindly and efficient supervision of Miss
Esther G. Payne, who has served the Home faithfully for many years.
Mrs. Virginia M. Lord, our Matron, has been quite successful in developing and maintaining among the residents of the Home who are in
sufficient good health to occupy their rooms in the main building, a social
atmosphere in keeping with the ideals of our Fraternity; and to provide
them with the comforts and diversions which make life worth while for
those who can no longer fight the battle of life.
The ~ookkeeping department is operating very efficiently. All of the
accounts and records are up to date and in first class order under the
able supervision of Mr. E. C. Hildebrand.
Our commissary and purchasing department is efficiently managed by
Mr. Paul Reichert. Receiving and distribution of supplies are carefully
supervised. Being familiar with qualities and prices, he is in a position

119

to take advantage of any opportunity that may present itself where a
saving can be effected.
·
All other departments are functioning quite satisfactorily; however,
there is need for improvement which will be made when and if we are
able to obtain efficient help.
Due to conditions over which we have no control, the operating expense
of the Home has increased materially in the last year. More employees
and higher wages are a major portion of the increase, and increases in
prices account for the balance.
The improvements and necessary repairs which we have been able to
accomplish during the past year have put our buildings in good condition,
and the grounds and gardens present a more pleasing appearance. Our
water supply has been inadequate for several months and as a result
we have been compelled to purchase water from the Public Utilities
Company of Niles, which is quite expensive. The answer may be a new
well if attempts to increase the supply in the present well do not succeed.
The farm land is still under lease. The receipts from that portion retained
for the Home use was very poor due to the drought suffered in this section.

With one or two minor exceptions all recommendations for changes
or alterations at the Home made by the State Fire Marshal, as well as
those made by our Insurance Broker, have been complied with. The recommendations for changes on our elevators, made by the Pacific Coast
Engineering Department of the Employees Group have been referred to
the the Pacific Elevator Company of San Francisco. They inform us that
due to the fact that they have so many requests for such changes it will be
some time before they can attend to the matter for us.
The many programs which were presented by various groups throughout the year, a complete list of which will be found in another part of our
report, have all been excellent, enthusiastically received and immensely
enjoyed by the members of the Home family. We feel that special mention
should be made of the East Bay Past Matrons' Association's visitation,
which was made on August 16th with about 600 in attendance, and in their
generous manner presented to the members of the Home 7,634 glasses of
jelly and jam, 30 jars of assorted relishes and 76 delicious home made
cakes. Following a luncheon served in our banquet room in honor of
Grand Matron Birdie Bassett and her corps of Grand Chapter officers,
Orient Chapter as hostesses and Past Grand Matron Willa Jane Hellwig
as Chairman, a very impressive program was presented in our auditorium.
Mrs. Louise Wood, President of the association, presided. Grand Matron

Bassett was introduced and made a very interesting and impressive
address.
The East Bay Masters' and Wardens' Association's visitation is also
worthy of special mention. A very large delegation from this fine organization visited the Home on September 22, with Brother Howard Kaulhach,
President, in charge of arrangements. After partaking of a barbecue
served in the banquet room, a very interesting and enjoyable program was
presented in our auditorium. .
For many years past, R.K.O., Columbia, United Artists, Warner Bros.,
M.G.M. and Twentieth Century-Fox film distributing companies of San
Francisco have been and are still providing gratis to the Home excellent
weekly programs which the Home family enjoys very much. To these fine
organizations we want to express our grateful thanks and deep appreciation for their generosity.
The fine messages brought to us every Sunday by the Reverend gentlemen of the Ministerial Association of Southern Alameda County are
always appreciated by a large number of the members of our Home. We
would feel remiss, indeed, if we failed to extend to these Reverend gentlemen our sincere thanks. Our library is kept well supplied with hooks,
magazines and periodicals which enable our members to keep well posted
on current events. The members who are unable to find the hooks they
desire on our shelves are able to secure them from the Alameda County
Library, a branch of which is in our library.
During the year the Trustees have visited the Home, both individually
and collectively, as have other Grand Lodge officers. We were honored
with a visit from the Grand Master and Mrs. Moore on March 21, 1947.
The members of the Home arranged a reception in their honor. Grand
Master Moore addressed the assemblage, after which he and Mrs. Moore
spent a pleasaQt evening chatting with the members of the Home family.
Mrs. Lord and I wish to express our deep appreciation to the Trustees
and other Grand Lodge officers for the assistance they have given us in
solving some of the problems with which we have been confronted.
In conclusion we wish to express to our employees our sincere thanks
for the loyal services they have rendered. We also want to thank the
members of the Home for the valuable assistance that they have rendered
during the year.
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES R. EUBANKS, Superintendent.
