REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT-COVINA HOME

To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of Californw:
Herewith is presented my second annual report as Superintendent of the
Masonic Home for children at Covina.
Home Membership

This year ends with a Home membership lower than that of previous
years due to the few qualified applicants during the year and an unusually
large class graduating from High School.
During the past year 18 children were admitted. This was an increase
over the admissions for each of the three previous years. A total of 21 left
the Home--ten after graduation and eleven at parent's request. All
Masonic Homes for children are operating with decreased memberships
during these years of prosperity. Already, however, there seems to he an
increase in inquiries which indicates that the services of this Home will
he in greater demand as post war conditioi.is develop.
Aµerations Program
The work of alteration and refurnishing the buildings was started in
the spring. Installation of steel fire stairways and remodelling of baths
has involved considerable work in the buildings. This has made it necessary to change the routine living program considerably to meet the
emergency. This somewhat extensive program will not he completed until
late fall of 1947.

122

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Summer Program
All except the youngest children have had camping experience with
Y.M.C.A., Y.W.C.A. or Scout groups or at Yosemite. We are especially
grateful to Brother W. D. Crosby, the members of Pohona Lodge No. 689
and the Yosemite Masonic Club for their generous assistance with a
Y~semite Va.lley ~amp for our older boys and girls. A few older boys
en1oyed a High Sierra pack trip. Some have participated in a summer
work program which has given them contact with the outside.
Graduates, After-Care, Home Alumni
This Home has always been proud of the bo.ys and girls who have
g~own to young adulthood under its supervision. That pride continues
with the.te~ youn~ people ~ho completed High School this year. Seven
are contmumg their education at Universities or Junior Colleges, while
three are employed.
·
Those not having a parent who can assume the responsibility are looked
after, ~ounselled and assisted by the Home staff until they are entirely
on their own. Scholarship money is made available for those who need
assistance in college. Alumni of the Home have assembled for a Reunion
Day, an annual custom. Alumni reunion dinners in San Francisco and
Los Angeles have been held during the year.
Health Program

Daily chmc visits average 28 per day or an average of 136 visits per child
for the year. The daily average number of bed patients in the hospital
during the year has been 2.12 or an average of 10.33 days per child for
the year. All children are examined regularly by Dr. Magan and his
associa~~s who have supervised the Home health program for many years.
I? addition to the usual colds, flu, poison oak and expected children's

GRAND LODGE. OF CALIFORNIA

Report of Masonic Homes Endowment Board
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
It is with pleasure that your Masonic Homes Endowment Board pre·
sents herewith their fifteenth annual report, covering the period from
August 1, 1946, to July 31, 1947, inclusive.
HISTORY

The necessity for an Endowment Fund was recognized from the time
of the dedication of the Home at Decoto in 1898. Records show that the
matter was discussed among the Brethren and at Grand Lodge, but the
establishment for such a Fund was indeed slow. However, the seed was
planted and the desire was in the hearts and minds of the thinking Masons,
and slowly but surely it came to fruition.
In 1909, our late Brother, Jacob Hart Neff, passed on, leaving the
residue of his estate amounting to $12,688.97 to the Home at Decoto.
This brought the matter squarely before Grand Lodge and at the annual
Communication in 1910, it was ordered that the Neff bequest be entered
as the first donation to a Permanent Endowment Fund.
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board was created by action of
Grand Lodge (Constitution and Ordinances, Article V) and consists of
fifteen members. The purpose of such a Board was to enlighten the
Brethren regarding the work and needs of the Homes, and to afford an
opportunity to make contributions for their support. In short, the purpose
of the Board is, "to study, devise, and carry out plans for the securing of
adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of California." The personnel of the present Board and the indicated date of the expiration of
their appointment is as follows:

PROGRESS •

It has been the policy throughout the years that the Board pursue an
educational program in accordance with the purposes of its creation.

124

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

During the past year, we have endeavored to continue this program and
found the interest among the Brethren in our living testimonials for the
charity work of Masons in California. We have followed a strict econom·
ical plan without sacrificing in securing our ultimate objective. The
actual cost in this promotion work has been only a small fraction of 1 %.
The growth of the Fund is the one and ~nly answer to the success of
the Program. Such phenomenal accomplishment can only be obtained
when working with a responsive group. The Craft throughout the Jurisdiction is showing, not only a continuing, but an increased interest in the
Endowment Fund Program. The contributions through the Lodges for the
past year were $186,398.55-this amount from 43,708 contributors. This
well exceeds in membership contribution and individual contributors any
preceding year.
We wish to pay special tribute to the fine Masons who have served on
the Board during the past. Particularly, should we be proud of their
leadership, their interest and devotion to their work, and above all, their
accomplishments.
Much credit is due the Masters, Secretaries and other officers of the
of the constituent Lodges. Your Board expresses their gratitude to these
fine Masons as well as to the Committee Chairmen and many individual
Brethem who have constantly aided us in our work. Particularly, are
we grateful to the hard-working Inspectors who are more and more
molding the Endowment Fund Program into their activities. But above
all, we express a special thanks tQ the Grand Master who has consistently
cooperated throughout the year.
FUTURE

The answer to our efforts-accomplishment is in our hands. We know
how and what has. been done. We hold the key to the future. It is our
recommendation that the present program be continued with such em·
bellishments and improvements as will aid the cause. Pressure or
coercion on none, but an opportunity for all. We ask that the sum of
$8,000 be appropriated for the purposes of the Board in carrying on
its work.
We enlist your perusal and study of the following financial report
.. trusting it will be an inspiration for the future, and the hope that in the
not too distant future, the income from our Endowment Fund will be
ample to carry on the work in our two great Homes.

Report of Board of Control
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Eighteen years ago Grand Lodge created a Board of Control, consisting
of five members, to supervise and control Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus and to so direct their affairs that they might be operated
efficiently and economically.
Past reports of the Board of Control to Grand Lodge are in themselves
testimony that this authority has been wisely used and that Boards of
Relief and Employment Offices have developed efficiently and that their
operations have been conducted economically. These records show manv
thousands of dollars saved Grand Lodge by this method of handling reli~f
and employment.

130

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
BOARDS OF RELIEF

Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction are permitted by Grand Lodge
to form Boards of Relief. These boards operate under a compact and
by-laws which are signed by masters of the lodges and approV'ed by the
Board of Control and the Grand Master. Their work is directed by a board
of trustees or directors, usually chosen from among the masters and
wardens of the member lodges. They select a secretary whose duty it is to
actively manage the operations of that Board of Relief. The purpose for
which these offices are founded is to aid sojourning brethren, their wives,
widows and orphans, and all others entitled to relief under the jurisdic·
tion of the Grand Lodge of California. Only temporary relief is contem·
plated, however they are not restricted in ofiering such relief as in their
judgment the circumstances may warrant.
All Boards of Relief receive their entire financial support from the
local lodges. A uniform per capita assessment is agreed upon by the board
of directors or trustees, which is limited only by the maximum which has
been set up within their compact. They shall visit the sick, investigate
relief applications, supervise all Masonic funerals in the district for
visiting brethren and may establish and maintain Employment Offices.
At present we are operating 17 Boards of Relief within our jurisdiction.
They are located at Bakersfield, East Bay, Fresno, Glendale, Honolulu,
Long Beach, Los Angeles, Pasadena, Richmond, Sacramento, San Bernar·
dino, San Diego, San Francisco, San Jose, Santa Barbara, Santa Monica
and Stockton. These represent some 262 lodges or a Masonic member·
ship of approximately 104,000. The statistical reports from these Boards
of Relief show that they have conducted 792 funerals during the past
Masonic year, made 2112 calls upon the sick, administered relief or in·
vestigated 2336 cases and handled 825 cases involving other types of
relief. Many services were rendered which are not a part of this report
but which are none the less valuable to the individual member and his
family.
Their report shows, that, during the year, ·they disbursed for relief
approximately $31,000. That they are in a stable financial condition is
indicated by the figures reported to the Board of Control on their con·
solidated balance sheet, which shows a net worth of over $77,000.00.
Your particular attention is again directed to the fact that all of these
Boards of Relief are entirely self supporting and that not one cent has
been contributed by Grand Lodge.
It has been customary, however, for Grand Lodge to reimburse Boards
of Relief for any money expended for relief wherein the Lodge of the
brother so aided or his Grand Jurisdiction fail to acknowledge the obliga·
tion. This year, out of some $31,000 expended on relief, only one board
has requested reimbursement and it is asking Grand Lodge for $10.00.

The compacts by which Boards of Relief operate, permit the organiza·
tion and operation of Masonic Employment Services. Seven such offices

~s Angeles, Sacramento, San Diego and San Francisco. With the excep-

In our empl~yment services there are 218 lodges with a membership

$42,~0 to operate for the year and their combined net worth as shown
by their balance sheets, as of July 31, 1947, was $6,700.

BOARD OF CONTROL

The Board of Control met in San Francisco on January 25th to plan
our work for the year.
A meeting was held in Long Beach on April 11, 12, and 13, to which
the representatives of all the Southern California Boards of Rel_ief and
Employment Services were invited. Only Pasadena, San Bernardmo and
Santa Barbara were absent. At this meeting several items of major
importance were considered.
The Glendale Board of Relief had been called upon to conduct sixty
sojourner funerals during the year which placed an unfair burden on
the three lodges making up the active membership of that Board. Further
study of this problem will be required. .
.
A Southern California lodge had voted unanimously to join one of our
Boards of Relief. At a subsequent meeting another vote was taken and
it was their unanimous decision to withdraw from the Board~ Both of
these actions were out of order as they were taken prior to presentation
to the Board of Control, which is a requirement of their comp(!ct. Officially they were not members of the Board of Relief until their application
had been approved by the Board of Control and the Grand Master. Therefore they could not withdraw from that to which they did not belong.
· Another item of importance had to do with the appropriations of
Grand Lodge to the support of Employment Offices. In the past it was the
custom to consider requests for appropriations upon the basis of the
amount requested by the individual Employment Office. This system could
easily lead to an unfair distribution of Grand Lodge aid in favor of one
or more of our offices. The Board of Control, therefore, adopted the
following rules as an equitable and logical basis in determining a fair
appropriation, and made it effective as of August 1, 1947.
1. That the receipts and expenses allocated to Employment Services
must be in like ratio, i.e., whatever percentage of the total expense is
charged against Employment Service, a like percentage of total receipts
must be devoted to Employment Service.
2. That Grand Lodge will not contribute an amount greater than the .
local per capita allocation to Employment and
3. That revenues from endowments, bequests, gifts, and other Masonic
bodies will not be included in applying these rules.
The Board of Control invited all of the Northern California offices to
meet with them in Fresno on June 6, 7, and 8. All offices had repre-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

133

eentatives present. This was an important meeting and we were able to
adjust a misunderstanding within one of the Boards of Relief.
We also voted at this meeting to adopt the uniform system of records
for the Employment Offices, which had been under consideration for
months.
An emergency developed in Los Angeles which required the calling
of a special meeting of the Board of Control. We accordingly met on
August 1, 2, and 3. Hearings were held with our Los Angeles brothers
and recommendations were made which were later adopted in their
entirety, and which seem to be the solution to the immediate problem.
Members of the Board of Control have attended the Masonic Breakfasts in San Francisco, Long Beach, Sacramento, East Bay and Fresno
and the conference meeting in Los Angeles. The Board of Control is now
in session and will continue its meeting throughout this entire communication of Grand Lodge.
We fully realize that there are yet many problems to be solved in order
to attain maximum efficiency in organization and operation. Varying
conditions in different localities tend to complicate ultimate solutions.
We believe, however, that by continued vigilance and careful study,
proper methods will be found which will operate under all possible
conditions.
Relief is being efficiently and economically managed with no one entitled to help ever turned away. The Employment Service has become an
extremely important part of our Board of Relief. We believe that much
has been saved our lodges by placing brethren in employment thus preventing many of them from coming to us as relief cases. It works as a
perfect balance to the Relief service, in that it gives a man a chance to
help himself, thereby strengthening his morale and saves the resources
of Relief for those who cannot help themselves.
That our present method is not perfect is illustrated by the many
changes that the Board of Control put in operation this year. Some criticism of the systems used by our Employment Offices resulted in a decision
by the Board of Control, with the approval of the Grand Master, to
engage a nationally known firm of accountants to make a complete survey
of all Employment Offices and to recommend a uniform, efficient, and
economically sound method of handling records, one which would lend
itself to rapid and accurate annual audit. This survey dealt only with the
mechanical operation of these offices and was not concerned with finances,
Grand Lodge has always required an annual financial audit of all offices
under the supervision of the Board of Control and no question has ever
developed as to the accuracy of these records.
In consequence of the above mentioned survey, a uniform record
system for our Employment Offices was put in operation as of August 1,
1947. By this procedure, the statistics accumulated will be uniform and
an audit of the transactions of each office can be made with a minimum
amount of work.

APPRECIATION

Now let us compare that with one of our own cases which developed
in a Board of Relief. About five years ago a brother from the State of
--~died. We gave him a Masonic burial. He left a widow and a young
son, a partnership burdened with debt and no insurance. The widow
secured work through our Employment service and through diligence and
thrift was working out her problem. A little over two years ago she was in
an automobile accident. Her back was broken and she was paralyzed from
the neck down. Saviiigs were soon exhausted and she had to be transferred
to the County hospital. Her son was taken in by friends. Some assistance
was received from the father's Lodge. Swnmer employment and weekend jobs helped the boy in his support, at the same time he was making
the long trips to see his mother. Her damage suit was set for trial a year
ago last June. It seemed as hopeless as did her recovery. She passed away
in February 1946. The Board of Relief took over the affairs of the boy,
buried his mother, collected a small death benefit, had a guardian appointed and had the damage suit settled without trial with a very liberal
settlement. They appointed a substitute executor for the father's estate
and will wind up this complicated problem with about $5,000 for the
boy's support and education.
This case will continue more or less under the guidance of our Board
of Relief for the next two years when the boy will become of age.
.
You will note the smooth, efficient operation of relief which is typical
of cases handled in this jurisdiction. No red tape, but hour upon hour of
time wisely spent until the case is finally completed. No publicity or
desire for praise, just another job well done.
The Board of Control solicits any criticism or suggestion from this
Grand Lodge and from members of the Craft. The Board of Control
pledges itself to maintain its control and supervision over Boards of
Relief and Employment Services and to so direct their management that
they will continue to be operated with efficiency and economy.

The Board of Control is indebted to the Most Worshipful Grand
Master the Grand Secretary and his assistants, and many other, Grand
Lodge ~fficers for their cooperation and helpful suggestions. Our report
would not be complete were we to overlook this debt.
The Secretaries of our Boards of Relief and the Managers of our Employment Services have been most cooperative ~ their underst~ndi~g of
our common problems. It is a pleasure to work with.men of theu cahbe~.
We are all indebted to them for their loyalty to theu work and for theu
enthusiastic support of all our principles. Their records justify the confi·
dence which we have placed in them.
Our contacts with the Directors and Trustees have been an encourage·
ment to us in our work. Their interest in the problems of relief and
employment and the proper management of their offices has proved to us
that the responsibility has been wisely placed.
During the year we lost the services of Brother Leo Bruck, Secretary
of the San Francisco Board of Relief, Brother Fred M. Thompson,
Secretary-Manager of the San Diego Board of Relief and Employment
Service, Brother J. Herbert Smith, Secretary of the San Bernardino Board
of Relief and Brother Jack Work, Manager of the Los Angeles Employ·
ment Service. For many years these Brothers had served our Boards
faithfully and well. We regret the loss of their services.
We sincerely thank our Masonic Brethren who have aided us in . the
solution of many difficult problems. Even in the most delicate situations
we have found them most willing to set aside personal prejudices in
favor of harmony and understanding.

Report of Special Committee on
George Washington Memorial
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In view of the uncertain state of the policies of Grand Lodge with
reference to the George Washington Masonic National Memorial and with
a view to action in a definite way by our Grand Lodge concerning that
project, you named the Deputy Grand Master, the Chairman: of the
Finance Committee and the Chairman of our Grand Lodge Committee on
the Washington Memorial as a Special Committee and requested their
attendance in Washington, D.C., at the annual meeting of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association on February 22,

1947.
Your Committee was accordingly in attendance at that meeting and
also attended a meeting of the . Board of Directors of that organization
when our Grand Master propounded some pertinent questions relative
to cost and the possibility of completion and probable date. The architect of the work was present at that meeting and answered questions so
far as the same could be answered in view of the uncertainties of material
and labor costs and the ability of the organization to raise the necessary
funds to complete the work and the time when such funds would be
available.
Little or nothing was learned from either the Directors or the architect
that we had not already learned from a study of th.e reports published
annually.. .But we did learn that no departure from past methods, or
plans for increased activity, existed either as to actual construction, or
the raising of the necessary money to complete and endow the project.
The Board, with few changes, had remained in office for many years, and
probably would remain in office until some cataclysm shall occur to jar
them loose.
We think, however, that much was gained by our "on the ground"
inspection, observation and inquiries. We feel that the reason for lack
of progress both as to the Memorial itself and the raising of the funds
could have been brought to us, impressed upon us, and explained to us,
in no other way. It is difficult to realize the state of stagnation that is
apparent from an "on the ground" examination.
.In going over past reports of the Association with the picture of things
at the Memorial in mind, it would appear that the present Board of

137

Directors, with some exceptions, may have been too long in office, and
may have become set in their ways and processes of thought. Under
present methods followed by the Board, it is hardly likely that any member of this Committee will live to see the Memorial completed and fully
endowed. Your Committee is firmly of the opinion that changes must
be made in the administrative organization before much, if any, improvement will appear. By reason of the plan of organization, this will require
action on the part of the Board of Directors, themselves, and therefore it
may be a remedy is not likely soon to be effected. We have some recommendations along this line, some of which, we hope, may be acceptable
to the Board. These are stated later in this report.
This want of new ideas and enthusiasm can become, as it did once
before in a somewhat similar situation, the thrall that kills. Let us not
permit this Association to follow in the footsteps of its illustrious predecessor, the Washington National Monument Society, which, for that
same lack of initiative and enthusiasm, permitted the great obelisk on
the Mall to lie untouched and uncompleted for more than twenty years,
and until, finally, and only, through means of an appropriation by
Congress, out of the public funds, were the finishing touches put upon
it. We trust that means will be adopted which will revive this association
before it becomes necessary to appeal to the public resources.
·
ESSENTIAL PRELIMINARIES

The study which your committee has devoted to the project leads us
to the conclusion that certain things are essential preliminaries to a successful outcome of this monument to Masonry, namely:
1. That a limitation be placed by official action of the Board upon
further changes in plans and specifications, to the end that the cost of
the completed structure may be kept within the bounds of reason.
2. That a definite sum be fixed upon for the costs of administration
in an annual budget to be adopted which costs should be limited and
possibly curtailed.
3. That in any annual budget, an ample and definite sum be budgeted,
and later set aside in money for investment, to constitute a fund to cover
depreciation, obsolesence, and replacement.
4. That as nearly as possible, a definite sum be fixed for the cost of
completion by men competent and skilled in the art and practice of con·
struction; that when so fixed, the work of completion be limited to such
fixed sum, in order that the Grand Jurisdictions of the country may be
informed of the extent of their obligation.
The above mentioned figures having been arrived at by competent
authority, it is the unanimous opinion of your Committee, that this
Grand Jurisdiction should prepare itself financially by the creation of
a fund to meet the outlay at the proper time of a sum of money which
shall be our just proportionate part of the total necessary to be raised
for the completion of the Memorial and the establishment of an Endow-

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ment Fund the income from which would be of adequate size to meet the
essential needs, administration, maintenance and repair and for clepreciation, obsolesence and replacement. Such proportion to he based upon
the Masonic population of the United States for the year 1932, as heretofore.
This Grand Jurisdiction should also contribute the proportion of all
expenses heretofore incurred and to be incurred up to the time it pays
to the Association its just proportion of the needs of the Memorial.
While your Committee is prepared to and does hereinafter recommend
the immediate adoption of such legislation as may be necessary or thought
desirable to provide the funds required, your Committee is utterly
opposed to releasing any of such funds to the Memorial Association as
now constituted lest they be frittered away without accomplishing the
purposes for which they are to be designed. To that end, we make our
fifth suggested preliminary essential to success, namely:
·
5. We believe that such changes should be made in the set-up of the ·
Association that the area of the United States shall be divided into twentyone districts, as nearly equal in Masonic population as may be practicable, not more than one District to a State, however, and that the
Board of Directors of the Memorial Association be composed of twentyseven directors to be selected by suitable means, one each from the
several districts into which the United States may be divided, and one
each from The General Grand Chapter Royal Arch Masons, The General
Grand Council Royal and Select Masters, The Grand Encampment
Knights Templar, The Supreme Council A. & A.S.R., Northern Jurisdiction, and The Supreme Council A. & A.S.R., Southern Jurisdiction,
each of .said Directors so selected to serve for a term of three years; that
State Chairmen be appointed, one to each Grand Jurisdiction, upon
nomination of the Grand Lodges in the several jurisdictions and not by
Grand Masters or the Memorial Association; that State Chairmen be
given definite duties and responsibilities; and, finally, that no Director
be permitted to serve more that two terms consecutively.
ESTIMATES OF TIME AND COST

The meeting which we attended is described in the Annual Report as
"The 37th Annual Meeting." This report indicates that at the close of
that meeting there had been raised from the inception of the project to
and including February 22, 1947, the total silln of $5,088,681.34, or an
average of $137,532 each year. This average is based in part of course
on the early years when enthusiasm ran high. Some years will show less
than half the average. The donations to the Building Fund at the recent
annual meeting amounted to $120,169, including two donations from
non-Masonic organizations. However, we will assume that $120,000 is an
average sum that may be expected to be raised in the immediate future
under present methods of administration. How long, then, may we
expect it will he before the Memorial is completed and adequately
endowed, if its business continues to be conducted as in the past, and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

139

what will be the total annual carrying charges which it will be necessary
to add to any estimates of the cost of completion ?
To answer the question will involve considerable speculation as to
the ultimate cost for the reason that the future costs of labor and material
and the time when the association will be financially able to complete the
work are all matters of conjecture. So far as the costs are concerned, the
best figure that we were able to obtain was the architect's estimate of
cost of completion of building and grounds based upon 1940 costs. This
figure was $1,074,095. Since that time we all know there has been a great
increase in the cost of labor and materials. The architect estimates this
increase to be 30 percent. The gist of the information that your Committee has obtained through inquiries among contractors, material men and
statistical reports ranges from 50 percent to 100 percent higher than in
1940.
We believe the top has been reached and that somewhat lower prices
may be looked forward to ere the association will be ready to complete
the structure. With this view of the situation in mind, we believe we
will be safe in adopting 60 percent over the 1940 figures as a conservative
figure. On such a basis, the present and near future cost of completion,
according to the existent plans, would be $1, 718,552. For no apparent
justifiable reason there has always been an attempt to underestimate
costs, and this may as well apply to the recent estimate of the architect
as to other items. Including the contributions received at the annual
meeting of 1947, there is on hand available for construction purposes,
the sum of $527,153.33, which leaves $1,191,398.67 yet to be raised
before funds will he available for completion of the construction work ·
of the Memorial and grounds.
.
We should here point out that when we speak of time of completion
herein, we are contemplating only the financing. It may be that the
actual construction work could be delayed even beyond the period req~ired for financing with large resultant savings. As to that, only time
will tell.
It should be pointed out also that the figure quoted above, of $1,191,398.67, is merely the amount needed to complete the building and the
grounds and that to this figure must be added the proposed Endowment
Fund of $4,000,000 of which there is now on hand $181,161.89; leaving
$3,818,838.11 yet to he raised; to these also must he added the annual
cost of maintenance and administration.
It may be noted fµrther that it appears from the report of the pro·
ceedings of the Association for the year 1946, that the Supreme Council
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite for the Southern Jurisdiction
of the U.S.A. donated $100,000 for the furnishing of part of the second
Boor; and that John H. Cowles, Sovereign Grand Commander of that
body, personally donated $5,000 for the completion of the ninth floor.
· At the annual meeting just closed, it was reported that The Mystic
Order of the Veiled Prophets of the Enchanted Realm had appropriated

COMMENTS ON MEMORIAL AFFAIRS

The foregoing discussion of cost and time of completion of financing
is based upon present, and recent past interest in the project shown by
the Grand Jurisdictions of the United States, the present plan of organization and the present plans of promotion of the project and its financing. All this can be altered; new interest created, the donations greatly
augmented and the time of completion and endowment greatly shortened
if this, and other Grand Jurisdictions, now inactive, are awakened to the
situation and its needs.
We believe that the lack of interest in California for many years past
is due wholly to lack of information and opportunity to participate in the
affairs of the Association. It is true that for a short period in the past,
one of our most able and beloved Past Grand Masters has been a mem·
her of the Board of Directors of the Association. That, however, means
little so far as greatly affecting the conduct of its affairs. The influence of
one or two such men may be good, but may be completely ineffective. ·
What we need is a whole new Board of men of similar caliber.
A committee report made at the instance of the Board of Directors of
the Association in 1945, recommended certain changes in the operation,
plans for completion of building and landscaping, which would have
materially reduced the ultimate cost of the project, and increased interest
in and speeded up the financing. This report had much to commend it.
The report, as might have been expected, was not adopted.
1£ the recommendations hereinafter made should be adopted by Grand
Lodge, California may expect to add to the annual donations, either as
direct gifts or as reserved funds available when conditions warrant placing them at the disposal of the Association, the sum of $40,000 annually. 1£ the action of this Grand Lodge should induce other Grand Lodges
to take similar action, possibly this sum might be doubled. If such should
be the case, money for the completion of the Memorial might even be
available within a period of five years and the endowment within a short
period thereafter, provided, of course, that the Board of Directors show
the proper spirit of cooperation. ·
All through its study of the Memorial, the Committee has been caused
to stop and ponder from time to time if there were a reason for the wholly
inadequate estimates promulgated by the Association, and why the
Masons of the country have not been better informed of the affairs of the
Association. It has occurred to us that possibly this lack of information
and misinformation may be the cause of their want of interest in this
. very fine and commendable undertaking.
It is noticeable that many jurisdictions, as California, for example,
have not shown proper interest. It is the belief of this Committee that a

Report of Special Committee on
Centennial Arrangements
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The special committee on the Centennial Arrangements appointed by
the Grand Master begs leave to report as follows:
In 1950 the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of California will
have completed the first hundred years as a star in the cluster of the
American Grand Lodges. It has had a long, interesting, active, honorable,
successful and truly Masonic career. It's history is contemporaneous
with that of the great State of California, which is holding an elaborate
centennial celebration in 1950. The Grand Lodge was organized by three
Lodges in the roaring days of the gold discovery in California and
through the years it has matched the developments of the Golden State
and now stands among the foremost Grand Lodges of America, in membership and in Masonic achievement.
It is not only appropriate, but highly desirable, that the occasion be
celebrated in a memorable and splendid manner and that all Grand
Lodges with which we are in amity be invited as our guests to participate
in our fraternal hospitality and to join in our jubilee.
The State of California and the California Grand Lodge are not accustomed to half measures and if a centenary celebration is held we must
go all out to make it commensurate with the dignity, character and
reputation of Grand Lodge. Your Committee therefore recommends:
( 1) That the Centennial Celebration be held in San Francisco.
(2) That the Centennial Celebration be held in 1950 contemporaneously with the one hundred first Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California.
(3) That the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee on
Centennial Arrangements.
( 4) That a per capita tax be levied on the constituent Lodges of
25 cents per member for the next three years to provide for the expenses
of the Centennial Celebration of Grand Lodge, which funds shall be carried in a special fund and any part thereof not required for the purpose
for which the same was levied to be returned pro rata to the Lodges pay-·
ing the same.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In accordance with a resolution adopted at the 1946 communication of
Grand Lodge the Most Worshipful Grand Master appointed the undersigned committee for the purpose of studying and recommending .a Retirement Plan for the employees of the Grand Lodge of California and
the Masonic Homes of California.
In making its recommendation for the appointment of this committee
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes stated that in the opinion
of the members of that Committee "A careful study and a definite plan
of retirement should be before Grand Lodge for its consideration."
Therefore your Committee has had in mind the preparation of a defi·
nite plan and not the fixing of a policy which may or may not protect
employees in the future. We know that this communication of the Grand
Lodge cannot bind a future communication but we are mindful of the fact
that no arrangement or plan can be considered as definite unless the
employee is given assurance that so far as is possible it will be adhered to
and a moral if not legal responsibility placed on future Grand Lodge
communications.
,
Therefore under this restriction your committee has not considered any
informal plan such as fixing retirement benefits according to· his needs
whenever it is considered that retirement is desirable for a particular
employee which is what has been done in the past both on the part of
Grand Lodge and also the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes.
Generally speaking definite pension plans fall into two categories:
a self insured plan, and a plan under which an insurance company is
employed and payments made to that company.
Under a self insured plan it is necessary to employ an actuary and an
attorney and enter into a contract with a trust company and place the
retirement funds with it beyond the control of the employer. While there
is much merit in this plan your committee is in favor of an insurance
plan. While it might cost more in the beginning its operation will relieve
Grand Lodge employees of much responsibility that they would have
under a self insured plan.
Your committee has been in consultation with Brother Ralph L. Low,
who is an authority on pension plans, and has requested him to formulate
a plan to be underwritten by an insurance company, with a bank as
trustee, setting up a Retirement Plan for eligible employees of the Grand
Lodge of California and the Masonic Homes of California. The proposed
plan as prepared by Brother Low, attached hereto and made a part of
this report, includes estimated costs which we believe to be substantially
correct, and is submitted to the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California for its consideration.
In connection with this report your committee makes the following
recommendations:

(10) The plan relieves the employee of fear for his future, and thus

C. SUMMARY OF THE ADVANTAGES TO THE EMPLOYEE
(1) An old-age retirement income is assured the employee.
(2) He obtains what amounts to an increase in salary.
(3) This indirect salary increase does not increase his income tax
liability.
( 4) The plan usually provides protection for his family as well.
(5) The plan provides the employee with a fund that indirectly constitutes a private unemployment reserve fund.
( 6) The plan provides a similar indirect disability reserve fund, and
may provide outright disability benefits.
.
(7) The plan relieves the employee of worry over his old-age problems
and assists him in their solution.
D. ESSENTIALS OF A SENSIBLE PENSION PLAN.
1. The plan must he actuarially sound. The operation of an unsound
program is frequently worse than none at all, because it raises false
hopes, destroys confidence, and fails to solve the problem. Moreover, it
must he actuarially sound in order to qualify for the tax exemptions.
2. It must be practical. If work is such that employees are unfit after
55 or 60, it would he absurd to designate 70 as the normal retirement
age. Contributions from the employees should he well within their ability
to pay. In short, the plan should be workable, practical, and simple
enough to he understood and appreciated.
3. It must he flexible. Tremendous economic and social changes have
occurred during the past ten years, and it is reasonable to assume that
the changes may he as great during the next decade. It is therefore of
ubnost importance to have a plan that can he kept abreast of the times.
4. It must he attractive to the employee. This requires a plan that is
fair and equitable to all, providing benefits of sufficient amount to assure
a comfortable retirement income and a proper share of the fund in the
event of termination of service after a reasonable length of time.
5. It must ,be profitable to both employer and employees. This point
is of major importance because you cannot expect the employees to become enthusiastic about a plan that could perhaps he duplicated through
their own efforts, nor can you expect the employer to become interested
unless he can realize an immediate return in improved efficiency and
increased good will that has a greater cash value than the amount of
money invested.
E. The pension trust using individual insurance, endowment or annuity contracts for each employee is ideal for smaller groups. It is relatively simple, quite flexible, and provides a very high degree of safety
and guaranteed values for each employee.

A BRIEF FOR PENSIONS
A. OLD-AGE SECURITY has become a prime political, economic and
social problem; and with it, adequate provision for the retirement of
aged and incapacitated employees has become a definite modern business
problem. Such provision for employee retirement grows more important
every day as a result of our high-speed, mechanized production system
and its trend toward the individual's early withdrawal from active industrial life. The growing interest in employee retirement may be traced
to several sources.
FIRST, industry has come to accept the validity of the doctrine that
depreciated man-power needs eventual replacement just as much as does
depreciated plant equipment.
SECOND, interest in the problem of employee retirement may also be
traced to the recent political emphasis upon social objectives generally,
and old-age security particularly.
THIRD, the idea of employee retirement comes at least in part from a
growing social consciousness on the part of business generally.
B. SUMMARY OF THE ADVANTAGES TO THE EMPLOYER IN A SOUND PEN·
SION PROGRAM.
(1) The plan stabilizes employment and reduces turnover in personnel.
(2) The plan increases the morale, good will and loyalty of the
employees.
(3) The plan builds good will among members of the employee's
family.
( 4) It enables the business to retire its employees at a given age, and
thus avoids the carrying of "dead wood"-inactive or semi-active manpower.
(5) The plan provides an incentive for the employee to apply himself
more diligently to his work.
( 6) The plan enables the employer to maintain a higher level of plant
efficiency.
(7) The plan provides tangible rewards ~or long periods of service
with the company.
.
(8) The plan enables the employer to obtain a better class of worker.
(9) The plan stimulates thrift among the employees.

A sound, workable plan is set forth on the following pages, giving

.·

Death Benefits:
Two types of annuity contracts will he issued to eligible members of
the Plan. The death benefits will differ as follows:
1. Insurable members will he covered under a contract providing a
death benefit of $1,000 for each $10.00 of monthly income at retirement.
2. Uninsurable members will he covered under a regular retirement
annuity contract which provides for a death benefit equal to the total
deposits made, or the cash value, whichever is the greater.
Each employee, through the Trustee, shall have the right at all times
to change the beneficiary designation under his policy. The proceeds of
his policy after his death shall not he subject to any claims of the trustee
or the employer, and all proceeds shall he paid to his beneficiary or
family by the insurance company in the manner he has directed.
All income arrangements payable at retirement are based on a continuation of the income for the lifetime of the employee. 1£, however, his
death occurs within 10 years of the date of his retirement, then the income will he continued to his beneficiary for the remaining portion of
the 10 year period. In other words, he has 120 months certain guarantee
of the income in the event of his death.

FORMULATION OF THE PLAN

Eligibility:
(a) All present employees, who have completed two or more years of
continuous service and are not over age 571h, shall he eligible. ·
(h) New employees and those not now eligible, shall he eligible after
two years of continuous service, provided they are not over age 57;.'2
when first eligible.

years of service at or prior to age 571/2, shall he provided for under an
infor~al plan. See subsequent page entitled "Older Employees."
Retirement Age:
The normal retirement age for all participants under the plan shall
he age 65. .
Retirement Benefits:
(a) Retirement benefits shall he calculated at 2% of present salary
(including hoard and room) for each year of past and future service, less
estimated basic Social Security benefits, if any.
(h) Maximum benefit, 50% of salary. (Including Social Security.)
( c) Minimum benefit, $25.00 per month.

All contracts provide for the payment of dividends at the end of each
year, beginning with the first policy year. All dividends will he used to
reduce future premiums.

Employees shall contribute 2% of compensation (including hoard and
room) and the employer shall pay the balance of cost necessary to provide all benefits under the plan.

Earlier Retirement:
With consent of the employer, earlier retirement may he granted, hut
not earlier than age 55. Retirement benefits will he on a reduced basis,
actuarily computed.

Salary increases or decreases shall he recognized under the Plan. No

retirement age.

income policies will he h~ld by the trustee.

GENERAL

The plan which is being presented is provided for under Section
165(a) and 23(p) of the Revenue Act of 1942 as amended, under the
title of "Pension Trusts."
The plan will be operated under the terms of an agreement between
the Employer and a corporate trustee. The Employer will appoint a
Pension Committee or Pension Manager, who will represent the Employer in its dealings with the Trustee.
The agreement may be modified, changed, or terminated at any time at
the will of the Grand Lodge or the Board of Trustees. In the event of the
termination of the plan, all funds in the trust must be turned over to the
member employees in the respective amounts to which they are entitled.
Such funds may take the form of cash or paid-up endowments. No part
of the trust funds shall ever revert to the Employer.

SUMMARY

The Plan as arranged when combined with the program for "Older
Employees," provides an equitable and proportionate pension for all
employees of the Grand Lodge and Masonic Homes who were not over
age SS when employed, and who would have completed at least 10 years
of service by retirement age, (Age 6S).
Employees who complete 2S or more years of service receive SO percent
of their average salaries (including the estimated salary equivalent for

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

157

board and room). Employees who complete more than 10 years but less
than 2S years receive proportionate retirement benefits. A few Grand
Lodge employees are covered under Old Age Social Security, which benefits are included in determining benefits payable under the plan. None
of the employees of Masonic Homes are currently covered under Social
Security.
The plan, if adopted, will assist materially in attracting and holding
a better class of employees in the future. This will reduce labor turnover,
which is now quite high.
In final analysis, the plan provides for employees when they grow
old, protects their families if they die, and also gives them intermediate
benefits.
Referred to Committee on Finance.
Report of Special Committee on
Masonic Magazines
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of Grand Lodge:
Your Committee to whom was referred the matter of Masonic Maga·
zines in general and also the publication of a Grand Lodge Magazine
beg leave to report:
MASONIC MAGAZINES

Every Grand Master for the past ten years at least seems to have had
to give consideration to the un-Masonic and unethical practices of private
publishers of so-called Masonic Magazines.
There seems to he little to complain of from the editorial point-of-view
although there have been times when even this portion of the publication
was subject to criticism.
However, the situation relative to the commercial features of the magazines, the solicitation of advertising and the misrepresentations made in
connection therewith are matters which call for serious condemnation
of many of such enterprises. There are exceptions which should he made
when listing these shortcomings hut the statement applies to more of
them than to those to which it is not applicable.
Instances of the management, or solicitors, falsely representing their
magazine to he an official Masonic publication, of collecting money for
advertising not justly due them, and of receiving money for advertising
in "special editions" not published as promised and failing to repay the
deposit made by the would-he advertiser, are only a few of the matters
brought to the attention of the Grand Master during his term of office.
In the opinion of your Committee these actions are reprehensible and
unworthy of any Mason or enterprise claiming connection with or using
the name of Masonry. At first glance the thought occurs, why does
Grand Lodge permit them to continue to publish?
There are several answers to this question. In the first place, Grand
Lodge has for many years permitted, and perhaps in some instances
encouraged, the publication, until, in a sense, such a business in the

158

159

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

hands of an individual proprietor has become a vested right of which
he cannot be deprived. Then again, Grand Lodge has on all occasions
denied any connection, supervisory or otherwise, with these enterprises
and can hardly at this late date undertake the responsibility that would
flow from an attempt to now supervise them. Again it might be said that
the proprietors, editors and managers are, as Masons, subject to the
control of the Grand Master and of Grand Lodge, but, the answer to that
is that, in many instances, we would say in the majority of instances of
such un-Masonic conduct, that the perpetrators are not members of the
Craft and therefore not amenable to its rules, regulations, edicts and
decrees.
There remains one and only one way your Committee sees in which
this deplorable situation is open to attack and that way is provided by
Section 34, sub. 13th of the Constitution, wherein the Grand Master is
empowered to forbid traffic with, or the aiding or supporting any business representing itself to be Masonic or using any name or words implying a connection with Masonry which shall indulge in un-Masonic or
unethical conduct.
By this provision every member of the Craft in California and every
officer of a Lodge could be forbidden to give any advertising or subscrip·
tion to such an interdicted magazine or to furnish it with Masonic news
or trestle boards, under penalty of expulsion for un-Masonic conduct if
the order were disregarded. Such action would be drastic and any Grand
Master might well hesitate to invoke the power granted him by its terms,
but the authority is there for use whenever the Grand Master sees fit
to use it.
We feel this provision of our Ordinances is sufficiently clear and
explicit and broad enough in its application, to effect the purpose ·without
further legislation, and we so recommend.

membership. Evidently neither Masonic instruction nor the activities of
the Craft interest the others.
·
Another jurisdiction puts out a magazine of sixteen pages, without
advertising. Its contents are well edited, of general interest and worthwhile. It also is free for the asking. Here, too, 15 percent of the mem·
bership have asked to be put on the mailing list.
Another jurisdiction puts out a magazine of thirty-five pages. The
subscription price is one dollar per annum. The Grand Secretary reports
that 6 percent of the members are subscribers.
Another jurisdiction puts out a fine magazine of twenty pages with
practically no advertising at a subscription price of one dollar per annum.
Less than 5 percent of the membership are on the mailing list.
One Grand Secretary reported that their Grand Lodge issued a 16·page
monthly. We were furnished copies. It was above the average in contents
and editing. It was mailed to all members on the roll and is supported
by a small per capita tax. This tax fails to meet the expense by about
$2,000 a month. The query arises how long a small jurisdiction can
continue to suffer such a drain upon its resources.
If our Grand Lodge should decide an official magazine should be
undertaken by this jurisdiction, then, it must also decide whether it shall
be published at the expense of Grand Lodge by appropriation from its
general fund, by a per capita tax or by paid subscription.
Your Chairman spent a half day at the office of the Board of General
Activities of the Grand Lodge of New York which publishes the two
magazines issued in that jurisdiction. One of these, "The Masonic Out·
look," is issued upon subscription of one dollar a year and is chiefly for
Lodge officers and Masonic students. The other, "The Family Magazine,"
is a bi-monthly of about fourteen pages and cover which goes out to all
members free of charge. The first carries a small amount of strictly
Masonic advertising. The latter, as yet, carries no advertising but it is
expected to do so later. The membership in New York is about 275,000.
We are informed that there are about 18,000 paid subscriptions to the
"Outlook," and we were informed that if the subscriptions could be built
up to 25,000 it would carry itself financially. The cost of publishing the
"Family Magazine" and mailing to members is is about $75,000 per
annum for six issues.
In order that we might have something definite to offer Grand Lodge
in the way of estimated expense, if the project of publishing a magazine
is adopted, we obtained from publishing firms estimates on the cost of
publishing a magazine 9 x 12 inches, 20 pages and cover, to be issued
monthly or bi-monthly in quantities of around 175,000, the lowest. of
these is as follows:

A GRAND LODGE MAGAZINE

Your Committee has explored the field of official Grand Lodge magazines of the United States and Canada and finds that fourteen Grand
Jurisdictions do publish something more than a mere bulletin. A number
of them put out magazines of a worth and character not equalled by any
privately published in California. Some of them carry advertising and
some do not. These magazines are usually about 8¥2 x 11% and carry
from 8 to 48 pages.
There is also a variety of plans for defraying the expense. Some are
financed by Grand Lodge appropriation from general funds. Some
are financed by a per capita levy and some by voluntary subscription
with deficits covered by Grand Lodge appropriation.
One of the jurisdictions publishes a very worthwhile paper of approx·
imately fifty pages, without adverti~ing. It contains matter of a general
instructive nature in part, and in part news of lodges and officials of local
interest. .This magazine may be had at no expense by merely asking to

If ten pages of hand-set advertising is included in make up,
an additional................................................................,............ $80
The cost of addressing and mailing would be additional to
the above figures.
There is also to be considered the cost of setting up and maintaining
the office force and equipment necessary to carry on this new enterprise.
Addresses of all members on the roll must first be obtained from the
Secretaries of Lodges. This will involve the complete time of at least
one clerk, first, in the preparatl.on of the master list from which addresso·
graph plates can be made, and then, in maintaining it up to date. The
salary for this clerk would probably be not less than $1,800 per year.
The making up of 175,000 addressograph plates would be the next
step. These plates must be kept up to date by changes in addresses when
magazines for lack of delivery are returned by the Post Office Depart·
ment. Judging by the experience of others the expense connected with
the returns from the Post Office and cost of changing plates would probably run around $3,000 per year.
We have assumed that the thought back of the appointment of this
Committee was that it would be the wish of Grand Lodge if such a magaz~e were published that it would go out to all members in the jurisdic·
hon free of cost and without advertising. In that event an estimate of

To this should be added the cost of the initial set-up of approximately

item alone is $26,250.
If on the other hand, it is planned to charge an annual subscription,
your Committee again judging from the experience of others believes
that it would not be safe to estimates that more than 15 percent of the
membership would become subscribers which would make a total subscription list of about 26,000 on the present membership in this juris·
diction. With an annual subscription price of $1.25, judging from the
experience of the jurisdiction of New York, the enterprise, after the
initial expense of setting up the necessary machine for operation, could
be expected to pay its own way without assistance from Grand Lodge.
· This would be for a 20-page and cover magazine without advertising.
We are informed that advertising should bring about $2.50 per
thousand subscribers per page issue. We are of the opinion that advertising should not be solicited, but that advertising of suitable character
when offered should be accepted as a means of reducing expense of
publication.

If it should be found after a period of operation that the annual subacription price of $1.25 produced greater income than necessary to meet
the expense, the subscription price could be reduced but your Committee
is of the opinion that it should in no event be made greater than $1.25
per annum.
CONCLUSION

Your Committee after careful consideration of the problems involved
in the institution of the project of publication of an official magazine
confess that they feel they are unable to make definite recommendations ·
except as to two features of the proposed program.
1. We are definitely and unanimously opposed to the publication of
any magazine unless it is to be a worth-while, well-edited and high-class
publication.
2. We are likewii;1e unanimously opposed to a free distribution of
such a paper to all members in the jurisdiction because of the heavy
expense to Grand Lodge, a large part of which would be a waste.
We are of the opinion, however, that much good could result from such
a publication if properly edited and managed. We are also of the opinion
that the question of whether or not such an effort is to be made should be
decided by the Masons themselves by actual subscriptions. We therefore
recommend that the whole matter go over to the next Annual Communication; that the incoming Grand Master appoint a Committee of three
consisting of brethren qualified by experience and acquaintance with the
publishing business to survey the field and ascertain whether there be
available men able and willing to assume the burden of editing and
managing such a business; whether subscribers to the number of at least
25,000 can be secured for such a paper; what amount of money should
be appropriated by Grand Lodge as a working fund; and generally to
present to Grand Lodge a prospectus of available men and materials
and probable number of subscribers together with their recommendations
thereon.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM B. OGDEN, Chairman,
KENT 0. S EYMOUR,

Report of Committee on De Molay Activities
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Probably the most serious problem confronting law enforcement and
social agencies today is that of juvenile delinquency and what to do
about it. Statistics show that a very large proportion of commitments
to correctional institutions consists of persons under 23 years of age.
The question is: What can we, as members of the Masonic fraternity,
· do about it? The consensus of opinion is that education along proper

163

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

lines during the £ormulative period of the youth will do more to prevent,
or at least improve, present conditions than any other known measures.
As a part of such education it would seem that we, as individual Masons,
could profitably give vigorous and enthusiastic support to such groups
as De Molay, Boy Scout and other similar organizations.
That this training brings results is indicated by the fact that, on good
authority, seldom if ever does a youth, who either has been or is a member of De Molay, become involved with law enforcement agencies. De
Molay teaches boys during an impressionable period, the difference
between right and wrong and guides their thoughts into proper channels.
When a young petitioner kneels at the Altar of a De Molay Chapter and
is pledged to the seven cardinal virtues of Filial Love, Reverence, Courtesy, Comradeship, Fidelity, Cleanliness, and Patriotism the impression
left on his mind will largely control his future conduct, and do not
forget, Brethren, that on those shoulders rests the future of our beloved
country.
Lack of previous experience made it necessary that your committee
exercise caution and proceed in such a manner as to preclude making
commitments not in keeping with the directives contained in the resolution adopted at our last Communication. In the interest of closer contact
and economy of operation, and with the permission of the Grand Master,
Brother Ray Kimbell of San Francisco was asked to serve as vice·
chairman for the North and he, as well as all of the committee members,
did a grand job considering the fact that they had to start from scratch.
There were contacted a considerable number of Lodges, both directly
and through various Inspectors, seeking to create among the membership
an active interest in De Molay. In a number of instances arrangements
were made with a De Molay Chapter to exemplify one of the degrees at
a stated meeting of the Lodge, and with very gratifying results. Many
Chapters were visited with a view to ascertaining whether or not they
were in need of advisory help. This type of visitation will be made much
easier in the future by virtue of a bulletin which will be sent to the
·various Chapters from the office of the Active Member of the Grand
Council advising them of the existence of the committee and suggesting
their active co-operation.
Out of our experience to date, the following recommendations are
made:
That a De Molay Activities Committee be continu~d as a special committee of the Grand Lodge.
That a communication from the Grand Master be sent to the Master of
each Lodge in the jurisdiction and to the Inspectors of each Masonic
district requesting their active and sympathetic co-operation with the
work of the committee.
That, to give the advantage of new ideas, two members be replaced
each year by new appointments.

That an appropriation in the sum of five hundred dollars be made to
cover the necessary expenses of the committee, for the ensuing year.
To set a boy's uncertain feet upon the path of character,
Guide eager young hands to usefrilness,
Direct and steady the arm of inexperience, and
Teach young manhood which way lies true success.
Here is a task worthy of the best and busiest of us.

Report of the Committee on Masonic History Publication
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History Publication reports as follows:
Work of the Committee during the past year has been purely a work
of investigation and its recommendations will be on the basis of our
investigation.
We find that a great amount of work has been done by the History
Committee over a period of a great many years. Their files are replete
with individual Lodge histories, stories and incidents of famous Masonic
characters and happenings, and a wealth of material is available for the
publication of a history of One Hundred Years of Masonry in California.
Many individual lodges have published histories of their own Lodge
and these are all in the files. We find literally hundreds of human interest
stories, which could be woven into a history that would have great interest
£or the rank and file of California Masons.
The files are in excellent shape and each individual lodge has a section
giving outstanding events of that particular lodge, also showing the
survey made a number of years ago by the History Committee.
We do find a lack of up-to-date information from many of the lodges,
and our recommendation on this will appear later in this report.
Most Worshipful Brother Leon Whitsell, Past Grand Master, chairman
of the History Committee for many years, has done a notable job in
collecting this information and seeing tliat all is in proper order.
We find that no manuscript has been written, covering the material
which is available and before your Masonic Publication Committee can
proceed any further, it will be necessary for such a manuscript to be

166

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Today, as you have already heard, our membership is the greatest it
has ever been. Our finances are better than ever and best of all our
enthusiasm and desire for progress is unbounded.
In another two years our Grand Lodge will be one hundred years old and
it is fitting and proper that this History of One Hundred Years of California Masonry be published for our Centennial Celebration at that time.
With the above thought in mind we respectfully urge and submit the
following Resolutions and move their adoption:
1. In order to bring down to date the history of each individual Lodge,
that the incoming Grand Master require that every Lodge individually
be required to appoint a history committee in their individual Lodge
and give a written brief history of that Lodge to Grand Lodge, within
ninety days from date of receipt of such request from the Most Worship·
ful Grand Master.
a. That the incoming Grand Master also ask all the living Past Grand
Masters to give a summary of their year as Grand Master, so that same
can be a matter of record.
2. We recommmend that a manuscript be prepared by a competent
man who understands the compilation of facts, figures, and human in·
terest stories. Because of the time that would be required to do this work,
we believe that such a man should be on a salary basis and devote his
entire time to this work. This would entail, necessarily, stenographic ·
services, ample equipment, office space, supplies, and so forth.
3. That Most Worshipful Brother Leon Whitsell have supervision
of the writing and preparation of the manuscript of the History of
Masonry in California and to complete such manuscript as efficiently
and expeditiously as possibly with the help and aid of the Publication
Committee.
.
4. That the Publication of History Committee be continued till this
work is completed and off the press.
5. That Grand Lodge appropriate the sum of $10,737.50 to be used
to defray the necessary expense incident to writing and preparing this
manuscript for publication. It is estimated the several items of expense
will be along the following lines: Man to write manuscript, $2,800;
stenographic expense, $1,600; rent of space $l,800; the balance to be
used for rental of equipment, supplies, traveling expense, and so forth .
These figures of course are approximate. Monthly expense account should
be submitted to the Grand Secretary for payment and could be paid by
him upon presentation of same with the approval of the Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
W. I. KOHNKE, Chairman,
JOHN T. BOND,
A. F. HEUER,

Report of Trustees of Masonic Club House at Berkeley
To the Most Worthy Grand Lodge of California:
As president of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club at Berkeley,
it is again my privilege to report to you briefly on the affairs and operations of that institution.
The year just past has been crowded with activity, featured by large
attendances. The facilities, which were designed for the activities of
250 to 300 members, have been strained to provide for the 700 to 1,000
members which lately have been in attendance. As a result of this extra
use repairs and alterations in the physical plant, now nearly twenty-five
years old, have been extensive. In this era of high costs they have been
expensive. Notwithstanding the liberal treatment which we received at
your hands last year, our operations resulted in a deficit of $1,714.51.
Our reserve, therefore, is impaired to that extent.
Repairs referred to, brieflly stated, were: Replacement of oil furnace
by a gas furnace; alterations to doors and exits to meet safety requirements properly insisted upon the fire chief of the city of Berkeley; flame
proofing of upholstery, etc.; new water heater; and a variety of items,
ranging from repairs to exterior cornices to alterations to the main entrance door and steps. These aggregate $5,499.
We are under a debt of gratitude to Brothers Dragon, Schmidt and
Hardman, architects, all members of One Thousand Oaks Lodge, who
have generously given of their time and professional services in the
preparation of plans and specifications and supervising the making of
these alterations. They have declined all compensation therefor.
Our proposed budget for 1947-1948 is rather staggering, amounting
as it does to $21,286.43. Of this $7,000 represents repairs and replace·
ments, including painting, estimated at $4,000; replacement of the above
deficit of $1,714.51; roof work, estimated at $220, which must be done
at once. A substantial amount of work on furnishings is also most urgent.
There is no use in waiting further for a decline in costs, as that prospect
appears dim.
The activities /of the students during the past year have been very
extensive and elaborate .. They have presented more than the usual number of problems for the trustees and more than the usual daily run of
perplexities to our excellent hostess, Mrs. Morton. At my request she
has again given us a brief report. It reads:
"Again i_t is my privilege to report to you the special events, activities,
and daily use by the members of the Masonic Club House at Berkeley.
"Our expectations were more than realized. The attendance at the
special events of the fall term approximated 10,000; daily use 350. The
spring term total for special events approximated 9,500; daily use 300.
A grand total of 60,000 enjoyed the use of the Club House during the fall
and spring terms.
"From these figures you should be able to appreciate the inestimable
value to the students of this 'Club home' on campus.

"The members wish me to express to Masonry their heartfelt gratitude."
Some change in the name is being made to meet the new statute pre·

I believe the Institution continues to merit your generous support.
Respectfully submitted,

SPRING SEMESTER

The school year of 1946·1947 found membership in the club reaching new highs
within the ken of all of us. Totals for the Fall Semester were well over 800 and in the
Spring 731, reflecting an almost proportionate drop in enrollment at the University.
The clubhouse and its manifold facilities were used to the fullest throughout this
period. The members, though parts of a very large group, were extremely active and
manifested great interest in the club. The girls who carried on the tradition& and
activities of the club during the war years, the younger fellows who missed the grand
combat, and the returning veterans have been blended all together in this past year,
and now are emerging as a strongly cohesive group with mature attitudes.
As a representative of the group it gives me the greatest pleasure to express the
thanks and appreciation of the members of the Grand Lodge and to Masonry for the
maintenance of a social institution where lifelong friendships may be formed. in
which a nice environment is maintained, and where the member may follow his
bent, be it study, dancing, politics, or just rest from the strain of university life.
On the following pages are a listing of activities of the members of the club for the
school year 1946·1947 with approximate attendance figures fo~ each gathering.
Respectfully and gratefully,
[signed) FRANK D. FARGO,
President U. C. Masonic Club.
Spring Semester 1947.

Report of Committee on Lodge Financing
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing presents herewith its report
giving an account of activities during the past year.
. While the number of applications received and acted on pursuant to
the provisions of Sections 78 and 152 of the Constitution and Ordinances
were less in number than the previous year, yet there has been no decrease
in the actual work of the committee. Many inquiries on the subject of
lodge financing have been directed to your committee. Where con·
venient and practicable these have been answered by direct personal
contact and in other cases by correspondence.
It is the observation of your committee that a number of contemplated
new Temples have, in the discretion of the Lodges, been deferred by
reason of government regulations, mal-distribution of building materials
and record high costs.
Following is a brief history of the applications which have passed
through your committee:
HENRY KNOX LODGE NO. 662--LOS ANGELES

This Lodge presented a form of resolution creating and establishing
a building fund for the purpose of receiving contributions, donations
and endowments. Your committee saw no objection to the purposes set
forth in the resolution and gave its consent.
SAN MARINO LODGE NO. 685--SAN MARINO

San Marino Foundation, Inc., applied for approval of their organiza·
tion, submitting the Articles of Incorporation and By-laws, a financial
statement of the organization and excerpts from the minutes of San
Marino Lodge No. 685. The committee consented to the San Marino
Foundation, Inc., as a vehicle for raising funds and, subject to further
consent, erecting and operating a building for San Marino Lodge. The
consent as to the means for raising funds was limited to the raising of
funds by donation, gift, devise, and bequest. It was stipulated in the
consent that no land be purchased or contract for building entered into

171

or other financing arranged without first submitting such contemplated
action to the committee.
POINT LOMA LODGE NO. 620--SAN DIEGO

During the year 1946 your committee approved an application from
this Lodge to invest $1,600 in a building site in Ocean Beach Park, San
Diego. A subsequent application was received asking consent to the
incorporation of Point Loma Masonic Temple Association, controlled
by the Lodge, and to be used as a vehicle for raising a building fund. To
further the undertaking and permit the Temple Association to take title
to the property in question approval was requested for the investment of
$2,000 from Lodge funds in voting memberships of said Temple Associ·
ation. This approval to nullify that previously given the Lodge to invest
$1,600 in a building site and take title thereto. Your committee gave
consent and approval.
ARCADIA LODGE NO. 547-ARCADIA

This · Lodge requested the committee's approval to the purchase of
68 shares of stock of the Arcadia Masonic Temple Association, Inc., at
$25 a share. The purchase of these shares would give the Lodge twothirds of the entire stock outstanding, all other stock being owned by
the Arcadia Eastern Star. Financial statement accompanying the request
showed sufficient cash funds on hand to make the purchase and the
approval of the committee was given.

NATOMA LODGE NO. ~FOLSOM
In order to preserve for Masonic usage the building in which this
Lodge had been renting and meeting since 1880, nine members of the
Lodge and three members of the Eastern Star purchased the building
for $6,000 when it was put on the market for sale in the early part of
1946. An offer by the purchasers to permit the Lodge to acquire the
property at their cost was referred to this committee.
With the cooperation of Brother Walton E. Holmes of Sacramento
acting for the committee the Masonic Hall Association of Folsom was
incorporated to take title to the property. Approval was given to Folsom
Lodge to invest $3,060 in the Hall Association from some $7,300 cash
and government bonds in their general fund in consideration of the
equity ownership in the corporation going to the Lodge.
Independent appraisal placed a valuation of $7,750 on the property
and engineers report in part stated the building was in good condition
structurally and complied with building code regulations.
The committee, after reviewing estimates of revenue, consented to the
purchase for $6,000 by a payment to each of the twelve present owners
of $250 with a three year note for the balance with interest at 5 per cent,
or a lessor amount in cash and a larger note according to the wishes of
the sellers.
