Inquiries with respect to lodge financing and related subjects were
directed to the committee by Golden State Lodge No. 358, Fairfax Lodge
No. 556, Welcome Lodge No. 255, Sun Garden Lodge No. 530, Menlo
Park Masonic Temple Association, Trona Lodge No. 684, Lindsay Lodge
No. 416, Oxnard Lodge No. 341, Valley Forge Lodge No. 587, El
Segundo Lodge No. 507, San Dimas Lodge No. 428, Redwood Empire
Lodge No. 683, Suisun Lodge No. 55, Kaweah Lodge No. 665, Elmhurst
Lodge No. 610, Military Service Lodge No. 570, Stanislaus Lodge No.
206, Bakersfield Masonic Temple Association, Woodland Lodge No. 156,
Madera Lodge No. 280, Porterville Lodge No. 303, Nicolaus Lodge No.
129, Meridian Lodge No. 667, Brea Masonic Temple Association, Hanford Lodge No. 279, an.d Alexander Douglas Potts, Inspector District
No.103.
In the main these inquiries covered requests for information. Those
that contemplated financing and building had not progressed to a point
where a committee decision was called for, therefore, in responding no
consent or approval was given.
Our contact and association with officers and members of Lodges has
been most pleasant. However, from experience gained in dealing with the
problem of lo.dge financing we feel that it would be beneficial, not only
to the committee, but to i;onstituent Lodges as well, if some clarification
of the provisions of Sections 78 and 152 of the Constitution and Ordi-

Through legislation adopted by this Grand Lodge in 1946, the Committee on Lodge Financing was made a standing committee of five members. When legislation was passed creating the committee in 1942 the
Jurisprudence Committee in its report stated in part:
"We feel that a committee should be large enough so that its membership could be dispersed throughout the state in order that a familiarity
with conditions would rest in some member of the committee withnut
imposing undue traveling upon the part of its members."
Each year since the inception of the committee the number of cases
before it have continued to mount and we feel that the purpose and use
of the committee to Grand Lodge would best be served if the number of
members were increased from five to seven. We, therefore, offer the
following resolution:
Resolved, That Sec. 70 of the Constitution and Ordinances be changed,
to wit:
Strike out "on Lodge Financing" immediately preceding "and on
Necrology" and insert "on Lodge Financing" immediately following "on
Clandestine Masonry."
To clarify Sec. 78, and to further provide for the necessary expense
of the committee, we recommend adoption of the following:
Resolved, That the following changes be made in Sec. 78 of the Constitution and Ordinances, to wit:
Strike from the first line of Sec. 78, sub. (a) the word "five" and
insert "seven" in lieu thereof.

180

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Strike from the second line of Sec. 78, sub. (a) the word "two" and
insert "three" in lieu thereof.
Strike from the first line of Sec. 78, sub. (b) the word "lodge."
Insert " ( 1)" after word "refinancing for" in first line, sub. (b).
Insert "(2)" immediately preceding "the leasing" in second line,
sub. (b).
Insert "(3)" in second line after words "three years," sub. (b).
Insert "contracted for" in eighth line, sub. (b). So that Sec. 78 (b)
will read as follows:
(b) No financing, or refinancing, for (1) the purchase of lands or
buildings, or (2) the leasing for a longer term than three years, or (3)
for the erection, construction, or alteration or any building requiring the
expenditure of more than two thousand five hundred dollars, shall be
entered into by any Lodge, or by any building company, trusteeship,
partnership or corporation representing itself or themselves as Masonic
in character, or operating for the benefit of Masons, Masonry or a Masonic Lodge or Lodges, without first obtaining the written consent of
said Committee; nor shall any such purchase, leasing, erection, construction or alteration be entered into, contracted for, or commenced, whether
or not the same involves the immediate expenditure of Lodge funds, without first obtaining the aforesaid consent.
Add a sub-section (d) to read as follows:
78(d) The members of the Committee shall be reimbursed for their
necessary expenses incurred in the performance of the duties appertaining to their office; said claims, when approved by the Grand Master,
shall be paid as provided in Section 72 hereof.
In 1944 an amended Section 152 was adopted. Legislation was enacted in 1946 deleting the word "trustees" from said section. In rewriting
this section and eliminating the word "trustees," the wording of the old
section prior to 1944 amending, was used. We feel this should be corrected, and in addition some clarification of the law made and we therefore
offer the following .resolution:
Resolved, That Sec. 152 of the Constitution and Ordinances as now
written be repealed and the following be enacted in lieu thereof:
Sec. 152. A Lodge may invest its fonds in securities prescribed as legal
for savings banks by the laws of the State of California or by the laws of
the territory in which the Lodge is located;
Provided that after first obtaining the consent of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Lodge Financing, it may invest its funds as follows:
1. (a) In real estate embracing a building suitable for occupancy in
whole or in part by a Masonic Lodge, or (b) In land upon which it is
proposed to erect such a building, or ( c) In the erection of such a building upon land owned by the Lodge.
2. In memberships or shares, as the case may be, of a corporation
(a) which owns real estate embracing a building suitable for the occupancy in whole or in part by a Masonic Lodge, or (b) which owns land

upon which it is proposed to erect such a building, provided, however,
that the Lodge shall hold a control-interest in any such corporation or
shall by such investment acquire a controlling interest therein.
3. By making a loan evidenced by (a ) a duly executed Promissory
Note amply secured by a first lien against property of a class described
under Paragraph 1 above, or (b) a Promissory Note duly executed by a
corporation in which the Lodge owns a controlling interest.
Provided, however, that prior to making any such investment mentioned in Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 above, there shall first have been submitted to and approved by the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing, such of the following data as circumstances may direct :
(a) An appraisal or other evidence of the value of the land and
building involved.
(b) An appraisal or other evidence of value of the land upon which
the building is to be erected.
( c) Plans and specifications and estimates covering cost of construction for any building.
( d) Plans for financing same;
and provided, further, that under no circumstances shall Life Membership Funds of any Lodge be invested in securities other than those prescribed as legal for savings banks by the laws of the State of California
or by the laws of the territory in which the Lodge is located.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence approve the above suggested
amendment to Sections 70, 78 and 152 of Ordinances and recommend
their adoption by Grand Lodge.

TO THE APPLICANT

Having expressed a desire to become a Freemason, we presume you are
willing to consider thoroughly the step you propose to take. The exact nature
of our Institution being unknown to you, we deem It advisable that you should
be informed on certain points, the knowledge of which may affect your
decision to apply for membership.
Freemasonry Interferes neither with religion or politics, but has for Its
foundation the great principles of the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood
of Man. No Atheist can be a Freemason. Freemasonry strives to teach a man
the duty he owes to God, his neighbor and himself. In Inculcates the practice
of virtue, and makes extensive use of symbolism In Its teachings.
It cannot be too strongly emphasized that Freemasonry ls not to be
entered In the hope of personal gain or advancement. Anyone so actuated
will be bitterly disappointed. The aim of the true Freemason ls to cultivate
a brotherly feeling among men, and help whomsoever he can.
Freemasonry is not a benE>llt society. This fa.ct cannot be too strongly
emphasized. We do not subscribe so much a year to entitle us to draw sick
pay or other provisions for those who survive us. There are other excellent
societies founded for this purpose. No man should enter the ranks of Freemasonry In hope or expectation that he will derive any financial benefit
from It.
Loyalty to one's country Is an essential qualification In Freemasonry, and
only those are acceptable who cheerfully render obedience to every lawful
authority. Disloyalty In any form Is abhorrent to a Freemason, and Is regarded as a serious Masonic offense.
Your admission to the craft will entail certain financial obligations which
you should be able to discharge without detriment to yourself or those
dependent upon you. In addition to the fees payable upon the presentation of
this application, there will be an annual subscription for the support of your
lodge ·and occasionally you may be asked to contribute to the relief work
of the Craft.
Freemasonry · has In all ages Insisted that men should come to Its doors
entirely of thel·r own free will, and not as the result of solicitations, or from
feelings of curiosity, but simply from a favorable opinion of the Institution,
and a desire to be ranked among Its members.

Report of Committee on History
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your conunittee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report:
During the past year your conunittee has continued its research work
and has obtained much valuable information relative to many of the
early members of California lodges.
We have completed our exhaustive studies of the life and activities .of
John W. Geary and also the interesting history of Brother James McCall
Jones, the brilliant and distinguished lawyer and linguist, and the hard-

188

189

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

working delegate to the Constitutional Convention of 1849, who .so ably
assisted in the preparation of that historical document.

picture of Brother Smith in our present exhibit. This picture was taken
with Brother Harry Eugene Stafford.
We have assisted several of our constituent lodges in the research of
their local anniversary history and have answered hundreds of letters
of inquiry pertaining to masonry and members of the craft in the early
days in California.
Members of your committee have responded to a great many requests
to appear before lodges and discuss the different phases of the history
of masonry and early masonic characters in California.
The committee of three appointed by Penryn Lodge to investigate and
report on the occupation!" of the charter members of that lodge, submitted their report on April 10, 1947. After a thorough research they
found that the 17 charter members were operative as well as speculative
masons. They signed the petition for a dispensation on February 27,
1879, and were at that time working for Griffith and Griffith in the quarries near Penryn preparing stone which finally became a part of the
building which has been since used by the lodge. The books of Griffith
and Griffith fully bear out this conclusion. Your History Committee
several years ago, after a thorough investigation, arrived at the same
conclusion and reported that fact to Grand Lodge.
Within the past six months many historic public buildings situated on
the Mother Lode and in other sections of the state have been destroyed
by fire. Valuable records have thus been lost. With these irreparable
losses in mind, permit your committee to again respectfully urge the old
historic lodges to immediately take the proper steps to store old time
records in fire-proof vaults. Should these records be destroyed regrets at
your procrastination will not replace them. Some lodges have constructed
vaults even outside the lodge or temple's structure where it was not practicable or economical to construct the vaults within the lodge building.

We have also concluded our studies of the life and history of David D.
Cohon, who at one time was sheriff of Siskiyou County and finally was
connected with Huntington, Crocker, Stanford and Hopkins, the "Big
Four" of Central Pacific fame. He led a stormy life from the very first
and his financial connection with the Central Pacific group was finally
subject to extensive litigation,
We have also completed the story and history of the establishment of
masonry in the Philippine Islands, under the guidance of Harry Eugene
Stafford, who was chosen the first Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines. You will doubtless recall that in 1901 Brother Stafford
applied to the Grand Lodge of California for a dispensation to establish
the first Lodge in the Philippines composed of Americans. He applied to
the California Grand Lodge instead of to New York which was his
mother Grand Lodge. During his long and interesting career he pl~yed
a leading part in the activities of the fraternity in the Islands and the
story of his spectacular and colorful career reads like a scenario. Brother
Stafford had the distinction during the Spanish-American War of serving as physician and surgeon under General MacArthur's father. By reason of this service there developed a friendship with General MacArthur
himself which has continued even until the present day. Brother Stafford
served under Governors Taft and Woods, both of whom were Governors
of the Philippines. He also served under President Manuel Quezon. He
was captured in his residence at Bagio by the Japanese and was held
prisoner by them until General MacArthur returned to the Philippines.
Doctor and Mrs. Stafford are now living at Santa Cruz, California.
We have been in correspondence with Brother C. F. Chaussee of Hono·
lulu who is preparing the history of masonry in the Hawaiian Islands.
We were pleased to furnish him with all the informatio~ in the files with
respect to masonry and masons in that part of our California jurisdiction.
Brother John W. Smith is California's oldest mason. He is now a member of Santa Cruz Lodge No. 38, and resides in that city. Next Christmas
he will be 105 years old. He may be the oldest living mason in the United
States. He is in excellent health at present, although he has been ill
several times during the past year. His eyesight is remarkable and he
can read a newspaper without glasses. He is, however, quite deaf. He was
born in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia on December 25, 1842. As
a youth of 22 he enlisted in the Union Army at Circleville, Ohio, in 1864
and saw action in Tennessee and Georgia. He was a railroad engineer for
fifty-one years. He was raised in 1880 in Winnemucca, Nevada, and affiliated with Santa Cruz Lodge No. 38, on December 5, 1924. We have a good

Severaf years have passed since your committee has received historic
information from many of the lodges; therefore we respectfully urge all
lodges to have s'ome competent and willing brother forward to the committee within the next ninety days, any new historic material relative to
the lodge or its members, not already in the files of said committee. We
thus desire to have in our files down to date facts.
Especially are we anxious to receive the stories of the part which any
member of your lodge played in World War No. 2. Surely there is a
wealth of human interest in the activities of your members while in the
armed forces on the far-flung battle fronts.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
1. That the committee on Masonic History be continued during the
ensuing year.

At the last session of the Grand Lodge the committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommended:
"That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to investigate
the most feasible and advisable method of financing the rebuilding of the
Masonic Temple at Columbia, and the most economical method of maintaining same." This recommendation was approved by Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master accordingly appointed your humble servant on said

We found that the lot in question was owned by the Thomas P. Conlon
estate but the title is now vested in the California Park Commission.
Your committee now has on file a letter from Joseph R. Knowland,
chairman of the Park Commission, reading in part as follows:
"A satisfactory lease will be m11de by the State to whatever official
body may desire to enter into such a lease representing the masonic
fraternity of California."
We carried on an extensive search throughout the state by letter and
the radio, with the assistance of J. E. Carpenter of the State Chamber of
Commerce, to procure if possible an authentic picture of the temple as
it was in the "fifties." We were unable to find a satisfactory picture. We
did find the original architectural drawing. We were also able to secure
an authentic description of the building and its exterior and interior
appearance from old residents of Columbia who vividly remember it.
Brother William Mooser, one of California's leading architects, kindly
offered to prepare the necessary blue prints, plans and specifications, free
of charge, which he has done, and I desire to express to Brother Mooser
the grateful thanks of the committee for this voluntary service.
The old temple was a two story brick structure 50 ,feet by 30 feet
with standard sized doors and windows of that period and in all particulars complied with masonic law.
As we worked on this project we found it necessary to secure the help
and assistance of local members of the craft and upon our request,
Brother Donald M. Stewart, Master of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, has ap·
pointed a committee from that lodge, consisting of the following: Bros.
Louis Bach, Secretary of No. 8, Bert C. Bullock and H. E. Meyer.
We are pleased to report, that through the efforts of Louis Bach of that
committee, we have located the original bricks of which the temple was
constructed.
So in truth and in fact, we may be able to say that it will be a rebuilding of the temple with some of the original material. Very few buildings
have, after a lapse of fifty-six years, been reconstructed out of any of the
parts of the original.

historical shrine. When the old buildings now standing are fully restored

Report of Special Committee on
Masonic Temple at Columbia
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on rebuilding the Masonic Temple at Columbia begs
to submit the following report and recommendations:
The old mining town of Columbia in Tuolumne County is now a state
park under the jurisdiction and control of the California Park Com·
mission.
The legislature appropriated and set aside the sum of $50,000 for the
acquisition and restoration of Columbia as a State Park.
The Act provided that an additional sum of $50,000 'be raised by a
corporation named in the Act, "The Columbia Historical Park Associa·
tion."
Dr. James E. McConnell of Columbia is the president of said corpora·
tion and the chairman of this committee is a member of the Board of
Directors.
The required additional $50,000 was raised through contributions by
history minded Californians. At the last session of the legislature an ad·
ditional sum of $50,000 was appropriated for the purpose of providing
a master plan for the final restoration of this old mining town.
The work on the plan is now in the process of being prepared. However
the master plan will in no way alter or change the present plans for the
rebuilding the Masonic Temple.
In 1855 the temple of Columbia Lodge No. 28, was erected "nd con·
tinuously used until 1891 when the gravels gave out and the o1d lodge

192

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in structure and appearance as in the "fifties" and the buildings which
· have heretofore been torn down and destroyed are rebuilt, this old erstwhile ghost town will be the pride, not only of the Mother Lode, but the
pride of the entire State of California.
This old masonic temple should be rebuilt as it was in the "fifties"
and should be so maintained that the lodges of California that desire, may
sojourn to that historic spot and confer degrees on their candidates, upon
appropriate and convenient occasions.
The lower story should be prepared as a masonic museum.
I have no doubt that within a reasonable time, sufficient masonic items
of historical interest will be forthcoming and a museum could be established and maintained which would be of tremendous interest to members
of the craft and the laity as well.
With respect to the probable cost of maintenance of the building in
its entirety, I do not deem it is necessary at this session to submit figures
for the reason that it will be at least one year before the temple can be
built and ready for occupancy. At the next session of Grand Lodge, plans
for custodian service and full cost of maintenance thereof can be submitted by an appropriate committee for the sanction and approval of
Grand Lodge.
The years 1949 and 1950 will be red letter years in California history
as well as Masonic history,-194~he IOOth anniversary of the start
of the gold rush. 195~the admission of California into the Union, and
the beginning of Grand Lodge masonry in California.
Thousands of history minded people from all over the United States
will visit our state. Men and women from the East will come seeking the
localities and scenes where their relations worked and labored and met
with either success or failure, during the hectic days of the greatest search .
for gold in the history of the world.
Letters pouring into the several state and historical agencies during
the past year give proof to the truth of this statement.
Masons from all sections of the Union as well as from foreign countries, will come to join with us in celebrating our first century of masonic
existence. Masonry should be ready for them.
The Mother Lode will be the great magnet drawing our visitors to those
localities in the mountains where masonic romance flourished and where
the Masonic Temple was in reality the religious center. for those hard
working and hard playing miners in the early days.
1£ the temple in this Williamsburg of the West is rebuilt and properly
maintained it will be a Masonic shrine to which the history hungry California Masons will visit and revisit and it will stimulate a healthy interest and pride in our past- a pride, not only in the minds of the older
members of our fraternity but also in the minds and hearts of the young,
virile, new members who must be prepared and equipped to carry on so
that masonry in California may ultimately reach that high destiny to
which its glorious past entitles it.

California masonry needs the stimulating influence of the years that
are gone; it needs to again commune with the strong masonic spirits of
the mountains-the spirits of men who in the long ago had visions and
in those visions saw and foretold the great part which masonry was destined to play in this state and its ever expanding institutions.
Let us rebuild the old temple in the mountains.
Let us provide under proper supervision that degrees may be conferred therein, that the members of our lodges may gain inspiration in
that atmosphere redolent with memories of the men who so many years
ago held high the banner of masonry in those old hills until the gravels
were exhausted and they were compelled to seek the illusive metal elsewhere.
Your committee submits the following resolution and moves its adop·
tion:
I. That the sum of $18,000 be appropriated and set aside for the rebuilding of the masonic temple on the old site in Columbia.
2. That three members of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, be appointed by
the incoming Grand Master as a committee on Masonic Temple at Columbia; that said committee be instructed and empowered to contract,
under the supervision of the incoming Grand Master, for the building oI
said temple in accordance with the plans and specifications as prepared
and submitted by Brother William Mooser, the architect, and now on
file with the Grand Secretary.
That said committee investigate and study the most feasible plan for
furnishing and maintaining the lodge room and museum, and to submit
their findings to the next annual communication of the Grand Lodge.

Report of the Board of Directors of the Masonic Club House
at the University of California at Los Angeles
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
As reported last year, the Club House was taken over during the War
first, by the Military Authorities, and later, by the Red Cross. This report,
therefore, covers the first full year's operations since restoration of possession and the completion of housecleaning and repairs necessary to our
reoccupancy.
During the year death deprived us of our beloved associate, Past Grand
Master Dana R. Weller. Brothers Ben G. Wright and Walter Berger, the
former Chairman, and the latter Secretary, have retired from the Board.
Each had been associated with the Club House from its inception. Their
wisdom and devoted service immeasurably contributed to its development
and success; they participated in the transformation of an isolated spot
in a vast barley field into a beautiful and useful edifice in the center of
a great cultural and business area having a present money value of
$250,000, and of inestimable worth as a Masonic contribution to the
development of American citizenship.
In accepting our gratitude for your generous cooperation, we feel sure
that you will join in our satisfaction over the manner in which the
Masonic Club House continues to fulfill the purposes of its founders.
Four hundred students currently avail themselves of its facilities, and
this number will probably reach six hundred during the current year. A
very large proportion are war veterans, and more than thirty of the latter .
are Master Masons.
The immense University enrollment (over 14,000 at tJ.C.L.A.) seriously aggravates the difficult housing situation. Many students are compelled to live in crowded and uncomfortable quarters, altogether unsuited
to study. The Club's study hall and other facilities do much to alleviate
this condition. They are utilized to capacity.
To meet a crying necessity, the students maintain a snack bar, where
sandwiches and light refreshments are available from 9 :00 A.M. to 4 :00
P.M. daily. They also serve a hot evening meal. Practically all of the
labor is performed by the students. They are responsible for operations,
which are on a cooperative non-profit basis. A number of our War veteran
students have stated that but for the economical service thus provided
they would be unable to carry on their college work.
To avoid interfering with studies, entertainment and other diverting
activities are not emphasized. Each Friday night there is an informal
student get-together, with dancing and games. Each Sunday night there
is a supper, usually attended by seventy-five to one hundred students. A
speaker on a musical or other short program is provided, aiming to close
at or near 9:00 P.M.
The Grand Master honored us by a visit. He met and was entertained
by about four hundred students. His interest and courtesy were greatly
appreciated.

195

It was our privilege also to receive a visit by Seniors and Juniors from
the Covina Home, which was greatly enjoyed. The boys and girls were
much impressed by the University Campus and the Club House. Alumni
students contemplate establishing a scholarship fund to be available to
boys and girls from the Home.
The vigilance and valued experience of Brother Klarquist have kept
Club House maintenance and repair down to a minimum. Eighteen years
of constant service requires that we anticipate depreciation expenditures
in the not distant future. Following expert advice, our books have consistently shown depreciation in the sum of $1,250 each year. The budget
allowance, however, has been only $1,000. It is proper that the budget
allowance should be increased to correspond with the books, and we so
request.
Budget of $15,065 for the ensuing year is submitted. Details are as
follows:

San Antonio Lodge No. 694, in the city of South Gate, county of Los,
Angeles.
Adopted.

The Grand Master has also referred to your Committee the following:
Belvedere Lodge No. 539 has requested the authority of Grand Lodge
to move its place of meeting from 3601 Yz East First Street, in the county
of Los Angeles, to the city of Monterey Park, a distance of about five and
one-half miles. The requirements of Section 140, Constitution, have been
fulfilled.
Your Committee is aware that the neighborhood surrounding Belvedere
Lodge's present place of meeting has undergone a decided change in the
type of population, and is now no longer a satisfactory source of potential
candidates. As a result, the Lodge no longer draws its new members from
Belvedere, and many of its members have moved away. This situation
is evidenced by the fact that only two members have been accepted from
the community of Belvedere in the last six years, and indeed the membership of the Lodge has increased by only nine in the past fifteen years.
Your Committee sincerely believes that Belvedere Lodge has exhausted
its usefulness in its present location. The city of Monterey Park is in a
rapidly developing section of San Gabriel Valley in which there is an
abundance of good Masonic material.
We are impressed with the fraternal solicitude which prompted Belvedere Lodge to seek the approval of its new Masonic neighbors to its proposed move, and the hearty welcome offered in return.
While the removal of a Lodge inevitably causes regret and sometimes
hardship to certain of its members, your Committee is of the opinion that
the broader interests of the Lodge should prevail, and recommends that
the application of Belvedere Lodge No. 539 to move to Monterey Park
should be granted, and its charter amended accordingly.
Fraternally submitted,
HAROLD A. MEYER,

Report of Committee on By-Law8
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the past year there has been considerable By-Law activity
among the Lodges.
Much of it was necessary because of the action of GrandJ.odge in
raising the minimum fee for Degrees to $50. Thirty-three Lodges came
up to $50, seventy-two raised their fees to $75 and thirty-six to $100 or
more. All of these 141 Lodges should be materially benefited by this
action.
Approximately 100 additional Lodges took action amending their
By-Laws as shown hereafter.
We are deeply appreciative of the splendid cooperation given by the
Grand Secretary in assisting the Lodge Secretaries in correctly carrying
through these amendments. It involved considerable correspondence in
some cases. As a result we have found all amendments in proper form.
Provision for Stated Meetings that might fall on holidays was made by
amendments to By-Laws in 18 Lodges. Special attention to such changes
in meeting dates when they occur are the responsibility of the Officers and
the Secretary of the Lodge.
During the past year one Lodge discovered that its By-Laws stated and
required a certain amount for the Three Degrees. For a number of years
this Lodge had only been charging approximately one-half this amount.
A number of other mistakes came to light this year concerning other
Lodges.
Our Committee join with the Grand Secretary in urging a careful
reading of the By-Laws by Lodge Officers. The Installation Ceremony instructs the Master to see that the By-Laws of his Lodge are strictly complied with. He should read them carefully when he takes office.
Our Committee have carefully examined all of the following amendments, which are listed here, and in the Grand Secretary's Report. All
have been approved by the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master as to
form and Masonic law requirements.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of
The Committee on Masonic Information, 1947
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of Californ'ia:

Your Committee on Masonic Information reports as follows:
Work of the Committee during the past year was interrupted by the
retirement of its Chairman, W. Bro. Reynold E. Blight, after many years
of able and conscientious labor in this field, and the loss of his guidance
and the benefit of his experience and knowledge has been keenly felt and
regretted by your Committee.
During the past year, the system of Quiz Programs, instituted about
six years ago, has been continued, though only two in a form somewhat
more elaborate than usual, accompanied. by a pamphlet of explanatory
matter called "The Charge," has been issued by your Committee. In
September a short comment on the Constitution of the United States was
distributed. A new plan of sending all this material through the Inspectors
was adopted and seems to he operating satisfactorily.
The importance of the subject and the possibility that this report may
stimulate further study of the problems which surround it seems to justify
a resume of Masonic Education in this Grand Jurisdiction. Masonic Education or, as now termed, Information, was undertaken in 1915. During a
third of a century, approximately $75,000 has been spent upon the various
projects yet, notwithstanding the time, effort, and money devoted to it,
the program has often been referred to and sometimes justified, as experimental. Every Grand Master during that period, with only two or three
exceptions, has stressed, in his annual report, the need for Masonic
instruction, urged its prosecution, and some have described it as a vital
requirement. None, however, have had the genius to say what it should
consist of or the magic touch to put a successful scheme into operation.
Nor is this to he wondered at when the difficulties of the matter are considered.
The history of the efforts seems to divide into five periods.
The first period, 1915-1924, witnessed a laudable undertaking and a
rather lavish expenditure of funds, $25,000 being disbursed during the
nine years. By 1923, the Grand Master was enabled to report that the
program had not fulfilled expectations. He asserted that the system was
faulty and that its proper conduct would require the entire time of an
Executive Secretary.
The second period, 1925-1931, covered seven years during which an
Executive Director, with office and assistant, was engaged, and a most
heroic effort was made at high pressure and with appropriations aggre-

205

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

gating $52,500, though possibly as much as $10,000 of that was not spent.
Pamphlets, circulars, letters and literature were sent out by the tens of
thousands to a mailing list of over 1,100. Addresses numbering into the
hundreds were delivered by the Executive Director and others. Educational Committees were functioning in 440 lodges, and a majority of the
Masters were indicating their approbation of the work. Yet, with all this
effort and expense and with the program at a pitch of intensity never
equalled before or since, unfavorable comment began to trickle through
to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Finance
to the effect that the membership were not getting value received, and one
or the other of those committees were constrained to concur in the continuance of the program on the basis that it was still in the experimental stage
and that the Committee on Masonic Education had been diligent and
faithful in the face of apathy and indifference. In the final year of this
period, 1931, the appropriation was cut to $2,500 and conditioned that
none of it should be spent without the special approval of the Grand
Master. But the Grand Master, though himself strongly in favor of Masonic
Education, approved no expenditure, appointed no Educational Committee, and the program came to an abrupt stop.
The third period, 1932-1936, was one of reappraisal and investigation,
beginning with the report of the Grand Master to the effect that Masonic
Education was a critical question and a crying need, but was subject to
widespread diversity of opinion; that the fraternal and progressive spirit
had been neglected in the Fraternity; that we had over-emphasized the
ritual which was only a means to an end, properly constituting only a
minor activity; and that, unless we could retain the fraternal spirit and
lively interest which characterized our early brethren, the usefulness of
Masonry was terminated. The following year, a special committee was
appointed to survey the whole subject. It made a well considered report,
the main points of which were as follows:
1. That, with the exception of intermittent groups, the general mem·
bership would not exert itself to acquire Masonic education;
2. That lodge officers, though willing to participate in the program,
did not carry through unless urged by Grand Officers;
3. That a proper program should be required by Grand Lodge;
4. That the candidate was the logical individual with whom to start
and his participation should be made prerequisite to his advancement;
and
5. That such a program need entail no considerable expense, if any
at all.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommended against
· a compulsory program, and this period of inaction ended with no educa·
tional work and no appropriation having been made during the five years.
The fourth period, 1937·1939, only three years in length, witnessed an
ambitious and aggressive attack upbn the problem, but the heroic charge

ended in ignominious retreat. The Committee on Masonic Education reported that the consensus seemed to favor the following:
1. That the program be confined to Masonic subjects.
2. That it should be directed to the candidate; and
3. That it should be voluntary.
The Committee formulated an elaborate program for instructing candidates, consisting of lectures on 40 topics, 10 of which were to be given the
candidate before initiation and 10 following each degree. The next year,
the New York Manual was borrowed and, with some modifications, re·
printed to the number of 10,000 copies of which 4,000 were distributed
at once. But again hope was dashed to the ground, for, almost immediately,
objections were made and the Chairman of the Educational Committee
was under the painful necessity of appearing before the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes and admitting that the Manual contained
matter not proper to be printed or written. The Manual was promptly
removed from circulation. Again the educational pointer turned back to
zero.
The period which we are now in began in 1940 with the declaration of
the Grand Master that the word, "education," was repellant and that
"advancement" would be preferable. The Committee on Masonic Education, in 1941, recommended that its name be changed to "Information,"
a term doubtless suggested by a popular radio program of the time, for
the report went on to say that the matter put out by the Committee must
be concise, interesting, and in challenging form; that the members did not
like profound long-winded dissertations on abstract and abstruse themes;
they wanted facts not philosophy; capsules of pre-digested data shot at
them like radio announcements; and that the material must be revised to
fit the rapid fire procedure of quiz programs.
Embarrassing though it may be, the fact is that we are now and have
been for the past six years proceeding on the theory that the Freemasons
of California are incapable of absorbing anything but pre-digested food
shot from guns. If that be true, it raises several serious questions: What
has this Fraternity come to? Is this the end? If not, where are we headed?
What kind of education or information can be inculcated into such a body
of pupils? If our present appraisal is true, it would seem that Masonic
education is an idle and futile gesture, for the educational process necessarily contemplates one of two things: either a clientele able and anxious
to learn or a compulsory process such as that in our public schools.
Undoubtedly, a mistake has been made in assuming that we are driven
to one or the other of two extremes; either long-winded dissertations on
abstract and abstruse themes or the shallowness of radio quiz programs.
Are not schools and colleges turning out educated young men and women
by the tens of thousands each year without being impaled on either horn
of this supposed dilemma? Is it true that, among the 161,000 Freemasons
in California, there are none capable of digesting anything but infantile
mental pabulum?

206

207

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Your Committee has no hesitation in expressing doubt as to whether
Masonic Education is yet on the right road, or as to whether the present
system is worthy of a Grand Lodge of the size and standing of that of
California; nor does it have any intention either to obscure the delicacy.
and difficulty of the problem or to engage in platitudinous generalities to
allay the painful symptoms of the disease or te cover up the failure of its
remedies. For, if the solution of the Fraternity-wide problem has been
found anywhere, that fact has not become evident.
Let's not hunt scape goats. or blame each other for poor results. This is
a common problem worthy of the best talent. It is to be regretted that, on
several occasions in past years, educational efforts have been interrupted
by private, anonymous objections to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes or to the Committee on Finance with no disclosure of the nature,
ground or merits of the complaints and with no opportunity for inquiry
as to the accuracy of the testimony or the breadth of the trouble. Mention
is made of this, not because of any effect upon the Committee on Masonic
Education or Information, because that effect is of no importance whatever. It is important, however, to Grand Lodge, for it deprives that body
of information which might have been of great value, and it deprived the
Grand Lodge of the right to determine what, if anything, was wrong, and
whether corrective measures were not possible without completely terminating the then existing effort. No one will be found more ready than
your Committee on Masonic Information to receive and consider either
complaints or suggestions, and, if any other Committee or Committees be
included in the petition, so much the better. But every move should look
to a thorough investigation and determination and the application of the
proper remedy and not be designed merely to disrupt.
Permit us now to dissect the problem and direct attention to some of
the very fundamental truths which seem heretofore to have been overlooked.
1. What facts, theory or doctrine does the Grand Lodge expect the
Committee on Masonic Information to inculcate? The Grand Lodge has
not said. Obviously, it is not to teach what is in the ritual, for that is
already thoroughly taken care of. What is the Grand Lodge's authorized
and approved version of the history of Freemasonry? It has none, except
what is found in the ritual. What is the Grand Lodge's interpretation of
the symbolism of Freemasonry? It hasn't any, except the ritual. What is
the doctrine of the Grand Lodge about the philosophy, religion, or principles of Freemasonry? Obviously, nothing, except what is already taught
in the ritual. Therefore, if your committee circulates any information at
all, it must be in addition to, subtraction from, or modification of the only
authorized doctrine of Grand Lodge, viz., the ritual. Hence, we have the
anomaly of a Committee officially and solemnly authorized to disseminate
unauthorized materials. Furthermore, this must be expected to vary from
time to time as the personnel, resourcefulness, imagination, and concepts
of the Committee change.

2. As presently conceived, the process of Masonic information must
continue to be controversial, must inevitably give some dissatisfaction and
must arouse some criticism. This is so because no two Freemasons have
exactly the same concept of Freemasonry and many of them differ widely
in their views and in the phases of the subject which they think should be
emphasized. There is no more unanimity of taste ~.niong Masons on ~at
subject than there is in the choice of general readmg matter, recreation,
or other avocation.
3. Hitherto, Masonic education seems to have been considered in terms
of dollars. But real education, like real charity, is not proportional to
money spent.
4. Masonic education has been thought of as something that could be
pumped into the gasping Freemason as air is forced into the lungs of a
drowned man. But education requires effort on the part of both teacher
and the pupil.
5. It has been partly, but only partly, recognized that Masonic education is really a function of the lodge, not the Grand Lodge. The members
are almost wholly members of lodges not the Grand Lodge; the candidates
are candidates of the lodge, not the Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge,
through its Committee, should outline, suggest and direct, but the principal effort must be made by the lodges.
6. The idea is thoroughly ingrained that the lodges are officially required only to initiate, pass and raise candidates, and that su~h is ~eir
sole aim and ultimate objective. Lodges will and do accept mcreasmg
numbers of candidates until their officers are overburdened and neither
the lodges nor the officers have time or patience to learn or teach anything
outside the ritual.
7. The only fact thus far agreed upon is that the Fraternity is losing·
its peculiar individuality and savor, and that its gro~th, though rampan!,
is more vegetative than fruitful. It seems to be realized that mere repetition of the ritual is not cementing the newly raised Master Masons into a
brotherhood, but is leaving them sterile of any considerabl~ veneration
for the Society or understanding of its background and peculiar customs,
policies and purposes, so that Freemasonry is tending to become just
another of the numerous fraternal orders or "lodges" which abound
everywhere.
8. Symbolic Masonry has been too complaisant in allowing itself to be
regarded in many quarters as a mere elementary course or even an
obstacle to be taken or overcome in reaching the eminence supposed to
exist only in higher degrees and orders. It should display more confidence
in itself as a complete course of Masonic instruction.
Your Committee has reached the following conclusions:
I. That there is one critical period lasting a few weeks when Masonic
education or information is earnestly desired and will be avidly absorbed.
This is while the candidate is awaiting or passing through the degrees.

208

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The few who actually do not actually desire to learn, feel an obligation
to do so.
2. The material should appertain to Freemasonry alone.
3. The material should be authoritative by having received the approval of Grand Lodge.
4. It should be so phrased as to work a double purpose, viz., to give
some information and to arouse curiosity for more.
5. It must be a recognized, ·routine, regular part of lodge activities.
6. It will almost double the time and attention devoted to the candidate.
7. It may retard the rapidity of progression through the degrees. If it
accomplishes nothing more, that alone would be worth while.
8. Those who are not intelligent enough or interested enough to read a
book might be stopped on their way through the degrees. This would be a
distinct benefit to the Craft.
9. It must be frankly recognized as a new approach. If adopted at 'Bll,
it should be adopted with virtual unanimity and, thereafter, subjected
only to open, constructive criticism.
10. This job should not be left to Coaching Committees, for their duties
and talents are entirely distinct. Some other brethren in the lodge should
be entrusted with this function and, in recognition of their efforts and as
an indication of the importance of their position, a distinctive title should
be given them.
.
11. Educational work among the general membership should be encouraged, but should not be attempted as a primary or major objective
of Grand Lodge. We are so far behind that the effort to catch up would
prove to be disheartening. The benefits are to be expected in future; not
immediately.
As examples of what your Committee believes can properly be approved
by Grand Lodge for delivery to the candidate, two manuscripts have been
prepared which would be printed in attractive pamphlet form and delivered to the candidate, the first before and the other after his initiation.
Your Committee has not thought it advisable to prepare the remaining
two pamphlets, one to be delivered after the passing and the other after
the raising, until the reaction of Grand Lodge to the two now presented is
known.
In drafting these, your Committee has meticulously adhered to authorized doctrine, adding only such historical and explanatory matter as it
deems unlikely to be questioned.
Your Committee recommends:
1. That the two manuscripts hereto attached be referred to the Com·
mittee on Policy and General Purposes for approval; that with such
amendment as that Committee may recommend, such manuscripts be
approved by Grand Lodge; and that your Committee be authorized to
have the same printed and distributed to the lodges.

2. That your Committee on Masonic Information be continued for the
ensuing year.
3. That there be appropriated for the work of said Committee the sum
of $750.
4. That, if the printing of said pamphlets be approved, such appropriation be increased by an additional $500.
Dated October 1, 1947.

THOMAS ANDREW DILLE

Tom, as he was most affectionately known, was appointed Inspector
of the 78th Masonic District in 1927, and served in that high office until
ill health forced his retirement in 1942. He died November 8, 1946.
Thomas A. Dille was born in Greensboro, Indiana, December 17, 1873.
His boyhood was spent in Lincoln, Nebraska, and it was in the public
schools of that city that he received his education. He chose the law as
his profession, and following his graduation from the University of
Nebraska he practised in Salt Lake City, Utah, and later in Chicago,
Illinois. While practising in Chicago he received a most flattering o:ffer
to take the office of credit-man for the Pfeiffer Chemical Company of
St. Louis, Missouri, which position he held for two years. The lure of
the Pacific Coast attracted him, and when he received an invitation to
join the staff of the Fairbanks·Morse Company of Los Angeles in a similar position, he readily accepted. He later transferred his services to the
Public Relations Department of the Southern California Edison Co.,
which position he held until ill health forced his retirement.
Brother Dille was raised in Wilshire Lodge No. 445, in December,
1919, and served as Master in 1925. He was a member of the Scottish
Rite Bodies in Los Angeles, graduating in the class of June 5, 1920.
Tom Dille's name was a synonym for all that was good and fine in
Masonry. His knowledge of the ritual and the law, and his willingness
to aid newly appointed Inspectors, earned for him a unique place in our
Fraternity. May Almighty God grant him the peace he so richly deserves!

HARDUS POMEROY SORKNESS

In the innermost recesses of our understanding we know that death
is constantly at our side; that the Sword of Damocles hangs continuously
over our heads· that with every breath we draw we come nearer to the
tomb. Our dail~ observations furnish evidence that this is also true of
those we admire much and love most. With a full knowledge of these
truths the sudden passing of Dana R. Weller came as a grievous shock
to the Fraternity.
•
Dana Weller was made a Master Mason in his twenty-third year. His
ability and diligence elevated him to the Masters Chair. His qualities
of leadership were recognized by the Grand Lodge, and at the early a~e
of thirty-six he was elected and installed Grand Master of Masons m
California. He was a member of every branch of the York Rite of Free·
masonry, and held high office in several of its branches. He was a 33rd

Shortly after his birth on January 25, 1902, at Ashby, Minnesota,
Brother Sorkness' family moved to North Dakota, where the boy re·
ceived his grammar school training. The family later moved to Texas,
and it was in that State he graduated from high school. The great migration to Southern California shortly after World War I found the Sorkness family again on the move, and this time they found the land of
their dreams in the beautiful San Jacinto Valley. They settled in Hemet,
where young Hardus entered the automobile business with his father.
Feeling the call of the sea, he joined the United States Navy, and at the
termination of his enlistment returned to Hemet and entered business as
a radio technician, which line of endeavor he followed until the enactment of the Selective Service Law. With the establishment of the Local

212

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Board he was appointed secretary, which position he held at the time
of his death.
Brother Sorkness was made a Master Mason in San Jacinto Lodge
No. 338 on December 19, 1923. Served as Master in 1929-1932-1935,
and as Secretary in 1939. In the latter year he was appointed Inspector
of District 107, and served faithfully until his passing on April 15, 1947.
As evidence of the esteem in which he was held and the affection in
which he was regarded, his funeral was the largest Masonic gathering in
the history of the Valley.
WILLIAM LAWRENCE HOVIS

Appointed Inspector in 1928, William L. Hovis presided over the 79th
District for eighteen years. He was raised in Golden State Lodge No. 358
in the City of Los Angeles, but demitted in 1925 to become a charter
member of Southland Lodge No. 618. Recognizing his splendid qualifi·
cations, he was elected Master in 1928, serving with distinction. He was
also a member of the Chapter, Commandery, Scottish Rite, and the
Shrine.
Bill, as he was more familiarly known, had profound admiration for
the splendid work being accomplished by our Boards of Relief, and upon
his election as a Trustee of the Los Angeles Board he entered so enthusi·
astically upon his duties that his re-election was assured, and he served
continually until his death on November 1, 1946. He was honored in
1934 and 1935 by being elected Chairman, and from 1936 to 1946 he
was Treasurer of the Board.
Bill Hovis was born in Butler, Pennsylvania, June 12, 1883, the third
boy of the family. The mother died when he was a baby and the father,
seeking a more equitable climate in which to rear his family, moved to ·
Los Angeles in 1893. The boys attended the 30th Street School, and dur·
ing this period Bill occupied his spare time as an usher in the old Mason
Opera House.
Following his graduation from high school Brother Hovis was em·
ployed as salesman for the Haynes Stationers Company at First and
Spring Streets. Resigning from that company in 1919 he formed a part·
nership with Frank S. Baker under the firm name of the Hovis-Baker
Printing and Mailing Company, specializing in Masonic printing. In
1930 he sold his interest in the company to his partner and established
the Addressing Machine Equipment Company, of which he was the sole
owner. He was married in 1904 to Bessie McMurry of Kahoka, Missouri.
Bill Hovis was faithful to his duties, loved by the members of the
Craft, and admired by all. His absence is keenly felt.

WILLIAM PENN HUMPHRIES

History has never written a record more interesting than that of the
development of the great State of California. Those hardy pioneers who
crossed the plains in covered wagons, or who braved the fevers of

214

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Panama, or came around the Horn, and laid the foundation for the developments of California, which we now enjoy, are all gone. The passing
of time has removed most of the sons of those valiant souls. A few, how· ·
ever, still remain. One of the most prominent and most beloved of this
later generation, William Penn Humphries, died July 29, 1947, as he
was nearing his 76th birthday.
Brother Humphries was a direct descendant of American Revolutionary stock. He was born in the City of San Francisco on September 11,
1871, at the residence of his father, William Penn Humphries, at 976
Chestnut Street. His father was prominent in the early history of San
Francisco and being an engineer by profession he served his city as City
Surveyor during the hectic period of the Gold Rush.
Bill Humphries received his education in his native city. After grad·
uating from the Spring Valley Grammar School and the Urban Prepara·
tory Academy he entered the University of California, and graduated
with the class of 1892. He later attended both Harvard Law School and
Hastings Law School. He was admitted to the Bar in 1896 and practiced
his profession for the remainder of his life.
His Masonic career was outstanding. He served the Craft faithfully
for forty-six years. His activities extended to every branch of the Frater·
nity. He was raised July 16, 1901, in Oak Grove Lodge No. 215, in Ala·
meda. He demitted to Occidental Lodge No. 22 in San Francisco on
July 7, 1902, and served as its Master in 1920. He was a Past High Priest
of King Solomon's Chapter No. 95, Royal Arch Masons, and Most Excel·
lent Grand High Priest of the Grand Chapter in 1923. He was serving '
his 14th term as Grand Treasurer of these bodies at the time of his death.
He was Illustrious Master of California Council No. 2 Royal and Select ·
Masters, and in 1942 served as Most Illustrious Grand Master of the
Grand Council. He held membership in California Commandery No. 1,
Knights Templar, and was a member of Islam Temple of the Shrine.
The Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction, honored him with the 33rd Degree on December 16, 1939. Brother Humph·
ries rendered splendid service as a member of the Grievances Committee
of this Grand Lodge in 1934-5-6.
The breach left in our ranks by the passing of this distinguished Mason
will be recognized by all those who are familiar with the history of
Masonry in California. We ask God's blessing upon him, and peace to
his loving and kindly soul.
It is given to few men to write anything upon the pages of history, and
those few are soon forgotten.
Scientists tell us that this world has been a solid mass for more than
two billion years, and as two billion of anything is beyond the comprehension of the minds of most of us, they have simplified it by comparing
that figure with a novel of 500 pages, each page containing 400 words,
each word representing 10,000 years. By comparison the time you and
I will pass upon this earth, if we live the full three score and ten years

mentioned in the Bible, our life span would not cover the "period" that
ends the book.
·

Truth, and its beauty of ritual, comes to us from the dim ~ast- from
that hazy period, that borderland between the known and the unknown.
It has been preserved for us by the unselfish service of untold thousands
who have gone before. When the worldly accomplishments of our brethren w?om we now mourn are lost in the moldy records of time their

IN MEMORIAM
FRANK WILBER MIXTER
December 30, 1873 - May 22, 1947

By Will H. Fischer, Past Grand Master
The. life ?ist?ry of Past Grand Master Frank W. Mixter, who passed
away m this city on May 22 last, follows with remarkable fidelity to
patt~rn the sa~a of the self-made man, which through generations has
~nspued A?1e~cans to wor~, to ser~e and to achieve. It is not to be told
m pane~nc ~1gh.t or embehshed with florid phrase; it is instead a record
to be recited. 1~ s11?ple ';ords -:--- a record rich with deep significance in
these unfam1har tn~es m which we hear the strident preachments of
those who hold that the age of opportunity has passed, that self-reliance

216

217

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

is an outworn and futile doctrine and that our cares and burdens and
hopes should henceforth be the concern of paternalistic government.
The careers of Brother Mixter and men of his courage and character
refute these foreign and fallacious notions and confound those who give
them voice.
Past Grand Master Mixter, who came into mortal life December 30,
1873, at Pekin, Illinois, was the son of Horace Leander Mixter and Mary
Katherine Mixter. He was not born to wealth or position. He made his
bow to the world in obscurity; but from his earliest years he manifested ·
qualities which evidenced the probability of his ultimate triumph over
the adversities of his youth. While he was still a child his family moved
from Pekin to Peoria, Illinois, then to St. Louis, Missouri, thence to
Paris, Texas, and finally to Hot Springs, Arkansas.
During those tender years Frank learned to work and to save. He sold
newspapers and candy on the streets. He picked cotton. He worked as
a stock boy in a department store. He served as a laborer in a brick yard.
As and when he could, he attended public school. All this before he was
fourteen years of age. Work built sinew, toughened fibre, bred selfreliance and gave form and spur to the boy's ambition.
At the age of fourteen, Frank announced his desire to try his fortune
in California. Gaining parental consent, he set out alone and arrived at
Visalia, near which place resided a friend of his father. Immediately he
applied for employment at a Visalia drug store. He was accepted as an
errand boy and handy man, and as such he swept the store, dusted the
shelves and kept the oil lamps cleaned and filled and the wicks trimmed.
For five and a half years he continued these humble duties, but in his
spare time he devoted himself to the study of pharmacy and earnestly
added to his general education. At the age of twenty he was qualified
and admitted a licentiate pharmacist, the master of a profession with
which he was thereafter intimately associated throughout his life, first
as an employee, then as a partner and finally a sole owner. Thus engaged,
he resided first in Visalia, then in San Francisco and finally at Exeter
where he settled in the early part of 1905, continuing there for forty-two
years until his death.
He prospered in his profession and in other business activities, and
his interests expanded into banking. He was a director of the First
National Bank of Visalia, beginning in 1911 and continuing to 1930,
serving a portion of that period as vice-president. Subsequently, he was
vice-chairman of the board of the Visalia Branch of the Bank of America
and a member of the board of the Exeter Branch of the same institution.
As the reward of his years of careful attention to his affairs he gained
a comfortable competence.
Despite the hard work of his early life, Brother Mixter found occasions
for normal amusement and relaxation. As a youth he delighted in play·
ing baseball on the home-town team, and his interest in a good ball game
never waned. He was also an ardent fisherman and hunter. · During one

period he had an intense desire for a military career. He joined the
National Guard company at Visalia as a private, and two years later
was advanced to the rank of captain. On the outbreak of the Spanish
American War he was commissioned a lieutenant of Company E, Sixth
California Infantry. To his regret at the time he was not sent abroad,
his company being restricted to eight months of service at the Presidio
of San Francisco. In all, the young man was connected with the military
for twelve years.
Frank Mixter possessed a strong sense of civic responsibility. No
enterprise for the welfare of the people among whom he lived or of that
great inland empire, the San Joaquin Valley, lacked his support or his
active leadership. It was said of him that to secure his endorsement of
a community cause amounted to its automatic success. He was a powerful
supporter of the public schools, an organizer and member of the first
Board of Trustees of Exeter High School District. He was one of the
organizers and the first president of the Exeter Kiwanis Club, representing which he attended several international conventions. He also served
Kiwanis as lieutenant governor in 1938.
In the year 1924, when the great Central Valley Project was in its
infancy, the people of Tulare County keenly felt the importance of sending a strong representative to the Legislature. They induced Brother
Mixter to become a candidate for the Assembly and elected him in
November of that year. He served six years in the lower House and was
then advanced to the Senate where he served four 4-year terms, making
in all a legislative career of twenty-two years. During all that time,
Senator Mixter held a position of leadership in activities relating to the
development of the Central Valley Project and irrigation matters in
general. As an assemblyman he was a member of the Joint Interim
Committee on Water Resources and chairman of the Assembly Committee on Irrigation. As a senator he was for ten years chairman of the Committee on Irrigation and its successor, the Committee on Water Resources.
He was a member of the Committee on Agriculture, and for ten years was
a member of the Senate Committee on Military Affairs. For four years
he was chairman of the Senate Finance Committee and finally was chairman of the Committee on Revenue and Taxation. He served also on
numerous less important committees in both houses. Modest, quiet, not ·
given to oratory, attentive to duty, fair and courteous, Senator Mixter
held the profound respect and confidence and the sincere affection of his
associates and of the people he so ably represented.
Frank Mixter was raised a Master Mason in Visalia Lodge No. 128
in April, 1902. In 1911, he demitted to assist in organizing Exeter
Lodge No. 424 of which he became the first Senior Warden. He served
as Master in 1913 and again in 1915. He received the degrees of Royal
Arch Masonry in Visalia Chapter No. 44 in 1902, later demitting to
Exeter Chapter No. 122 in which he held every office including High
Priest. The degrees of the Council of Royal and Select Masters were

218

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

conferred on him in Fresno in 1917. He was Knighted in Visalia Com'mandery in 1902 and received the Scottish Rite degrees, including the
32nd, in Fresno in the winter of 1918-19. He was also a member of
the Shrine, the Sciots, and the Eastern Star. He became an Inspector in
February, 1917, and served with great devotion and fidelity until the
Communication of Grand Lodge in October, 1929, at which time his
Brethren elected him to the office of Junior Grand Warden. He was advanced to Senior Grand Warden in 1930 and to Deputy Grand Master
in 1931. At the Communica,tion in October, 1932, he was unanimously
elected and installed Most Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in Cali·
fornia, and in that exalted station served with great loyalty and distinction.
During Grand Master Mixter's tenure of office this country was at the
lowest point of the great depression. It was characteristic of him, therefore, that he devoted a large part of his time to matters arising from the
universal distress. His services in connection with unemployment among
Masons, difficult financial conditions of numerous Lodges, the activities
of the Board of Control and hoards of relief, rehabilitation and relief
following the earthquake of March 10, 1933, the affairs of the Masonic
Homes, and his appointment of the Endowment Fund Board under our
late Brother William P. Jeffries, were among the highlights of his admin·
istration.
On June 23, 1897, Frank W. Mixter and Miss Olive Pogue of Visalia
were joined in wedlock. Mrs. Mixter, five sons and one daughter survive.
Two sons, one grandson and Mrs. Mixter, as was the husband and father
of the family, are pharmacists. The sons are Norbert, Earl, Thomas,
Willard, and Chester, each of whom, in his profession or business, has
made an honorable and estimable place for himself. The daughter, Mrs.
Bert Ware, is the wife of a hanker at Shafter.
Frank Mixter was an honest man, a practical man, an affectionate and
faithful husband, a beloved father. He was a constructive legislator,
a sterling and .outstanding citizen. A loyal Mason, he loved and venerated the Craft. He was a firm believer in the wisdom, the omnipotence,
the compassion and the love of God. He was a reliable man. When he
perceived a duty he performed it, when he accepted a responsibility he
discharged it. His word was his bond. Across the record of his life lies
no shadow; upon his escutcheon, no stain.
It is appropriate, because they so clearly reflect the character and
attitude of Past Grand Master Mixter, th~t we should bring this modest
tribute to a close by quoting the concluding words of his message to
Grand Lodge at the Communication of 1933. They were as follows:
"Yesterday is behind us; let us prepare for tomorrow. Let us look to
that Great Divinity whom we adore for inspiration and guidance in
attending to the important matters before us. May we have faith in God,
faith in our institutions, and faith in our fellow men. And thus inspired
by faith, may. we have the courage to look with confidence toward the
morrow and the fulfillment of its brighter promise."

DANA REID WELLER
Eulogy by Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master
Grand Secretary

In twenty-one Annual Communications of this Grand Lodge I have
appeared before you to present or discuss matters of greater or lesser
importance. Always you have given a fraternal hearing to what I have
had to say. There have been occasions of levity in repartee between me
and some other Grand Lodge officer, and there have been those times of
sorrow as when, from this same platform, I conducted the last services for
my beloved predecessor.
On this occasion I shall need again your sympathetic hearing for I
stand before you in an attempt to put in words the heart throbs of this
Grand Lodge as it gives united thinking to the memory of Dana Weller.
I am hut the humble organ chosen to say as best I can that which we all
would like to hear. I shall not do it well hut perhaps I shall do it as well
as any other for there is none among us who can adequately give expression to those things which we would like to say concerning him who was
at once wise counselor, trusted confidant and loyal friend.
Desirable as it might he for me to say all that should he said, it is not
necessary, for what I shall fail to say will he said quietly in the hearts of
those who hear me.
Dana Reid Weller was horn in Duluth, Minnesota, March 24, 1874. He
came to California with his parents in June, 1875. He attended the public
schools and was admitted to the practice of the law on April 9, 1895.
During the Spanish war, he served as a Major of the Seventh California
Volunteer Infantry and later as Captain of the Forty-fourth United States
Volunteer Infantry in the Philippines. On January 1, 1918, he was ap·
pointed Judge of the Superior Court and later was appointed to the Appellate Court by Governor Stephens.
He was raised a Master Mason in Southern California Lodge No. 278
on January 27, 1897, and became its Master in 1904. He entered actively
into the affairs of Grand Lodge and was elected Grand Master of Masons
in California October 14, 1910, serving until October 13, 1911. He was
the first president of the Southern California Past Masters' Association.
He was chairman for a long period of the ritual committee of Grand
Lodge. For many years he was a member of the jurisprudence committee
and became its chairman in 1932. He received the Scottish Rite Degrees
in 1906 and in recognition of his pre-eminent services to the Rite the Rank
and Decoration of Knight Commander of the Court of Honour was conferred upon him in October, 1919. In 1921 Brother Weller was coroneted
a Thirty-third Degree Mason, and was elected Venerable Master of Los
Angeles Lodge of Perfection when Brother Wm. Rhodes Herve, 33°, was
chosen by the Supreme Council to he Sovereign Grand Inspector General
in California. He was a member of South Gate Chapter No. 98, Royal
Arch Masons, and of Golden West Commandery No. 43, Knights Templar.
He was also Past Master of Los Angeles Council, Royal and Select Mas·

221

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ters, and was Past Sovereign of San Gabriel Conclave No. 14 of the Red
Cross of Constantine.
It is as a Past Grand Master that we knew him best. He first attended
Grand Lodge in 1905 as Master of his Lodge and he has attended every
Session since that time with the exception of 1935 when he was compelled
to remain home because of illness, and in 1945 when we were in session
but one day. Thus it is that he attended forty Annual Communications
and because of that it is as .a Past Grand Master that we knew him best.
His contribution to Masonry in general, and to this Grand Lodge in particular, can not measured for there has yet been found no standard by
which to measure that which carries beyond the lifetime of a person,
transcends his earthly deeds and takes on that character which causes
future generations to bow in admiration, in respect, in gratitude.
His service to this Grand Lodge was not to be found in any narrow,
shallow groove. It was sometimes as the wise lawyer wrestling with a
problem of jurisprudence; at another time it was as the perfect ritualist
whose perfection lay not only in the words he spoke, but in the meaning
which he gave to them. Again it was as the steady hand that quietly fore·
stalled the impulsive action of those who had not reached his years of
judgment and discretion.
He sometimes r~se upon this floor to argue skillfully and courageously
for the point which he would make or the position he would defend, and
then again he stood in this selfsame spot where now I stand, and spoke a
word of quiet eulogy for some old and valued friend, in a manner equaled
by few and surpassed by none.
Sometimes he was at his best in the corner of a room, or in the corridor
where issues were discussed and sides were taken, and I can see and hear
him now as he accepted final disagreement, rolled a cigarette, smiled and
said, "I am going to be against you." And that he was skillfully, fairly,
kindly, and the graciousness with which he won or lost took all the sting
from defeat and permitted no pride of victory.
And now his active service to the Grand Lodge is at an end. The solid
worth of forty-three years of unselfish service will become more apparent
as the years go on. We must find new nien able to fill the place which he
has left, willing to give to it that same devoted service if we are to pay a
tribute to him that will be more lasting than the words I speak. The wisdom, the kindliness, the good judgment, the untiring service of Dana
Weller must be reincarnated in the livei of those of us who stay, if he is to
have the tribute which is rightfully his.
Whether "in that house not made with hands eternal in the heavens"
he has found new outlets for his Craftsmanship I can not say, but this I
· know: in this temple made by hands, for which he himself laid the corner·
stone, his Craftsmanship shall endure as long as Grand Lodge lives.
Whether in "that undiscovered country" to which he has gone he has
found the friends he sought I can not say, but this I know: in this discov-

ered country where he lived and moved and had his being, the friends he
made and kept now seek and find him still, and ever shall.

220

Whether in that Celestial Lodge above it is longer necessary to imitate
the example of celebrated artists, I can not say, but this I know: in this
lodge he imitated the example of a Celebrated Artist "in his truly exalted
and exemplary character, in his unfeigned piety to God and in his inflexible fidelity to his trust," and I know, too, that he met death "not as
a grim tyrant, but as a kind messenger sent to translate him from this
imperfect to that All-perfect, Glorious and Celestial Lodge above," and
there we leave him-Master Mason, Master Craftsman, Master Friend.

Report of Committee on Grievances
To the Mo8t Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

To your Committee on Grievances there has been referred a total
number of thirty-nine records. Twenty-six of these records will be covered
by this report, your Committee feeling that the determinations made by
the several Trial Commissions should be affirmed. The remaining thirteen
will be covered by separate opinions.
There are a number of practices in connection with Masonic disci·
plinary proceedings which seem to recur year after year and which we
have labored hard to eliminate, but without success. It therefore seems
appropriate to mention a few of them again.

In proceedings looking to automatic expulsion under Section 332 of
the Constitution and Ordinances, it is an absolute essential that the notice
prescribed by that section be sent by registered mail to the accused at

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

222

223

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
TRIAL RECORDS

"his last known place of address." This is the language of the statute. If
proceedings under that Section are taken promptly~ this la~t ~own plac.e
of address is usually the place of confinement, either a ~ail or a P.em·
tentiary. Where this is true, the notice must be sent by registered mail to
that place of address and not to the ordinary residence of the accused.
This is a jurisdictional requirement and failure to conform thereto re·
quires that the expulsion be set aside and new proceedings taken. There·
.
.
fore, we urge careful compliance with this requirement.
The forms for use in automatic expulsion cases are set forth ID Section
334. We recommend the use of these forms. Considerable difficulty may
thereby be avoided.
.
.
Almost invariably, each year we run across a record or two ID w~ich
nomination of Trial Commissioners is permitted. Section 299 provides .
that after the determination by the Lodge of the number of Trial Com·
missioners to be elected, not less than seven nor more than nine, "Each
member present will write the name of as many members of t~e ~odge
upon one ballot as shall correspond with the number of Commissioners
determined upon, and, upon counting the ballots, such members as shall
be found to have received a majority of all the votes cast, shall be declared elected as Commissioners. In case the full number should not be
elected upon the first ballot, another ballot will be had for the remainder,
again and again, until the full number of Commissioners shall have been
elected, each by a majority of the votes of those present."
It seems to your Committee that permitting nomination of Trial Com·
missioners is out of harmony with the language of the section just quoted
to you and that, therefore, such nominations should not be permi~ted.
The nominating of Trial Commissioners will not necessarily result m a
reversal. Ordinarily, such would only be the case where there has been a
packing of the Trial Commission which, in itself, would constitute a
Masonic offense. We are not unmindful of the fact that in several former
·instances Grand Lodge has ruled that placing names of Trial Commis·
sioners on nomination may not be improper. Nevertheless, your Com·
mittee feels that it is a practice which should be avoided.
We would also like to emphasize again the necessity of separate votes
by the Trial Commissioners upon each of the specifications and upon the
charge of Unmasonic conduct. Also, we would like to call attention to the
fact that a Master who directs the Junior Warden to prefer charges is
thereafter disqualified from presiding at the trial of the case.
Masonic trial procedure is really quite simple. It is very clearly prescribed in the Constitution and Ordinances. We recommend to Masters
a careful reading of these sections when they are confronted with a trial
in their lodge.

in the 26 trial records hereinafter enumerated. We have found in them
no errors of a substantial character and feel that in each instance substantial justice has been accomplished. These records are:
