At the last Annual Ca.mmunication of Grand Lodge, your Committee
on Grievances recommended the reversal of this case on the grounds that
the notice prescribed by our Law under Section 332 of the Constitution
had not been properly served upon the accused. The trial record then
showed that the notice had been sent to the Oakland address of the accused, whereas at that itme he was im~risoned in the United States Peni·
tentiary at McNeil Island, Washington. There was nothing to show that
he had ever received the notice, and consequently had not had the opportunity within 60 days to demand a trial, had he wished to do so. Such
attempted service of notice has bee~ uniformly declared by this Grand
Lodge to be insufficient. Accordingly the recommendation of this Committee that the case be reversed was accepted and adopted by Grand
Lodge.
Subsequently it has been called to the attention of your Committee,
and documentary evidence produced in support thereof showing conclusively that the notice had been forwarded to the accused from the
Oakland address, and received by him at the prison in sufficient time for
him. to have demanded a trial, had he desired to do so. Moreover the
accused has stated in writing that he had no desire to resist any action
the Lodge saw fit to institute in his case and expressed his willingness to
withdraw from Masonry, if that were possible, in order to forestall the
necessity of a trial.
Had these facts been known by your Committee, the recommendation
for reversal would not have been made. Since they are now established,
your Conimittee believes it to he its duty to call them to the attention of
Grand Lodge. Further, it is of the opinion that this Grand Lodge has the
inherent power to amend its action heretofore taken, and under the facts
now established to affirm the conviction.

mends its adoption:

of Brother H. S. be set aside, and that the action of :{layview Lodge No. 401

the same is hereby affirmed.

Trial Record No. I 080
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record No.
1080 begs leave to report as follows:
This trial record, being from San Bernardino Lodge No. 348, is be·
fore us for the second time.
Accused, a doctor, was convicted in the state courts of three counts of
abortion, a felony. The conviction on two counts was reversed by the
state appellate court because there was no corroboration of the testimony
of the women involved, they being accomplices. Accused was given probation by the superior court on the other count~

226

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Accused was tried masonically on specifications alleging this abortion
and the subsequent conviction, found guilty and expelled. This conviction was reversed by the last communication of Grand Lodge because the
record showed that at the trial accused was not permitted to call witnesses
in his defense but that the erroneous ruling had been made that the conviction in the state court conclusively established his guilt. Such conviction is prima facie evidence of guilt on a masonic trial but accused still
has the right to rebut it.
On the second trial amended specifications were presented charging in
three separate specifications the three acts of abortion which accused had
been originally tried and convicted of in superior court. The presiding
officer at the trial struck out the two specifications pertaining to the counts
which had been reversed by the appellate court and allowed no evidence
connected with those alleged offienses. By a vote of four to three the accused was found Not Guilty.
The action of the presiding officer is not allowing the two specifications
of abortion relating to the counts which had been reversed by the appellate court in the state criminal prosecution was erroneous. It has often
been held that even acquittal of a charge of crime in a state court Cloes
not bar prosecution and conviction in a masonic lodge for the unmasonic
conduct involved in the commission of such crime. Certainly the action
of the appellate court in holding that the judgments of conviction of two ·
counts should be reversed for technical reasons does not bar a masonic
trial based on the same accusations. The appellate court did not h~ld
accused to be innocent but only ruled that the conviction could not stand
because of the lack of sufficient corroborating evidence.
Without any implication from this committee that accused is either
Guilty or Not Guilty we feel that this matter should be again retried.
The certified copy of judgment of conviction on the one count is prima
facie evidence of guilt of that offense, but not conclusive. The evidence,
or some of it, given by witnesses in the superior court on the original
trial, (not before the grand jury), can be read on the masonic trial. Witnesses may be produced on either side if they still are available. Then the
trial commissioners should decide, regardless of anything that has hap·
pened in either state court or masonic proceedings in the past, whether
accused did or did not commit abortion as specified, and, if so, whether
it was unmasonic conduct. Commission of a felony would seem to be such
unquestionably. If the accm•ed is found guilty the commissioners should
then decide the penalty.
Although we dislike this second reversal in this matter we feel that
this case is sufficiently serious to warrant this action.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved: That the action of San Bernardino Lodge No. 348 in finding
C. A. P. Not Guilty be and the same is hereby reversed and set aside and
the matter remanded to the lodge for retrial.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1088
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Report of Grievance Committee-Case No. 1088--Brother R. D. M.
Willow Glen Lodge No. 676.
On August 7, 1946, Brother R. D. M. was charged with un-Masonic
conduct, in three specifications, which summarized are as follows: ( 1)
That he had been accused by the District Attorney on or about the 16th
day of November, 1939, with having committed the crime of grand theft;
(2) that he had been arrested on the said charge; and (3) that he had
been convicted of said charge in the Superior Court, and granted pro·
bation.
The accused was found guilty of the specifications, although no sepa·
rate ballot was taken on each specification, and the sentence was fixed by
the Commissioners at expulsion.
The facts and circumstances of the offense as appearing from the report
of the Probation Officer showed that the accused had accepted checks
from customers of the firm by which he was employed, which checks were
made out to him personally, with the understanding that the amounts
would be credited to their accounts. The accused claimed that he had been
in contact with his Home Office up until the day of his arrest, and that his
account would have been straightened out within a few days. However
this may be, it was shown to be a fact that at the time the probation report was filed that the total amount of money involved had been placed
in the hands of the Sheriff for restitution. In commenting on the case the
Probation Officer had this to say: "It seems doubtful if the transaction
involved any intent to defraud"; also, "It would appear that this present
difficulty might have been adjusted without a warrant being issued." In
any event, probation was granted to the accused for a period of two years,
without any disciplinary sentence of imprisonment.
With this brief resume of the facts, your Committee now passes along
to a consideration of the trial procedure itself. One of the essential requirements of any judicial proceeding is that of "due process," by which
is meant simply that a proper summons or notice must be given to the
accused, advising him of the charges pending against him, and notifying
him of the time and place of the hearing on said charges. The purpose of
such process is, of course, to give the accused an opportunity to appear
and answer said charges, if he elects to do so, or to offer any evidence in
explanation or mitigation of the accusation.

229

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our Maeonic Law recognizes the importance of these principles, and in
Section 308 of the Constitution and Ordinances prescribes that "1£ the
accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, the summons and copy
of the charges shall be issued and served upon the accused at least ten
days prior to the day appointed for the trial, and shall be serv~d per·
sonally by the Tiler or some other member of the Lodge authorized by
the Master for that purpose, or shall be left at his ordinary residence or
place of business. 1£ he be without the said juri~diction, but within the
State and his residence be known, they shall be issued and served upon
the a~cused at least thirty days before the day of the trial, and shall be
forwarded to his address by the Secretary, by mail or other usual mode
of conveyance, and service shall be complete from and after depositing ·
the same in the mail upon due proof thereof."
An examination of the trial record shows that these provisions of our
Constitution were not complied with in this case. The summons was
mailed on September 9, 1946 to the accused addressed to .him .in an.other
community without the jurisdiction of the Lodge, and directmg him to
appear on September 19, 1946, for the trial. The accu~ed ~id not app~ar
at the trial and there is nothing in the record by which it could be m£erred that' he waived the right granted to him by the Constitution to
have at least 30 days notice thereof. A strict compliance with this
fundamental principle of due process has always been considered juris·
dictional by this Grand Lodge, and the failure to observe it i~ this case,
vitiates the proceedings, in the opinion of your Committee.
There are two other matters which should be mentioned in connection
with this trial, not in any spirit of criticism, but rather as helpful suggestions in the conduct of future trials. It was noted above that two of the
specifications of un-Masonic conduct were the accusation of the accus~d
by the District Attorney, and the subsequent arrest thereon. These m
themselves are of course merely preliminary steps to bring one charged
with crime before a proper tribunal. In our Civil Law they do not over·
come the presumption of innocence which clothes every person charged
with crime, and do not import any inference of guilt. Therefore they cannot be the basis of any specification of un-Masonic conduct under our
Masonic Law. And it may be pointed out that even one convicted of a
criminal offense in our Civil Courts, may elect, nevertheless, to have a
Masonic trial and submit all the facts and circumstances of his case to
the judgment 'and consciences of his brethren who are elected to try him.
In this manner Masons retain exclusive jurisdiction over their brethren
and reserve to themselves the sole authority of trying a brother for unMasonic conduct.
The second point is that our Constitution requires, upon the filing. of
charges, that a special meeting be called for the purpose of electmg
Trial Commissioners, and that notice thereof be sent to the brethren.
(Sections 295 and 296 of the Constitution and Bylaws). In the case being reviewed, this requirement of our Law was not followed, as the

record shows that Trial Commissioners were elected at a stated meeting,
with visitors being present.
For the reasons above set forth, your Committee offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved: That the action of the Commissioners of Willow Glen Lodge
No. 676 expelling Brother R. D. M. from the rights and privileges of
Masonry, be and the same is hereby reversed and the case be remanded
to the Lodge for further and proper proceedings.
Adopted.

a general Finding of cruelty, without any specific Findings as to what
acts of cruelty the defendant in that action, who rs the accused here, committed. Neither the Trial Commission nor your Committee has a transcript of the evidence in the divorce action. We feel, however, that we
may safely assume that the evidence there introduced followed quite generally along the lines testified to by this husband and wife before the
Trial Commission.
. The testimony in this case is quite typical of the usual run of the mill
so-called "Cruelty cases" upon which divorces are granted in California
to the extent of many thousands per year. There is neither a charge nor
evidence that the accused used any physical force upon his wife. The
evidence by the wife is to the effect that the husband stayed out nights
until 11 or 12 o'clock and in a few instances until 1 or 2 o'clock and on
one occasion to around 4:30 A.M. On this latter occasion, the husband
testified that he was in attendance upon a celebration of a Shrine Patrol.
The wife intimated that the accused associated with another woman. The
evidence fails utterly and completely to show any sexual relations between the accused and the so-called other woman. The Trial Commission
was therefore entirely right in having the accused found Not Guilty of
the Second Specification. In fact, a contrary Finding should be reversed
as not supported by any evidence. The only affirmative evidence upon
the subject in the record shows that the accused on some occasions did
eat lunch with a group of office employees when the woman mentioned
was in the group; that the accused assisted the other woman in making
out some insurance papers when her husband was killed in the war and
that on an occasion the accused drove from Sacramento to Reno in a car
owned by the other woman for the purpose of attending and acting as
best man at a wedding. Five people made the trip in the same car and the
party left in the morning and returned about 11 P.M. of the same day.
The evidence by the accused is to the effect that he and his wife separated for a period of a month a number of years before; that while they
had gone back together, there had never been a full and complete reCOJ!·
ciliation; that they had been on the verge of one or more subsequent
separations; that harmony did not exist between them, family arguments occurred, and the two of them simply could not get along together
-in other words, a typical case of incompatibility.
Without dispute, the evidence shows that the accused made provision
for the support of his wife and child at the time he left the family home;
that thereafter, a court order was made fixing the amount of support
money which the accused should pay and with that order the accused has
abided meticulously. The divorce decree also divides certain properties,
both real and personal, between the parties.
The Third Specification upon which the accused was found guilty by
a vote of 4 to 3 contains a clause that the accused was, in fact, consorting

233

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

with another woman, not his wife. In this connection, however, we call
attention to the fact that the accused was found not guilty of this precise
charge in the second specification and to our previous assertion that the
evidence is insufficient to support such a charge.
Your Committee is unable to agree with the expulsion of this member
of our Fraternity. We do not applaud his separation from his family nor
do we place any stamp of approval upon his association with the so-called
other woman, however trivial or innocent such association may have
been. We regret that one of ou~ members has become involved in a divorce
proceeding and that it has been found necessary for the court to dissolve
the marriage relation, but we are unwilling to advise Grand Lodge that
the creation of a situation sufficient to warrant the courts to grant a
divorce on the ground of cruelty is a justification for the expulsion of a
member of our Fraternity found guilty of such cruelty. We quite readily
agree that the evidence in some divorce cases might well warrant the
expulsion of the member involved but we do not think this is such a case.
We therefore offer and move the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved: That the finding of Guilty of the accused F. X. A. and the
fixing of the penalty at expulsion be and the same hereby is set aside
and reversed.

The record in this case shows that in the particular transaction here
involved the accuser had accepted a listing of certain real property for
sale. The price was quite cheap for the property. A sale at this price was
thereupon effected to a dummy at the price fixed by the owner. Practically
an immediate resale was made at profit. Both transactions, that is, the
original sale and the resale, were handled through the same Title com·
pany and apparently through the same or a companion escrow. The.ac·
cused secured the money on the check of the Title company which repre·
sented the profit on the deal, turned this money over to the so called
dummy and the dummy, in turn, paid the money to the accused to apply
on a loan which the accused had previously made to the party acting a~
the dummy in this transaction. In passing, it should be noted that the
accused and the accuser had made other deals very similar in character
in which they had received a profit on the resale of properties which
profit they joined in withholding from the original owners.
A real estate agent or broker, representing an owner in the sale of a
piece of property, owes to his principal the duty of exercising honesty
and good faith. To make a secret profit, as was testified to by both the
accuser and the accused, is a reprehensible act, dishonest, a violation of
the law, and a fraud upon the principal. This was recognized by the
accuser for he testified (page 26) that such a practice is neither ethical
nor legal. The accused likewise admitted the illegality of such a trans·
action and so testified (pages 64 and 76) .
We therefore have the odd situation of the accuser as well as the ac·
cused having admittedly engaged in an illegal and improper transaction.
Yet the accuser asks that the accused be disciplined because the accuser
failed to secure the profits resulting from such transaction. To inflict
discipline on one and not upon both would be obviously unfair. The fact
of the matter is that the profit of $1,219.75 belongs to neither of them but
is legally and in good conscience the property of the principal they were
representing and from whom they had collected a commission, for selling
his property. Therefore, it should be obvious that the accused did not
cheat, wrong or defraud the accuser nor did he embezzle funds belonging
to the accuser.
.
Because of the fact that both the accuser and the accused admit, and
the record shows, an illegal transaction, knowingly participated in by
both of them, your Committee feels that both of them should be brought
to the bar of Masonic justice on proper charges. They belong to different
lodges in the same locality. We feel that the Grand Master, at the request
of Grand Lodge, should designate a neutral lodge to try this matter; that
the Junior Warden of the designated lodge should be instructed to prefer
charges against both the accuser and the accused charging them with
unmasonic conduct_for their actions in defrauding their principal out of
the $1,219.75 profit resulting from the real estate transaction above re·
£erred to.
We therefore offer and move the adoption of the following resolution:

Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1101
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Trial Record No. 1101 presents an- unusual situation and, in the
opinion of your Committee on Grievances, requires an unusual dispo·
sition.
The accuser is, and for some time has been, engaged in the real estate
business. The accused was a former associate with the accuser in that
business. In the present case, the accuser charged the accused with un·
masonic conduct, setting forth two specifications. The first of these speci·
fications in substance charged the accused with having embezzled the sum
of $1219.75 which was then and there the property of the accuser. By a
unanimous vote the Trial Commission found the accused not guilty of
this specification. Your Committee agrees with this finding for a variety
of reasons, some of which are technical in character as will hereafter
appear.
The second specification charged that the accused had knowingly and
intentionally cheated, wronged and defrauded the accuser. No vote was
ever taken on this specification. The Trial Commission, without a finding
of guity on either specification, nevertheless found the accused guilty of
unmasonic conduct and by a vote of five to two fixed the penalty at repri·
mand. This situation, alone, would require a reversal of this case for there
can not be a finding of unmasonic conduct unless there is first a finding
of guilty on a specification of fact which would support the conclusion
of unmasonic conduct.

234

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Be it Resolved: That the finding of the accused guilty of unmasonic
conduct and the fixing of the penalty at reprimand be and the same
hereby is set aside and the proceeding dismissed; that the Grand Master
be requested to designate a neutral lodge for the trial of charges to be
preferred against both the accuser and the accused; that· the Junior
Warden of the designated lodge be instructed to file charges in accordance with the views expressed in this report; and that, because of the
technical character of the matter, the Master of the lodge to which the
matter is referred should designate counsel to act with and advise the
Junior Warden if he be not a lawyer.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. ll 05
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances begs leave to report as follows:
RE: Trial Record No. 1105, S. I. R., Pacific Lodge No. 136.
The accused was convicted in the United States District Court by verdict of a jury of the offense of stealing property of the United States and
was sentenced to serve one year and one day in the federal penitentiary
at McNeil Island. The alleged offense was the diverting of a large quantity of steel from the U. S. Navy station at Treasure Island to an iron
works in San Francisco for which accused received $1,100, he being a
trusted civilian employee of the navy on Treasure Island at the time.
Proceedings were started by the lodge soon after the commitment of
accused to prison for his automatic expulsion under Section 332 of the
Constitution. Accused, however, demanded a trial, as was his right under
that section. Charges were filed with three specifications, ( 1) the stealing
of the government property, (2) the conviction of the accused in the U.S.
District court and (3) his imprisonment in the federal penitentiary. Due
service was made on the accused, and, having been paroled by the trial
date, he appeared in his own behalf.
Certified copies of the indictment against him and of the judgment of
conviction were introduced as a prinia facie case against the accused.
The master struck out the second and third specifications of the charges,
correctly ruling that the commission of the criminal act might be a masonic offense but that the conviction and imprisonment arising therefrom
are not masonic offenses in themselves.
The accused testified at great length, and a proper adjournment was
taken to allow him to search for corroborating evidence. This he was
unable to obtain.
Briefly, his testimony was to the effect that he had made a deal with a
sailor named Frates on Treasure Island to buy the steel in question and
had paid him in cash, and Frates was to pay the money to the supply .
officer who he, Frates, stated had the legal right to sell this surplus property. The steel was hauled to the iron works from which the accused received partial payment before his arrest.
--- -· ··--..

235

On being first investigated by the F.B.I. and naval authorities accused
had denied the accusation and had told the story about Frates. The naval
authorities denied the existence of any such person on Treasure Island
but accused still insists there was such a sailor. However he finally agreed
to admit guilt of the theft on an assurance (he claims ) that he would get
probation.
However, after being indicted and upon getting an attorney he pleaded
Not Guilty and was tried by a jury and found guilty. At the trial he told
the story about the deal with Frates, etc. as before.
Upon the conclusion of the Masonic trial the five commissioners acting
found accused guilty of the first specification and guilty of unmasonic
conduct. The vote for expulsion was three to two in favor of it. As the
total number of commissioners elected had been seven this, therefore, was
not a majority vote, and on a vote for .suspension the ballot was five to
none in favor of it, and the penalty was therefore fixed at suspension and
the matter duly reported to the lodge.
Accused has filed a notice of appeal.
The evidence as briefly outlined above amply supports the finding of
the commissioners as to the guilt of the accused.
As to the penalty we feel that where a Mason has committed a felony,
unless there is some evidence of mistake, misunderstanding, or extenuating circumstances the more severe penalty should be applied. The automatic proceeding provided by Section 332 of the Constitution in cases of
felony convictions calls for expulsion. If the accused elects to be tried
and the commissioners of the lodge find that he did in fact commit the
felony of which he was convicted the penalty should be the same as under
the automatic procedure.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Be it Resolved: That the finding of guilt by the trial commissioners in
this case be and the same is affirmed but that the penalty be and the same
is hereby fixed at expulsion.
Adopte~.

Trial Record No. 1112
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom has been referred Trial
Record No. 1112, Friendship Lodge No. 210, reports as follows:
The specifications of un-Masonic conduct were only that the accused
was charged in the Police Court with gambling, arrested, posted $200.00
bail, and failed to appear before the Court, whereupon bail was forfeited. No Masonic offense was thus charged because arrest and forfeiture of bail are not sufficient proof of un-Masonic conduct. The
testimony before the Trial Commission did not go beyond proof of the
foregoing charge; therefore there is no proof of un-Masonic conduct on
the part of the accused.
On the trial the accused volunteered that he had accepted bets orally
from certain customers at his cigar store, which bets he later placed with
or forwarded to bookmakers. There is a question whether such conduct
constituted bookmaking as defined by California Law; but in any event
this admission does not prove the offense of gambling, which was the
only charge the accused was called upon to face.
Therefore the conviction of un-Masonic conduct is neither charged
in the specifications nor proven at the trial and must be reversed, without
prejudice of course to the right of the accuser to charge the accused with
bookmaking should he be so advised.
We propose the following resolution:
Resolved: That the action of Friendship Lodge No. 210 in Case No.
1112 be reversed and set aside.

Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1116
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom has been referred Trial
Record No. 1116, Enterprise Lodge No. 70, reports as follows:
A Brother Past Master of this Lodge preferred charges of un-Masonic
conduct against another Brother of the Lodge. It was specified that the
accused Brother drove an automobile while under the influence of intoxicating liquor and caused a collision with another automobile resulting
in property damage and injury to persons.
No transcript of the testimony heard by the Trial Commissioners has
been furnished to Grand Lodge other than a record of the proceedings
in the form of Minutes reciting in brief the testimony of the several
witnesses who appeared.
The accuser testified that the accused had pleaded guilty in the Justice's
Court to drunk driving (Veh. Code Sec. 502) and had been fined $50.00
and had his driver's license suspended for 30 days. The accuser testified
to other facts which he had gleaned from newspaper accounts of the
accident but these facts, of course, must be disregarded as hearsay so the
only testimony before the Trial Commission was the bare record of a
plea of guilty of drunk driving without injury to property or person.
Witnesses for the accused testified that he was a man of sobriety, that he
drank some but had never been intoxicated. The accused testified that on
the evening of the accident he had been in Oroville to visit a buddy who
had served with him in the Army during the last war; that he did have
several drinks but thought he was in condition to operate his car and
that he thought the accident was because he fell asleep on his way home;
that he pleaded guilty in the Justice's Court because he desired to avoid
further publicity.

After consideration of the whole matter the Commissioners unanimously foun.d the accused not guilty of un-Masonic conduct.
The accuser has written a letter to the Grand Master which we think
constitutes an appeal from this decision of the Lodge. In the letter the
accuser complains that he was not given the right to challenge individual
members of the Trial Commission, and that certain members of the Trial
Commission were prejudiced in favor of the accused, and that they were
in error when they found the accused not guilty.
However, the Minutes of the trial recite that no objection was made by
either party to any of the Commissioners. This disposes of the first and
second contentions of the accuser.
So far as the asserted error in finding the accused not guilty is concerned, it is to be observed that the only competent evidence against him
was his plea, fine, and suspension of license in the Justice's Court. Your
Committee is of the opinion that the Trial Commission gave the proper
weight, effect and value to the testimony of the accused and his witnesses
and that the finding of not guilty of un-Masonic conduct was proper
under all the circumstances of the case.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That in Record No. 1116 the judgment of the Trial Commissioners be and the same is hereby affirmed.
Adopted.

Report of Committee on Clandestine Masonry
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
This Committee was first appointed in 1928 by Grand Master Hutaff
upon the recommendation of Grand Master Fisher and this will be its
19th annual report submitted to you.
The policy established by this Grand Lodge concerning clandestine
Masonry is clear and may be briefly summarized as follows:
_
That every man, be he white, black, yellow or red, and whatever his
belief in God, is eligible to be a Mason, provided he is qualified and
found worthy. That no organization of clandestine or irregular origin
can ever, as such become Masonic. That the only way to be healed Masonically is for the individual or individuals comprising any clandestine
organization to repudiate it, and to petition for the degrees of Masonry
in the regular way. That it is inadvisable to legislate against clandestine
Masonry.
Under this policy the activity of this Committee has been confined to
gathering the data concerning all movements of clandestine character and
furqishing the information to regular Masons and Lodge officers affected
thereby in the various areas throughout the State. It has not been the
policy of this Committee to publish anything concerning such informa-

242

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tion, not even in the printed proceedings of this Grand Lodge. The
Committee recognizes that that which is unnamed soon languishes into
oblivion uncoffined, unknelled and unknown.
· ·
A second line of activity has been to function as an investigator and
furnish information and counsel to those charged with any prosecution
in connection with clandestine Masonry concerning the policy and attitude of regular Masonry. A third and last line of activity has been to
counsel with local Lodge officers as to means and methods to be employed
to suppress the spread of spurious Masonry. In this connection the
Committee has been vigilant to track down racketeers, to prevent whereever possible impositions upon good men who have the sincere desire to
become regular Masons and thus to prevent this termite from affecting
the soundness of this Grand Lodge.
Within the scope of this line of activity the Committee has spent a busy
year. The prosperity of the times has greatly encouraged and made
possible the spread of this clandestine activity. · Notwithstanding this,
there has not been brought to the attention of the Committee any instance
where these clandestine groups are poaching generally upon good Masonic material. There are isolated cases of individuals who have been
imposed upon and in these instances steps are being taken whereby some
of the imposters will be made to suffer and restitution made to the victim.
The general activity of this spurious movement is no different than
that already reported to the Grand Body upon many previous occasions
and it is not necessary to here reiterate that which has already been said.
WARREN E. LIBBY, Chairman,
JoHN ALPERS,
ORI.A A. PRATT,
FRED P. Rou LLARD,
HIRSCHEL SCOTT,
CLAY CALDWELL,
WILBUR B. GIBSON.

Adopted.

RESEARCH COMMITTEE

The Grand Master recommended that the Lodge Research Committee
be abolished. Your committee is advised that said committee has made
considerable investigation of the feasibility of establishing Research
Lodges and it is satisfied after such investigation that it is not feasible
to establish such lodges unless dual membership was permitted in this
State. There are not many men who desire to join such lodges and those
contacted have expressed a disinclination to demit from their mother, or
present, lodges to join a Research Lodge. Your committee is of the
opinion that a new form of lodge for research only should not be set
up by this Grand Lodge unless the members thereof could retain their
present lodge memberships. Your committee concurs in· the Grand Master's recommendation that the said committee be abolished.
Adopted.

As to requests of other jurisdictions for the conferring of degrees on

legal residence is in the jurisdiction applying, (b) giving his exact legal

The Grand Master reports that in the last six months of the Masonic
year 1946, California Lodges conferred 899 Courtesy Degrees, while
lodges of other jurisdictions conferred 423 for us, and that in the last six
months of the Masonic year 1947, we conferred 341 Courtesy Degrees
for other jurisdictions while they conferred 148 for us.
It is somewhat difficult to avoid the surmise that the condition reflected by these figures is due at least in considerable part to the hegira
of the last few years from eastern jurisdictions into California. Many of
those from out-of-state upon whom we have conferred the degrees by
courtesy probably came to be permanent residents of California. It
likewise appears that a considerable number elected in California Lodges
and now requesting to receive the degrees in other jurisdictions have
definitely given up residence within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.
This gives cogency to the Grand Master's observation that "A Masonic
Lodge is or should be a part of the community life, and its members
should be residents of the community or area in which the lodge is
located," and that men coming here or permanently departing this State
who earnestly desire to become Master Masons should obtain demits or
waivers from the jurisdictions from which they remove and become
members of lodges where they are permanently to make their homes.
The subject of Courtesy Degrees runs back through our legislation for
many years. It is unnecessary to review the numerous references thereto
in which our laws abound. It is interesting to note, however, that at our
Communication of 1927, Grand Secretary John Whicher dealt with the
subject in some pointed paragraphs in his report, from which I quote:
"I respectfully renew the suggestion I made last year that we adopt the
policy of refusing to confer degrees by courtesy upon men who actually
hold residence within our jurisdiction, except when proper reasons may
be shown why the candidate should remain a member of the requesting
lodge. Under our present policy, we merely add names to the rosters of
outside lodges with no resulting addition to the moral or material
strength of Masonry. Our lodges have conferred 377 Courtesy Degrees
for other jurisdictions and have requested like favor to the number of
66 degrees."
With reference to Brother Whicher's observations, the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes reported as follows:

MASONIC CLUBS

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under con·
sideration that section of the Grand Master's report entitled, "Masonic
Clubs," and respectfully reports as follows:
The Grand Master indicts "Masonic clubs, clubs of Masons and
Masonry clubs" on five counts, all of which are set forth in full in his
report, and which you doubtless have read. They may be summarized as
follows: ( 1) that they detract from attendance, interest and participation
in the regular work of Lodges, (2) that they are sometimes guilty of
violating lodgeroom decorum, (3) that some charge dues and spend their
money for purposes not authorized by Grand Lodge, (4) that some of
them are beholden to and hold charters from a national organization
and are thereby subjected to influences constituting an invasion of "the
rights of this Grand Lodge," and (5) that they tend to deter sojourning
Masons from affiliation with Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction, thus
"definitely interfering with the processes of Masonry."
There are now, and for a period of years have been, a· considerable
number of Masonic clubs functioning in California, many of which are
conducted in accordance with the spirit and purpose of Masonry. There
are others, no doubt, as discovered by the Grand Master, which at least
occasionally are guilty of practices calculated to reflect upon the prestige
and good name of our Institution and which, if it possesses proper means
.of proceeding, Grand Lodge should suppress.
Much evidence, in the opinion of your Committee, could be adduced to
support an argument that well-conducted Masonic clubs, instead of de·
tracting from attendance, interest and enthusiasm in Lodge work are definitely stimulating the same. There are, no doubt, Masters and Wardens
now serving in office whose interest in the work of their respective Lodges
was first developed by their participation in club activities. They have
visited the sick. They have assisted the widows and orphans of deceased
or distressed Masons. They have discharged the homely, human duties

Adopted.
MASONIC INFORMATION

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration the report of the Committee on Masonic Information and with
reference thereto offers the following:
In the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes the
report of the Committee ori Masonic Information is a brilliant contribution.to the subject with which it deals and in its recommendations points
the way to a great advance in the solution of a problem which has vexed
Grand Lodge during a third of the century and has cost approximately
$75,000. The Committee points out that "notwithstanding the time, effort,
and money devoted to it, the program has often been referred to and
sometimes justified, as experimental. Every Grand Master, with only two
or three exceptions, has stressed in his annual report the need for Masonic
instruction, urged its prosecution, and some have described it as a vital
requirement. None, however, has had the genius to say what it should
consist of or the magic touch to put a successful scheme into operation."
The Committee on Masonic Information makes a searching review of
the activities above referred to. This review is divided into five periods,
each of which is thoroughly discussed.

250

251

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee, in its own language, "dissects the problem" and
directs attention to fundamentals which have been overlooked. Of these
there are eight, all clearly stated. We believe the first of them is worthy
of quotation here, as follows:
"l. What facts, theory or doctrine does the Grand Lodge expect the
Committee on Masonic Information to inculcate? The Grand Lodge has
not said. Obviously, it is not to teach what is in the ritual, for that is
already thoroughly taken care of. What is the Grand Lodge's authorized
and approved version of the·history of Freemasonry? It has none, except
what is found in the ritual. What is the Grand Lodge's interpretation of
the symbolism of Freemasonry? It hasn't any, except the ritual. What
is the doctrine of the Grand Lodge about the philosophy, religion, or
principles of Freemasonry? Obviously, nothing except what is already
taught in the ritual. Therefore, if your Committee circulates any information at all, it must be in addition to, subtraction from, or modification
of the only authorized doctrine of Grand Lodge, viz, the ritual. Hence, we
have the anomaly of a Committee officially and solemnly authorized to
disseminate unauthorized materials. Furthermore, this must be expected
to vary from time to time as the personnel, resourcefulness, imagination,
and concepts of the Committee change."
The Committee finds, correctly we think, that "there is one critical
period lasting a few weeks when Masonic education or information is
earnestly desired and will be avidly absorbed. This is while the candidate
is awaiting or passing through the degrees."
The Committee then proceeds, on the basis of the foregoing conclusion,
to outline its proposal ·for a significant departure in the activities of
Masonic Information. This comprehends the presentation to each applicant for the degrees after his election but prior. to his initiation, of an
attractively printed pamphlet covering the history of Freemasonry, its
foundations such as the Gothic Constitutions, the story of Gothic Architecture, the transition from purely operative Masonry to theoretic or
speculative Masonry, information concerning records of the early Lodges,
the formation of the Grand Lodge of England, the introduction of the
Craft into America, old tenets and customs of the Craft, the doctrine of
Freemasonry, what the Institution regards as the proper attitude of the
individual Mason, and many other matters calculated not only to inform
the mind of the applicant but also to establish within him a deep respect
for Freemasonry.
It is proposed that following the initiation of the candidate another
pamphlet shall be presented to him by the Officers of his Lodge, the same
referring to Apprentices, their status and relationship to their Lodges,
appropriate information relative to Lodges, historical or otherwise, and
a great deal of other material and advice which, in our opinion, should
prove extremely interesting to the entered Apprentice, and indeed which
could be read and re-read by every Mason.
If Grand Lodge approves the recommendations of this Committee

similar pamphlets will be provided for Fellowcrafts and Master Masons.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes heartily approves the
proposals of the Committee on Masonic Information.
We therefore approve the recommendations of the Committee on
Masonic Information as follows:
1. That the two manuscripts herein referred to be approved by Grand
Logde; and that your Committee be authorized to have the same printed
and distributed to the Lodges.
2. That it be made the duty of the Secretary of each Lodge to send,
to each candidate, along with the notice of the favorable ballot upon
such candidate, a copy of the pamphlet entitled, "Address to the Candidate," and to hand to each Candidate, at the close of the Charge in the
Entered Apprentice Degree, a copy of the pamphlet entitled, "Book of
the Entered Apprentice."
3. That your Committee on Masonic Information be continued for the
ensuing year.
We understand that the recommended appropriations have been considered and will be reported upon by the Committee on Finance.
Adopted.

LIFE MEMBERSHIP

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration a resolution offered by Brother E. A. Troxel, Past Master of
Elysian Lodge No. 418, proposing that Sec. 253 of our Ordinances, pro-

252 .

253

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

viding for life memberships, be amended to require that a Lodge fix a
sliding scale of fees for life memberships computed according to the age
of the member and the dues charged by a Lodge. Younger members would
pay a proportionately higher fee than older members.
Under our present law a Lo.dge may establish a system of life mem·
bership by a resolution which must he approved by the Grand Master
fixing a fee which in the judgment of the members of the Lodge is just
and equitable, provided that it be not less than $150.00 if the dues of pte
'Lodge are $12.00 a year and greater or less in proportion as the dues of
the Lodge are greater or less than $12.00.
Brother Troxel proposes a definite scale of fees to he charged, based
on the ages of the members. This particular scale is worked out on the
basis of $12.00 annual dues and can be adjusted up or down proportion·
ately as the dues fixed by the Lodge are higher or lower than $12.00. The
scale of fees is too long to repeat here but a Brother of 22 years would
pay $335.00, while a Brother of 60 years would pay $200.00. We have
not had an opportunity to determine whether the scale of fees is actuarily
sound or not but we have no doubt that Brother Troxel has spent a great
deal of time and thought in working it out. However, we feel that should
Grand Lodge consider adopting such a plan more time and thoughl
should be spent in working out a scale of fees not only for $12.00 annual
dues but also a different scale for Lodges charging amounts other than
$12.00 a year.
We cannot agree with the reasoning of this proposal. We must remem·
her that most of the Lodges of our jurisdiction do not have life member·
ship and that the legislation in effect at present is permissive only, Grand
Lodge having taken no action whatever on whether life memberships are
desirable or not desirable for Lodges.
To pay dues is a Masonic duty, and the regular payment of dues by
individual members undergirds the strength of our institution. If a
Lodge, in its wisdom, accords its members the privilege of paying a fixed
sum, and thus procure an immunity from dues for life, it rests with the
individual members whether or not they take advantage of that privilege,
but the duty is still incumbent upon them to pay dues, either annually, or
for life in advance. Every person pays the same amount of dues whether
he is young or old, whether he goes to Lodge or is very inactive, and
this equality of members, so far as paying dues is concerned, is another
factor that adds strength to our institution. If a person is in distress or
unfortunate he may have his dues remitted, and this is just and right.
To Your Committee it appears that the proposal for a fixed scale of fees
smacks somewhat of commercialism. The fees are fixed not on an equal
basis, but according to age, and on the theory that' if a person is going ·
to live longer then he should pay more.to enjoy a life membership, and
that if a person is well along in years the cost of the fee is discounted,
as it were.
There is no question that yo~ger men by purchasing life memberships

in their Lodges might outlive the actual payment if it is figured in dollars
and cents. We feel however that Masonic membership should he figured
in terms other than dollars and cents, and in a way that is just and equit·
able to all.
We have a feeling also that the proposed resolution would invade the
rights of the individual Lodges. While we have many rules and regula·
tions by which the Lodges are governed, generally speaking Lodges are
left to manage their own financial affairs, and we feel that they should not
be required to adopt a scale of life membership fees which they might
consider unwieldly and unworkable.
We therefore recommend that the proposed legislation be not adopted.
Adopted.
MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred to
it the suggestion by the Grand Master with reference to the erection of
a Masonic Memorial Temple to be used as the meeting place and headquarters for this Grand Lodge.
We agree with the Grand Master that it is eminently fitting that con·
sideration be given to finding a more suitable meeting place for this
Grand Lodge. While many of us who have sat in this hall for years have
certain sentimental attachments there is no question that it is very inconvenient for many who attend, and if a more suitable meeting place
could be secured or erected which would house our growing Grand Lodge
activities it would be eminently fitting and proper. In addition we feel
that the erection of such a building would be the most fitting, most useful
and most lasting Memorial which could be erected to the Masons who
have served their country.
Probably we all agree that if a suitable building could be erected in
a proper place without financial worry we would all vote for it unhesi·
tatingly. However, there are many phases to a problem of this kind,-the
disposal of the old building, the location of the new building, particu·
larly with regard to accessibility, the proper medium through which the
building is erected, either by the formation of a building company or
by Grand Lodge direct. Some of your committee do not feel themselves
entirely in accord with the suggestion of the Grand Master that the power
be placed in a committee to erect a building, but we cannot disagree without knowing more about the whole project.
The greatest factor however in connection with this proposal is finance,
and it is quite likely that the whole project will stand or fall according to
whether or not Grand Lodge wishes to embark on a program of financing
this project.
Therefore, while individually we might be very much in favor of the
plan, since the problem is mainly one of finance we feel that it would be
premature for us to express an opinion or make a recommendation until
Grand Lodge has decided whether or not the project is feasible from a
financial standpoint. This matter has been referred to the Finance Com-

255

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mittee and until the Finance Committee has made its report, and Grand
Lodge has taken action thereon, we feel that we cannot make a recom·
mendation.
Adopted.

THE FREEDOM TRAIN

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has studied with
interest the resolution introduced by Brother Arthur Joel, Inspector of
the 48-A Masonic District. Brother Joel proposes that the Grand Master
be empowered and directed to appoint a committee through which the
advent of the Freedom Train in the State of California may be properly
publicized to all Masons and Masonic Lodges in this jurisdiction so that
Lodges may advise their members and all Masons to visit the Freedom
Train and to influence others to avail themselves of this great opportunity.
We feel indebted to Brother Joel for his alertness and thoughtfulness
in bringing this matter to the attention of the Grand Lodge and are cer,.
tain that his proposal will find ready response in the hearts and minds
of all of the brethren of this great state.
When the Freedom Train arrives in our town we shall see a modern
streamlined train guarded by a picked company of United States marines
and having on display some of the most precious documents of our his·
tory including the original draft of the Declaration of Independence
showing the changes made by Thomas Jefferson.
We believe that we as Masons and as citizens should pay due heed to
the advent of the Freedom Train and all that it implies and that the Grand
Lodge should urge and encourage all Ma!'ons to visit it.
There are many reasons why this should he done. The Freedom Train
already has been scorned and snee~ed at by those who are not in sympa·
thy with our concept of free government and the ideals represented by
the Freedom Train and the quiet presence of large numbers 9f our citi·
zens wherever the Train stops will be a solemn and dignified reproach
to those who would cast aspersions on these hallowed symbols of our
liberties.
To visit the Freedom Train is a duty incumbent upon all good citizens
just as saluting our flag, exercising our right of franchise and performing
the many privileges of citizenship in the ordinary walks of life.
There is however a better and more cogent reason for our participation
in this great event. We have a great heritage in our country. Our standard
of living, our freedom of opportunity, our inherent civic rights are beyond
comparison with those of any other country or civilization and yet we are
too prone to take them for granted and to feel that our forefathers guaran·
teed us freedom for all time.
If the advent of the Freedom Train will enable us to envision more
clearly the ideals upon which our government was founded, if the sight
of these precious documents will enable us to realize anew the heroism, the
suffering, the sacrifices and the unflinching integrity of purpose which
brought them into being and bring home to us the necessity of alertness

Adopted.

· Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to whom was referred
the resolution presented by W. Harry L. Buckalew, Master of Las Palmas
Lodge No. 366, have had the same under consideration and beg leave
to report as follows:
The resolution relates to the failure of a member to act when appointed
upon an lnv~stigation Committee and asking Grand Lodge to declare
such neglect or refusal, with certain excusable circumstances, to constitute Un-Masonic conduct.
Grand Lodge has often been criticised for burdening the craft with
much legislation and for interfering unjustifiably in the internal affairs
of constituent lodges.
Your ..Committee are of the opinion that the proposed legislation is
objectionable from either of the foregoing standpoints. Every Master
of a Lodge has it within his own power and authority to enforce any
order necessary for the proper administration of the affairs of the Lodge
and legislation upon the subject is unnecessary.
We, therefore, recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
Respectfully submitted,

The Constitution of the United States
An address delivered before the Grand Lodge of Masons in California at San Francisco on Thursday, October 16, 1947, by William R. McKay, Judge of the
Superior Court of Los Angeles County, Chairman of the
Grand Lodge Committee on Constitution Month Observance.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Would it be an unlicensed trespass of the imagination to conceive that
on the night preceding that 30th day of April, 1789, when from the
balcony of the City Hall the Chancellor of the State of New York admin·
istered to George Washington the solemn oath faithfully to execute the

264

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

office of President of the United States and to the best of his ability to
preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States, in the
visions of the night the guardian angel of the Father of our Country had
appeared before him in the venerated form of his mother and, to cheer and
encourage him in the performance of the momentous and solemn duties
that he was about to assume, had delivered to him a suit of celestial
armor - a helmet consisting of the principles of piety, of justice, of
honor, and of benevolence with which from his earliest infancy he had
hitherto walked through life in the presence of all his brethren; a spear
studded with the self-evident truths of the Declaration of Independence;
a sword, the same with which he had led the armies of his country through
the war of freedom to the triumphal arch of independence; a cor8e·
let and cuisses of long experience and habitual intercourse in peace and
war with the world of mankind, his contemporaries of the human race,
in all their stages of civilization; and last of all, the Constitution of the
United States, a shield embossed by heavenly hands with the future
history of his country. Yes, gentlemen, on the shield-the Constitution
of the United States--was sculptured by forms unseen and in characters
then invisible to mortal eyes the predestined and prophetic history of
the one confederated people of the North American Union.
lri the bosoms of this people thus heterogeneously composed there was
burning, kindled at different furnaces, but all furnaces of afiliction, one
clear steady flame of liberty. Bold and daring enterprise, stubborn endurance of privation, unflinching intrepidity in facing danger, and
inflexible adherence to conscientious principles had steeled to energetic
and unyielding hardihood the characters of the primitive settlers of all
these colonies. The members of that convention, in going about the
great work before them, deliberately laid aside the means by which all
preceding legislators had aimed to accomplish a life work. In founding
a-strong and efficient government adequate to the raising up of a power·
ful and prosperous people their first step was to reject the institutions in
which other governments entrusted their strength and prosperity and
which they had at least regarded as the necessary conditions of stability
and order. The world had settled down into the belief that a hereditary
• monarch was necessary to give strength to the executive power. The
framers of our Constitution provided for an elective chief magistrate
chosen every four years. Every other country had been betrayed into
the admission of a distinction of ranks in society under the absurd impres·
sion that privileged orders were necessary to the permanence of the social
system.
The framers of our Constitution established everything on the purely
natural basis of a uniform equality of the elective franchise to be exercised by all the citizens at fixed and short intervals. In other cowitries
it had been thought necessary to constitute some one political center
towards which all political power should tend and at which, in the last
resort, it should be exercised. The framers of the Constitution devised

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

265

o!

a scheme c~nfe~erate and representative sovereign republics united in
a happy d~s~nbut10n ?f powers _which, reserving to the separate states
all the political functions essential to local administration and private
justice, bestowed upon the federal government those and those only
require~ for the service of the whole. Thus was completed the great
revolutionary movement; thus was perfected that mature organization
of a free system destined, as we trust, to stand forever as the exemplar of
popular government; thus was discharged the duty of our fathers to
themselves, to the country, and to the world.
In every country, I care not what its form of government0 there must
?e so~eone or .so.met_hing sup~eme above all. In an empire it is emperor;
m a ~mgdo~ it is ki~g_; _hut m a republic the only sovereign is the law,
and JUSt as m every civilized country to offer violence to the sovereign is
treason to the state, so in a republic to offer violence to the law is the
highes_t crime against the nation and the greatest menace to its future.
Ours is a government of law, and when I saw "law" I do not mean
simply that which we write upon the statute books. I mean that great
body of wisdom and justice which is the fruit of all the ages to which
the wise and just men of the Orient, of Greece, of Rome, of eve~ civilized
country since have contributed-that great body of the law which we
feel in our hearts expresses the highest wisdom and the most exalted
sense of justice of the best men of all time.
It is true, ours is a government by the majority, but it is something
vastly more. When our forefathers met at Independence Hall in Phila·
delphia to frame the Constitution they were familiar with the lessons of
histor~. They knew that republics had risen and fallen throughout the
c~ntunes because of.the,~anny practiced by the majority in those republics, and so they said, There are some rights so sacred that they must
be placed forever beyond the power of even the largest majority." They
said, "The right to worship God in accordance with the dictates of one's
own conscience is a right so sacred and precious that no majority should
take it away and that the law would protect the humblest individual in
the exercise of that sacred right." They read history. They knew that
the m?me~t man emerged from savagery the instinct of property developed m his heart. They knew that all progress and all civilization were
based upon that concept, with others, and so they said that, no matter
W:hat t~e passion or the whim of the majority, the property of the individual is beyond the power of the majority and the humblest individual
in all the land cannot be deprived of that property except by due process
of law, and law in that larger sense which I attempted to define a moment
ago. So the liberty of the individual and those incalculable rights which
we denominate our Bill of Rights were made the basis of our government.
Why, my Brethren, tyranny is just as odious to the American citizen
whether it is practiced by a crowned monarch or whether it is practiced by .
a mob. Justice and righteousness were made the cornerstone of our

266

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

government and not the passing whim of any majority, no matter how
large. That is the thing which distinguishes the American republic
from all the republics of the past; that is the thing which has made us
great and prosperous; and that is the thing which has made us an example to all the liberty-loving people of all the world.
I wonder if we realize just how much we mean as a people, not only
to ourselves, hut to all the world. I wonder if we realize what the force
of our example has been. I .wonder if we understand that this government which I have attempted feebly to describe has been the inspiration
of every enlightened statesman in the world and of every measure looking
to an enlargement of human liberty. America has been a solace to the
patriot dying in other lands because, though he has fallen, his failing
vision beholds as recompensing hope for his sacrifice the Flag of America and he dies content in the faith bestowed by that symbol that one
day men will be free throughout the earth. It has been said often, and
it is everlastingly true, that America is the best and the last hope of mankind. If we should fail, which God forbid, where in all the world may
the broken spirit find refuge? Where beneath the shining heavens will
there be found a haven for those who have failed, for those whose dreams
have not come true, for those who seek a land of liberty, a land of right•
eousness, a land of law? We will not fail-we cannot fail-if we do
our duty, but the time has passed when we can remain silent regarding
those fundamentals of government and permit the enemies of social
order everwhere to occupy the center of the stage. The time has come
when we must take issue with those who, infatuated with chaotic dreams,
are seeking to undermine the bulwarks of government, when we can no
longer refrain from exercising and proclaiming the truth- truth as virile
today as was a hundred years ago--that "eternal vigilance is the price
of liberty."
I do not subscribe to the doctrine somewhat prevalent at the moment
that the past should he scrapped, that it can be of little use to us in solving the problems of this new era, nor to that twin monstrosity, that anything of today or tomorrow that is consistent with what has gone before
is a menace to mankind. Out of the past come the lessons of experience.
·Out of the past come incentive and inspiration. Out of the past come
memories of courage and self-sacrifice, of loyalty and devotion.
The time is not far distant when the elements of society in the United
States that have been rudely and wickedly disturbed by reason of the great
holocaust through which we have just passed must be readjusted and the
old order of things re-established, possibly with modifications growing
as necessities out of the shock they have sustained.
It seems that a century of trial has somewhat dulled the halo about
democracy to fools and those of little faith, though the great optimism
has abated sectarian fury, abolished legal slavery, protected and enlarged
manhood suffrage, mitigated much social injustice, increased kindness
and gentleness, preserved the form of the Union, conquered its wilder-

nesses, developed great agencies of culture, and made itself a symbol of
prosperity. But it also developed new and hateful masters in politics
and new shapes of temptation and wrong-doing, and after a generation
of amazing constructive efforts, without sufficient leisure, perhaps, for
ethical consideration, it is in danger of its own strength, and it must discover and protect itself with its own strength.
I am not railing against great constructive forces, or uttering cheap
prophecies of damnation. I am simply claiming that democracy, like a
man's character, is never clear out of danger. It is not selfishness nor
corruption alone which we have to fear, for we have vanquished these
before, hut as much the temper of despair and faithlessness which blinds
the eyes of our youth to the heroic simplicity and love of freedom at the
heart of the American people.
But I have no fear of the future. I think, looking around upon the
country at present, that even if it would seem to us at times that there
are gravest perils which confront us, that even though there may be
evidence of weakening in our character, notwithstanding this I say,
I believe the great American commonwealth contains elements which
alone can continue to he the leaders of civilization-the elements of
fundamental power, abiding virtue, public and private. Wealth will not
preserve a state; it must be the aggregation of individual integrity in
its members and in its citizens that shall preserve it. That integrity,
I believe, exists deep-rooted among our people.
Sometimes when I read accounts of vice here and there eating into the
hearts of the people, I feel inclined to become pessimistic ; but when
I come face to face with the American and see him in his life, as he truly
is; when I reflect upon the great body of people that stretch from one
side of this country to the other, their homes perched on every hill and
nestled in every valley, and recognize the sterling virtue and the kind of
character that sustains it, built on the rock of those principles that our
fathers transmitted to us, my pessimism disappears and I know that not
only for this immediate time, hut for many long generations to come,
with that reservoir of virtue to draw from, we shall sustain and carry
both ourselves and the whole human race forward.

AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS

Following precedent, yo~r committee has again employed Brother
Walter Parker to audit the accounting records of the Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, Masonic Homes, and the Endowment Fund.
The audit indicates that all receipts and disbursements have been
properly recorded and that all moneys and securities are on hand. A copy
of the report has been filed with the Grand Secretary. It will be printed
in the Annual Proceedings. The cost of the audit was, to Grand Lodge
$250 and to the Masonic Homes $800.
This is an increase over former years to Grand Lodge of $100 and to
the Masonic Homes of $200.
REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER

This Grand Lodge officer is again entitled to the commendation of
Grand Lodge for the able manner in which he is handling the manifold
financial transactions of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, and the
Endowment Fund.
The auditor's report indicates that all records are in good order and
all moneys and securities properly on hand.
The report of the Grand Treasurer indicates the extent of the financial
transactions to which he must give attention.
Last session of Grand Lodge appropriated $1,200 for the use of the
Grand Treasurer in caring for the expenses of his office. Of this amount
$1,002.80 was required. For the coming year we recommend an appro·
priation of $1,200, with the understanding that should the Grand Treasurer find this sum not sufficient to properly care for the expenses of this
office for the year, whatever additional amount he may find is needed is
to be considered appropriated.
REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY

Our Grand Secretary reports a membership of 173,917, the greatest
in our California history. All activities are flourishing in a healthy
manner.
Obviously these gratifying conditions are reflected in the Grand Lodge
office where duties and responsibilities are also increasing. Selling and
shipping of supplies are surprisingly large time consumers. Extensive
correspondence and telephone services are constantly increasing. The
receiving, recording, and faithful caretaking of a growing volume of
legacies and securities imposes a greater load on the office.

TRAVELING EXPENSES OF GRAND MASTER

This committee again wishes to follow previously established precedence in encouraging the Grand Master to travel as extensively as he finds
it expedient to so do and expresses the thought that the visitations of
the Grand Master to all parts of the Jurisdiction are of distinctive advan·
tage to the craft. The growth of the Jurisdiction makes additional drafts
upon the time of the Grand Master, both in administering the affairs of
Grand Lodge as well as for visitations. Due to this growth and these
demands, it is difficult to determine what the requirements of his expenses
may be.
·
Your committee has discussed both with the outgoing and the incoming
Grand Master the needs for the coming year. Basing its judgment upon
these discussions, it is budgeting $7,000 for the purpose of covering the
Grand Master's expenses, with the understanding, however, that it is
to be left to his good judgment to decide how much, if any, additional
he may consider necessary to expend in properly performing the duties
of his office and that should the amount which is being allowed prove
insufficient a recommendation for an additional amount should he presented to the next session of the Grand Lodge.
Your Committee on Finance recommends an appropriation of $7,000
to cover the traveling expenses of the Gr and Master.
GRAND MASTER' S STENOGRAPHIC SERVICES

For a number of years an allowance for stenographic services for the
Grand Master has been made. In order that the Grand Master may
properly perform the duties of his office it is essential that he should have
the proper stenographic service. It is also entirely proper that Grand
Lodge should pay for such services. For the year just closed the Grand
Master was allowed $1,200 for this purpose. The full amount was needed.
The message of the Grand Master amply displays the extent of the
work required of our Grand Masters.
The incoming Grand Master at the present time does not find need of
a secretary. It is the conclusion of this committee that to properly take
care of all the requirements of his office a permanent secreta_ry sho'lild
be employed. This means that an appropriation greater than that of
a year ago will be required.
Your committee therefore recommends an appropriation of $2,000
for the purpose of covering the expenses of the incoming Grand Master
in employing stenographic service.

PORTRAIT OF LA WREN CE C. KELLEY

Last year this committee recommended an appropriation of $300 for
the purpose of having painted the portrait of Brother Lawrence C. Kelley,
who, as the membership will recall with sorrow, was taken by death
within two weeks of the time of his installation as Grand Master.
It developed during the year that an appropriate portrait could not
he obtained for the allowance made. After much effort by Past Grand
Master William' Rhodes Hervey and our Grand Secretary, a price of $600
for the painting of this portrait was finally obtained. A discussion was
had with the Grand Master and the chairman of the Committee on
Finance, after which it was concluded best to have the portrait painted
at the additional cost, this due to the fact that to delay would mean that
those who best knew Brother Kelley would not see his portrait. The
Grand Master thereupon ordered the painting of the portrait at this price,
in which the chairman of the Finance Committee concurred.
Your committee therefore recommends that the action of the Grand
Master in ordering the portrait painted at an additional cost of $300
together with the framing of same for $30 he approved.

TRAVELING EXPENSES OF GRAND LECTURER AND ASSISTANTS

The regulations of Grand Lodge provide that the expenses of the Grand

maintain the excellence of the esoteric work of the Order, shall he reimbursed to them. Last Grand Lodge appropriated $2,500 to cover these
expenses. Of this amount $2,355.39 was expended.

$2,500 will he needed.
Your Committee on Finance recommends the appropriation of this
sum.
REIMBURSEMENT OF EXPENSES OF INSPECTORS

Grand Lodge regulations provide that the expenses of the Inspectors,
incurred in visiting the lodges under their jurisdiction and under such
regulations as may he set up by the Grand Lecturer, shall he returned
to them out of the funds of Grand Lodge. It is entirely proper that Grand
Lodge should sustain this expense.
Attention is again called to the outstanding work which is being performed by these Masonic servants and the great amount of time and
expense they ai:e out and particularly to the very small amount of return
which is requested. This past year the same record has been made by
this excellent corps of officers.
A year ago the appropriation made by Grand Lodge to take care of
these expenses was $3,000. Of this amount $2,641.95 was asked for.
In discussing with the Grand Lecturer the amount which he considers
should he set up to cover the traveling expenses of the Inspectors, he has
suggested an allowance for this purpose of $3,000. He also calls to the
attention of this committee the provision originally adopted that the
Inspectors in the metropolitan districts should not he allowed any expense
for the use of their cars and advises he regards this as an injustice and
now recommends that all Inspectors throughout the jurisdiction should
he reimbursed for the use of their cars on an equal basis.

lear.

GRAND LODGE WEEK ACTIVITIES

In the report of the Committee on Finance at the last Communication
and approved by a vote of Grand Lodge a suggestion was made that

activities at the present session, including the annual get-together dinner,
entertainment of Grand Lodge officers, distinguished guests, their ladies
and Grand Lodge members and the annual pilgrimage to the Decoto
Home.
A great deal of praise is due Andrew Burke and the members of the
Activities Committee for their efficient handling of their work, for although the price of meals at the get-together dinner was raised $1 per
plate and other expenses were similarly increased, yet the committee
has accomplished its work in the finest style, at a total expenditure of
about $100 less than the suggested sum.
Your Committee on Finance therefore recommends that all expenses
incurred for Grand Lodge activities during this week be paid out of the
funds of Grand Lodge, subject to the requisite audit.
This committee is unable to recommend an appropriation for the

Activities Committee again endeavor to keep its expenditures within
the same limits as this year; namely, $4,000.

In 1943 the Lodge found itself unable to longer keep up the full pay·
ments on the agreement and appealed to Grand Lodge for help. Grand
Master Wood ordered the payment to the surviving spouse of $150
monthly, with the understanding that it was to be regarded as a loan to
the Lodge and that the Lodge was to repay to Grand Lodge not less than
$50.00 monthly.
This arrangement was approved by the Finance Committee and a
similar arrangement was approved by Grand Lodge for the years 1944,
1945 and 1946. During the· past two years the Lodge has been able to
repay to Grand Lodge $100 monthly. Up to October first of this year
Grand Lodge has advanced $7,800. The Lodge has repaid $5,000, leaving a balance due Grand Lodge of $2,800.
Mrs. Bush, the surviving spouse, is still alive although well passed
eighty years of age. To keep the contract in good standing the payments
must continue to be paid.
Your Committee on Finance therefore offers the following resolution
and recommends its adoption:
Resolved: That there be paid from the funds of Grand Lodge monthly
to Sotoyome Lodge No. 123, a sum not to exceed $150, during the lifetime of Mrs. Bush, with the understanding that such sum shall be used to
fulfill its obligation to Mrs. Bush and that all sums advanced, including .
the amount heretofore paid, shall be considered as a loan to Sotoyome
Lodge and be repaid by such Lodge in a sum of not less than $100 per
month, until the full amount advanced shall have been repaid, together
with interest thereon at the rate of 3 per cent per annum.
