GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC NATIONAL ME MORIAL

There has been referred to this committee that portion of the Grand
Master's address dealing with the Memorial and also the report of the
Special Committee appointed by the Grand Master.
This committee has studied the report of the Special Committee with
great care. It shows that this Special Committee not only took the necessary time to attend the annual session of the Memorial Association and
thus obtain first hand information of the Memorial and of the activities
of the Association, but also made a careful analysis of the financial prob·
lems confronting the Memorial. It all displays great care and study and
is the first complete and analytical study that has appeared dealing with
the affairs of the Memorial.
It is to be noted the report is critical of the administration of the Memorial. This Committee feels this criticism is justified and sustains the
position heretofore taken by Grand Lodge. While we are reluctant to
recommend further appropriations to the Memorial, yet we see no other
way out and have the faith and good name of the Masons of the nation
preserved.

281

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Your Committee on Finance is therefore in full accord with the recommendations made by the Special Committee, that a $1.00 donation be
required of the initiate and that a 15 cent per capita be levied; both of
these recommendations to be continued in effect until the full amount
due from this Grand Jurisdiction as its proper proportion of the amount
necessary for completion and endowment and for costs of administration,
operation and maintenance and also to pay for its proper proportion of
monies to make up our deficit for past years.
·
It should be directed to the attention of Grand Lodge that, although a
policy for the raising of all funds that may be properly due from this
Jurisdiction to the Memorial Association has been recommended by the
Special Committee and that it is entirely proper and your Committee
on Finance is in accord with the recommendation that Grand Lodge shall
at this time adopt a policy for the ultimate raising of our Jurisdiction's
full share of the total cost of the Memorial and yet, this Grand Lodge
session cannot bind future Grand Lodges on the per capita levy and therefore in presenting the resolution for the levy it must, of necessity, he made
for this year alone.
This committee is also very much in accord with the recommendation
that all funds raised by the per capita levy (including the $25,770.45 now
in the treasury of Grand Lodge, accumulated from the per capita levy of ·
15 cents of a year ago), shall he placed in a special fund to be known
as the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Fund and not to be
paid over to the Memorial Association until Grand Lodge, or the committee composed of the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer and Chairman of
the Finance Committee (as recommended in the report of the Special Committ~) shall determine. It is understood that such funds shall be invested
in such securities as are provided for in the investment of endowment
funds.
It also seems to this committee that the conclusions of the Special Committee on the Memorial are correct, namely, that any sums donated by
the Initiates should not be impounded, but should be paid to the Memorial Association at least annually. It is the recommendation of your
Committee on Finance that all donation!i made by the Initiates should be
deposited in the endowment fund of the Association to be kept in perpetuity, the income therefrom alone to be used for the operating expenses
of the Association.
Your Committee on Finance therefore recommends that that portion
of the report of the Special Committee on the George Washington Masonic National Memorial, recommending the $1.00 donation required of
the Initiate, he referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for proper legis·
lation. It also presents the following resolution:
Resolved: That a per capita of fifteen (15¢) cents be levied, the pro·
ceeds to .be placed in a fund known as the George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Fund, said fund to be impounded and to be remitted
to said Memorial Association only at such time as authorized by some

future communication of Grand Lodge, or by a committee composed of
the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer and the Chairman of the Finance
Committee, and be·it further
Resolved: That the sum of $25,770.45 now on hand from the per capita
levy of last session be placed in said fund, under the same restrictions
as are such funds that may be collected from subsequent levies, and that
all monies now in or hereafter to be placed in the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial Fund shall, at all times, be under the con·
trol of Grand Lodge and should Grand Lodge determine, after an ap·
propriate time has elapsed, not to donate any or all of said funds to said
Memorial, then Grand Lodge shall have the power, by appropriate action,
of making other disposition of said monies.

MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Your Committee on Finance has had referred to it by the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes that portion of the Grand Master's ad·
dress suggesting the appointment of a special committee, pointing toward
the construction of a Masonic Memorial Temple, it being thoughtfully
anel clearly pointed out by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that the ultimate determination of the feasibility of such a Temple will
be based on financial grounds rather than as a matter of policy.
It is well known that the Grand Lodge hall has been inadequate for
many years to handle the members in attendance and it has become more
and more apparent in the last few years that the lay-out of Grand Lodge
headquarters is unsatisfactory for efficient operation. The Grand Master
is to be highly commended for bringing this matter to the attention of
Grand Lodge, as well as for pointing out the desirability of having the
Temple available for our centennial celebration, if possible.
However, as pointed out by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, in their report on the subject, the ramifications of the subject are
so varied and wide that your Committee on Finance is unable to draw an
intelligent conclusion concerning the erection of a new Temple from the
facts now available.
It is therefore recommended that a special ·committee be appointed to
investigate all phases in connection with the feasibility of the erection
of a Masonic Memorial Temple, to report its conclusions at the next
annual communication of this Grand Lodge and that said committee be
charged with determining, as accurately as possible, the location, the size
and scope of the temple and the estimated cost thereof, including land,
building and furnishings; that it prepare a budget of operating expenses
and income of the Masonic Memorial Temple. It is also to determine the
disposition of the Grand Lodge interest in the present temple and investi·
gate the possibility and probable cost of remodelling the present Grand
Lodge offices and hall to make them adequate for the best operation of
Grand Lodge.
It is further recommended that an appropriation of $1,000 be furnished

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this committee, with which to undertake the necessary surveys, with the
understanding that if this amount is inadequate for the performance of
its duties such additional sums as may be approved by the Grand Master
for the use of this committee are hereby authorized.

COLUMBIA LODGE HALL

Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration the report
of the Most Worshipful Leon 0. Whitsell, on the rebuilding of the old
Masonic Temple in the old town of Columbia. It also has had extensive
discussions with the M. W. Brother.
As the committee understands it, there is at the present time no part of
the old building now existing, nor will Grand Lodge or any Masonic
entity hold title to the lot on which the building is to be erected. It will
be necessary to erect the building through the consent of and on ground
leased from the State Park Commission for that purpose.
Your Committee on Finance is in sympathy with the plan to rebuild
this old Temple. However, in its judgment the information now on hand
is not sufficient to warrant the recommendation of an appropriation. The
following information should be furnished to the committee:
Complete plans and specifications of the proposed building, so that
further checking might be made on the probable cost.
·
A list of the proposed funishings for the building, together with an
estimate of the cost of same.
The proposed plan for the future use and occupancy of the building,
together with an estimate of the cost of operation and maintenance.
Complete information as to the plans of the State Park Commission for
the restoration of the old community, together with information as to
progress already made.
Until this information is received this committee has concluded to withhold any recommendation for an appropriation.
It must be borne in mind that after the hall is once built there will be
a constant recurring expense for its operation and maintenance. Provision for these expenses must be made and cannot be left to uncertain
agencies. It appears to this committee that the only certain way of pro·
vi ding for these expenses is by Grand Lodge assuming this additional
obligation.
Your Committee on Finance therefore feels that it should have as complete an estimate as possible of the full responsibilities which Grand
Lodge will have to assume before making any recommendations.

CENTENNIAL ARRANGEMENTS COMMITTEE

There has been referred to your Finance Committee the report of the
Centennial Arrangements Committee. Your Committee is in accord with
the full report of the committee, together with the various recommendations which it makes.
It should be pointed out, however, that in presenting a resolution for
the per capita levy we cannot bind future Grand Lodges and therefore
the levy can only be made for this year.
It also appears to this committee that more definite plans for the celebration probably will be developed before the next session of Grand
Lodge and also a more accurate estimate of what the actual expenses may
be, therefore the next Grand Lodge will be the better enabled to determine whether the full three years per capita levy will be needed.
Your Committee on Finance offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption :
Resolved: That a per capita of 25 cents be levied to provide for the
expenses of the centennial celebration of Grand Lodge, the sum derived
therefrom to be carried in a special fund.

The financial affairs of the Lodge are somewhat tangled. The Lodge has
on hand $5,200, of which amount $4,200 was received from insurance,
and a damage claim against a contracting firm and its insurance carrier
for $25,000. It is thought that $8,000 will be eventually recovered from
this damage claim.
The Lodge has had prepared plans and specifications for a new building with an estimated cost for its erection and furnishings of $25,000.
The Lodge requests a loan from Grand Lodge of $15,000.
At the time of the publicati~n of the last Roster this Lodge had a mem·
bership of sixty-six. It is receiving some petitions each year, the representative advised about seven annually. He reports that Camptonville is
a reasonably substantial community and his estimate is that it will remain so.
It is obvious that the ability of the Lodge to rebuild on the plan outlined will depend on the amount which it may collect on its claim for
damages. It is believed that it will receive not less than $7,500 and prob·
ably $8,000.
It has been a long established policy of Grand Lodge that whenever a
lodge, through calamity, has suffered damage to its temple beyond its
own ability to sustain, that it can apply to Grand Lodge for assistance.
The conclusions of your Finance Committee are,~
That the Lodge is entitled to help from Grand Lodge;
That the Lodge should not be required to await the next session of
Grand Lodge before receiving the nece8sary help for the rebuilding of
its temple.
That this Lodge should exhaust all its own avenues of assistance before leaning on Grand Lodge for help.
That the assistance to be reridered by Grand Lodge to this Lodge should
be leh to the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge Financing and the
Chairman of the Committee on Finance to determine.
The recomme~dation of your Finance Committee therefore is, that
whatever amount these two Chairmen may recommend, but not to exceed
$13,000, be appropriated and paid to Gravel Range Lodge No. 59, with
the understanding that such an amount will complete the building and
furnishings of the temple, the terms of such advance to be left to these
two Chairmen to determine.

IN GRAND LODGE
MORNING SESSION

Friday, October 17, 1947
Grand Lodge was called on at 9 :30 A. M., the Grand Master presiding.
The following prayer was offered by the Grand Chaplain:
Great Architect of the Universe, Our God and Our Father:

We have beheld in the Book on the Altar thy words: Behold I have set
before thee a new heaven and a new earth.
In the glory of a new morning which thou hast given us, we come to thee
on the closing day of the Communication to thank thee. Forgive us if we
have failed thee or our brothers.
In awe and reverence we stand before thee. We would not become so
familiar with thee as would breed the contempt of men, but we would talk
with you as our father.
You see, God, as men we are thankful for what Masonry means to us.
For the rich heritage of the ancient landmarks, for the Masons and Lodges
all over the world, for the Lodges in our jurisdiction and for the nearly
175,000 men in them, for their Masters and officers, Inspectors, for the
past and present officers of Grand Lodge, for all the work that is done in
Grand Lodge office under the direction of Lloyd Wilson, our able, efficient
and affable Grand Secretary, for the officers of Grand Lodge, and most
especially for our Grand Master, John Moore. He has gone from South
to North, from East to West of this State and across the waters, always our
Grand Master in all of the genuineness, honor and dignity of his exalted
office, but always our brother John in the outreach of his personality, his
thoughtfulness, his consideration, his eagerness to be of service, his
remembering and calling the brethren by name, his smile, his integrity,
his faith, his fortitude, and above all, his great and good manhood. He
has truly been a friend.

In a fellowless firmament;

Where highways never ran;
But let me live by the side of the road
And be a friend to man.

294

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The W. Herbert R. Hargrave acted as Master of Ceremonies and the
officers elected and appointed were installed by the retiring Grand Master
in due and ancient form.
The newly-installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with
a Past Grand Master's lapel button, in which was set a beautiful diamond.
The Charles Albert Adams insignia was transferred from the retiring
to the incumbent Grand Master and the other chair officers exchanged the
Arthur S. Crites lapel pins. .
The M. W. John Stewart Ross, Past Grand Master, invested the retiring
Grand Master with the apron of a Past Grand Master.
The M. W. James B. Gist, Past Grand Master, on behalf of the members
of Grand Lodge presented a gift to Mrs. John R. Moore, and it was
accepted by the retiring Grand Master in her behalf.
At 5 :00 P. M., all business being completed, Grand Lodge was closed
in due form.

Grand Master.

GRAND LODGE AUDIT
September 19, 1947
Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the books of account and records of the Grand Lodge F. & A.
M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1947, and submit herewith the
following statements :
Grand Lodge Funds
Exhibit A: Statement of Grand Lodge cash received and disbursed by the
Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer, August 1, 1946 to July 31, 1947.
Grand Secretary's Accounts
Exhibit B: Resume of cash received August 1, 1946 to July 31, 1947.
Exhibit C: Statement of cash received and disbursed for Special FundsWar Relief and Plaridel Temple (Manila) Building Fund, August 1, 1946 to
July 31, 1947.
Schedule 1 : Statement of Grand Lodge per capita dues collected from 1946
annual returns.
Schedule 2: Statement of Masonic Homes per capita dues and $25 contributions collected during the year 1946-1947.
Schedule 3: Comparation of budget and expenditures 1946-1947.
Grand Treasurer's Accounts
Exhibit D: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1946 to
July 31, 1947.
Exhibit E: Statement of assets and liabilities, July 31, 1947.
Exhibit F: List of investments, July 31, 1947.
Comments
The revenue from ~r capita dues and other sources exceeded the expenses
and appropriations by ~2,573.55, as shown by Exhibit E.
All per capita dues, as reported on the 1946 annual returns from constituent
Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Schedules 1 and Z show proof of the revenue
due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1946 returns and the $25.00 Homes
contribution reports for the first three quarters of the fiscal year 1946-47. The
total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total cash received from the Lodges
by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries. Disbursements were made by checks and supported by vouchers properly approved by
the Committee on Accounts. All bank balances were verified by correspondence
with the depositaries. Certified lists of the securities were received from the Anglo
California National Bank, which holds the securities for safe-keeping. The
securities as recorded in the books of account were checked to these lists and
found to be in agreement. All interest and dividends due thereon were received
and accounted for. Government bonds purchased during the year ainounted to
$30,000.00. No securities were sold.
We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements fairly present the
financial condition of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California as at July 31,
1947, and the result of its operations for the fiscal year 1946-47.
Respectfully submitted,
Bumtows, PARKER & COMPANY,
Certified Public Accountants.
Walter A. Parker.

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND AUDIT
September 13, 1947.
Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1947, and submit herewith the
following statements :
·
Exhibit A : Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1946,
to July 31, 1947.
Exhibit B: Statement of Endowment Fund assets, July 31, 1947.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund, July 31, 1947.
Exhibit D : Statement of income and capital accounts for the fiscal year
ended July 31, 1947.
Schedule 1: Securities on hand, acquired prior to July 31, 1946.
Schedule 2: Securities received and purchased during the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1947.
Schedule 3 : Statement of securities redeemed and sold.
Comments
Cash:
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest due was received and turned over to the Masonic Homes. The
total income received by the Homes from the Endowment and Luckenbach
Funds amounted to $62,706.11.
Securities:
Securities on hand that were acquired in prior years are listed on Schedule 1.
Securities received through contributions and bequests and bonds purchased
during the current year are listed on Schedule 2. Securities redeemed and sold
during the current year are listed on Schedule 3.
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed at
market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual value
is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment Fund
were received from the Anglo California National Bank. The records were
checked to these lists and the securities not listed were found in the office of
the Grand Secretary and were inspected by us.
Increase in Fund:
The combined assets of the Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund
show the following increase for the current year :
Amount of funds, July 31, 1947.--.......................- ..............- ................ $2,989,976.31
Amount of funds, July 31, 1946.................................-........................... 2,519,307.13

309

Other Endowment Funds:
For the past several years the Masonic Homes' records have carried two
annuity funds which are to be turned over to the Endowment Fund at the death
of the several beneficiaries. During the current year the beneficiary under the
George and Harriet Wadleigh Annuity Fund died, th~refore the fund consisting
of $1,222.63 in cash and $15,000.00 of government bonds was transferred to the
Endowment Fund.
The other fund, the Harriet C Wadleigh Endowment Fund shows a balance
of $23,983.87 at July 31, 1947. Detailed reports on these two' funds are shown
on our Schedu~e B-10 and B-11 of our report on _the Masonic Homes.
The Masoruc Homes also holds several pieces of real estate for the account of
the Endowment Fund. Whenever a sale is made, the proceeds will be transferred
to the Endowment Fund.
Certijicate:
Vo(~ certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements set forth the financial
condition of the Endowment Fund as at July 31, 1947.

Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS, PARKER & COMPANY,

Certified Public Accountants.
Walter A. Parker.

MASONIC HOMES AUDIT
September 24, 1947.
Masonic Homes of California,
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:
We have audited the books of account and records of the Masonic Homes
of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1947, and submit herewith the
following statements:
Statements or Funds and Properties

Exhibit A : Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1946
to July 31, 1947.
Exhibit B: Balance sheet, July 31, 1947.
Schedule B-1: Statement of securities owned, July 31, 1947.
Schedule B-2: Statement of Entertainment Fund.
Schedule B-3 : Statement of Students' Loan Fund.
Schedule B-4: Statement of Summer Camp Fund.
Schedule B-5: Statement of Post-War Reserve Fund.
Schedule B-6: Statement of Charles L. Patton Fund.
Schedule B-7: Statement of C. N. Flint Trust Fund.
Schedule B-8: Statement of C. N. Flint Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-9: Statement of C. N. Flint Annuity "Morgan" Fund.
Schedule B-10: Statement of George and Harriet Wadleigh Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-11: Statement of Harriet Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-12 : Statement of Verbarg Fund.
~chedule B-13: Statement of Lee R. Talbert Fund.
Schedule B-14: Statement of George M. and Florence G. Perine Endowment Fund.
Schedule B-15: Statement of Decoto Monthly Grant Fund.
Statements of Revenue and Expense
Exhibit C: Statement of Revenue and Expense 1946-47.
Exhibit D: Statement of Direct Operating Expense-Decoto.
Exhibit E: Statement of Direct Operating Expense-Covina.
Schedule D-1: Detailed Operating Expense-Decoto.
Schedule E-1: Detailed Operating Expense-Covina.
Comment11

Cash:
All recorded receipts were properly accounted for and deposited in the
proper funds bank account. All interest due on securities and notes was received
and accounted for, except those marked with an asterisk on the securities
statement, Schedule B-1. Disbursements were made by checks and supported
by proper vouchers. Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the
depositaries and reconciled to the books.
The 1946 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the amounts
due to the Homes thereon, plus the $25.00 contributions received for the first
three quarters of the current year, agreed with the amount turned over to the
Treasurer of the Homes by the Grand Secretary.
Securities:
A detailed list of all securities owned by the Masonic Homes is shown on
our Schedule B-1. Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost, all other securities
were received by donation and are listed at market value at the time donated.
When the market value is unknown, a nominal value of $1.00 is used for
purpose of record.

316

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Life insurance policies are recorded at the amount due at the death of the
insured, if determinable, and the premiums are fully paid-up; otherwise a
value of $1.00 is recorded.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as at July 31,
1947. Interest payments were received on all four notes.
The older real estate is recorded at the assessed value at the time of donation. Real estate donated during the past several years has been recorded at a
value of $1.00.
All securities were accounted for as held by the Anglo California National
Bank, or in the office of the Grand Secretary. Those held by the bank were
verified by a certification from the bank, those in the office of the Grand Secretary were inspected.
Other Funds:
The Masonic Homes has numerous separate funds which have been created
for definite. or special purposes. Full details of these funds are shown on the
attached statements, Schedules B-2 to B-15, inclusive. Payments due from the
annuity funds in accordance with the contracts and agreements, were made.
All interest due on the securities in these funds was received and deposited
in the proper bank accounts. All bank balances were verified by correspondence
with the depositaries. The securities were verified by certification from the
Anglo California National Bank which holds them for safe-keeping.
Total Funds of the Homes:
A summary of all funds connected with the Masonic Homes as at July 31,
1947 is shown below:

General:
Sufficient examination and tests were made of the revenue and expense
accounts to satisfy ourselves as to the general correctness of the accounting
records. Detailed distribution of the operating expenses of the Homes was made
by the Decoto and Covina offices and were accepted as correct after we had
verified amounts by totals.

accompanying statements present fairly the financial condition of the Masonic
Homes of California as at July 31, 1947 and the result of its operations for the
year 194647.
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS, PARKER & COMPANY,

REPORT OF CORRESPONDENCE COMMITTEE
FOREWORD
The function of the Correspondence Committee is to inform you what
is happening elsewhere and what other Grand Lodges are doing in things
Masonic. This year, you will travel, via excerpts from their reported pro·
ceedings, to some 60 Grand Jurisdictions all over the globe.
Apparently, the foremost thought in the minds of these Masons is the
point of the story of an old negro man, hungry and out of work, who
called at a white home for some help. The white man directed him around
to his back yard and said, "I will pay you a dollar if you will move
that pile of rock to the other corner of the yard where my wife wants
to build a flower bed." The negro was willing. After an absence of
about two hours the white man returned and found the old negro sit·
ting in the center of the yard on part of the rock which he had moved.
He was asked, "How are you getting along?" The negro replied, "Boss,
I was doing fine until I stopped to rest and then I forgot in which direc·
tion I was going."
From our review this appears to be a time when most Grand Lodges
are thinking about the direction in which they are going. The background
of this thinking is a mixture of worry and optimism as we face a
world divided in two. The idea is echoed that we should adhere to our
Masonic principles, and that with this as a common denominator our
fraternity can have a tremendous potential influence in the world of
tomorrow.
In many jurisdictions there is a great deal of debate as to what the
future holds in view of our widespread membership increase. Some
figures may be interesting. In 1934, out of some 15,000 lodges in this
country, there was a total membership of about 3,000,000, and a loss that
year of about 150,000. Ten years later, in 1944, the total membership was
about 2,700,000, but with a gain of about 162,000. If that rate of gain
is maintained, we shall exceed our all-time high. In this connection, we
observe that the southern Grand Lodges were the heaviest losers and
now are the greatest gainers. Some Grand Masters think that these addi·
tions to our ranks is healthy. Disagreement comes from a number of
places, however, with references to "poor material" and "degree mills."
The answer is made that we must assimilate the new brethren and keep
alive their interest.
Some Grand Lodges are sw~nging toward a reinterpretation and a
liberalization of doctrine. The subject of physical qualifications con·
tinues to provoke diversity of opinion. Others approach the subject with a
reverence for tradition. Along with the liberal trend of thinking, one
Past Grand Master of Massachusetts has stated that our fraternity should
bring itself into line with modern speculative Masonry by imparting its
lessons in language more understandable today than by what was said to

464

be "the antiquated and outmoded allegories and symbols of ages past."
Issue is joined immediately over this trend by other comment which
reminds us that while some adjustments to the tempo of the times may be
advisable, we would do well to heed the advice, "make haste slowly." We
are told that at least in our temples we can refrain from the all too
prevalent "go-getter" tactics which often cause only physical and mental
exhaustion, premature old age and nervous ailments.
There is expressed considerable concern over the possibility of liberal·
ization to the point of innovation. We are cautioned in this respect that
when differences and questions arise in our affairs the problems in many
cases may be solved quickly by recourse to Masonic law and to the reason
for the law; remembering that the law is a rule in force until changed
by an established method. Historically, we revere law as the guardian
of our liberty. No less so should we be guided, it is said, by Masonic law,
and its basis, in the affairs of our Craft.
Your reviewers find the usual local differences among the Grand
Lodges in the rituals and administration. But, while they steer their
sovereign groups down separate paths, they travel in the same general
Masonic direction, and they do merge and unite on our fundamental
universality. This is shown by the conduct of brethren who think alike on ·
the spiritual and moral virtues, and who meet everywhere in Masonic
friendship. It also appears to point toward one workable way of achiev·
ing international brotherhood.
Our report contains information as to the general condition of the
Craft abroad, and especially the needs and progress of our brethren who
were mistreated during the recent war. The United States has about two
thirds of the Masons of the world. It will take time to rehabilitate those
in the one third abroad who suffered pillage and suppression. Recently
when the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands was
in San Francisco, he expressed to your chairman deep appreciation for
the help of California during and after the war with Japan. He singled
out our Grand Secretary for special commendation on his contribution
to the program of assistance.
As we estimated the overall situation this year, there is felt an irre·
sistible sense of pride and security as we observe the recurring emergence
of the leaders of our Craft. Combined, they form a Niagara of strength.
On the whole, their wise statesmanship is at a high level and continuous
in character. We can say with confidence, therefore, in the words of James
Russell Lowell :

Arizona, 1946 (Proceedings) :
The Grand Master at this time invited Brother John R. Moore, Senior
Grand Warden of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, to address the Grand Lodge. He, in a very able manner delivered
a most interesting address. Brother Moore also brought to this Grand
Lodge the greetings of the Grand Master of California, together with the
greetings of 156,525 Masons of the same state.

Idaho, 1946 (Correspondence Committee) :
The Grand Lodge of California is the Mother Grand Lodge of the
Philippines, and a grand job of mothering she has done in recent years
in keeping in touch with the members, receiving from them their dues
in trust, and issuing certificates of good standing. More recently she
undertook a relief campaign for them, both in California and in other
Grand Lodges from which final returns are not yet in, but the Grand
Master says the response was "very generous."

Iowa, 1946 (Correspondence Committee) :

In his conclusion (Gilbert C. DeForest, Grand Master) are three paragraphs worth careful and general thought:
We should not forget the continued fulfillment of the purpose for which we became Masons. While this varies with each individual Mason, it is connected with
the well-being and improvement of mankind through the application of the principle
of good to the individual man.
In a world torn with prejudice and ill will we can and should he known as men
of goodwill. When others scoff at this or that creed, race or sect, we should, with
the tolerance of perfect understanding, assist the world to a better understanding.
We should hate nothing hut hatred and intolerance.
We must respect our indiv:idual personalities, we must support our rights as
indiv:iduals, but in supporting those rights we must accept the responsibilities which
go with those rights, and those responsibilities can best be discharged by that
service which comes from loyal enthusiasm and clear, unbiased thinking.

In its entirety it was an excellent message with the thought clearly
expressed in classic English.

North Dakota, 1946 (Correspondence Committee) :
The War Activities Committee (California, 1945) evidently knows the
evils of being busybody little helpers who can easily make a nuisance of
themselves as witness these well-timed words from its report:
Too many people look upon the veteran as being in a class by himself, whereas he
wishes to be treated as any other human being. He wants to know where he can
go for information when he wants it, but he does not want to be "adjusted." He
has proven, by what he has gone through that he is quite capable of adjusting
himself. We must impress him with our willingness and desire to help him and

We believe that this is the proper spirit.

Hence, Masons may consider these ancient hut pertinent words as a rule of

determine the most eligible life." Masonically speaking, the most eligible life is
Masonry in action. It is ingrained and ingrafted into the breast of every true lover

CORRESPONDENCE REVIEWS PER SE
For several years now, we have diligently perused the proceedings of
Grand Lodge sessions throughout the world. We agree with all other
reviewers that these reviews can be of great value.
Our method is to treat the wealth of material somewhat as does Missouri, namely, make it your·mission to keep the craft informed as to the
status of Freemasonry in the world.
When our search discloses a common factor in several or many proceedings, we cite enough examples to give the reader a cross-section view
of the subject, although not necessarily a 49-state commentary. We also
print our reviews in the proceedings so they will be available to all the
world. Several jurisdictions, as for instance Kentucky, publish their
correspondence reviews in their monthly Grand Lodge bulletins.

Missouri, 1946 (Correspondence Committee) :
At the head of this article dealing with the Masonic world we have
inserted a section of the Missouri law which sets forth the duties of the
writer of this report-to keep the Missouri craft informed as to the status
of Freemasonry in the world. For this reason we have never called this
report a review because it is more than that. It is a resume of Masonic
acts and thought as expressed in Masonic newspapers, proceedings, and
correspondence. In preparing it the writer has read over two hundred
and fifty volumes of proceedings of Masonic bodies; he has gleaned much
information from the Masonic press, and during the present year has
traveled almost 50,000 miles by air, auto, train, and boat, contacting
Masonic groups in half a hundred jurisdictions.
There are some who are wedded to the old style of review in which
each state is taken up separately; this may have been satisfactory when
Freemasonry was trying to find itself and endeavoring to secure uniformity. Today the membership want to know what is happening in other
parts of the world and especially the status of Freemasonry since the war
has ended. They are entitled to know for there are few Masonic magazines to give this information.

New York, 1945 (Grand Secretary):
In the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge every year there appears in the
last part of the book a review of worldwide Masonry. In the last three
years this was prepared by Right Worshipful Brother James E. Craig,
and is a very comprehensive review of the whole worldwide Masonic
situation.
I have a great many questions asked me, about Masonry here, there
and everywhere, all of which would be unnecessary if you read that
review.
Brother Craig has spent a great deal of time on that review every year,
by compiling from Grand Lodge Proceedings all over the world the
important matters they have considered and the important trend of the
Masonic world; and so I would suggest to you brethren that when you
get your Proceedings, don't read just the first few pages, but turn to the·
back of the book and read the report of the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence, and you will find there a very comprehensive survey of
Masonry throughout the world, the problems which engage their attention, the questions which they are considering, and you will get a picture
of worldwide Masonry which you would not otherwise get in any other
place.

Illinois, 1946 (Grand Orator):
CALL TO ACTION ?
Throughout the Masonic, as well as the profane world, from Briti3h
Columbia and Nova Scotia to Tasmania and New South Wales, and in
each of our own 49 jurisdictions, Grand Masters, Grand Orators, guest
speakers, ministers and high government officials-unanimously sound
one theme--one exhortation-"Masonry, here is your challenge! The
new world and the new order.seeks
Mentally tall men who live above the fog,
Conscious of their duty here and now!"
/. Edgar Hoover in an address given on September 29, 1947, issued
thi-3 warning: "Crime is on the increase and will not wane until the
American people make it their predominant and national purpose to
be morally stable, spiritually sound and physically and mentally
clean."

Illinois, 1946 (Committee Report) :
They picked the boy up out of school or industry, giving him high
pressure training in the art of war, made him a part of an immense
machine. Some one thought out everything for him-he did not have to
worry about clothes, food, housing, etc. Some one looked after these things
for him, and while he may not have liked the meals, or the bed, or the
clothing, he had them, and he looked forward to the time when it would
be over and he would be back home where there was peace and quiet,
maybe a wife and a home.
And what does he come back to? Everything in a turmoil-no clothes,
scarcity of food, and in many cases to a housing condition that is beyond
the wildest imagination. Strikes affecting him directly or indirectly,
crooked schemes and deals to get his savings. In many cases job promises
not fulfilled, and many that have been will be up after they have worked
the year. Veterans with degrees but no work history except three or four
years of war, and who wants them? The veterans who are going to school
now under the G. I. Bill, many will come out when the buyers market
has changed to a sellers market. Where are they going?
Is there any wonder that these veterans need counselling and help
from some organization that will talk to them with understanding of
their many problems?
Is Masonry in Illinois going to follow the crowd who are forgetting
because the uniforms have been laid aside, the flags are down and the
bands have stopped playing, or will they continue the service to these
veterans which is a thousand times more important to morale, to the
community and to our country than all the service we rendered for their
pleasure while they were in the service?

Right in the midst of our Masonic fraternity is the answer to the cry of
old:
God give us men a time like this demands,
Men whom the lust of power does not kill;
Men whom false tempting offers cannot buy;
Men who possess opinions and a will;
Men who have honor-who will not lie;
Men who can stand before a demagogue
And damn his treacherous flatteries with a vow;
Mentally tall men who live above the fog,
Conscious of their duty here and now!

Illinois, 1946 (Correspondence Committee) :
The deadliest enemy Freemasonry has ever had was the bitter and
sen~less hatred felt for it by Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany, and Falangist

Spam. Freemasonry was utterly crushed in those countries where Axis
nations were in power. All Masonic property was confiscated or destroyed
and prominent Masons were imprisoned or put to death. First hand
information concerning the atrocities against Masons and Masonry in
Europe has recently been secured by the Commission appointed by the
Masonic Service Association, whose investigations were aided by the
President of the United States.
Events during the last ten years have presented a challenge to Masonry
and to all men of good will to convince the world that the future safety
of humanity depends upon the general adoption of those principles of
fraternity and brotherly love which have always been the basis upon which
the superstructure of Freemasonry has been erected. Upon a general
and steadfast belief in these principles we are convinced the permanent
peace of the world depends.

Kentucky, 1945 (Grand Master):
These thoughts bring forth two important questions--ls the abolition
of war the peculiar mission of Freemasonry? And, is Freemasonry
capable of accomplishing such a stupendous undertaking?

478

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A few facts that are in reach of all is the only reply that can be given
these questions: First, Freemasonry teaches morality, taking the Holy
Bible as its rule and guide in faith and practice. Second, Masonry
teaches universal brotherhood of mankind. Third, it is a lamentable fact
that other societies, even the worshippers of the one true God, the followers
of Jesus Christ, have waged terrible wars against each other; as such,
there is not, in the history of all time, an instance of Masonic WarMasons against Masons, or Masonic violence of any kind. She has busied
herself in the erection of the temple of peace; her apron has remained
pure and unspotted; her hands unstained with blood.
As in the past-so in the oncoming years, let this institution stand for
stability in government-the antagonist of needless change; for religious
toleration-the freedom of belief and of unbelief; for the largest measure
of liberty-liberty regulated and restrained by law. Let it stand for all
that the sure test of time has shown to be ennobling and enlightening to
humankind.

Kentucky, 1946 (Grand Master):
Freemasonry in Kentucky has, during the preceding twelve months,
experienced its greatest numerical growth in a quarter of a century6,262 being our net gain. The growth of our moral strength can only be
recorded by history; but it is our hope that the quiet and moral force has
turned the minds of men toward the pursuits of peace and stimulated them
to the most exalted desires and aspirations; that the results of the noble
precepts will be discernable in the practical working of our government.
It is our prayer that each free and accepted craftsman will strengthen
Masonry agains the shock of time; the persecution of its opponents; the
fiery vengeance of disappointed ambition; the hatred of despotism and
bigotry; and the anathemas of ecclesiasticism. If so, it shall stand firm
and unshaken, an impregnable fortress against the assaults of malice and
envy, amicl the throes and turmoil of world-wide contending faction
which are surrounded by howling tempests of fear, superstition, ruin,
and decaying philosophies. As long as the world suffers and people are
oppressed, so long as the philanthropist is vitally needed, so long as
governments are imperfect, so long as science is inexhaustible, so long as
man seeks God, so long as there is a wailing, agonizing humanity, the
world will have need of Freemasonry.
Therefore, my brethren, let us unite in an effort to exhibit to the world
the strength of honest conviction; let us defend and protect that which
physical powers and heroic fortitude has preserved as fundamental
principles; let harmony, purity, and zeal combine to elevate the standard
of Masonry upon a basis as firm and imperishable as those eternal
principles which have ever constituted its glory and reputation. Amen.

Nebraska, 1946 (Grand Master) :
Since Masonry is devoted to people it follows that we as Masons must
be concerned with our fellow man and how people get on together. This
thought brings in the dynamics of Masonry. It may be that too long we
have stressed the speculative aspects of Masonry. The world needs
operative Masons-not operative in the sense that skills in the building
trades are required, but operative in that we work within the light to
better the world and improve the welfare of mankind. There is much to
be done. We have just gone through the most costly war of ·all time.
Indeterminable amounts of money have been spent, and property destroyed. Thousands of our youth are sick and maimed. Many thousands too,
are in their graves and as many homes are left desolate. These are the
ghastly relics of war. And, now that fighting has ceased, we find that
scars on our society have been accentuated and new ones have appeared.
All is not well with the human family. Masons should do something about
it. Through the processes of speculative Masonry we should be impelled
to work within the light to correct the ills of society.

Constitution Hall in Philadelphia with other members of the craft, after
many weeks of tireless labor in carving out the immortal principles of a
free people as set forth in the Constitution of the United States, was asked
by someone in the crowd: "Mr.. Franklin, what have you given us?"
Measuring his words carefully, Benjamin Franklin replied: "We have
given you a Republic, if you can keep it."
When the Fathers of the American Republic wrote the Constitution of
the United States, and the record reveals that over half of the signers
were Masons, they gave to the people of America the most inspired law
ever conceived. It is because of the freedom that document guarantees
that the American people have progressed more in the short span of their
existence than any nation of people on earth. It was not the product of a
day, for temporary use, to be altered and adapted at will to the mood of
the hour. It was refined from the crucible of time, and until the last
fifteen years those original ideals of freedom remained intact, unchanged
and immovable. The so-called liberal interpretation now being placed on
that sacred document by those clothed with power to preserve it makes
one recall again the admonition of Benjamin Franklin: "We have given
you a Republic, if you can keep it."

The ability of the American people to keep that Republic and maintain
the individual liberty which it guarantees, it seems to me, has never
faced so severe a test as that which it faces today.
When I was a youngster going to school, I was taught that I could do
what I would with mine own. If any law was ever passed by any subdivision of government infringing on my rights as an American citizen,
I had redress before the highest court in the land, if need be - The
Supreme Court-and all would be well. The picture was indelibly imprinted on my mind of those nine learned men, chosen from without the
length and breadth of our land-not as a reward for political reciprocity
or liberal thinking in interpreting the law-but for their outstanding
ability as jurists of their day, guarding the rights of the people, from the
highest to the lowest, as if their very lives depended upon it. Their's was
a sacred trust and they regarded it as such. And I was proud to be even
a small part of such a system of government, never thinking the admonition of Benjamin Franklin would echo again: "We have given you a
Republic, if you can keep it."
Those nine old men-guardians of our rights-have passed into
oblivion. Their memory will linger in the minds of liberty-loving
Americans. They served their country well and were a credit to the
honorable profession of law. During their tenure of trust of the rights of
the people and of industry and free enterprise, monumental decisions
were made; decisions recognized everywhere by barristers as masterpieces, and regarded by them as established landmarks of the profession.
They were faithful to their trust and enjoyed the confidence of the people.
While the Constitution was in their custody there was never any reason
to question our ability to keep and maintain the Republic.
The replacements of those nine old men, seven of whom came from
public or political life, represent another school of thought. They were
not selected, primarily, for their superior qualifications as jurists or
their proven ability as disseminators of the law. Under their so-called
protective hands, the trend of American government has given rise to
apprehension by all thinking Americans. We have looked upon the various changes and freak laws that have interfered with personal liberty and
free enterprise and industry as a series of nuisances soon to pass away.
On the face, they appeared to be temporary aberrations in an otherwise
normal atmosphere. But as the years have passed, we have come to realize
that those supposedly experimental remedies, written as emergency
measures, are not temporary at all, but in reality are here to stay and are
changing our way of life.
Out in this western country, the rights of possession and doing what
we will with our own were firmly implanted in our minds and hearts by
our forefathers-those early settlers who blazed the way and made it a
fit place for us to live. They knew what it was to see men fight and die
over a water hole or a drift fence or a stray calf or the open range. That
which was theirs, they protected with their lives, if need be. Perhaps it is

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

because of that heritage down through the years that makes us wonder if
we will be able to keep the Republic when we have witnessed organized
forces take over and remain, unmolested, in our great industrial factories,
destroying patterns and machinery and property worth millions, without
recourse or even reproach from our government.
On the other hand, and in reverse, we have seen the army of the United
States, on orders from Washington, take over a business in a large
industrial city and bodily remove the manager .t herefrom because he
differed with the government on how he should operate his business.
When the Supreme C~urt decides that a farmer, raising his own
produce, must pay toll to a trucker's union if he drives his own truck h.1side
the city limits of an eastern metropolis, doesn't it make you wonder if we
will be able to keep the Republic?
In the last several months, we have witnessed the travesty of two of the
guardians of the rights of the people airing their petty and personal
differences before the people of America and the world. Never before,
in the history of the Court, has the dignity of that august body been
threatened in such a manner. Broadcast over the radios and published in
every paper m the land, I'm wondering what young America is going te
thmk when their tutors relate to them, as they did to you and me, that
the highest tribunal is made up of men who are the pick of the land in the
profession of law. Won't they too, question our ability to keep the Republic?
Probably the thought uppermost in the minds of all of you is: Where
does this all fit into the pattern of Freemasonry? As a Lodge of Free·
masons, it has no place on our Masonic trestleboard for formal action,
but as individual American citizens, if we give due recognition to the
labor of those Brethren who landed on these shores nearly two centuries
ago; if we recall the part they played in establishi~g this great Rep~bli~,
pushing the frontiers ever westward ~nd undergomg great ?ardships. m
the doing; if we appreciate the blessmgs of freedom and hberty which
they left in our care; then, I say to you Brethren, it does fit in if we are to
keep the Republic?
Every Mason, I think, should be a good citizen, and ~very ~ood citiz~n
should take an interest in his government and be an active mmuteman m
the preservation of the greatest Republic o'!1 Go~'s f?otstool. I:Ie s?ould
keep himself informed of the trend of the times, m his home city, m the
State and in the Nation. And every time one of those fundamental
prin~iples on which this Nation was created is h~nging in the balance, he
should lend his voice and his pen, not as a spellbmder or a flag-waver, but
as an American citizen who loves his country and appreciates the rights
and privileges guaranteed him under our form of government.
As Freemasons, we are admonished to practice out of the Lodge those
great moral duties which are inculcate~ in i~; In the wor.d~ o.f John Adams,
a Mason and a signer of the Declarat10n: Let us, as idividuals, dare to
read, to think, to speak and to write. Let us recollect and impress upon

our souls the views and ends of our forefathers in exchanging their
native country for dreary, inhospitable wilderness, and recollect that it
was liberty, the hope of liberty for themselves and for us and ours, which
conquered all discouragements, dangers and trials."
If you will but look about, my Brethren, you will observe that Masons
are the leaders in nearly every community in the land just as they were
leaders when the Republic was founded. Equipped and schooled as we are,
what an opportunity we have as individual Masons to spread the gospel
of brotherly love, liberty and justice and the pursuit of happiness as we
go about from day to day in our contacts with our fellowmen: on the
street, in our homes, and in our places of business. Not only should we
be expert as ritualists in the conferring of our degrees, but we should be
expert as representatives of the good things of life outside the confines
of our meeting places, assuming our responsibilities as good citizens
and holding fast to the tenets that make up a true American.
There is the right of every man to stand on his own two feet and with
his own hands and talents to carve out a place for himself and his family.
There is the right of a woman to look hopefully ahead, raising up her
brood in dignity and self-respect, undictated to save by her own mother
wisdom and her own conscience.
There is the right of a boy to lead the hale, free life of boys, flying kites
when the wind blows, playing cops and robbers when he wants to, going
to school when he must-and out of it all somehow to shape up a future.
There is the right of a small child to its chance for health and love and
laughter-to a good start toward who knows what useful life in the years
to come.
And then there is the right of us all to worship God as we see fit.
These are simple things, Brethren, these things that spell America
and add up to freedom. So simple, so wholesome, it seems strange that
men would even want to change one word or the meaning of one word
in that great document which guarantees them. That which is good makes
itself known, no matter how loud the clamor of denial. That which
deserves to live, lives on and on.
What nobler thing could we ask, my Brethren, than to have it said
that from our ranks came the leaders and in our ranks was found the
overwhelming force that helped preserve the American way of life and
that left our government as we had found it: A government of just and
equitable laws and not a government of men? Life is a battle all the way,
and the things worthwhile will come and stay with us only when we fight
for them. And only those things are worth fighting for.
As individuals, we all sometimes dream of great deeds and high
rank, a way from the humdrum and the pettiness of the ordinary. Yet
success in life is not necessarily occupying a lofty place or doing conspicuous work. Success in life is being the best that is in us, right where
we are. Rattling around in too big a job is worse than filling a small one
to overflowing. The immediate task of every man and every Mason, as an

They gave us a Republic, my Brethren; let us do all we can as true
Americans and good Masons to keep it and pass it on to our children.

In April of this year, I took the liberty of addressing the United
Nations Conference, the President of the United States and the Secretary
of State advising them "t4at the members of our Masonic Fraternity
are giving to the purposes of this meeting their unqualified assent and
moral support. We share in the common hope that out of it may come a
realization of the universal cry of civilized humanity that ways of peace
and persuasion be substituted for the ways of force and power." The full _
statement appeared in the June-July issue of the Masonic Outlo~~· .and
many of you have probably seen it. I have heard no adverse cntlc1sm,
and trust that you will approve it and that it will be made a part of these
proceedings.
·
The San Francisco charter will not in itself secure world peace. The
carrying out of its provisions will require the wholehearted support of
all right thinking men and women. Masonry is world wide, and wherever
we can help with our influence and good will in such matters as all good
men are agreed upon, we ought to make that influence felt.

Oklahoma, 1946 (Grand Master):

Freemasonry has a kit of tools, which, if properly used, will do more
toward cementing the nations of the world together than all of our armies,
navies or diplomatic corps. To attain these ends and reach this goal, we
shall have to labor in our chosen profession of Freemasonry with untiring
efforts; sustained and encouraged by our faith in ultimate victory. We
must not doubt that this is so.
Our sons and daughters have envisioned a brighter, more tolerant
world. What shall our answer be when they ask, "What are you doing
to rid the world of greed, hatred, intolerance, suspicion and fear? What
are you doing to perpetuate the victory we have won? Somewhere, from
the land-back-of-the-setting-sun, somewhere, from the Valhalla of glorious
warriors they, who cheerfully paid the price, are intently listening for the
answer as they throw down the gauge and dare us to carry on. Brethren,
will you-will Freemasonry accept the challenge?

We are talking about a world where "nations shall beat their swords
into plowshares," and where they shall know war no more.
Masonry can and must be a factor in bringing in this new day for mankind. Its fellowship crosses all boundaries of nations and creeds. Ever}\'
where throughout the world are members of the craft who will help to
bring the spirit of Masonry to the practical solution of our common
problems. It can be said, without danger of contradiction, that the ?nly
basis of a lasting world peace is to be found in the fundamental philosophy of Masonry.
Here, again, we are brought face to face with a challenge and a_n ·
opportunity. Foreign Grand Jurisdictions have been persecuted, their
temples and records have been destroyed, Grand Masters have been
killed. Every effort has been made by the enemy to wipe out every trace
of Masonry. It was one of the first institutions to be attacked when
dictators rose to power. Its principles and practices were contrary to all
that the dictators stood for. Yet in spite of persecution, imprisonment,
murder and destruction, many lodges have continued to function underground. Physical violence could not kill the spiritual ideal.

fessions of the universality and the indestructibility of the spirit of
Masonry-and stop there? Or are we going to thank Almighty God that
we have been spared like treatment, and do something to help these

I would that I could somehow speak to you from the heart of Masonry

If we are going to build a temple, the first thing we do is to select a site.

for King Solomon's Temple, I think that we will find the very site that

The Jewish Talmud savs that the selection of the site for King Solomon's Temple came abo~t in this wise: It was a field left by a father

that harvest. And that night the brother over at this end of the field began

Washington, 1946 (Historian):
Down through the ages from time immemorial, man has been reaching
out, striving, struggling, fighting, dying for that which we are pleased to
call "Liberty." Representative government, the right to worship as one
desires, freedom of enterprise, were not gifts of the gods. They were not
just laid in man's lap with the statement, "Here they are. Take pleasure
in them." They are the results of the battle of mankind, and have been
bought and paid for in blood, suffering and misery, by wars between
nations, by civil wars and revolutions.
These freedoms have existed for hut a short duration of time. We have
just observed that within the space of two centuries men were imprisoned
even in enlightened England for expressing a religious belief not pre·
scribed by government authority. And within that period we heard
a King of England stating that freedom did not consist in the right of
the people to have a voice in the government.
Freedom is something comparatively new. Let us not forget that it did
not come to us because it is our right, but because our forerunners ·paid
for it. And of late is it not possible that we of America and Britain have
come to value our liberty too little? Is it not well to bring home to us
the long struggle through which freedom has come to us, and the price
paid? Have we not just taken too much for granted?
Let us stop and think. We have just passed through another great war,
a war for freedom, for national liberty, for freedom to worship as one
desires. This war has been for the preservation of free men under the
democratic government of free nations. The whole war directed against
us aimed to impose autocracy and to enforce submission. The whole
trouble with us is that we have been willing to repeat as a mere platitude

489

that the price ?f liberty is vigilance, and then have yawned, taken a look
around, and did not feel so sure about the vigilance.
. The diffi~ulty has always been with the application of the doctrine of
hhe~ty. W1~h every stage of social advance life gets more complicated.
National umty appears to us more difficult and complex than it did to
our grandfathers. The road is longer than we thought. The march more
arduous.

There were so many requests received for service to visiting Mas~ns

'

for patients, sending and receiving telegrams, long distance and office
telephone calls, ambulance and wheel-chair cases, ordering flowers,
cashing checks. Sometimes a listening ear is all that is needed; again
a word of cheer to the discouraged and despondent.
The work has had to keep pace with the growth of the city and the
Mayo Clinic. Population in the city has trebled, as have registrations
at the clinic, during these years of my service. The work is also national
in scope. During the year 1938, I kept a record of cases by States and
found patients from 47 States, 7 Canadian Provinces, and 11 other
countries on my list. There are six hospitals and two convalescent homes
in Rochester and a new hospital with 1,500 beds is to be erected as soon
as possible. As hospital accommodations increase, more members of
the Craft will be hospitalized and in need of fraternal assistance. This
service is made possible by the Grand Lodge of Minnesota.
Since the beginning of the office in 1922, we have contacted 81,834
Masons or their relatives who have visited Rochester for Mayo Clinic
assistance. During the same time, 208,871 calls have been made upon
people in hospitals, hotels, and convalescent homes, and there have been
17,417 personal office calls by these people. During the depression years,
we have been called upon many times to find employment for Masons
and relatives of Masons and of recent years, during housing and hotel
shortage, we have been called upon to find rooms for 6,311 people.
We have assisted in over 600 ambulance cases and nearly 600 wheelchair cases. Many patients come to Rochester and find themselves short
of funds, and as a result, we have cashed for them over $71,000 in checks
and have handled over $43,000 additionally, for these patients.

Tasmania, 1946 (Grand Master) :
It follows from what I have said that we do not simply belong to an
Order. Masonry has survived the shocks of time and the fall of mighty
empires, not because it is a kind of pleasant social club, nor even because
it is a philanthropic institution whose main purpose is to distribute charity to the poor and needy amongst us. It is something far beyond that.
Masonry has exercised a profound influence in the world and still continues so to do because there are sufficient Masons who find in it an
opportunity for self discipline and the exercise of those talents which
they place at the disposal of the community at large. It must give us all
satisfaction when we find Masonic brethren leading the community in
acts of selfless service. Our Order expects more of us than exemplary
conduct, it has the right to expect of us that we place at the disposal of
Masons and non-Masons alike that which is best in us. For thus and thus
only are we erecting for ourselves an edifice which will outlast these
mortal bodies of ours. We are in the world to give of our best, we are
true Masons in heart and outwardly when that is done. It is the glory of our
Masonic art that opportunity within the Lodge and beyond it is so given
to us.

FOREIGN MASONRY

Iowa, 1946 (Committee) :
Your committee has carefully investigated the situation of Freemasonry
throughout the world at the present time.
Outside the British Commonwealth of Nations, Scandinavia, Holland,
and Switzerland on the Continent of Europe and in Asia, it is, to say the
least, chaotic, and in such an indefinite condition that we do not at this
time deem it wise or advisable to extend further recognition to, or establish fraternal relations with, any of the revived or new Masonic powers
of those countries until their origin, standing, and adherence to the principles hitherto enunciated by this Grand Lodge are fully established to
the complete satisfaction of this Grand Lodge. This recommendation
applies also to certain bodies claiming at this time to be regular Grand
Lodges in exile.
At the same time we extend to all those bodies professing and calling
themselves Masons, wheresoever dispersed, who comply with these principles, our warmest sympathy and encouragement and urge them, as
rapidly as possible, to furnish to us and all other regular Grand Lodges
proof that they are within the pale of Masonic legitimacy.
Turning now to the Western Hemisphere, we find a peculiar situation.
We have reports indicating that general Masonic conditions in Mexico,
Central, and South America have greatly improved ; other reports, also
reliable, tell us that, apparently due to the Latin temperament, which
does differ from ours, ideas seem to change from time to time, and the
standards of lodges today are not as they were a short time ago; that
some organizations calling themselves "Masonic" are in reality political
groups of one sort or another, without ritual, initiation ceremony, or
Masonic authorization; and that some Grand Lodges, which only recently
appeared to conform to our standards, have since permitted the removal
of the Volume of Sacred Law from the Altar, obligate their initiates on
the Book of Constitutions, and have admitted women to membership.
These reports convince this committee that we should proceed with
caution and, before extending formal recognition, be positive that the
Grand Lodge under consideration does fully conform to the standards
which we consider essential.
Maine, 1947 (Correspondence Committee) :
A resolution was adopted inviting the Grand Master, at his discretion,
to enter into fraternal relations on behalf of the Grand Lodge with any

496

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Grand Lodge or Grand Orient throughout the world which shall be, by
direct descent or Masonic healing, an off-shoot of the mother Grand
Lodge.
It is with profound regret that we report this action by our esteemed
sister jurisdiction of New York. Through the years, the regular Grand
lodges of the world have established definite standards of recognition,
which, while differing in minor details, unanimously agree in prescribing
certain fundamental qualifications without which no body can be accounted as Masonic. Foremost of these qualifications are two, derived
directly from the Ancient Landmarks of the Craft. The first of these
requires belief in God, the second the presence of the Volume of Sacred
Law upon the altar. Without these qualifications, there can be no Masonry. The Grand Lodge of New York, along with all other legitimate Grand
Lodges, has repeatedly asserted this doctrine, and has declared bodies
.
violating it to be unmasonic and clandestine.
The resolution under consideration appears to ignore these fundamentals, and to authorize the recognition of bodies not possessing these
essential qualifications. To say the least, the language of this resolution
is most unfortunate, is certain to be misunderstood, and may well cause
a breach in the harmony of the Masonic world.
.
Should any Grand Master of New York, under this resolution, attempt
to recognize as Masonic any body which has abandoned its belief in God,
or which has removed the Great Light in Masonry from its altars, he
would be attempting that which is beyond the power of any man or body
of men. The Grand Lodge of New York is a great and powerful body, but
there are limits to its power. It cannot make that Masonic which is unmasonic. It cannot abrogate a Landmark.
It is our earnest hope that our New York brethren will amend and
clarify this resolution at their next communication, so that the profane as
well as the Masonic world may be assured that the largest American
Grand Lodge is still loyal to the fundamental principles of Freemasonry.

the Grand Lodge of Maine extends fraternal recognition to a sister Grand
Lodge she thereby acknowledges that body as her Masonic peer, endued
with every attribute of Masonic sovereignty which she herself possesses.
Moreover, she thereby sets the seal of her official approval upon the
Masonry taught and practiced by the body recognized, and, to a certain
degree, makes herseH responsible, in the eyes of the profane as well as
the Masonic world, for the Masonic deportment of that Grand Lodge and
its subordinates.

Maine, 1947 (Grand Master) :
One of the most important problems confronting our American Grand
lodges at the present time is that occasioned by the applications for recog·
nition currently being made by various bodies in Continental Europe,
Mexico, and South America. Some of these bodies hail from countries
ravaged by the war, others from lands where Freemasonry has had to
struggle hard for existence against the forces of bigotry and persecution.
These applications deserve sympathetic, careful, and intelligent consideration; but we must not allow ourselves to be stampeded by sentiment
into any hasty or indiscriminate recognition of doubtful organizations.
In our desire to demonstrate the universality of Freemasonry, we must
not permit the sacrifice of those fundamental principles which alone
make Masonry Masonic.
Formal Grand Lodge recognition involves far more than a mere admission that the Masons under a certain obedience are not clandestine. When

New Mexico, 1946 (Grand Master):
During the period when practically the entire world was engaged in
open warfare, the committees on foreign relations of a number of our
Grand Lodges made reports on requests for recognition which concluded
with the recommendation that no action he taken until following the
cessation of hostilities or until conditions in general became settled.
The sincerity of such recommendations has not been questioned, hut
it is my humble opinion that during the periods of turmoil and unrest
we need most to he firmly united and working together in harmony, to
the end that the leavening influence of the principles and precepts which
we profess to champion shall have a tremendously greater force and
effect. If the lump may not be leavened through the influence of our
teachings alone, then let us not neglect to do all we can regardless of
whose shall he the praise for the final accomplishment. Whether we lead
or follow in this endeavor, it is first necessary that we put our own house
in order.
New York, 1945 (Joint Report Committee on Jurisprudence and Foreign Correspondence) :
This "ostracized" group of Grand Lodges is composed mainly of
brethren practising "Latin" Freemasonry as distinguished from AngloSaxon Freemasonry. The latter, in membership, far outnumbers the
former. The Anglo-Saxon embraces the British Commonwealth of Nations, Switzerland, Holland, Canada, the United States, and the Scandinavian countries (with modifications) . The Latin embraces much of
Western, Central, and Southern Europe, Africa and Asia Minor, and
Central and South America. Both branches, in addition, are spotted
here and there over the world. We give here but a general picture. Now
briefly as to the issues which divide the two:
Anglo-Saxon Freemasonry charges Latin Freemasonry with concerning itself with political questions; and with the absence of the Bible from
the Altar. In addition, we American Masons charge it with violations of
Masonic law by invasion of our territory.
Latin Masonry retorts that the practices which are disapproved are
defensive for Freemasonry's survival in certain countries, and also where
governments are unfriendly. Latin Masonry also asserts that it conforms
strictly to the provisions of the "Anderson Constitutions" as adopted in
the beginning by the mother Grand Lodge; that it is not irreligious, but

498

liberal as provided by the Anderson Constitutions; that it v~olated .no
Masonic interjurisdictional law when it chartered Lodges m fo.re1gn
countries, because there was and is no such law enacted by the family of
Grand Lodges.
.
.
.
Here briefly and in general terms are recited the issues which have
divided the Masonic Fraternity the world over.
Both groups presently are functioning throughout the world. Both
are seeking to serve mankin~ by contributing their utmost to th~ ca~se
of permanent peace. That service they share, and much more - JUStlce,
charity, brotherhood, righteous living, education, the quest for truth and
happiness.

FOREIGN RELIEF
During 1945 the Masonic Service Association sent a delegation to
Europe. Recommendations made have been generously complied with by
most Grand lodges.

Arizona, 1946 (Grand Master) :
In the matter of contributing relief to our brethren in Europe, I feel
that we should go a little more slowly and that this problem is closely
related to our future recognition of European grand lodges. This is
a matter which might well be put in the hands of our correspondence
committee, which committee, after having investigated the situation, and
having determined which grand lodges in Europe we should recognize,
can then direct our funds to those grand lodges.

District of Columbia, 1946 (Grand Master):
During the summer of 1945, the Masonic Service Association sent a
committee of four distinguished American Freemasons abroad to make
a first-hand investigation of the needs of our brethren in the occupied
and devastated countries of Europe. By the co-operation of President
and Past Grand Master Truman, the State Department, the Army, the
Diplomatic Corps, this committee was enabled to accomplish in six weeks
abroad what might have taken a less fortunate group six month11 to do.
As a result of the investigation, an appeal was made to all United
States Grand Lodges for a voluntary contribution of ten cents per capita,
to assist European brethren to re-establish their scattered and disinte·
grated Masonry.
In the belief that he gives twice who gives quickly, and that if the job
was to be done at all it should be done at once, I authorized the drawing
of our check for $2,517.10 for this purpose. The fund contributed by
Grand Lodges, individual Lodges and interested brethren is now in excess
of $115,000 and has resulted in such expressions of gratitude, such
thankfulness to American Masonry for extending the right hand of
fellowship to those in bitter need, as to touch the heart.
I ask the approval of the Grand Lodge for my action.

Missouri, 1946 (Grand Master): '
The Masonic Service Association renders a vital service in the relief
of distress. It is hard to see why Masons should hesitate to pool their
efforts through such an organization, when, to me, at least, it is so obvious
that the old saying, "in unity there is strength," is just as applicable here
as anywhere else. Of course it costs some, but, as I see it, the amount is
small when compared to the good that can be done, and is being done
by that organization. Personally, I want to compliment M.W. Brother
Carl Claudy, the executive secretary of the M. S. A., for his faithful and
efficimt service to the fraternity throughout the world. He has furnished
the leadership whereby we are able to send relief to those who need it,
and le certain that it is going where we want it to go. His organization
make' and maintains the contacts throughout Europe and elsewhere
through which our contributions to the needy brethren of Europe and
the Far East can flow with speed and certainty. More power to the
M. S. A. ! I consider that the small sum it costs us is well worth _the
price, and much more.

Florida, 1946 (Grand Master) :
I recommend, therefore, that Grand Lodge create a Committee on
Masonic Education, having three sub-committees, as follows:
Sub-Committee on Masonic Practice;
Sub-Committee on Masonic Work;
Sub-Committee on Masonic Law.
This committee should be composed of a general chairman and the
chairmen and members of those sub-committees and to be responsible to
and report to the Grand Lodge and to the Grand Master in the recess.
I recommend, further, that the duties, methods and organization of
such sub-committees be generally as follows:
( 1)

SUB-COMMITTEE ON MASONIC PRACTICE

Duties: To inculcate a knowledge and observance in our daily lives
of those principles and ideals of Masonry which have made our fraternity great.
(2) SUB-COMMITTEE ON WORK
Duties: To be the custodians of our secret work and to guard it from
change and innovations; and make recommendations to Grand Lodge as
to any required changes, particularly where necessary to eliminate innovations and keep to the old work.
(3)

SUB-COMMITTEE ON MASONIC LAW

Duties: To prepare and have printed a comprehensive summary of
our Masonic law, not including matter contained in our local laws, including the structure of our ancient form of Masonic government, and an
outline of the origin and present status of the rights, privileges and prerogatives of the Craft in their particular Lodges, of the Grand Lodge and
of the Grand Master.
